p.seg: 1.1 Jìng Pínggōng asked Shī Kuàng:
"What is the way of a ruler?"
He replied:
"The way of a ruler
is to be serene and non-interfering,
devoted to universal love,
inclined to appoint the worthy,
broadening his sight and hearing
to observe all directions,
not stubbornly immersed in popular customs,
not constrained by those around him,
with expansive foresight,
standing alone with lofty independence,
frequently examining achievements,
to oversee his ministers—
this is the conduct of a ruler."
Pínggōng said:
"Excellent."
1.2 Qí Xuānwáng said to Yǐn Wén:
"What are the affairs of a ruler?"
Yǐn Wén replied:
"The affairs of a ruler
involve non-action and the ability to tolerate subordinates.
For few tasks make compliance easy,
simple laws make them easy to follow;
thus the people do not incur guilt through governance.
The great way accommodates the multitude,
great virtue tolerates subordinates;
the sage does little, yet the world is governed.
The 'Shū' says:
'Wisdom makes one a sage.'
The poet said:
'In Qí there are level paths,
may your descendants preserve them.'"
Xuānwáng said:
"Excellent."
1.3 King Chéng enfeoffed Bó Qín as the Duke of Lǔ,
summoned him, and advised:
"Do you know the way of being a superior?
Those in high positions
must respect their subordinates,
follow virtue and heed remonstrance,
opening the door to unfettered speech,
restraining oneself in calm to support them,
not intimidating remonstrators with authority,
nor blocking their words,
but broadly collecting their counsel
to select what is commendable.
Having civility without martial prowess
fails to awe subordinates;
having martial prowess without civility
makes the people fear but not feel close;
when both are practiced,
authority and virtue are achieved;
once achieved,
the people feel close and submit.
Purity reaches upward,
cunning flattery is blocked below;
remonstrators gain access,
loyalty and trust accumulate."
Bó Qín bowed twice, accepted the mandate, and took his leave.
1.4 Chén Línggōng acted perversely and spoke improperly.
Xiè Yě said:
"Chén will perish!
I have repeatedly admonished the ruler,
but he does not listen and loses more dignity.
For the superior's influence on subordinates
is like wind bending grass:
east wind bends it west,
west wind bends it east,
the grass follows the wind's direction.
Thus a ruler's actions must be cautious.
One who plants a crooked tree
cannot expect a straight shadow.
A ruler who does not straighten his conduct or respect his words
cannot maintain the title of emperor,
nor hand down a illustrious reputation.
The 'Yì' says:
'When a gentleman in his chamber
speaks words
that are good,
even a thousand miles away they are responded to,
how much more by those nearby?
When in his chamber
he speaks words
that are not good,
even a thousand miles away they are opposed,
how much more by those nearby?
Words from his person affect the people;
actions from nearby are seen afar.
Words and actions
are the pivot of a gentleman;
when the pivot moves,
it determines honor or disgrace.
Words and actions
are how a gentleman moves heaven and earth;
can they not be cautious!'
Heaven and earth move, and all things transform.
The 'Shī' says:
'Be careful in your speech,
respectful in your demeanor,
and all will be gentle and good.'
This refers to it.
Now my lord is not cautious thus but indulges recklessly;
if not perishing, he will be assassinated."
Línggōng heard this,
deemed Xiè Yě's words demonic, and killed him.
Later, he was indeed assassinated by Zhēng Shū.
1.5 Lǔ Āigōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"I hear gentlemen do not gamble—
is this true?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"It is."
Āigōng said:
"Why do they not gamble?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Because it involves two opposing moves."
Āigōng said:
"With two moves,
why does that prevent gambling?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Because it concurrently follows a wicked path."
Āigōng was alarmed.
After a pause,
he said:
"So this is how much gentlemen detest wicked paths!"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"If a gentleman's hatred for wicked paths is not intense,
then his love for good paths cannot be intense either;
if his love for good paths is not intense,
then the people's closeness to him cannot be deep.
The 'Shī' says:
'Before seeing the gentleman,
my heart is anxious;
but having seen him,
having encountered him,
my heart is joyful.'
This shows how deeply the 'Shī' cherishes the good path."
Āigōng said:
"Excellent!
I hear gentlemen help others achieve good,
not evil;
without Kǒngzǐ,
how would I have heard such words!"
1.6 Héjiān Xiànwáng said:
"Yáo kept the world in his heart,
focused on the impoverished,
grieved for the people's suffering,
worried about all living beings' hardships.
Thus if one person was hungry,
he would say:
'This is because I starved him.'
If one was cold,
he would say:
'This is because I chilled him.'
If one committed a crime,
he would say:
'This is because I led him astray.'
His benevolence shone and righteousness stood firm,
his virtue was vast and influence broad;
thus without rewards, the people were motivated,
without punishments, they were governed—
first forgiving, then instructing—
this was Yáo's way."
In Shùn's time,
the Yǒumiáo clan did not submit;
their reason was
the great mountain to their south,
Diàn Mountain to their north,
Lake Dòngtíng's waves to the left,
Pénglí's rivers to the right—
relying on these barriers,
they remained unsubdued.
Yǔ wanted to attack them, but Shùn refused,
saying:
"My instruction and persuasion are not yet exhausted."
After thorough instruction,
the Yǒumiáo clan requested submission.
The world heard of this,
criticized Yǔ's approach,
and attributed the virtue to Shùn.
1.7 When the Duke of Zhōu ascended to the Son of Heaven's position,
he disseminated virtue and bestowed beneficence,
which became even more illustrious the farther it reached.
The twelve pastoral overseers,
each with three men,
were sent out to raise up the people of distant regions.
Those who suffered hunger and cold without clothing or food,
those involved in legal disputes who lost their positions,
and those with worthy talents who went unrecognized
were to report to the Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven received their rulers at court,
he would bow and invite them forward,
saying:
"Could it be that my governance and teachings have shortcomings?
Why is it that the people under your care include those suffering hunger and cold without clothing or food,
those involved in legal disputes who lost their positions,
and those with worthy talents who remain unrecognized?"
When these rulers returned,
they would summon their state's senior officials and relay the Son of Heaven's words.
The common people, hearing this,
all rejoiced and said:
"This is truly the Son of Heaven!
How can he reside so deeply and distantly yet see us so clearly?
How could we possibly deceive him!"
Thus, the role of pastoral overseers is to open the four gates,
enlighten the four directions of vision,
and extend the four directions of hearing.
Therefore, those nearby feel close to him,
and those far away feel at peace.
The Book of Songs says:
"Pacifying the distant and enabling the near,
thus securing our king."
This is what it means!
1.8 Xiànwáng of Héjiān said:
"Yǔ stated that if the people have no food,
then I cannot command them;
if achievements are made but do not benefit the people,
then I cannot encourage them.
Therefore, he dredged rivers to guide the waters,
cut through the Yangtze to connect its nine tributaries,
and channeled the five lakes to stabilize the Eastern Sea.
The people indeed labored hard,
yet they did not complain or suffer,
because the achievements benefited the people."
1.9 When Yǔ went out and encountered a criminal,
he descended from his carriage, inquired, and wept for him.
His attendants said:
"The criminal did not follow the way,
hence this happened.
Why does Your Majesty grieve for him to such an extent?"
Yǔ said:
"The people under Yáo and Shùn
all took the hearts of Yáo and Shùn as their own.
Now that I am the ruler,
the common people each take their own hearts as their guide.
That is why I grieve."
The Book of Documents says:
"If the common people have faults,
they reside in me alone."
1.10 The people of Yú and Ruì sought to have their dispute settled by King Wén.
Upon entering King Wén's territory,
they saw his people yielding to become shì and senior officials;
entering his capital,
they saw his shì and senior officials yielding to become high ministers.
The two states said to each other:
"Their people yield to become shì and senior officials,
their shì and senior officials yield to become high ministers,
then surely their ruler would also yield the world and not occupy it."
The two states,
without even seeing King Wén in person,
yielded over what they had disputed,
returned the land as neutral territory, and went back.
Confucius said:
"How great!
The way of King Wén,
it cannot be surpassed!
He transformed without moving,
achieved without acting,
respectfully and cautiously composed himself, and Yú and Ruì settled themselves."
Therefore, the Book of Documents says:
"Only King Wén's reverence and caution."
This is what it means.
1.11 King Chéng and Tángshū Yú were at leisure,
when the king cut a phoenix tree leaf into a guī-tablet and gave it to Tángshū Yú,
saying:
"I grant you this fiefdom."
Tángshū Yú was pleased
and told the Duke of Zhōu.
The Duke of Zhōu came to inquire:
"Has the Son of Heaven enfeoffed Yú?"
King Chéng said:
"I was merely jesting with Yú."
The Duke of Zhōu replied:
"I have heard
that the Son of Heaven has no jesting words.
When the Son of Heaven speaks, the scribes record it,
the musicians chant it,
and the scholars proclaim it."
Thereupon, he enfeoffed Tángshū Yú in Jìn.
The Duke of Zhōu Dàn can be said to have been skilled in persuasion;
with one statement, he made King Chéng value his words more,
clarified the duty of loving his younger brother,
and secured the support of the royal house.
1.12 In the time of Yáo,
Shùn served as Minister of Education,
Xiè as Minister of War,
Yǔ as Minister of Works,
Hòujì as Minister of Agriculture,
Kuí as Director of Music,
Chuí as Chief Artisan,
Bóyí as Minister of Rites,
Gāoyáo as Chief Judge,
and Yì in charge of driving game.
Yáo, though physically adept and skillful,
could not perform any one of these roles himself.
Yáo was the ruler, and the nine served as his ministers.
What was the reason for this?
Yáo understood the affairs of the nine offices,
enabling the nine to each undertake their duties,
all excelling in their posts,
thus accomplishing the nine achievements,
and Yáo thereby completed his work and ruled the world.
Therefore, understanding people
is the way of the ruler;
understanding affairs
is the way of the ministers.
The ruler's way is to know people,
the ministers' way is to know affairs.
Do not disrupt the old laws,
and the world will be well-governed.
1.13 Tāng asked Yīyǐn:
"For the three senior lords, nine ministers, twenty-seven senior officials, and eighty-one scholars,
is there a way to know them?"
Yīyǐn replied:
"In the past, Yáo knew people upon meeting them,
Shùn appointed people and then knew them,
Yǔ promoted them based on their achievements.
These three rulers' methods of selecting the worthy
all differed yet succeeded,
yet there were still errors,
let alone employing without standards and following one's own judgment,
arbitrarily appointing people,
which is bound to lead to great errors.
Therefore, if the ruler lets ministers present their own abilities,
then there will be no mistakes even in one out of ten thousand."
1.14 Why does the king select the worthy?
The king obtains talented and worthy individuals to assist him,
and only then can he govern well.
Even with the wisdom of Yáo and Shùn, if capable ministers are lacking,
then the ruler's grace will not flow,
and transformative beneficence will not spread.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler on the throne
is careful in selecting officials,
diligent in seeking the worthy.
He establishes four assistants to support himself,
and employs the talented to govern the offices;
he honors their ranks,
and enriches their emoluments;
the worthy are advanced to glory and honor,
the incompetent are retired to labor.
Thus, the ruler has no lingering worries,
the subordinates harbor no evil,
all officials can govern,
ministers delight in their posts,
grace flows to all living beings,
and beneficence moistens even the plants and trees.
In the past, Yú Shùn had Yǔ on his left and Gāoyáo on his right,
and governed the world without leaving his hall,
such is the effect of employing the capable.
1.15 King Wǔ asked Tài Gōng:
"Why is it that some states fall into peril and ruin despite promoting the worthy?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"Promoting the worthy but not employing them
means having the reputation of promoting worthies without attaining the substance of truly having worthies."
King Wǔ said:
"Wherein lies the error?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"The error lies in the ruler's fondness for minor virtues alone,
thus failing to obtain true worthies."
King Wǔ said:
"What does it mean to be fond of minor virtues?"
Tài Gōng said:
"The ruler delights in hearing praise and does not detest slander,
taking the unworthy for worthy,
the unvirtuous for virtuous,
the disloyal for loyal,
the untrustworthy for trustworthy.
Such a ruler considers reputation as merit,
and defamation as crime;
those with merit go unrewarded,
those with crime go unpunished;
those with many partisans advance,
those with few partisans retreat.
Therefore, ministers form cliques and obscure the worthy,
officials form factions and abound in treachery;
loyal ministers die unjustly due to slander,
treacherous ministers are rewarded undeservedly due to praise,
and the state appears in peril and ruin."
King Wǔ said:
"Excellent,
today I have learned the truth about slander and praise."
1.16 King Wǔ asked Tài Gōng:
"Why is it that some, despite obtaining worthies and respecting scholars,
are still unable to achieve good governance?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"Being unable to decide independently,
but deciding based on others' words—
that is calamity."
King Wǔ said:
"What does it mean to decide based on others' words?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"Being unable to determine whom to dismiss,
they dismiss based on others' words;
unable to determine whom to select,
they select based on others' words;
unable to determine what to do,
they act based on others' words;
unable to determine whom to punish,
they punish based on others' words;
unable to determine whom to reward,
they reward based on others' words.
Thus, the worthy are not necessarily employed,
the unworthy not necessarily dismissed,
and scholars not necessarily respected."
King Wǔ said:
"Excellent,
how does such a person govern the state?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"Such a person dislikes hearing about his own faults,
but enjoys hearing about others' faults;
dislikes hearing about his own evils,
but enjoys hearing about others' evils.
Therefore, he cannot achieve good governance."
King Wǔ said:
"Excellent."
1.17 Duke Huán of Qí asked Nìng Qì:
"Guǎn Zhòng is now aged,
and will soon leave me and pass from the world.
I fear that laws and decrees will not be implemented,
many will neglect their duties,
the common people will suffer and complain,
and the state will be full of bandits and thieves.
What should I do to prevent wickedness from arising
and ensure the people have sufficient clothing and food?"
Nìng Qì replied:
"The key lies in obtaining worthies and appointing them."
Duke Huán said:
"How does one obtain worthies?"
Nìng Qì replied:
"Open the paths for them,
observe and employ them,
honor their positions,
increase their emoluments,
and make their names illustrious.
Then scholars under heaven
will eagerly come forth."
Duke Huán said:
"Although I have promoted and employed worthy scholars,
without your grace in visiting me,
there would be no commoner of extraordinary talent
coming to my door seeking audience."
Nìng Qì replied:
"This is because Your Majesty observes without clarity,
promotes without prominence,
employs with doubt,
appoints to low offices,
and offers meager emoluments.
Moreover, there are five obstructions why the state fails to obtain scholars:
the ruler does not favor scholars,
with flatterers by his side—first obstruction;
those who speak of beneficial matters are never employed—second obstruction;
blocked and obscured,
one must rely on close attendants to be noticed—third obstruction;
interrogations exhaust the accused with words,
punishing them excessively by law—fourth obstruction;
officials follow their desires,
usurping state power and commands—fifth obstruction.
Remove these five obstructions,
and heroes will arise together,
worthies and wise men will come to serve.
If the five obstructions remain,
they obscure the sentiments of officials and people above,
and block the paths of worthy scholars below.
Therefore, the governance of enlightened kings and sage rulers
is like rivers and seas that accept all,
thus long remaining masters of all streams.
Enlightened kings and sage rulers accept all,
thus living in peace and longevity.
From this perspective,
those who secure the ruler and benefit the people are not limited to one scholar."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent,
I will record these five obstructions as a foundational warning."
1.18 Duke Jǐng of Qí asked Yàn Zǐ:
"I wish to follow you, Master, and improve Qí's governance.
Is this possible?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"I have heard that
a state must have competent officials before governance can be improved."
Duke Jǐng changed countenance, displeased,
saying:
"Although Qí is small,
how can it lack competent officials?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"This is not what I meant.
In the past, when our former lord Duke Huán was physically weary,
and his speech inadequate,
then Xí Péng attended him.
When his attendants made many errors,
and punishments were unjust,
then Xián Zhāng attended him.
When he lived unrestrained and indulgent,
and his attendants were intimidated,
then Dōng Guō Yá attended him.
When fields were neglected,
and the people unsettled,
then Nìng Qì attended him.
When military officers were negligent,
and soldiers lax,
then Wáng Zǐ Chéng Fù attended him.
When virtue and righteousness were lacking,
and trustworthiness declined,
then Guǎn Zhòng attended him.
The former lord could use others' strengths to supplement his shortcomings;
use others' abundance to compensate for his insufficiency.
Thus, his commands reached far without opposition,
and his armies attacked the guilty without defeat.
Therefore, feudal lords paid homage to his virtue,
and the Son of Heaven bestowed sacrificial meat upon him.
Now, Your Majesty has many faults,
yet not one scholar has been heard of to address them,
hence I say officials are not competent."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Excellent."
1.19 Duke Jǐng said to Yàn Zǐ:
"I hear Gāo Liáo associates with you, Master.
I request to meet him."
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"I have heard that
those who fight for territory
cannot become kings;
those who take office for emoluments
cannot achieve good governance.
Although Gāo Liáo has been like a brother to me for long,
he has never corrected my faults,
nor supplemented my shortcomings.
He is merely an official serving for salary.
How could he be sufficient to assist Your Majesty?"
1.20 King Zhāo of Yān asked Guō Wěi, saying:
"My territory is small and my people few.
The people of Qí have taken eight cities of Jì,
and the Xiōngnú have driven Lóufán to submission.
With my lack of virtue,
I have inherited the ancestral temple,
but fear endangering the altars of soil and grain.
Is there a way to preserve them?"
Guō Wěi said:
"There is,
but I fear Your Majesty cannot use it."
King Zhāo rose from his mat,
wishing to hear it.
Guō Wěi said:
"The ministers of an emperor -
their title is minister,
but in reality they are teachers;
the ministers of a king -
their title is minister,
but in reality they are friends;
the ministers of a hegemon -
their title is minister,
but in reality they are guests;
the ministers of an endangered state -
their title is minister,
but in reality they are captives.
Now if you, King, face east,
pointing with your eyes and commanding with your breath to seek ministers,
then the material for servants will come;
if you face south to hold court,
maintaining the rituals of bowing and yielding to seek ministers,
then the material for officials will come;
if you face west with equal courtesy,
treating them with respect,
not relying on authority to seek ministers,
then the material for friends will come;
if you face north, clasping your hands and retreating deferentially to seek ministers,
then the material for teachers will come.
In this way, at best you can become a true king,
at worst a hegemon,
depending on Your Majesty's choice."
The King of Yān said:
"I wish to learn but have no teacher."
Guō Wěi said:
"If the King truly wishes to promote the Way,
I ask to pave the way for the talented men of the world."
Thereupon the King of Yān always placed Guō Wěi in the seat of honor facing south.
After three years,
Sūzǐ heard of this,
and came from Zhōu to Yān;
Zōu Yǎn heard of this,
and came from Qí to Yān;
Yuè Yì heard of this,
and came from Zhào to Yān;
Qū Jǐng heard of this,
and came from Chǔ to Yān.
When these four men had all arrived,
they indeed enabled weak Yān to conquer strong Qí.
Now Yān and Qí were not countries of equal power that could contend in battle,
the reason it was so
was due to the strength of these four men.
The Book of Songs says:
"With many officers, well arrayed,
King Wén secured his state."
This expresses the meaning.
1.21 When King Zhuāng of Chǔ had subdued Duke Bó of Zhèng,
and defeated the Jìn army,
General Zǐ Zhòng spoke three times inappropriately.
King Zhuāng returned,
passed through the district of Shēn Hóu,
who offered food,
but by midday the King had not eaten.
Shēn Hóu asked for punishment.
King Zhuāng sighed deeply and said:
"I have heard:
if a ruler is a worthy ruler,
and also has teachers, he will become a true king;
if a ruler is a middling ruler,
and also has teachers, he will become a hegemon;
if a ruler is an inferior ruler,
and his ministers are all inferior to him, he will perish.
Now I am an inferior ruler,
and my ministers are all inferior to me,
I fear I will perish.
Moreover, sages are never absent from the world,
worthies are never absent from the state,
there are worthies in the world but I alone cannot obtain them -
as for one like me living,
what is the use of eating!"
Thus King Zhuāng, having subdued a great power in battle,
and having won the allegiance of the feudal lords through righteousness,
was still sorrowful and fearful,
aware that sagely wisdom did not reside in himself,
regretting his own lack of virtue,
and longing to obtain worthy assistants,
forgetting to eat until midday -
he may be called an enlightened ruler.
1.22 An enlightened ruler has three fears:
first, being in a high position yet fearing he might not hear of his faults;
second, being successful yet fearing he might become arrogant;
third, hearing the most profound words of the world yet fearing he might not be able to put them into practice.
How do we know this is so?
Formerly, King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè fought with the men of Wú,
defeated them greatly,
and annexed the Nine Yí tribes.
At that time,
he stood facing south as ruler,
with three close ministers,
and five distant ministers,
and commanded his assembled ministers:
"Whoever hears of my faults and does not report them will be punished with mutilation."
This is an example of being in a high position yet fearing he might not hear of his faults.
Formerly, Duke Wén of Jìn fought with the men of Chǔ,
won a great victory over them,
burned their army,
and the fire did not extinguish for three days.
Duke Wén withdrew with a worried expression,
and his attendant said:
"You have greatly defeated Chǔ,
why do you now have a worried look?"
Duke Wén said:
"I have heard that only sages
can achieve security through military victory.
As for those who win through deception,
they are never free from danger -
this is why I worry."
This is an example of being successful yet fearing he might become arrogant.
Formerly, Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng,
understood their words,
and delighted in their principles.
At the first morning court in the first month,
he ordered a grand sacrifice to be prepared,
and presented it to his ancestors.
Duke Huán stood facing west,
while Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng stood facing east.
Duke Huán praised them, saying:
"Since I have been able to hear the words of these two men,
my eyes have become clearer,
my ears have become sharper.
I dare not keep this to myself alone,
but wish to recommend them to my ancestors."
This is an example of hearing the most profound words of the world,
and fearing he might not be able to put them into practice.
1.23 Duke Jǐng of Qí went out hunting,
saw a tiger on the mountain,
and saw a snake in the marsh.
Returning,
he summoned Yànzǐ and asked him:
"Today when I went out hunting,
I saw a tiger on the mountain,
and a snake in the marsh.
Is this perhaps what is called an ill omen?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"The state has three kinds of ill omens,
but these are not among them.
Having worthies but not knowing them -
this is the first ill omen;
knowing them but not using them -
this is the second ill omen;
using them but not trusting them -
this is the third ill omen.
What are called ill omens
are precisely like these.
Now seeing a tiger on the mountain -
that is the tiger's home;
seeing a snake in the marsh -
that is the snake's den.
Going to the tiger's home,
going to the snake's den and seeing them -
why should this be an ill omen?"
1.24 King Zhuāng of Chǔ was fond of hunting,
and a minister remonstrated with him:
"Jìn and Chǔ are rival states.
If Chǔ does not plot against Jìn,
Jìn will certainly plot against Chǔ.
Is Your Majesty not perhaps indulging too much in pleasure?"
The King said:
"I hunt in order to seek out men of talent.
Those who charge through thickets to stab tigers and leopards -
by this I know their courage;
those who seize rhinoceroses and wrestle with wild oxen -
by this I know their strength;
when the hunt is over and they share what they have obtained -
by this I know their benevolence.
Through this method,
I have obtained three talented men,
and Chǔ has thereby been secured."
Therefore it is said:
"If one has determination, then nothing is without purpose" -
this expresses the meaning.
1.25 During Tāng's reign, there was a great drought for seven years.
The Luò River cracked and streams dried up,
sand boiled and stones melted.
Thereupon, he sent people holding a three-legged cauldron to pray to the mountains and rivers,
teaching them to pray thus:
"Is it because governance is not restrained?
Or that the people are suffering?
Are bribes circulating?
Are slanderers flourishing?
Are palaces being built?
Are women's petitions rampant?
Why does the rain not fall so extremely!"
Before the words had finished, the heavens poured down heavy rain.
Thus, heaven's response to humans
is like a shadow following the form,
an echo imitating the sound.
The Book of Songs says:
"Above and below, offerings are made and buried,
no deity is not honored."
This speaks of the distress of drought.
1.26 During the time of Yīn's Tàiwù,
mulberry and grain trees grew in the courtyard,
appearing at dusk
and reaching an arm's span by dawn.
The historian requested to divine at Tāng's temple,
and Tàiwù agreed.
The diviner said:
"I have heard:
Auspicious signs
are the forerunners of blessings;
if one sees an auspicious sign but does evil,
then blessings will not arise.
Ominous signs
are the forerunners of disasters;
if one sees an ominous sign but can do good,
then disaster will not come."
Thereupon, he attended court early and retired late,
inquired after the sick and mourned the dead,
and on the third day, the mulberry and grain trees vanished on their own.
1.27 Gāozōng,
also known as Wǔdīng,
was elevated and honored by his ancestors,
hence titled Gāozōng.
After Chéng Tāng,
the ways of the former kings declined,
laws were violated,
and mulberry and grain trees grew together in the court,
reaching an arm's span in seven days.
Wǔdīng summoned his prime minister to inquire.
The prime minister said:
"Though I know,
I dare not speak;
ask Zǔ Jǐ."
Zǔ Jǐ said: 'Mulberry and grain trees,
being wild grasses,
yet growing in the court—
does it signify the state's demise?'"
Wǔdīng was terrified,
disciplined himself and cultivated virtue,
reflecting on the governance of past kings,
reviving fallen states,
continuing severed lineages,
promoting reclusive talents,
and clarifying the way of caring for the elderly.
Three years later,
barbarian tribes from afar, through multiple translations, came to court from sixteen states.
This is called the lord who preserves the perishing and continues the severed,
hence he is elevated and honored.
1.28 Sòng suffered a great flood,
and a person from Lǔ came to offer condolences, saying:
"Heaven has sent excessive rain,
filling valleys and streams,
extending to your land,
causing worry to your governance,
so I humbly offer condolences."
The person from Sòng replied:
"I, the unworthy,
have been negligent in fasting and purification,
failed to maintain the city walls,
and misused the people untimely,
so heaven has sent calamity,
and even troubled you with worry;
I accept this reproach."
A gentleman heard this and said:
"Sòng is nearly there!"
Someone asked:
"What does that mean?"
He said:
"In the past, Xià's Jié and Yīn's Zhòu did not acknowledge their faults,
and their fall was swift;
Chéng Tāng, King Wén, and King Wǔ knew to own their faults,
and their rise was vigorous.
To err and correct it
is as if one had not erred.
Hence it is said:
They are nearly there!"
The people of Sòng heard this,
rose early and retired late,
attended court early and left late,
mourned the dead and cared for the sick,
and exerted themselves within the realm.
After three years,
the harvests were abundant and governance peaceful.
Had the people of Sòng not heard the gentleman's words,
the grains would not have been plentiful and the state not tranquil.
The Book of Songs says:
"Support me in bearing the burden,
and show me bright virtue."
This refers to this.
1.29 King Zhāo of Chǔ fell ill,
and divination indicated:
"The Hé River is causing the trouble."
The ministers requested to offer three types of sacrificial animals.
The king said:
"Stop.
In ancient times, the former kings divided lands and set territories,
and sacrifices did not extend beyond one's own domain.
The Jiāng, Hàn, Suī, and Zhāng rivers are within Chǔ's domain.
The arrival of fortune or misfortune
should not exceed this.
Though I lack virtue,
the Hé River is not one for which I could incur offense."
Thus, he did not perform the sacrifice.
Zhòngní heard of it and said:
"King Zhāo can be said to understand the great way;
it is fitting that he did not lose his state!"
1.30 During the time of King Zhāo of Chǔ,
there were clouds like red birds
flying alongside the sun
for three days.
King Zhāo was troubled by this
and sent a messenger on a relay horse
eastward to ask the Grand Historian Zhōu Lí.
Zhōu Lí said:
"It will bring harm to the king's person,
but it can be averted by having the Prime Minister and the Minister of War intercede."
When the Prime Minister and Minister of War heard this,
they fasted overnight and bathed,
preparing to offer themselves in prayer.
The king said:
"Stop.
That Chǔ has me
is like a body having a chest and ribs;
that it has a Prime Minister and Minister of War
is like a body having thighs and arms.
If the chest and ribs are ill
and transfer it to the thighs and arms,
how can that mean discarding the person?"
1.31 Duke Wén of Zhū divined about moving to Yì,
and the historian said:
"It benefits the people but not the ruler."
The duke said:
"If it benefits the people,
it is my benefit.
Heaven gave birth to the multitude and set up rulers for them
to benefit them.
If the people are benefited,
I must share in it."
An attendant said:
"Life can be prolonged;
why does the lord not do so?"
The duke said:
"My duty lies in shepherding the people;
the shortness or length of life
is a matter of timing.
If the people are benefited,
what greater fortune is there?"
Thus, he moved to Yì.
1.32 King Zhuāng of Chǔ, seeing that heaven showed no portents and earth produced no calamities,
prayed to the mountains and rivers, saying:
"Has heaven forgotten me?"
This ability to seek faults from heaven
surely means he would not reject admonishment;
in safety, he did not forget danger,
thus he could ultimately achieve hegemonic success.
1.33 Tāng said:
"Medicine and food are first tasted by the lowly,
then reach the noble;
medicinal words are first offered to the noble,
then heard by the lowly."
Thus, medicine and food being tasted by the lowly
before reaching the noble
is teaching;
medicinal words being offered to the noble
before being heard by the lowly
is the Way.
Therefore, having others taste food
before eating it oneself
allows one to gain more flavor;
having others taste words
before hearing them oneself
allows one to gain fewer words.
Hence, the enlightened ruler regarding words
must listen to them through others,
must hear them through others,
must select them through others,
must take them through others,
must gather them through others,
must store them through others,
must implement them through others.
Thus, the Way becomes clear when acquired through numerous means,
becomes illustrious when practiced through numerous means,
becomes stored when applied to all things through numerous means.
Therefore, those who seek the Way
do not use their eyes but their hearts,
those who take the Way do not use their hands but their ears.
1.34 King Wén of Chǔ fell ill,
and told his ministers:
"Guǎn Ráo confronts me with righteousness,
restrains me with ritual,
I feel uneasy with him around,
do not miss him when he's absent,
yet I gain from him,
so I must ennoble him while I still can;
Shēn Hóu Bó encourages me to do what I desire,
does what pleases me before I do,
I feel at ease with him around,
miss him when he's absent,
yet I lose from him,
so I must dismiss him while I still can."
The ministers consented,
so he ennobled Guǎn Ráo as a senior official,
and sent Shēn Hóu Bó away with gifts.
As Shēn Hóu Bó was going to Zhèng,
the king said:
"You must be cautious,
for as a person you are unvirtuous,
yet you desire to control others' governance -
do not go to Lǔ, Wèi, Sòng, or Zhèng."
He did not listen,
and went to Zhèng.
After three years he gained control of Zhèng's government,
but within five months the people of Zhèng killed him.
1.35 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was boating with Luán Jī,
and was about to throw him into the river,
saying:
"I once favored music and beauty,
and Luán Jī provided them;
I once favored palaces and towers,
and Luán Jī built them;
I once favored fine horses and skilled drivers,
and Luán Jī sought them out.
Now I have valued scholars for six years,
yet Luán Jī has never recommended one -
this promotes my faults and suppresses my virtues."
1.36 Someone said to Zhào Jiǎnzǐ:
"Why don't you reform, my lord?"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I will."
His attendants said:
"My lord has no faults,
why reform?"
The lord said:
"My agreement
doesn't necessarily mean I have faults,
but I want to attract those who would admonish me.
If I reject this now,
I would be rejecting admonishers,
and admonishers would surely stop coming -
then my faults would be imminent."
1.37 Hán Wǔzǐ was hunting,
the game had been gathered,
the hunting chariots assembled.
A messenger came reporting:
"The Duke of Jìn has died."
Wǔzǐ said to Luán Huáizǐ:
"You know I love hunting,
the game is gathered,
the chariots assembled -
may I finish the hunt before paying condolences?"
Huáizǐ replied:
"When the Fàn clan was destroyed,
they had many supporters but few admonishers.
Now I, toward you,
am a supporter,
while Lěi, toward you,
is an admonisher -
why not ask Lěi?"
Wǔzǐ said:
"Does Lěi want to admonish me?
If you admonish me,
why need Lěi?"
So he stopped the hunt.
1.38 Shī Jīng was playing the zither,
Marquis Wén of Wèi rose to dance,
chanting:
"Let no one contradict my words."
Shī Jīng took his zither and struck at the marquis,
missing him,
but hitting his tasseled crown,
shattering it.
The marquis turned to his attendants saying:
"For a minister to strike his lord -
what is the punishment?"
The attendants said:
"The punishment is boiling."
They dragged Shī Jīng down one step.
Shī Jīng said:
"May I speak one word before dying?"
The marquis said:
"Speak."
Shī Jīng said:
"When Yáo and Shùn were lords,
they only feared no one would contradict their words;
when Jié and Zhòu were lords,
they only feared someone would contradict their words.
I struck at Jié and Zhòu,
not at my lord."
The marquis said:
"Release him,
this was my fault.
Hang the zither on the city gate
as my tally of error;
do not repair the tassels
as my warning."
1.39 Duke Jǐng of Qí was touring at Lóu,
when he heard of Yànzǐ's death.
The duke rode in a plain-clothed carriage driven swiftly,
thinking himself too slow,
he dismounted and ran.
Realizing he couldn't outrun the carriage,
he rode again.
By the time he reached the capital,
he had dismounted and run four times,
weeping as he went.
Arriving,
he fell on the body and wailed:
"You, great officer, day and night admonished me,
leaving no detail untouched,
yet I remained self-indulgent and unrestrained,
accumulating the people's resentment and blame.
Now Heaven sends disaster to Qí,
not on me but on you, Master -
the altars of Qí are in danger,
to whom will the people appeal now!"
1.40 Seventeen years after Yànzǐ's death,
Duke Jǐng was drinking with his ministers.
The duke shot and missed the target,
yet the hall unanimously cheered,
as if with one voice.
The duke changed countenance and sighed deeply,
laying aside his bow and arrows.
When Xián Zhāng entered,
the duke said:
"Zhāng!
Since I lost Yànzǐ seventeen years ago,
I've never heard of my faults,
yet today I shot and missed the target,
and the cheers came as if with one voice."
Xián Zhāng replied:
"This shows these ministers' incompetence.
Their wisdom insufficient to recognize your faults,
their courage insufficient to confront your majesty -
yet there is one thing.
I have heard:
"If the ruler favors something,
his ministers will submit to it;
if the ruler craves something,
his ministers will consume it."
Just as the inchworm turns yellow when eating yellow things,
and turns green when eating green things.
Does Your Majesty still harbor flattering words?"
The Duke said:
"Well said.
In today's conversation,
you are the ruler,
and I am the subject."
At that time, sea fishermen presented fish,
and the Duke bestowed fifty cartloads to Xián Zhāng.
Xián Zhāng returned,
with fish carts blocking the road,
patted his charioteer's hand and said:
"Those who earlier chorused approval,
all desired such fish.
In the past, Yànzǐ declined rewards to rectify his ruler,
thus faults were not concealed.
Now the ministers flatter to seek profit,
so they emerge in unison to sing praises,
as if with one voice.
Currently, my assistance to the ruler hasn't been manifested to the masses,
yet I accept these fish,
this would contradict Yànzǐ's principle and comply with flatterers' desires."
He firmly declined the fish and did not accept it.
The gentleman says:
"Xián Zhāng's integrity,
is the legacy of Yànzǐ's conduct."
1.41 Heaven gives birth to humans,
not to make them rulers;
Heaven establishes rulers,
not for the sake of position.
If a ruler,
acts on personal desires without regard for his people,
this is not upholding Heaven's will,
forgetting what his position properly entails.
Such a one,
the Spring and Autumn Annals does not grant capable rulership but treats as barbarians.
The Earl of Zhèng hated one man and thereby abandoned his army,
hence there is the saying "barbarians do not act as rulers."
If the sovereign does not reflect on this,
having already lost sincere intent,
how can he understand?
Therefore it is said:
"Those who hold states must not fail to study the Spring and Autumn Annals."
This refers to that.
1.42 When men of Qí assassinated their ruler,
Duke Xiāng of Lǔ seized a spear and rose saying:
"How dare a subject kill his ruler?"
Shī Jù said:
"The ruler of Qí could not govern properly,
appointed unworthy men,
indulged one man's desires,
to oppress the nature of thousands,
which is not the purpose of establishing rulership.
His death,
was self-inflicted.
Now you, my lord, do not grieve for the lives of thousands,
but mourn one man's death,
how mistaken is that?
His ministers were already without principle,
his ruler also not worth pitying."
1.43 Confucius said:
"King Wén resembles the first year,
King Wǔ resembles the spring king,
the Duke of Zhōu resembles the first month.
King Wén had Wáng Jì as father,
Tàirén as mother,
Tàisì as consort,
King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu as sons,
Tài Diān and Hóng Yāo as ministers -
his foundation was excellent.
King Wǔ rectified himself to rectify his state,
rectified his state to rectify the world.
He attacked those without principle,
punished the guilty,
with one action the world was set right,
his deeds were upright.
Spring brings its season,
all things attain life;
the ruler brings his way,
all people attain order.
The Duke of Zhōu bore himself and the world followed him,
his sincerity was utmost."
1.44 Honoring the ruler and debasing ministers
is achieved through power,
but when power is lost, authority topples.
Thus when the Son of Heaven loses the Way,
the feudal lords become honored;
when feudal lords misgovern,
the great ministers rise;
when great ministers neglect office,
the common people thrive.
From this perspective,
when superiors do not fail yet inferiors succeed,
has never occurred.
1.45 Confucius said:
"If the Way of Xià had not perished,
the virtue of Shāng would not have arisen;
if the virtue of Shāng had not perished,
the virtue of Zhōu would not have arisen;
if the virtue of Zhōu had not perished,
the Spring and Autumn Annals would not have been written.
The Spring and Autumn Annals were written, and thereafter gentlemen knew the Way of Zhōu had perished."
Thus superior and inferior damage each other,
like water and fire extinguishing one another.
The ruler must not fail to examine this and greatly empower his ministers,
for this strengthens private gates and destroys the public house.
If the ruler does not examine this,
the state will be in peril.
Guǎnzǐ said:
"Authority cannot be placed in two places,
governance cannot come from two gates."
Therefore it is said:
"When the shin is larger than the thigh, walking is difficult;
when the finger is larger than the arm, grasping is difficult."
When the root is small and branches large,
they cannot be properly employed.
1.46 Sīchéng Zǐhǎn served as minister of Sòng,
and said to the ruler of Sòng:
"The state's danger or stability,
the people's order or chaos,
lie in the ruler's exercise of rewards and punishments.
When rewards are appropriate, the worthy are encouraged;
when punishments fit, the wicked desist.
If rewards and punishments are inappropriate,
the worthy are not encouraged,
the wicked do not desist.
When wickedness colludes,
deceiving superiors and obscuring the ruler,
to contend for ranks and emoluments,
one must be cautious.
Rewards, gifts, and concessions
are what people like -
Your Majesty should administer these;
penalties, punishments, and executions
are what people hate -
I request to take charge of these."
The ruler said:
"Excellent.
You handle the odious matters,
I practice the good ones,
I know I won't be laughed at by the feudal lords."
Thereupon the ruler of Sòng administered rewards while Zǐhǎn handled punishments.
The people knew the power of penalties
rested solely with Zǐhǎn,
the great ministers drew close to him,
the common people attached themselves to him.
Within a year,
Zǐhǎn expelled his ruler and monopolized the government.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not weaken the ruler and strengthen the minister."
Lǎozǐ said:
"The fish should not leave the deep;
the state's sharp weapons
should not be lent to others."
This refers to that.
2.1 The art of being a minister lies in
following orders and reporting back,
never daring to act arbitrarily,
upholding righteousness without improper compliance,
not seeking rank for its own sake,
ensuring benefit to the state,
and supplementing the ruler's efforts.
Thus, they attain honor and their descendants are preserved.
Therefore, ministers' conduct falls into six upright and six wicked types.
Practicing the six upright leads to glory,
while committing the six wicked brings disgrace.
Glory and disgrace are
the gateways to fortune and misfortune.
What are the six upright and six wicked?
The six upright are:
first, those who perceive crises before they sprout,
before signs appear,
clearly foreseeing the pivots of survival or demise,
the essentials of gain and loss,
preventing issues before they arise,
enabling the ruler to stand exalted in glory,
praised by all as filial—such are sage ministers;
second, those with humble minds and pure intent,
promoting goodness and understanding the Way,
encouraging the ruler with ritual and righteousness,
advising on long-term strategies,
supporting his virtues,
rectifying his faults,
achieving success in endeavors,
attributing merits to the ruler,
not claiming credit alone—such are good ministers;
third, those who humble themselves,
rising early and retiring late,
tirelessly recommending the worthy,
frequently citing ancient deeds,
to sharpen the ruler's will,
hoping to benefit
the state, altars of land and grain, and ancestral temples—such are loyal ministers;
fourth, those who discern the hidden,
foresee success or failure,
preventing and remedying early,
restoring stability,
plugging gaps,
cutting off sources of trouble,
turning calamity into blessing,
ensuring the ruler's perpetual peace—such are wise ministers;
fifth, those who uphold laws and statutes,
serving in office diligently,
declining salaries and rewards,
refusing gifts,
dressing neatly,
eating and drinking modestly—such are steadfast ministers;
sixth, those who, when the state is in turmoil
and actions go unadvised,
dare to confront the ruler's stern countenance,
speaking bluntly of his errors,
undeterred by execution,
dying to secure the state's peace,
unrepentant for their deeds—such are upright ministers.
These are the six upright.
The six wicked are:
first, those content in office, greedy for pay,
engrossed in private affairs,
neglecting public duties,
hoarding wisdom,
concealing ability,
while the ruler starves for counsel,
thirsts for strategies,
yet they refuse full dedication,
drifting with the currents,
watching and waiting—such are useless ministers;
second, those who call all the ruler says good,
all he does right,
secretly seeking his preferences to offer them,
pleasing his ears and eyes,
flattering and accommodating,
joining him in pleasure,
heedless of future harm—such are sycophant ministers;
third, those inwardly treacherous,
outwardly cautious,
glib-tongued and ingratiating,
yet envious of the worthy,
promoting favorites by highlighting strengths and hiding faults,
demoting others by exposing weaknesses and concealing merits,
causing the ruler to err in appointments,
misapply rewards and punishments,
and nullify commands—such are treacherous ministers;
fourth, those whose wit covers faults,
eloquence promotes persuasion,
twisting words into elegant rhetoric,
dividing kin internally,
sowing discord in court externally—such are slanderous ministers;
fifth, those monopolizing power,
manipulating state affairs for personal gain,
forming cliques to enrich their families,
augmenting their authority,
forging royal decrees for self-aggrandizement—such are usurping ministers;
sixth, those misleading the ruler with wickedness,
plunging him into injustice,
forming cabals,
obscuring his clarity,
speaking persuasively at court,
changing tales outside,
blurring right and wrong,
confusing truth and falsehood,
seizing opportunities to shift blame,
attaching accordingly,
spreading the ruler's disgrace throughout the land,
known to neighboring states—such are ministers of ruin.
These are the six wicked.
Worthy ministers follow the six upright ways,
avoiding the six wicked arts,
thus ensuring stability above and order below,
joyful in life,
remembered in death—this is the art of being a minister.
2.2 King Tāng asked Yī Yǐn:
"How do the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, Senior Officials, and Exemplary Scholars differ?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"The Three Dukes
comprehend the Great Way,
adapt to change endlessly,
discern the nature of all things,
and penetrate heavenly principles.
Their words suffice to harmonize yīn and yáng,
align the four seasons,
and regulate wind and rain.
Such individuals
are elevated as Three Dukes.
Thus, their duties
constantly revolve around the Way.
The Nine Ministers
ensure seasonal timeliness,
dredge canals,
repair dikes,
plant trees,
cultivate the five grains splendidly,
mastering geography.
They enable what was impassable and
benefit what was unprofitable.
Such individuals
are elevated as Nine Ministers.
Thus, their duties
constantly revolve around virtue.
Senior Officials
live among the people, sharing their lot,
take and give in common interest,
understand human affairs,
act as if guided by a plumb line,
unharmed by speech,
their words in society
bring no harm to themselves,
facilitate passage at borders and bridges,
fill treasuries and storehouses.
Such individuals
are elevated as Senior Officials.
Thus, their duties
constantly revolve around benevolence.
Exemplary Scholars
understand righteousness without losing heart,
achieve merits without monopolizing rewards,
are loyal and upright, strongly remonstrating without deceit,
forsaking selfishness for public good, speaking with legal measure.
Such individuals
are elevated as Exemplary Scholars.
Thus, their duties
constantly revolve around righteousness.
Therefore, with the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness established, the world is well-governed.
These four types
the enlightened king treats as ministers yet not as subjects."
Tāng asked:
"What does 'treat as ministers yet not as subjects' mean?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"There are four whom the ruler does not address as subjects:
paternal uncles—
ministers but not named as subjects;
elder brothers—
ministers but not named as subjects;
ministers of previous kings—
ministers but not named as subjects;
individuals of great virtue—
ministers but not named as subjects.
This is called great harmony."
2.3 Tāng asked Yī Yǐn:
"Why did the ancients establish the positions of the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, Grand Masters, and Various Scholars?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"The Three Dukes
are established to participate in the five affairs of state;
the Nine Ministers
are established to assist the Three Dukes;
the Grand Masters
are established to assist the Nine Ministers;
the Various Scholars
are established to assist the Grand Masters.
Thus, assistance upon assistance
is called the foundation of governance,
and when the foundation of governance is not lost,
internal and external affairs become as one."
2.4 Zǐ Gòng asked Confucius:
"Among today's ministers, who is worthy?"
Confucius said:
"I do not know.
In the past,
Qí had Bào Shū,
and Zhèng had Zǐ Pí,
who were worthy men."
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Then does Qí not have Guǎn Zhòng,
and Zhèng not have Zǐ Chǎn?"
The Master said:
"Cì,
you only know one aspect,
but not the other.
Do you consider recommending the worthy as being worthy,
or exerting strength as being worthy?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Recommending the worthy is being worthy."
The Master said:
"Indeed.
I have heard that Bào Shū recommended Guǎn Zhòng;
I have heard that Zǐ Pí recommended Zǐ Chǎn.
I have not heard that Guǎn Zhòng or Zǐ Chǎn recommended anyone."
2.5 Marquis Wén of Wèi was about to appoint a chancellor,
so he summoned Lǐ Kè and asked him:
"I wish to appoint a chancellor,
and it is between Jì Chéngzǐ and Zhái Chù.
Whom should I appoint?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"I have heard that
the lowly do not counsel the noble,
outsiders do not counsel insiders,
and the distant do not counsel the close.
I am distant and lowly,
and dare not receive your command."
Marquis Wén said:
"This is a matter of state,
and I hope you will not decline to advise me when facing such affairs."
Lǐ Kè said:
"It is because you have not observed carefully,
but it can be known.
For the noble, look at whom they recommend;
for the wealthy, look at whom they associate with;
for the poor, look at what they do not take;
for the destitute, look at what they do not do.
From this perspective,
it can be known."
Marquis Wén said:
"You may leave now,
for my chancellor is decided."
Lǐ Kè went out
and encountered Zhái Huáng.
Zhái Huáng asked:
"I heard that the ruler consulted you about the chancellorship,
but do not know who was ultimately appointed?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"Jì Chéngzǐ was appointed."
Zhái Huáng changed countenance and said displeasedly:
"Chù is disappointed in you."
Lǐ Kè said:
"Why are you so quickly disappointed in me?
When you recommended me to your ruler,
was it to form a clique with me to seek high office?
The ruler asked me about the chancellorship,
and I replied:
'It is because you have not observed carefully,
but for the noble, look at whom they recommend;
for the wealthy, look at whom they associate with;
for the poor, look at what they do not take;
for the destitute, look at what they do not do.
From this perspective,
it can be known.'
The ruler said:
'Leave now,
for my chancellor is decided.'
Thus I knew Jì Chéngzǐ would be chancellor."
Zhái Huáng said displeasedly:
"Why should Chù not be chancellor?
The guard of Xīhé
was appointed by me;
the internal historian for planning affairs
was appointed by me.
When the king wished to attack Zhōngshān,
I recommended Yuè Yáng;
when there was no minister to govern,
I recommended you;
when there was no tutor for his son,
I recommended Qūhóu Fù.
How am I inferior to Jì Chéngzǐ?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"You are not equal to Jì Chéngzǐ.
Jì Chéngzǐ enjoys a fief of a thousand zhōng,
with nine-tenths spent abroad and one-tenth at home,
to invite and engage scholars from all under heaven.
Thus, from the east he obtained Bǔ Zǐxià, Tián Zǐfāng, and Duàngān Mù.
Those whom he recommends
are teachers for rulers.
Those whom you recommend
are talents for ministers."
Zhái Huáng, startled, said with shame:
"Chù has misspoken to you,
and I beg to cultivate myself and then learn."
Before he finished speaking,
attendants announced that Jì Chéngzǐ had been appointed chancellor.
Thereupon, Zhái Huáng fell silent and changed color,
feeling ashamed within,
and dared not go out for three months.
2.6 The Prime Minister of Chǔ died.
Jǐng Gōng encountered Chéng Gōng Gàn and said:
"To whom will the prime ministership go?"
Chéng Gōng Gàn said:
"Probably to Qū Chūn?"
Jǐng Gōng angrily said:
"The people of the state think it will come to me."
Chéng Gōng Gàn said:
"Your resources are few,
while Qū Chūn's resources are abundant.
In righteousness, he attains the utmost concerns of the world,
and you consider him a friend.
The singing crane and the straw dog have very little wisdom,
yet you enjoy them.
Chīyí Zǐpí daily attends upon Qū Chūn,
and Sǔn Pō is his friend.
The wisdom of these two men
is sufficient to be prime minister,
yet they dare not claim their wisdom exclusively but entrust it to Qū Chūn.
Therefore, I say:
'Will the government not go to Qū Chūn?'"
2.7 Tián Zǐfāng was crossing the Western River
and visited Zhái Huáng.
Zhái Huáng rode in a canopied carriage,
shaded by an ornate cover,
with golden bridles,
fastened with mats and mats,
and such like,
with eighty such teams of four horses.
Zǐfāng saw him from afar,
mistook him for a ruler,
and as the road was narrow,
he descended his carriage and waited.
When Zhái Huáng arrived and saw Zǐfāng,
he alighted and hurried forward,
prostrating himself downwind,
saying:
"It is I, Chù."
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"Ah, you!
When I saw you from afar,
I thought you were a ruler.
But upon your arrival, I see you are a minister.
How have you reached such a state?"
Zhái Huáng replied:
"All this was bestowed upon me by my lord,
accumulated over thirty years,
hence I have come to this.
Taking advantage of leisure time,
I ventured into the open countryside,
and happened to meet you, sir."
Zǐfāng said:
"Why has your lord bestowed such lavish carriages upon you?"
Zhái Huáng replied:
"Formerly, the Western River had no defender;
I recommended Wú Qǐ, and the region beyond the Western River was pacified.
Yè had no magistrate;
I recommended Xīmén Bào, and Wèi was freed from the threat of Zhào.
Suānzǎo had no magistrate;
I recommended Běimén Kě, and Wèi was relieved of worries from Qí.
When Wèi wished to attack Zhōngshān,
I recommended Yuè Yāng, and Zhōngshān was captured.
Wèi lacked ministers to govern effectively;
I recommended Lǐ Kè, and the state of Wèi was greatly well-governed.
Thus, by recommending these five great officers,
my rank and emolument were doubled,
and that is why I have reached this state."
Zǐfāng said:
"Well done,
strive on!
The position of Wèi's chancellor
will not leave you for another."
Zhái Huáng replied:
"The lord's maternal younger brother has a Gōngsūn Jìchéng,
who recommended Zǐxià, and the lord treats him as a teacher;
recommended Duàngān Mù, and the lord treats him as a friend;
recommended you, sir, and the lord holds you in respect.
Those he recommended are teachers, friends, and those held in respect.
The ones I recommended
are all ministers who merely hold office and emolument.
How could I attain the chancellorship of Wèi?"
Zǐfāng said:
"I have heard that one who is personally worthy is virtuous,
and one who can recommend the worthy is also virtuous.
Your five recommendations are all worthy men;
strive on,
you will eventually attain the next rank."
2.8 King Wēi of Qí was touring the Jade Terrace,
when Chénghóu Qīng came to present matters,
with a great multitude of carriages and horsemen in his train.
The king saw him,
and said to his attendants:
"Who is this coming?"
The attendants said:
"It is Chénghóu Qīng."
The king said:
"The state is extremely poor;
why such a lavish procession?"
The attendants said:
"He who gives has reason to demand,
and he who receives has means to exchange;
Your Majesty might inquire into his explanation."
When Chénghóu Qīng arrived,
he presented himself, saying:
"It is Jì."
The king did not respond.
He said again:
"It is Jì."
The king did not respond.
He said again:
"It is Jì."
The king said:
"The state is extremely poor;
why such a lavish procession?"
Chénghóu Qīng said:
"Pardon my capital offense,
and allow me to explain."
The king said:
"Agreed."
He replied:
"Jì recommended Tián Jūzǐ for Xīhé, and Qín and Liáng were weakened;
Jì recommended Tián Jiězǐ for Nánchéng, and the people of Chǔ came bearing silk to court;
Jì recommended Qiánzhuōzǐ for Míngzhōu, and the people of Yān supplied livestock,
and the people of Zhào provided vessels;
Jì recommended Tián Zhǒngshǒuzǐ for Jímò, and in Qí there was sufficiency for all needs;
Jì recommended Běiguō Diāobózǐ for a high position, and the nine clans became closer,
and the people more prosperous.
Having recommended these several good men,
Your Majesty can rest your head and sleep;
why worry about the state's poverty?"
2.9 Duke Mù of Qín sent merchants to transport salt from Wèi,
and levied from the merchants.
A merchant bought Bǎilǐ Xī for the price of five ram skins,
and had him drive the cart to Qín.
Duke Mù of Qín inspected the salt,
and saw that Bǎilǐ Xī's ox was fat,
and said:
"The burden is heavy, the road long and perilous;
how is it that the ox is so fat?"
He replied:
"I feed it at regular times,
and drive it without violence;
when there is danger,
I go ahead or behind with my own person,
hence it is fat."
Duke Mù realized he was a gentleman,
and ordered the officials to prepare a bath, provide robes and headgear, and sit with him,
and the duke was greatly pleased.
Another day, when discussing governance with Gōngsūn Zhī,
Gōngsūn Zhī became very uneasy,
and said:
"Your lordship's ears and eyes are keen,
your thoughts and considerations thorough;
has Your Lordship perhaps obtained a sage?"
The duke said:
"Indeed,
I am pleased with the words of Xī;
he seems like a sage."
Gōngsūn Zhī then returned home to fetch a goose as a congratulatory gift,
saying:
"Your Lordship has obtained a minister for the altars of grain and soil;
I dare to congratulate on the blessing for the state."
The duke did not decline,
but bowed twice and accepted.
The next day,
Gōngsūn Zhī offered to yield his position as senior minister to Bǎilǐ Xī,
saying:
"Qín is situated in a remote place,
the people are crude and ignorant,
which is the root of peril and ruin.
I know myself inadequate to be above him,
so I ask to yield to him."
The duke did not consent.
Gōngsūn Zhī said:
"Your Lordship has obtained a sage minister for the state without using a matchmaker;
this is Your Lordship's blessing.
I, seeing a worthy, yield to him;
this is my blessing.
Now that Your Lordship has already obtained your blessing,
yet would make me lose mine;
is that acceptable?
I ask to finally yield it."
The duke did not consent.
Gōngsūn Zhī said:
"If I, unworthy, remain in a high position,
it means Your Lordship has lost the proper order;
for the unworthy to disrupt order
is my fault.
To advance the worthy and withdraw the unworthy
is Your Lordship's wisdom.
If I now remain in position,
I would be negating Your Lordship's virtue and opposing proper conduct as a minister;
I shall flee."
The duke then accepted.
Thus, Bǎilǐ Xī became senior minister to govern,
and Gōngsūn Zhī became the next minister to assist him.
2.10 Lord Jiǎn of Zhào was traveling from Jìnyáng to Hándān,
and stopped midway.
The carriage officer came forward and asked:
"Why are you stopping?"
Lord Jiǎn replied:
"Dǒng Ānyú is behind."
The officer said:
"This concerns the affairs of the three armies,
how can you, my lord, detain the entire army for one person?"
Lord Jiǎn said:
"Very well."
He drove another hundred paces and stopped again.
As the officer was about to remonstrate,
Dǒng Ānyú happened to arrive.
Lord Jiǎn said:
"Where the Qín road intersects with Jìn territory,
I forgot to have someone block it."
Dǒng Ānyú said:
"This is why Ānyú stayed behind."
Lord Jiǎn said:
"The precious jades of the office,
I forgot to have someone load them."
Came the reply:
"This is why Ānyú stayed behind."
Lord Jiǎn said:
"The envoy Zhú Guò is advanced in years,
his words have always served as law for Jìn state,
I forgot to have someone take leave and present gifts to him."
Came the reply:
"This is why Ānyú stayed behind."
Lord Jiǎn can truly be said to have examined himself inwardly and understood others outwardly!
Thus his person was at ease and the state secure.
The Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Chāng said:
"If a ruler could truly be like Lord Jiǎn of Zhào,
the court would not be in peril."
2.11 Yànzǐ was attending to Duke Jǐng,
and the morning was cold.
The Duke said:
"Please bring some hot food."
Came the reply:
"Yīng is not your kitchen servant,
I dare decline."
The Duke said:
"Please bring a fur robe."
Came the reply:
"Yīng is not your field and marsh steward,
I dare decline."
The Duke said:
"Then what are you to me, Master?"
Came the reply:
"A minister of the altars of soil and grain."
The Duke said:
"What is a minister of the altars of soil and grain?"
Came the reply:
"A minister of the altars of soil and grain
can establish the state,
distinguish what is appropriate between superior and inferior,
ensuring proper governance;
regulate the order of the hundred officials,
ensuring proper arrangement;
craft diplomatic communications,
that may be distributed throughout the four directions."
From this time onward,
unless the Duke observed proper etiquette,
he would not see Yànzǐ.
2.12 The Marquis of Qí asked Yànzǐ:
"How should a loyal minister serve his ruler?"
Came the reply:
"He does not die with him in calamity,
nor see him off when he goes into exile."
The ruler said:
"If I apportion land to enfeoff him,
bestow rank to honor him,
yet when the ruler faces calamity he doesn't die with him,
when the ruler goes into exile he doesn't see him off,
can this be called loyalty?"
Came the reply:
"If his advice is heeded,
the ruler will never face calamity in his lifetime,
so how would the minister die with him;
if his remonstrance is followed,
the ruler will never be exiled in his lifetime,
so how would the minister see him off.
If his advice is not heeded,
and he dies with the ruler in calamity,
this is a meaningless death;
if his remonstrance is not followed,
and he sees the ruler off into exile,
this is hypocritical behavior.
Therefore, a loyal minister is one who can impart goodness to the ruler,
but cannot join the ruler in facing calamity."
2.13 Yànzǐ was going to court,
riding in a worn-out carriage,
drawn by a feeble horse.
Duke Jǐng saw this and said:
"Alas!
Is your emolument so meager, Master?
How extremely poor your carriage is!"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Thanks to your grace,
I have been able to support my three clans and state acquaintances, all can live.
Your servant has warm clothes and sufficient food,
a worn-out carriage and a feeble horse,
to serve my person,
for your servant this is enough."
After Yànzǐ left,
the Duke sent Liángqiū Jū to give him a grand carriage and team of horses,
but after three attempts he still wouldn't accept.
The Duke was displeased.
He urgently summoned Yànzǐ.
When Yànzǐ arrived,
the Duke said:
"If you won't accept, Master,
I won't ride either."
Yànzǐ replied:
"You employ me to oversee the hundred officials,
I regulate my clothing, food, and maintenance,
to set an example for the people of Qí,
yet still fear they may become extravagant and neglect their conduct.
Now as for grand carriages and teams of horses,
if you ride them as superior,
and I also ride them as subordinate,
then when the people lack righteousness,
becoming extravagant in clothing and food while neglecting their conduct,
I would have no means to restrain them."
Thus he declined and did not accept.
2.14 Duke Jǐng was drinking,
with Chén Huánzǐ in attendance.
Catching sight of Yànzǐ,
he reported to the Duke, saying:
"I request to toast Yànzǐ."
The Duke said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"Yànzǐ wears clothes of black cloth,
a deerskin fur,
rides in a crude cart,
and drives a worn-out horse to court.
This is to conceal the gifts bestowed by the ruler."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
The cupbearer, holding a goblet, approached him,
saying:
"The ruler commands a toast to you."
Yànzǐ said:
"For what reason?"
Chén Huánzǐ said:
"The ruler bestowed upon you the ministerial rank to honor your person,
and favored you with a million to enrich your household.
Among all the ministers, none holds a rank more honored than yours,
nor a salary more generous than yours.
Yet now you wear clothes of black cloth,
a deerskin fur,
ride in a crude cart,
and drive a worn-out horse to court.
This is to conceal the gifts bestowed by the ruler,
hence the toast to you."
Yànzǐ rose from his mat and said:
"Shall I drink first and then explain,
or explain first and then drink?"
The Duke said:
"Explain first, then drink."
Yànzǐ said:
"The ruler bestowed the ministerial rank to glorify my person;
Yīng dare not accept it for glory,
but to carry out the ruler's commands.
Favored with a million,
to enrich my household,
Yīng dare not accept it for wealth,
but to disseminate the ruler's bounty.
I have heard that in ancient times, worthy rulers,
if a minister received generous gifts but neglected his state and clan,
would hold him at fault.
If, when handling affairs and keeping to his duties,
he proved incompetent,
they would hold him at fault.
If among the ruler's inner servants,
or my own father and brothers,
any were scattered in the wilds and outskirts,
this would be my fault.
Among the ruler's outer servants,
those under my charge,
if any were dispersed and lost to the four directions,
this would be my fault.
If armor and weapons were incomplete,
or war chariots not maintained,
this would be my fault.
But as for riding a worn-out cart and horse to court,
I believe it is not my fault.
Moreover, with the gifts from the ruler,
all of my father's kin have means to ride in carriages,
my mother's kin lack none in clothing and food,
my wife's kin suffer neither cold nor hunger.
Hundreds of families among the state's impoverished scholars rely on me to kindle their fires.
Is this concealing the ruler's gifts?
Or is it proclaiming the ruler's gifts?"
The Duke said:
"Well said!
Toast Wú Yǔ for me."
2.15 Yànzǐ was just eating
when the ruler's messenger arrived.
He shared his meal and fed him,
yet the messenger was not full, nor was Yànzǐ full.
The messenger returned
and reported this to Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Alas!
The master's household
is as poor as this!
I did not know;
this is my fault."
He ordered an official to deliver a district of a thousand households to Yànzǐ.
Yànzǐ bowed twice and declined,
saying:
"Yīng's household is not poor.
Through the ruler's gifts,
the bounty covers three clans,
extends to friends and companions,
and relieves the common people.
The ruler's gifts are generous indeed!
Yīng's household is not poor.
I have heard that
to take generously from the ruler
and generously bestow upon others
is to act as ruler in place of the ruler—
a loyal minister does not do this.
To take generously from the ruler and hoard it
is merely storing in boxes and chests—
a benevolent person does not do this.
To take generously from the ruler and have no way to use it,
so that upon death the wealth passes on,
a wise person does not do this.
I have also heard that for a minister,
in advancement, not serving the superior is considered loyalty,
in retreat, not overpowering the inferior is considered integrity.
Cloth of eight shēng,
food of one dòu,
is sufficient!"
The messenger returned three times,
yet he persistently declined and did not accept.
2.16 Chéng Chéngzǐ said to Chīyí Zǐpí:
"How do you compare with Cháng?"
He replied:
"If the ruler dies, I do not die;
if the ruler perishes, I do not perish."
Chéng Chéngzǐ said:
"Then how do you regard Cháng?"
He replied:
"Not yet dead, he avoids death;
not yet perished, he avoids perishing.
What death or perishing can he have?"
2.17 To follow commands that benefit the ruler is called compliance;
to follow commands that harm the ruler is called flattery;
to oppose commands that benefit the ruler is called loyalty;
to oppose commands that harm the ruler is called rebellion.
If the ruler has faults,
and one does not remonstrate or contend,
it will endanger the state
and topple the altars of land and grain.
One who can speak fully to the ruler,
staying if employed,
leaving if not,
is called an admonisher.
One who, if employed, may live,
if not employed, will die,
is called a contender.
One who can unite in wisdom and strength,
leading subordinates to firmly correct the ruler,
so that even if the ruler is uneasy,
he cannot but listen,
thereby resolving the state's great troubles,
removing the state's great harms,
achieving respect for the ruler and stability for the state,
is called a supporter.
One who can resist the ruler's commands,
reverse the ruler's actions,
take on the ruler's authority,
to secure the state in peril,
remove the disgrace of the sovereign,
so that campaigns suffice to accomplish the state's great benefits,
is called a rectifier.
Thus, those who are admonishers, contenders, supporters, and rectifiers
are ministers of the altars of land and grain.
Enlightened rulers honor and respect them,
while benighted rulers consider them their enemies.
Hence, they are rewarded by enlightened rulers
and killed by benighted ones.
Enlightened rulers delight in inquiry,
benighted rulers delight in solitude.
Enlightened rulers elevate the worthy and employ the able, enjoying their achievements;
benighted rulers fear the worthy and envy the able, destroying their works.
Punishing the loyal and rewarding the treacherous—
this is what is called extreme darkness,
the reason for the downfall of Jié and Zhòu.
The Book of Songs says:
"Thus, not heeding,
the great mandate was overturned."
This refers to this.
2.18 Jiǎnzǐ had ministers Yǐn Chuò and Shè Jué.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Jué loves me;
he admonishes me never in public.
Chuò does not love me;
he admonishes me always in public."
Yǐn Chuò said:
"Jué loves your dignity,
but not your faults;
I love your faults,
but not your dignity."
Confucius said:
"A gentleman indeed is Yǐn Chuò!
He criticizes to the face, not praises to the face."
2.19 Gāo Liáo served under Yànzǐ,
for three years without fault.
Yànzǐ expelled him,
and his attendants remonstrated, saying:
"Gāo Liáo has served you, Master, for three years,
yet without being granted any rank you expel him,
is this right in principle?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"I, Yīng,
am a man of narrow talents,
who can only be straightened by being supported from all four corners.
Now this man served me for three years,
yet never corrected my faults,
therefore I expelled him."
2.20 Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"I, Cì, know how to be subordinate to others,
but do not yet know the way to be properly subordinate."
Confucius said:
"Being subordinate to others
is like being soil, is it not?
Plant in it and the five grains grow;
dig it and sweet springs emerge;
grasses and trees take root in it;
birds and beasts are nurtured by it;
the living stand upon it;
the dead enter into it;
it accomplishes much yet never speaks.
To be subordinate to others
is indeed like being soil!"
2.21 Xúnqīng said:
"The young serve the old,
the lowly serve the noble,
the unworthy serve the worthy,
this is the universal principle of the world.
There are those who are noble yet cannot lead,
and those who are lowly yet are ashamed to be subordinate,
this is the mind of treacherous people.
If one never departs from a treacherous mind,
and one's actions never leave the path of treachery,
yet seeks to be praised by the multitude,
is that not difficult indeed!"
2.22 Gōngshū Wénzǐ asked Shǐ Qiú:
"Wǔzǐ Shèng has served Zhào Jiǎnzǐ for a long time,
yet his favor never wanes,
why is this?"
Shǐ Qiú replied:
"Wǔzǐ Shèng is widely learned and capable, yet holds a low position;
the ruler treats him intimately and keeps him close,
he responds with diligence and humility;
if treated distantly and kept at a distance,
he remains respectful without showing resentment.
When involved in state affairs at court,
he does not display his favor outside;
when the ruler bestows emoluments upon him,
knowing contentment, he declines them,
therefore he can endure long."
2.23 The "Great Oath" says:
"Those who collude with inferiors and deceive superiors shall die;
those who collude with superiors and deceive inferiors shall be punished.
Those who participate in state governance yet bring no benefit to the people shall be dismissed;
those in high positions who cannot recommend the worthy shall be expelled.
This is how to encourage good and dismiss evil."
Therefore, the Commentary says:
"Those who harm the good are the mutilators of the state;
those who obscure the good are the slanderers of the state;
those who accuse the innocent
are the villains of the state."
2.24 The "Royal Regulations" say:
"Those who use ghosts and spirits, astrological timing, and divination to mislead the people
shall be executed."
2.25 Zǐlù was magistrate of Pú,
and to prepare for floods,
he repaired ditches and canals with the people in spring.
As the people were weary and suffering,
he gave them a basket of food and a pot of soup.
Confucius heard of this,
and sent Zǐgòng to stop him.
Zǐlù was indignant and displeased,
and went to see the Master, saying:
"I, Yóu, fearing that heavy rains would come
and cause floods,
repaired ditches and canals with the people to prepare,
and as the people were lacking food,
I gave them a basket of food and a pot of soup,
yet you, Master, sent Cì to stop me,
why?
You are preventing Yóu from practicing benevolence.
You teach benevolence yet forbid its practice,
I, Yóu, cannot accept this."
Confucius said:
"If you thought the people were hungry,
why did you not report to the ruler,
to open the granaries and provide them with food,
instead of giving them your private charity?
This fails to make clear the ruler's kindness,
and only shows your own virtue and righteousness.
Stop quickly and all will be well,
otherwise, you will soon face punishment!"
Zǐlù accepted this in his heart and withdrew.
3.1 Confucius said:
"The noble person focuses on the root,
when the root is established, the Way grows."
If the root is not straight, the branches will surely be crooked;
if the beginning is not vigorous, the end will surely decline.
The Book of Songs says:
"The plains and marshes are leveled,
the springs and streams are clear."
When the root is established, the Way grows.
The principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals is that
where there is a correct spring, there will be no chaotic autumn;
where there is a correct ruler, there will be no endangered state.
The Book of Changes says:
"Establish the root and all things are ordered;
miss by a hair's breadth,
and the error will be a thousand miles."
Therefore, the noble person values establishing the root and emphasizes setting a proper beginning.
3.2 Marquis Wǔ of Wèi asked Wúzǐ about the first year of a reign,
Wúzǐ replied:
"It means the ruler must be careful about the beginning."
"How to be careful about the beginning?"
He said:
"Make it correct."
"How to make it correct?"
He said:
"Be wise and discerning.
Without wisdom and discernment, how can one be correct?
Hear much and select from it,
this is how to become wise and discerning.
Therefore, in ancient times, when a ruler began to govern,
he would listen to every word from his ministers,
grant an audience to every scholar,
ensure that every commoner's petition reached him,
speak with every inquiring member of the royal clan,
and not turn away visitors from all directions,
this can be called avoiding obstruction.
Distribute emoluments fairly,
apply punishments appropriately,
ensure the ruler's heart is benevolent,
consider the people's benefits,
and eliminate the people's harms,
this can be called not losing the people's support.
The ruler's person must be upright,
his close ministers must be selected carefully,
ministers should not hold multiple offices,
those who hold power over the people should not be from a single clan,
this can be called not monopolizing power.
These are all the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals and the root of the first year of reign."
3.3 Confucius said:
"In conducting oneself, there are six roots;
when these roots are established,
one becomes a noble person.
In establishing one's character, righteousness is essential, but filial piety is the root;
in observing mourning, ritual is essential, but grief is the root;
in battle formations, order is essential, but courage is the root;
in governing, principles are essential, but ability is the root;
in ruling a state, ritual is essential, but the heir is the root;
in cultivating talent, timing is essential, but effort is the root.
If the root is not firmly set,
do not seek to enrich the branches;
if your relatives are not pleased,
do not seek external relations;
if you cannot complete tasks,
do not take on many undertakings;
if what you hear and record is not expressed,
do not engage in much talk;
if those nearby are not pleased,
do not seek to cultivate distant ties.
Therefore, returning to the root and cultivating what is near
is the Way of the noble person."
3.4 What heaven gives birth to,
and what earth nourishes,
nothing is more precious than humans.
Among human relationships, none is greater than the affection between father and child,
and the duty between ruler and minister.
The way of the father is sageliness,
the way of the son is benevolence;
