the way of the ruler is righteousness,
the way of the minister is loyalty.
A worthy father, for his son,
nurtures him with kindness and benevolence to bring him up,
and educates him to help him mature.
He cultivates his sense of duty,
restrains his falseness,
guides him in timely moderation,
and is cautious in his discipline.
When the son is over seven years old,
the father selects for him a wise teacher,
chooses good friends for him,
preventing him from encountering evil,
gradually accustoming him to goodness from a young age,
so that he transforms early.
Thus, a worthy son in serving his parents,
in his speech and expressions,
ensures that nothing offends their ears;
in his walking and movements,
his appearance does not offend their eyes;
and in his humble posture, nothing offends their hearts.
A nobleman serves his parents to accumulate virtue.
The son is
the foundation of the parents,
and there is no command that he should not obey.
To disobey a command
is only to harm the parents.
Therefore, whatever brings comfort to the parents,
the son provides it all.
A worthy minister in serving his ruler,
from the day he accepts office,
regards the ruler as his father,
the state as his family,
and the scholars as his brothers.
Thus, if there is anything that can bring peace to the state and benefit the people,
he does not avoid its difficulties,
nor fear its toils,
to fulfill his duty.
Therefore, his ruler also assists him,
to help him achieve his virtue.
For the ruler and ministers, and the common people,
mutually serve as each other's foundation,
like an endless cycle.
The Master also said:
"No human conduct is greater than filial piety."
When filial conduct is cultivated within,
a good reputation spreads abroad.
This is called establishing it at the root,
so that glory and splendor naturally flourish.
The ruler takes the minister as his foundation,
the minister takes the ruler as his foundation,
the father takes the son as his foundation,
the son takes the father as his foundation.
Those who abandon their foundation
see their glory and splendor wither.
3.5 Zǐlù said:
"One who carries a heavy load on a long journey does not choose where to rest;
one with a poor family and elderly parents does not choose his salary when taking office.
In the past, when I served my two parents,
I often ate the fare of wild herbs,
yet carried rice for my parents from a hundred lǐ away.
After my parents passed away,
I traveled south to Chǔ,
with a hundred chariots following me,
stores of grain reaching ten thousand zhōng,
sitting on layered mats,
dining with rows of tripods.
But I wish I could return to the times of eating wild herbs and carrying rice for my parents—
that can no longer be regained.
A dried fish on a string—
how long before it is eaten by worms?
The lifespan of one's parents
passes as quickly as a glimpse through a crack.
When plants wish to grow,
frost and dew may not permit it;
when a worthy wishes to care for them,
his two parents may not wait."
Therefore it is said:
"With a poor family and elderly parents, one does not choose his salary when taking office."
3.6 Bóqín and Kāng Shū Fēng paid court to King Chéng,
and visited Zhōu Gōng,
but were caned three times after three visits.
Kāng Shū Fēng looked alarmed
and said to Bóqín:
"There is a man named Shāng Zǐ,
a worthy person;
let us go see him together."
Kāng Shū Fēng and Bóqín went to see Shāng Zǐ and said:
"We two,
recently went to court to see King Chéng,
and visited Zhōu Gōng,
but were caned three times in three visits.
What is the reason for this?"
Shāng Zǐ said:
"Why don't you two go together to see the south side of the southern mountain?
There is a tree there
called the 'qiáo'."
The two went to the south side of the southern mountain,
saw the qiáo tree,
standing tall and upright, bearing fruit and reaching upward.
They returned and reported to Shāng Zǐ.
Shāng Zǐ said:
"The qiáo tree
represents the way of the father."
Shāng Zǐ then said:
"Why don't you two go together to see the north side of the southern mountain?
There is a tree there called the 'zǐ'."
The two went to the north side of the southern mountain,
saw the zǐ tree,
lush and full, bearing fruit and bowing down.
They returned and reported to Shāng Zǐ.
Shāng Zǐ said:
"The zǐ tree
represents the way of the son."
The two,
the next day went to see Zhōu Gōng,
entered the gate and hurried in,
ascended the hall and knelt.
Zhōu Gōng stroked their heads,
comforted them and fed them,
saying:
"From whom have you learned the ways of a nobleman?"
The two replied:
"We saw Shāng Zǐ."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"A nobleman indeed
is Shāng Zǐ!"
3.7 Zēngzǐ was weeding melons and accidentally cut their roots.
Zēngxī, in anger,
took a large stick and struck him,
and Zēngzǐ fell to the ground.
After a while he revived,
sprang up suddenly,
and came forward saying:
"Earlier, Shēn offended you, father.
In using your strength to teach Shēn,
I hope you have not been harmed?"
Then he withdrew, screened himself, played the qín and sang,
wishing to let Zēngxī hear his singing,
to show he was calm and well.
Confucius heard of this
and told his disciples:
"When Shēn comes,
do not admit him."
Zēngzǐ, thinking himself innocent,
sent someone to ask Confucius why.
Confucius said:
"Have you not heard that Gǔsǒu had a son named Shùn?
When Shùn served his father,
if sought for work,
he was always at his side;
but if sought to be killed,
he was never to be found.
For a light beating he would stay,
for a heavy beating he would flee,
to escape the violent rage.
Now you offered yourself to await the violent rage,
standing still without leaving,
risking death to plunge your father into unrighteousness—
what lack of filial piety is greater than this?
Are you not a subject of the Son of Heaven?
To kill a subject of the Son of Heaven—
what crime would that be?"
With Zēngzǐ's ability,
and being a disciple in Confucius' school,
yet not realizing his own fault—
how difficult it is to dwell in righteousness!
3.8 Hán Bóyú committed a fault,
and his mother caned him.
He wept,
and his mother asked,
"In the past when I caned you,
I never saw you weep.
Why are you weeping now?"
He replied,
"In the past when Yú committed offenses,
the caning used to be painful.
Now mother's strength has declined,
and the caning no longer causes pain,
that is why I weep."
Therefore it is said:
When parents are angry with you,
do not take it to heart,
do not show it in your expression,
deeply accept their punishment,
and make yourself worthy of their compassion and pity—
this is the highest level;
when parents are angry with you,
do not take it to heart,
do not show it in your expression—
this is the next level;
when parents are angry with you,
take it to heart,
and show it in your expression—
this is the lowest level.
3.9 When adults have virtue,
and youths have accomplishments,
this is the teaching of the Great Learning.
To prohibit at the time before it occurs is called prevention,
to act when it is appropriate is called timeliness,
to observe each other in goodness is called polishing,
to teach without overstepping the proper sequence is called gradual instruction.
To prohibit only after it has occurred,
then there will be resistance and it cannot be overcome;
to learn only after the time has passed,
then it will be laborious and difficult to achieve;
to teach in a mixed and disorderly manner without sequence,
then it will be ruined and chaotic beyond management;
to study alone without friends,
then one will be isolated, ignorant, and poorly informed.
Therefore it is said:
There is brilliance in the Pìyōng,
there is worthiness in the Pàngōng,
in the fields and villages throughout the land,
multitudes move in harmony,
gathering to present gifts as pledges,
and there are groups for cultural refinement.
3.10 Zhōu Shàogōng at nineteen years of age,
having shown correctness was capped,
and once capped could become a regional lord or feudal prince.
During the time of human infancy and childish ignorance,
without seeking teachers to correct fundamentals,
there is no means to establish oneself and preserve one's nature.
The young are necessarily ignorant,
the ignorant act recklessly;
the ignorant acting recklessly,
cannot preserve themselves.
Mèngzǐ said:
"People all know to use food to cure hunger,
but none know to use learning to cure ignorance."
Therefore those with good material in their youth,
must be diligent in study and inquiry,
to cultivate their nature.
If people today could truly temper their talents,
make sincere their spirit and intelligence,
perceive the responses of things,
penetrate the essentials of the Way,
observe the beginnings and ends of affairs,
survey the realm without exterior,
wander freely within the boundless,
roam beyond the dust of the world,
standing eminent and independent,
transcending and leaving behind the worldly,
this is where the highest sages let their spirits travel.
However, people of recent ages,
cannot dwell in leisure with thoughtful minds,
playing the qin and reading books,
contemplating antiquity,
befriending worthy scholars,
studying, inquiring, discussing, and debating,
daily thereby finding contentment.
Keeping distant from worldly affairs,
clearly distinguishing benefit and harm,
calculating gain and loss,
to observe fortune and misfortune.
Establishing righteousness and setting standards,
to serve as models and patterns,
exhaustively tracing roots and branches,
investigating the actual circumstances of affairs,
having a legacy after death,
and honor and fame during life,
these are all achievements that human talent can build.
Yet the reason none can accomplish them,
is stealing leisure, laziness, and懈怠,
having too many idle days.
Therefore they lose the foundation and have no fame.
Learning,
is the foundation for establishing reputation and personhood.
With appearance and form equal,
those who adorn their looks are pleasing;
with innate nature and quality alike,
those who study and inquire are wise.
Thus grinding, whetting, carving, and polishing are not metal,
yet can sharpen metal;
the Shī and Shū standing apart,
are not myself,
yet can sharpen the mind.
Those who inquire and seek knowledge,
rising day and night,
sharpen their inner selves and increase wisdom to distinguish principles.
Therefore they preserve their persons completely,
and establish themselves without peril,
if scholars desire to deeply understand and broadly examine to leave a glorious name,
yet do not love the way of inquiry and seeking,
then they are cutting off the root of wisdom and blocking the source of intelligence,
how can they establish their person!
Though the qíjì is swift,
without meeting Bólè,
it cannot reach a thousand lǐ;
though the Gānjiàng is sharp,
without human strength it cannot cut by itself;
though the Wūháo bow is excellent,
without a bow frame,
it cannot string itself,
though human talent is high,
without pursuing study and inquiry,
it cannot reach sagehood.
Water accumulates to form rivers,
then jiāolóng are born there;
earth accumulates to form mountains,
then yùzhāng trees grow there;
learning accumulates to form sagehood,
then wealth, honor, dignity, and eminence arrive.
A fur robe worth a thousand gold,
is not made from one fox's pelt;
the rafters of towers and temples,
are not from one tree's branches;
the laws of the former kings,
are not from one scholar's wisdom.
Therefore it is said:
Inquiry is the root of wisdom,
reflection and consideration are the path of wisdom.
The Zhōngyōng says:
"Loving inquiry is close to wisdom,
diligent practice is close to benevolence,
knowing shame is close to courage."
Accumulating the small to achieve the great,
is this not only true of Zhòngní!
Learning is that by which one returns to one's nature, governs one's character, and exhausts one's talents.
Drawing near to the worthy and pursuing learning,
is how one cultivates virtue;
discussing and forming friendships,
is how one mutually reaches [improvement].
The Shī says:
"Like cutting, like filing,
like carving, like polishing."
This refers to this.
3.11 Now, to clear land and grow grains
for sustaining life and conducting funerals,
to refine metals and minerals and mix herbs to cure illnesses and pains,
to know how to build houses to shelter from heat and rain,
and to erect towers and pavilions to avoid dampness.
At home, they know to be affectionate to their parents;
in public, they know to honor their ruler;
internally, there is distinction between men and women;
externally, there are bonds of friendship.
This is the virtuous teaching of the sages.
The Confucians received and transmitted it,
to educate and instruct later generations.
But now, the wicked people of recent times
instead criticize the Confucians,
saying:
"What use are the Confucians?"
Such people
do not understand the foundation.
They are like those who eat grains and wear silk,
yet disparage farming and weaving;
those who ride on boats and carriages,
use and enjoy them,
yet disparage the craftsmen;
those who eat from pots and steamers,
relying on them for livelihood,
yet disparage the potters and founders.
This means their words contradict reality and their actions are blind at heart.
Such people,
do not cherish their own flesh and blood,
nor befriend the talented scholars,
they are the outcasts of the Three Dynasties,
and are not pardoned by the rulers.
Therefore, the *Book of Songs* says:
"Throw them to the jackals and tigers;
the jackals and tigers will not eat them.
Throw them to the barren north;
the barren north will not accept them.
Throw them to the vast heavens."
This refers to them.
3.12 Mèngzǐ said:
"People know to manure their fields,
but do not know to manure their minds."
Manuring the fields is nothing more than benefiting the sprouts to gain grain;
manuring the mind means changing one's conduct,
and attaining what one desires.
What is manuring the mind?
Broad learning and extensive knowledge;
what is changing conduct?
Cultivating one's nature and curbing excess.
3.13 Zǐsī said:
"Learning is what enhances talent;
whetting is what sharpens the blade.
I have once secluded myself and pondered deeply,
but it is not as swift as learning;
I have once stood on tiptoe to see afar,
but it is not as broad as climbing high for a wide view.
Hence, calling out with the wind,
the voice does not become louder, yet many hear it;
waving from a hilltop,
the arm does not grow longer, yet it is seen from afar."
Thus, fish rely on water,
birds rely on the wind,
plants and trees rely on the season.
3.14 Confucius said:
"That which one can engage in all day without tiring,
is it not only learning!
One's physique is not worth admiring,
one's courage and strength are not worth fearing,
one's ancestors are not worth praising,
one's clan and surname are not worth mentioning,
yet what can make one known throughout the land and illustrious among the feudal lords,
is it not only learning!
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Without error, without forgetfulness,
following the old statutes.'
This refers to learning."
3.15 Confucius said:
"Lǐ,
a gentleman must not fail to learn,
and when meeting others, must not fail to cultivate appearance.
Without cultivation, there is no foundation;
without foundation, one loses principle;
losing principle, one lacks loyalty;
lacking loyalty, one loses propriety;
losing propriety, one cannot stand firm.
That which shines from afar,
is cultivation;
that which grows brighter up close,
is learning.
It is like a stagnant pond:
rainwater pours into it,
reeds and rushes grow in it,
but looking from above,
one knows it has no source."
3.16 Gōnghùzǐ said:
"Those who rule a state must not fail to study the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Those born into nobility
become arrogant;
those born into wealth
become proud.
Born into wealth and nobility,
yet without a mirror and self-satisfied,
few avoid ruin!
The *Spring and Autumn Annals*
is the mirror for the state.
In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
there are thirty-six regicides,
fifty-two fallen states,
feudal lords fleeing,
unable to preserve their altars of soil and grain—many such cases,
and none did not first see the signs and then follow the path."
3.17 Jìn Pínggōng asked Shī Kuàng:
"I am seventy years old,
and wish to learn, but fear it is too late."
Shī Kuàng said:
"If it is late,
why not light a torch?"
Pínggōng said:
"How can a subject jest with his ruler?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"How would a blind minister dare jest with his ruler?
I have heard that
to learn when young
is like the sun at dawn;
to learn in prime years
is like the sun at noon;
to learn when old
is like the light of a torch;
to be old and not learn
is like groping in the dark at night.
The brightness of a torch—
is it not better than walking in darkness?"
Pínggōng said:
"Well said!"
3.18 Héjiān Xiànwáng said:
"Tāng said that those who learn the way of the sage kings
are like the sun;
to dwell quietly in solitary thought
is like a fire.
To abandon learning the way of the sage kings
is like forsaking the sunlight;
how can solitary thought alone,
like the light of a fire,
only reveal the small,
and not apply great wisdom?
Only learning can broaden and illuminate virtue and wisdom."
3.19 Liángqiū Jù said to Yànzǐ:
"I will never catch up to you, Master, even till death!"
Yànzǐ said:
"I have heard:
those who act often succeed;
those who walk often arrive.
I am no different from others,
but I constantly act without ceasing,
constantly walk without resting,
hence it is hard to catch up."
3.20 Nìng Yuè
was a humble man from Zhōngmóu,
who suffered the toil of farming,
and said to his friend:
"What can I do to escape this hardship?"
His friend said:
"Nothing beats learning;
study for thirty years, and you may achieve success."
Nìng Yuè said:
"I will do it in fifteen years.
When others rest,
I will not dare to rest;
when others sleep,
I will not dare to sleep."
After fifteen years of study, he became the teacher of Zhōu Wēigōng.
Now, a runner may be fast,
but stops after two *lǐ*;
a walker may be slow,
but does not stop even after a hundred *lǐ*.
With Nìng Yuè's talent and long perseverance,
becoming a teacher to feudal lords—
is it not fitting indeed!
3.21 Confucius said to Zǐlù:
"What do you love?"
Zǐlù said:
"I love long swords."
Confucius said:
"That is not what I meant.
I meant that if you apply learning to your existing abilities,
how could anyone surpass you?"
Zǐlù said:
"Is learning really beneficial?"
Confucius said:
"A ruler without remonstrating ministers will misgovern;
a scholar without instructive friends will mishear.
To rein a wild horse, one does not drop the whip;
to handle a bow, one does not discard the straightener.
Wood marked with the ink-line becomes straight;
a person who accepts advice becomes sage.
Receive learning and value questioning—
who would not then succeed smoothly?
To slander benevolence and detest scholars
is to approach punishment.
A gentleman cannot but learn."
Zǐlù said:
"The bamboo on the southern mountain
grows straight without bending—
cut it and shoot with it,
it penetrates rhinoceros hide.
So what need is there for learning?"
Confucius said:
"If you add feathers to its end,
sharpen its tip to a point,
would it not penetrate even deeper?"
Zǐlù bowed twice and said:
"I reverently accept your teaching!"
3.22 Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"May I set aside ancient learning
and act according to my own ideas,
is that acceptable?"
Confucius said:
"It is not.
Once a man of the Eastern Yí admired the customs of Zhūxià;
when his daughter
was widowed,
he arranged for her a secret husband,
so she never remarried.
Though she never remarried,
this was not the meaning of chastity.
A man of Cāngwú,
having married a beautiful wife,
offered to exchange her with his elder brother.
Loyal though it was,
it was improper.
Now you wish to discard ancient learning and follow your own ideas—
how can you know your ideas won't mistake wrong for right and right for wrong?
If you stray from the proper beginning,
though you may wish to regret it later,
it will be difficult!"
3.23 A wall thick but with weak foundations
may not collapse immediately,
but when floods come,
it will be the first to crumble;
a tree with shallow planting,
roots not deep-set,
may not fall immediately,
but when gales rise
and torrential rain comes,
it will be the first to be uprooted.
A gentleman dwelling in a state
that does not exalt benevolence and righteousness,
nor honor worthy ministers,
may not perish immediately,
but once extraordinary changes occur,
with chariots racing and people fleeing,
pointing as disaster arrives,
only then does he fret, throat dry and lips parched,
gazing heavenward with sighs,
hoping perhaps Heaven might save him—
is that not too late?
Confucius said:
"If one is not cautious beforehand,
but regrets afterward,
even regret cannot help."
The Book of Songs says:
"Now he sobs and weeps,
but what can sighing avail?"
This means not first rectifying the root but allowing anxiety about the branches.
3.24 Lord Yú asked Péng Chéngzǐ:
saying,
"Artisans improve with time and practice,
but beauty fades with age.
If one does not, in youth,
accumulate skills of mind and art
to prepare for fading beauty,
since beauty must end before old age,
and wisdom does not differ from childhood,
then when desirable looks,
so elegant and fine, are nearly gone,
how shall the incapable body find support?"
Thus, one with skills
does not burden the body yet never diminishes,
while beauty cannot remain forever lush."
3.25 Duke Huán of Qí asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What should a king value most?"
He replied:
"He should value Heaven."
The duke looked up at the sky.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The Heaven I speak of
is not the vast blue sky.
A ruler of people
should take the common people as Heaven.
If the people support him, there is peace;
if they assist him, there is strength;
if they oppose him, there is danger;
if they betray him, there is ruin."
The Book of Songs says:
"If a man is unvirtuous,
others resent him from all sides."
When the people resent their superiors,
and the state does not proceed to ruin,
such a thing has never occurred.
3.26 Xiànwáng of Héjiān said:
"Guǎnzǐ stated, 'When granaries are full,
people know礼节;
when food and clothing are sufficient,
people know honor and disgrace.'
Grain is that by which
the state thrives,
men and women remain fair,
ritual and righteousness are practiced,
and people's hearts are put at ease.
The Shàngshū lists five blessings, beginning with wealth.
When Zǐgòng asked about governance,
Confucius said:
'Enrich them.'
Only after they are rich
should they be educated.
This is the foundation of governing a state."
3.27 Duke Wén met Jiù Jì,
whose ancestral temple leaned against the western wall.
The duke asked:
"Who lives to the west?"
He replied:
"Your aged minister."
The duke said:
"I will expand your residence westward."
He replied:
"My loyalty
is not as strong as the old minister's efforts—
his wall collapsed, yet he did not rebuild it."
The duke asked:
"Why did he not rebuild it?"
He replied:
"One day without sowing
means a hundred days without food."
The duke went out and told his attendant.
The attendant bowed his head to the carriage rail and said:
"The Lǚxíng states:
'If one man does good,
millions rely on him.'
Your enlightenment,
is the blessing of all ministers."
Thereupon he decreed throughout the state:
"Do not build excessive palaces
that encroach on people's homes;
construct walls in due season,
do not disrupt farming work."
3.28 King Gōng of Chǔ had many favored sons,
and the position of crown prince was unsettled.
Qū Jiàn said:
"Chǔ will surely face much turmoil.
When a single hare runs through the streets,
thousands chase after it,
but once one person catches it,
the thousands will no longer run.
When shares are undetermined,
one hare running
causes thousands to be disturbed;
when shares are settled,
even the greedy know to stop.
Now Chǔ has many favored sons,
and the legitimate position has no master,
turmoil naturally arises from this.
The crown prince
is the foundation of the state,
and the hope of the common people.
The state being without foundation,
and causing the people to lose hope,
severs its root.
Once the root is severed, there is disruption and chaos,
just like the running hare."
King Gōng heard this,
and established King Kāng as crown prince.
Later, there still were the rebellions of Prime Minister Wéi and Prince Qìjí.
3.29 When Duke Xiāng of Jìn passed away,
the heir was young,
and Zhào Xuānzǐ served as regent.
He said to the high officials:
"Establishing a young lord
risks many troubles,
I propose we establish Yōng.
Yōng is older,
and is in Qín,
which is a great state,
sufficient to be our support."
Jiǎ Jì said:
"Better to choose Prince Lè,
who is favored in the state,
the late lord loved him and had him serve in Dí,
and Dí is sufficient to be our support."
Mù Yíng held the crown prince and cried out in the court:
"What crime did the late lord commit?
What crime did his heir commit?
You abandon the legitimate heir not to establish him,
and seek a lord from outside?"
She left the court,
holding him to see Xuānzǐ,
saying:
"You fear troubles,
hence wish to establish an older lord,
but once the older lord is established and the young lord grows up,
troubles will surely come."
Xuānzǐ was troubled by this,
and thus established the crown prince.
3.30 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ appointed Xiāngzǐ as his successor,
Dǒng Ānyú said:
"Wúxù is untalented,
now you appoint him as successor,
why?"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"This man, in his character, can endure humiliation for the state."
Another day,
Zhì Bó drank with Xiāngzǐ and poured wine over Xiāngzǐ's head,
the officials requested to kill him.
Xiāngzǐ said:
"When the late lord established me,
he said 'he can endure humiliation for the state',
did he say 'he can stab people'?"
After ten months,
Zhì Bó besieged Xiāngzǐ in Jìnyáng,
Xiāngzǐ divided his troops and attacked him,
greatly defeating Zhì Bó,
and lacquered his head to make a drinking vessel.
4.1 For scholars and gentlemen who have courage and act decisively,
if they do not use it to establish integrity and uphold righteousness,
but to die recklessly for an unworthy cause,
is it not grievous!
There are scholars who sacrifice their lives to achieve benevolence,
face harm to establish righteousness,
relying on principle and reason without avoiding mortal danger,
thus able to have their names passed down through the ages after death,
without courage and resolve,
who can accomplish this?
4.2 Zǐlù said:
"If one cannot endure hardship and toil,
cannot be content in poverty,
cannot lightly face death,
yet says 'I can practice righteousness',
I do not believe it."
In the past, Shēn Bāoxū stood in the court of Qín for seven days and seven nights,
weeping without ceasing,
and thus saved Chǔ;
if one cannot endure toil,
how can one accomplish this?
Zēngzǐ, in coarse clothes and worn-out robes, not yet whole,
with chaff for food, wild greens for soup, not yet full,
if righteousness did not accord, he would decline the position of high minister;
if not content in poverty,
how can one accomplish this?
Bǐgān, facing death, remonstrated even more loyally,
Bóyí and Shūqí starved to death at Shǒuyáng yet their will shone even brighter;
if one does not lightly face death,
how can one accomplish this?
Therefore, for scholars wishing to establish righteousness and practice the Way,
they must not consider difficulty or ease before acting;
to establish themselves and make their names known,
they must not consider advantage or harm before achieving it.
The Book of Songs says:
"That man,
is great and sincere."
If not a good, sincere, and intensely cultivated gentleman,
who can accomplish this?
4.3 Prince Bǐgān sacrificed his life to fulfill his loyalty,
Wěi Shēng sacrificed his life to fulfill his trustworthiness,
Bóyí and Shūqí sacrificed their lives to fulfill their integrity,
these four men,
were all renowned scholars of the world,
did they not love their own lives?
They believed that if righteousness was not established,
and their names not made known,
it would be a scholar's shame,
hence they sacrificed their lives to fulfill their conduct.
From this perspective,
low status and poverty,
are not a scholar's shame.
What scholars consider shameful
is when the world praises loyalty and the scholar is not among them,
praises trustworthiness and the scholar is not among them,
praises integrity and the scholar is not among them.
If these three are embodied in the person,
their name is passed down to later ages,
standing with the sun and moon without ceasing,
even in an age without the Way,
it cannot be tarnished.
However, this does not mean they love death and hate life,
nor that they despise wealth and honor and delight in poverty and low status.
Following the right path,
adhering to principle,
when honor and wealth come to them,
scholars do not refuse it.
Confucius said:
"If wealth were attainable,
even as a lowly official,
I would do it;
if wealth is not attainable,
I follow what I love."
This is the conduct of the great sage.
The Book of Songs says:
"My heart is not a stone,
it cannot be rolled away;
my heart is not a mat,
it cannot be rolled up."
This means not losing oneself.
Only by not losing oneself,
can one then overcome difficulties.
This is how scholars and gentlemen surpass the multitude.
4.4 Chǔ attacked Chén,
the west gate of Chén was burned,
and they made the surrendered people repair it.
Confucius passed by,
and did not bow from his carriage.
Zǐlù said:
"According to ritual,
passing three people, one dismounts,
passing two people, one bows from the carriage;
now those repairing the gate of Chén are numerous,
why does the Master not bow?"
Confucius said:
"I have heard,
if a state falls and one does not know, it is unwise;
if one knows but does not contend, it is disloyal;
if one is loyal but does not die for it, it is lacking integrity.
Now those repairing the gate of Chén cannot fulfill even one of these,
hence I do not bow for them."
4.5 Confucius visited Duke Jǐng of Qí,
Duke Jǐng offered him Lǐnqiū for his sustenance.
Confucius declined and did not accept,
and upon leaving said to his disciples:
"I have heard that a gentleman should receive emolument according to his achievements,
now I advised Duke Jǐng,
Duke Jǐng has not put it into practice,
yet bestows upon me Lǐnqiū,
his lack of understanding of me is indeed profound."
Thereupon he declined and left.
4.6 Zēngzǐ wore tattered clothes while farming.
The ruler of Lǔ sent someone to present him with a fief,
saying:
"Please use this to mend your clothes."
Zēngzǐ did not accept it.
The messenger went back and forth repeatedly,
but he still would not accept it.
The messenger said:
"You did not ask anyone for it,
someone offered it to you,
why do you not accept?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"I have heard that
those who accept gifts fear the giver,
while those who give become arrogant.
Even if you give without arrogance,
how could I not fear?"
He ultimately did not accept it.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"Zēng Shēn's words
are sufficient to preserve his integrity."
4.7 Zǐsī lived in Wèi,
wearing a padded gown without an outer layer,
eating only nine times in twenty days.
Tián Zǐfāng heard of this,
and sent someone to bring him a fox-fur coat,
fearing he would not accept it,
so he told him:
"I lend to others,
then forget about it;
I give to others,
as if discarding it."
Zǐsī declined and did not accept.
Zǐfāng said:
"I have, you have not,
why do you not accept?"
Zǐsī said:
"I have heard that
to give recklessly is no better than discarding things in a ditch;
though I am poor,
I cannot bear to make myself a ditch,
therefore I dare not accept."
4.8 Duke Xiāng of Sòng, Zīfù, was Crown Prince of Duke Huán.
Duke Huán had a younger son by a later wife named Mùyí,
whom the duke loved.
Zīfù, because the duke loved him,
wished to establish him as heir,
and requested of the duke:
"Please let Mùyí be established,
I will serve as his minister and assist him."
The duke said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"My maternal uncle is in Wèi,
and loves me.
If I am finally established, I cannot go there,
cutting off ties with Wèi,
which would be to betray my mother.
Moreover, I know I am not fit to be above Mùyí."
The duke did not consent.
He insisted in requesting the duke,
and the duke consented,
preparing to establish Mùyí.
Mùyí declined, saying:
"For the elder brother to be established and the younger below,
that is right;
now for the younger to be established and the elder below,
is not right.
If it is not right and you make me do it,
I will flee."
So he fled to Wèi,
and Zīfù followed him.
After three years,
Duke Huán fell ill,
and sent someone to summon Zīfù,
saying:
"If you do not come,
you will make me die of worry."
Zīfù then returned,
and the duke re-established him as crown prince,
after which Mùyí returned.
4.9 In Jìn, Lí Jī slandered Crown Prince Shēnshēng to Duke Xiàn,
and Duke Xiàn intended to kill him.
Prince Chóng'ěr said to Shēnshēng:
"For this matter,
it is not your fault.
Why do you not present your case?
If you do,
you will surely be cleared of blame."
Shēnshēng said:
"No.
If I plead my case,
Lí Jī will certainly be found guilty.
Our lord is old;
without Lí Jī, he cannot sleep peacefully at night,
nor enjoy his food.
How can I let our lord end his days in regret!"
Chóng'ěr said:
"If you do not plead,
then you should leave quickly."
Shēnshēng said:
"No.
To leave and avoid death
is to hate our lord.
To expose my father's faults
and gain praise among the feudal lords,
who would accept me?
At home, I would be trapped by my clan,
abroad, trapped by flight,
thus doubling my disgrace.
I have heard that
loyalty does not expose the ruler,
wisdom does not compound faults,
courage does not flee from death.
In this situation,
I will bear it with my life."
Then he fell on his sword and died.
A gentleman heard of it and said:
"It was Heaven's will, alas,
for the crown prince!"
The Book of Songs says:
"Luxuriant and bright,
they form this shell-patterned brocade.
Those slanderers,
have gone too far indeed."
4.10 During the time of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
there was an officer named Hú Tū,
who tutored Crown Prince Shēnshēng.
The duke established Lí Jī as his consort,
and the state was full of troubles.
Hú Tū claimed illness and did not appear at court.
After six years,
Duke Xiàn had the crown prince executed due to slander.
As the crown prince was about to die,
he sent a message to Hú Tū:
"Our lord is old,
and the state faces many difficulties.
If you, my tutor, would come forth to assist our lord,
I would die grateful and without regret."
He bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and died.
Hú Tū then resumed serving Duke Xiàn.
Three years later,
Duke Xiàn died,
and Hú Tū took leave of the high officials, saying:
"I received the crown prince's charge,
now my duty is done.
Rather than living long in this chaotic world,
I would rather die to repay the crown prince."
Then he returned home and took his own life.
4.11 King Píng of Chǔ sent Fèn Yáng to kill Crown Prince Jiàn,
but before he arrived, he had him warned, and
the crown prince fled to Sòng.
The king summoned Fèn Yáng,
who had the people of Chéngfù arrest him and bring him before the king.
The king said:
"The words came from my mouth,
entered your ears,
who warned Jiàn?"
He replied:
"I warned him.
Your Majesty initially commanded me:
'Serve Jiàn as you serve me.'
I, unworthy,
could not be disloyal.
Holding to your initial command,
I warned him.
Later I regretted it,
but it was too late."
The king said:
"How dare you come,
why?"
He replied:
"To be sent and fail in my mission,
then summoned and not come,
would be a double offense.
There is nowhere to flee."
The king then pardoned him.
4.12 Duke Líng of Jìn was tyrannical.
Zhào Xuānzǐ repeatedly remonstrated with him,
causing Duke Líng to resent it.
He sent Chú Zhīmí to assassinate him.
When Chú Zhīmí went early in the morning,
the bedroom door was already open.
Xuānzǐ, fully dressed for court,
found it still early,
so he sat and dozed off.
Chú Zhīmí withdrew,
sighed, and said:
"He does not forget to be reverent—
he is the pillar of the people!
To assassinate the people's pillar
is disloyalty;
to abandon the ruler's command
is untrustworthiness.
To have either of these faults,
it is better to die!"
Thereupon, he dashed his head against a locust tree and died.
4.13 There was a man of Qí named Zǐ Lánzǐ
who served Bái Gōng Shèng.
When Shèng was about to start a rebellion,
he told Zǐ Lánzǐ:
"I will undertake a great endeavor in the state,
and I wish to share it with you."
Zǐ Lánzǐ said:
"If I serve you and join you in killing the ruler,
that would be aiding you in your unrighteousness;
if I fear disaster and leave you,
that would be deserting you in your distress.
Therefore, I will not join you in killing the ruler,
to fulfill my righteousness.
I will sever my neck in the courtyard,
to carry out my resolve."
4.14 There was a scholar in Chǔ named Shēn Míng
who stayed at home to care for his father,
and his filial piety was renowned throughout Chǔ.
The king wished to appoint him as prime minister,
but Shēn Míng declined and would not accept.
His father said:
"The king wishes to make you prime minister;
why do you refuse?"
Shēn Míng replied:
"To abandon being a filial son to my father and become a loyal minister to the king—
why should I?"
His father said:
"If you receive a salary from the state
and hold a position at court,
you will be happy and I will have no worries.
I want you to be prime minister."
Shēn Míng said:
"Very well."
Thereupon, he entered the court,
and the king of Chǔ appointed him prime minister.
After three years,
Bái Gōng rebelled,
killing Prime Minister Zǐ Xī and Minister of War Zǐ Qī.
Shēn Míng prepared to go and die in the conflict.
His father stopped him, saying:
"To abandon your father and die—
is that acceptable?"
Shēn Míng said:
"I have heard that those who serve in office
give their person to the ruler and their salary to their parents.
Now that I have left you to serve the ruler,
should I not die in his crisis?"
So he took his leave and went,
leading troops to surround the rebels.
Bái Gōng said to Shí Qǐ:
"Shēn Míng
is a warrior of the realm.
Now he leads troops to surround me—
what should I do?"
Shí Qǐ said:
"Shēn Míng
is a filial son of the realm.
Go and seize his father with armed force.
When Shēn Míng hears of it, he will surely come,
and then you can speak with him."
Bái Gōng said:
"Good."
So he went and captured his father,
holding him at weapon point,
and sent a message to Shēn Míng:
"If you join me,
I will share the state of Chǔ with you;
if you do not join me,
your father will die."
Shēn Míng wept and replied:
"Once I was a filial son to my father;
now I am a loyal minister to my ruler.
I have heard that
he who eats another's food should die for his affairs,
and he who receives another's salary should exhaust his abilities.
Now I can no longer be a filial son to my father,
but must be a loyal minister to my ruler.
How can I preserve both?"
Seizing a drumstick, he beat the drum,
and eventually killed Bái Gōng,
but his father also died.
The king rewarded him with a hundred jīn of gold.
Shēn Míng said:
"To eat the ruler's food
and avoid the ruler's calamity
is not loyalty;
to secure the ruler's state
and cause one's father's death
is not filial piety.
These names cannot stand together,
and these deeds cannot be fully accomplished.
To live on like this—
what face have I to stand under heaven?"
Thereupon, he committed suicide.
4.15 Duke Zhuāng of Qí was about to attack Jǔ
and had guests in five chariots,
but Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu alone were not included,
so they returned home and refused to eat.
Their mother said:
"If you live without righteousness
and die without fame,
then even with five chariots,
who would not laugh at you?
If you live with righteousness
and die with fame,
then the guests of the five chariots
will all be beneath you."
Urged to eat, they then set out.
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu rode in the same chariot,
attending Duke Zhuāng as they advanced to Jǔ.
The people of Jǔ came out to meet them.
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu descended to fight,
and took three hundred armored heads.
Duke Zhuāng stopped them, saying:
"Stop now,
and I will share the state of Qí with you."
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu said:
"When you had guests in five chariots,
and Zhōu and Liáng were not included,
that was belittling our courage;
now, facing the enemy and in the midst of hardship,
you stop us with profit—
that is sullying our conduct.
To press deep and kill many
is our duty as ministers.
The benefit to Qí
is not our concern."
So they pressed forward to fight,
breaking the enemy lines and charging through formations,
until the three armies dared not oppose them.
When they reached the walls of Jǔ,
the people of Jǔ placed charcoal on the ground.
The two stood for a while,
unable to advance.
Xí Hóu Zhòng, who was the chariot right, said:
"I have heard that ancient warriors facing perils and difficulties
would remove obstacles with objects.
Come,
I will help you cross."
Xí Hóu Zhòng used his shield to lie upon the charcoal,
and the two crossed over him and entered,
looking back and weeping for him.
Huá Zhōu was the last to catch his breath,
and Qǐ Liáng said:
"Are you without courage?
Why do you weep so long?"
Huá Zhōu said:
"How could I be without courage!
It is that his courage was equal to mine,
yet he died before me—
that is why I grieve."
The people of Jǔ said:
"Do not die;
we will share the state of Jǔ with you."
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu said:
"To abandon our state and join the enemy
is not loyalty;
to leave our superiors and accept rewards
is not righteous conduct.
Moreover, we agreed at cockcrow,
but by midday you forgot—
that is not trustworthiness.
To press deep and kill many
is our duty as ministers.
The benefit to Jǔ
is not our concern."
So they pressed forward to fight,
killing twenty-seven men before they died.
When Qǐ Liáng's wife heard of it and wept,
the wall collapsed and the corner crumbled.
This is not how it began.
4.16 When the Yuè army reached Qí,
Yōngménzǐ Dí requested to die for it.
The King of Qí said:
"The sound of war drums has not yet been heard,
arrows and stones have not been exchanged,
long weapons have not crossed,
why do you insist on dying?
Is this the ritual for a subject?"
Yōngménzǐ Dí replied:
"I have heard that
in the past, the former king was hunting in the park,
the left hub made noise,
the chariot right requested to die for it,
and the king said:
'Why do you die?'
The chariot right replied:
'Because it made noise before my lord.'
The king said:
'The left hub making noise
is the fault of the craftsman.
What business is it of yours?'
The chariot right replied:
'I did not witness the craftsman's work,
but I witnessed it making noise before my lord.'
Then he cut his throat and died.
Did this happen?"
The King of Qí said:
"It did."
Yōngménzǐ Dí said:
"Now the Yuè army has arrived,
its clamor reaches my lord,
is it any less than that under the left hub?
If the chariot right could die for the left hub,
why can I alone not die for the Yuè army?"
Then he cut his throat and died.
That day,
the Yuè people withdrew their army seventy li,
saying:
"If the King of Qí has ministers all equal to Yōngménzǐ Dí,
they will cause the Yuè state to cease its sacrifices."
Then they led their army back.
The King of Qí buried Yōngménzǐ Dí with the rites of a high minister.
4.17 The Chǔ people were about to battle the Wú people,
the Chǔ troops were few while the Wú troops were numerous.
The Chǔ general Zǐ Náng said:
"If we attack this state, we will surely be defeated,
shaming our ruler and losing territory,
a loyal minister cannot bear to do this."
Without reporting back to the ruler,
he withdrew his troops and retreated.
When he reached the outskirts of the capital,
he sent someone to report to the ruler:
"I request to die."
The ruler said:
"Your retreat, great officer,
was for the sake of advantage,
and now it is indeed advantageous,
so do not die, great officer."
Zǐ Náng said:
"If those who retreat are without fault,
then rulers and ministers in later generations
will all adopt the reputation of disadvantage and imitate my retreat.
If so, then Chǔ will ultimately be weakened by the world.
I request to die."
He withdrew and fell on his sword.
The ruler said:
"If it is truly so,
I ask to fulfill the great officer's righteousness."
Then he had a tong wood coffin three inches thick made,
placed an axe and execution block upon it,
and paraded it through the state.
4.18 Sòng Kānggōng attacked Ā,
massacring Dānfù.
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"Before, I did not know myself,
thinking that with a thousand chariots, even ten thousand chariots would not dare attack;
with ten thousand chariots, the world would not dare scheme against me.
Now I am in Ā,
yet Sòng massacres Dānfù,
this means I have no means to stand firm.
I shall go and execute the King of Sòng."
Zhào then entered Sòng,
but for three months could not get an audience.
Someone said:
"Why not use an envoy from a neighboring state to see him?"
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"No,
if I use a neighboring state's envoy to assassinate him,
then envoys in later times will not be trusted,
the trust of bearing credentials will not be used,
and all will say:
'Zhào made it so.'
It cannot be."
Someone said:
"Why not use ministers to introduce a wandering scholar to assassinate him?"
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"No,
if I use ministers to introduce a wandering scholar to assassinate him,
then loyal ministers in later times will not be trusted,
persuasive scholars will not be considered,
and all will say:
'Zhào made it so.'
It cannot be.
I have heard that scholars of old,
when angered, would think of principle,
in danger would not forget righteousness,
and would certainly seek it through upright conduct."
After a year,
Sòng Kānggōng died of illness.
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"An incorruptible scholar does not disgrace his name,
a trustworthy scholar does not neglect his conduct.
Now I am in Ā,
yet Sòng massacred Dānfù,
this is disgracing my name.
I undertook to execute the King of Sòng,
but for a year could not achieve it,
this is neglecting my conduct.
If I live on like this,
what face have I to see the scholars of the world?"
Then he stood and withered away on Péng Mountain.
4.19 Bì Xī used the district of Zhōngmóu to rebel,
setting up fiefs and a boiling cauldron,
saying:
"Those who join me will receive lands,
those who do not join me will be boiled."
The scholars of Zhōngmóu all joined him.
Tián Jī, a junior from the north of the city, alone came last,
bared his upper body and prepared to enter the cauldron,
saying:
"Jī has heard that
for a righteous man, even if carriages and official caps are offered,
if it is unrighteous, he will not take them;
even if axes and executioners await behind,
he will not avoid dying for righteousness."
Then he bared his upper body and prepared to enter the cauldron,
but Bì Xī pulled him back and stopped him.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ massacred Zhōngmóu,
captured and took it over.
When discussing meritorious deeds,
he considered Tián Jī the first.
Tián Jī said:
"I have heard that an incorruptible scholar does not shame others.
If I thus accept credit for Zhōngmóu,
then the scholars of Zhōngmóu will be ashamed for life."
Then he carried his mother on his back,
and moved south to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ esteemed his righteousness,
and treated him as a Sīmǎ.
4.20 When Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated Duke Zhuang,
Xíng Kuǎikuì was returning from a mission to Jìn.
His servant said:
"Cuī Zhù has assassinated Duke Zhuang,
what will you do?"
Xíng Kuǎikuì replied:
"Drive on,
I shall enter and die to repay my lord."
His servant said:
"Our lord was unprincipled,
all the neighboring feudal lords
have heard of it.
For you, sir, to die for him—
is that not misguided?"
Xíng Kuǎikuì said:
"Well spoken,
you argue skillfully,
but it is too late.
Had you advised me earlier,
I could have remonstrated with him.
If my remonstrance went unheeded,
I could have left.
Now I have neither remonstrated
nor departed.
I have heard that one who eats his ruler's salary should die for his affairs.
Since I have eaten the salary of a disorderly ruler,
how could I now seek an orderly ruler to die for?"
Thereupon he drove his chariot into the capital and died.
His servant said:
"When others had a disorderly lord,
they still died for him;
since I have an orderly master,
how could I not die?"
Then he tied the reins and cut his throat in the chariot.
The gentleman, hearing of this, said:
"Xíng Kuǎikuì may be said to have maintained integrity and died for righteousness.
Death
is what people find difficult.
As for the servant's death,
though it may not fully accord with righteousness,
still it shows the intent of a determined man."
The Book of Songs says:
"Day and night never slackening,
to serve the one man."
This describes Master Xíng.
Mencius said:
"The brave man does not forget that he may lose his head."
This describes the servant.
4.21 King Zhāo of Yān sent Yuè Yì to attack Qí,
and King Mǐn fled.
When Yān first entered Qí,
hearing that Wáng Chù of Gàiyì was worthy,
issued an order to the army saying:
"Within thirty lǐ around Gàiyì,
do not enter,"
because of Chù.
Afterwards, he sent a man to tell Chù:
"The people of Qí largely esteem your righteousness,
I will make you a general,
and enfeoff you with ten thousand households."
Chù firmly declined the Yān man's offer.
The Yān man said:
"If you do not comply,
I will lead the three armies to slaughter Gàiyì."
Wáng Chù said:
"A loyal minister does not serve two lords,
a chaste woman does not change husbands.
The King of Qí did not heed my remonstrance,
therefore I withdrew to plow in the wilds.
Now that the state is destroyed and lost,
I cannot preserve it,
and now you coerce me with arms to become your general—
this would be aiding Jié in his tyranny.
Rather than live without righteousness,
it would be better to be boiled."
Thereupon he hanged his body from a tree branch,
threw himself forward, broke his neck, and died.
The great officers of the fallen Qí, hearing of this, said:
"Wáng Chù
was a commoner,
yet righteously would not turn from Qí toward Yān;
how much more should those in office, eating its salary?"
Thereupon they gathered together and went to Jǔ,
sought out one of the princes,
and set him up as King Xiāng.
4.22 Zuǒ Rú was a friend of Dù Bó,
and both were ministers to King Xuān of Zhōu.
King Xuān was about to execute Dù Bó,
though he was not guilty of any crime.
Zuǒ Rú pleaded with the king for him,
repeating his appeal nine times,
but the king would not grant it.
The king said:
"To set your lord aside and differ with your friend—
this is you."
Zuǒ Rú replied:
"Your servant has heard that
if the lord is principled and the friend unprincipled,
then one follows the lord to punish the friend;
if the friend is principled and the lord unprincipled,
then one leads the friend to oppose the lord."
The king angrily said:
"Change your words and live,
do not change them and die."
Zuǒ Rú replied:
"Your servant has heard that men of antiquity did not distort righteousness to follow others to death,
nor change their words to seek life.
Therefore, your servant can make clear your majesty's error,
and die for Dù Bó's innocence."
The king executed Dù Bó,
and Zuǒ Rú died for him.
4.23 Duke Mù of Jǔ had a minister named Zhū Lìfù,
who served Duke Mù
but went unrecognized.
In winter he dwelt in the mountain forests,
eating oak nuts and chestnuts;
in summer he dwelt in the river marshes,
eating water chestnuts and lotus roots.
When Duke Mù died in a crisis,
Zhū Lìfù prepared to go and die for him.
His friend said:
"You served your lord but went unrecognized,
now that the lord is in crisis,
for you, sir, to die for him—
I suspect it may not be proper?"
Zhū Lìfù said:
"At first, I thought the lord did not know me,
but if now the lord dies and I do not die,
that would indeed prove he did not know me.
I shall die for him,
to stir those in the world who do not know their ministers."
Thereupon he went and died for him.
4.24 King Zhuāng of Chǔ was hunting at Yúnméng,
shot a pheasant,
and captured it.
Shēngōng Zǐ Bèi attacked and seized it from him,
and the king was about to execute him.
A great officer remonstrated, saying:
"Zǐ Bèi is self-possessed;
his contending for the king's pheasant must have a reason.
Your majesty should investigate it."
Before three months had passed,
Zǐ Bèi fell ill and died.
At the battle of Bì,
Chǔ defeated Jìn.
Returning, the king rewarded achievements,
and Shēngōng Zǐ Bèi's younger brother came forward to request reward from the king, saying:
"When a man has achievement,
he is rewarded beneath the chariot."
The king said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"My elder brother read an old record which said:
'One who shoots a pheasant
will die
within three months.'
My elder brother
contended for it and obtained it,
hence he died prematurely."
The king ordered the archives opened and examined,
and indeed the record was there.
Thereupon he richly rewarded him.
5.1 Does the sage not treat the people of the world like newborn infants?
He feeds the hungry,
clothes the cold,
nurtures them,
rears them,
and fosters their growth,
fearing only that they will not reach greatness.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Lush is the sweet pear tree;
Do not cut it, do not harm it,
For Shào Bó rested beneath it."
The *Commentary* says:
"The lands east of Shǎn
were governed by the Duke of Zhōu;
the lands west of Shǎn
were governed by the Duke of Shào."
When Duke Shào was reporting on his governance,
it was the season of silkworms and mulberries,
and he did not wish to disrupt the people's affairs.
Therefore, he did not enter the city,
but instead lodged under a sweet pear tree to hold court and make judgments.
The people of the Shǎn region
all found their proper place,
and thus later generations remembered and sang praises of him.
Because they admired him, they spoke of him;
when words were not enough,
they sighed for him;
when sighs were not enough,
they sang of him.
The poet, being moved, reflects;
reflecting, he accumulates feelings;
accumulating, he becomes full;
being full, he expresses;
his expression follows the proper way and attains its place.
The people sigh at his beauty and offer their reverence.
That the sweet pear tree was not cut down—
how could governance and teaching not be practiced?
Confucius said:
"From the 'Gǎn Táng,'
I see the reverence of the ancestral temple.
How profound it is!
To remember a person,
one must love their tree;
to honor a person,
one must respect their position.
To harmoniously secure all things—
how close this is to the way of the ancient sages!"
5.2 The virtuous teaching of a benevolent person
truly stems from compassion within,
sincerity in the heart,
and an inability to restrain their feelings.
Thus, in governing the world,
they act like saving a drowning person.
Seeing the strong bully the weak in the world,
the many oppress the few,
the young and orphaned exposed and vulnerable,
the dead, wounded, captured, or enslaved,
they cannot bear such a state.
Therefore, Confucius visited seventy-two lords,
hoping that the Way might be implemented and his virtue applied,
so that the people might live fully nurtured,
the masses dwell peacefully on the land,
all things flourish joyfully,
and each finds happiness in their end.
Ultimately, he did not meet with opportunity,
so upon seeing the qílín, he wept,
grieving that the Way was not practiced,
and his virtuous influence did not spread.
Thereupon, he retired and composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
elucidating the way of the uncrowned king,
to show later generations.
He never ceased to think of bestowing his kindness,
nor ever forgot it;
thus, all kings honor him,
and aspirants take him as their model.
They recite his writings,
which are handed down to this day without cease,
all due to the reach of his virtue.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"I gallop my carriage, driving swiftly,
to thoroughly consult and plan."
This refers to such dedication.
5.3 When a sage king spreads virtue and bestows blessings,
he does not seek repayment from the people;
when offering suburban, mountain, ancestral, and seasonal sacrifices,
he does not seek repayment from the spirits.
When a mountain reaches its height, clouds and rain gather there;
when water reaches its depth, jiāolóng are born there;
when a gentleman attains the Way, fortune and prosperity return to him.
Those who accumulate hidden virtue
will surely receive open reward;
those with unseen good deeds
will surely achieve renowned fame.
In ancient times, when ditches and embankments were not maintained,
floods became a disaster for the people.
Yǔ dredged the Lóngmén,
opened the Yīquē,
leveled the land and tamed the waters,
enabling the people to live on dry land.
When the people were not affectionate,
and the five relationships were not harmonious,
Qì taught them the principles of ruler and minister,
the intimacy of father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
and the order of elder and younger.
When fields were not cultivated,
and the people had insufficient food,
Hòu Jì taught them
to clear land and plow grasslands,
fertilize the soil and plant grains,
ensuring that every household had enough.
Thus, the descendants of these three sovereigns
all became kings—
because they had hidden virtue.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
and ritual and righteousness were abandoned,
Confucius used the Way of the three dynasties
to instruct later generations,
and his legacy continues unbroken to this day—
because he had unseen good deeds.
5.4 The *Zhōu Sòng* says:
"Abundant year with much millet and rice;
also high granaries,
myriads and billions of measures;
for making wine and sweet liquor,
we offer to ancestors and ancestresses,
to complete all rituals,
and bring down blessings in great harmony."
The *Book of Rites* says:
"If the superior sacrificial animal is reduced, then the inferior is used;
if the inferior is reduced, then the sacrifice does not include all items."
This is because such discrepancies cause displeasure.
Therefore, the sage's relation to the world
can be compared to a hall full of people.
If in a hall full of drinkers,
one person alone is desolate, weeping in a corner,
then everyone in the hall will be unhappy because of it.
The sage's relation to the world
is like that of a hall full of people;
if even one person is not in their proper place,
then even a filial son would not dare to present his offerings.
5.5 Marquis Wǔ of Wèi was sailing down the Western River.
In midstream,
he turned to Wú Qǐ and said:
"How magnificent!
The impregnability of these rivers and mountains
is the treasure of the state of Wèi."
Wú Qǐ replied:
"[A state's security] lies in virtue, not in strategic terrain.
In the past, the Sānmiáo clan had Dòngtíng Lake on the left and Pénglí Lake on the right,
but because they did not cultivate virtue and righteousness, Yǔ destroyed them.
Where Xià Jié resided,
he had the Hé and Jì rivers on the left and Tàihuà Mountain on the right,
Yīquē to the south,
and Yángcháng to the north,
yet because his governance was unkind, Tāng exiled him.
The state of Yīn Zhòu
had Mèngmén to the left and Tàiháng to the right,
Chángshān to the north,
and the great river flowing to the south,
but because his governance lacked virtue, King Wǔ attacked him.
From this, we can see
that [security] lies in virtue, not in strategic terrain.
If you, my lord, do not cultivate virtue,
then everyone in this boat could become your enemy."
Marquis Wǔ said:
"Well said."
5.6 When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he summoned Grand Duke and asked:
"What should we do with their officials and masses?"
Grand Duke replied:
"I have heard that those who love a person
extend that love even to the crows on their roof;
those who hate a person
despise even their retainers.
Let us completely exterminate our enemies,
leaving none remaining.
What do you think?"
The King said:
"That will not do."
Grand Duke departed,
and Duke Shào entered.
The King said:
"What should be done about this?"
Duke Shào replied:
"Execute those who are guilty,
spare those who are innocent.
What do you think?"
The King said:
"That will not do."
Duke Shào departed,
and Duke Zhōu entered.
The King said:
"What should be done about this?"
Duke Zhōu said:
"Let each remain in their own dwelling,
farm their own fields,
without distinguishing between old and new subjects,
drawing close only to those who are benevolent.
If the common people have faults,
let the responsibility rest with me alone."
King Wǔ said:
"How magnificent! This is the way to bring peace to the world."
The reason why gentlemen are esteemed
is because they are benevolent and virtuous.
5.7 Confucius said:
"It is beautiful to dwell in benevolence.
If one chooses not to abide in benevolence,
how can one attain wisdom?"
The benevolent must act with forgiveness;
to commit one unjust act,
to kill one innocent person,
even if it brings high office and great position,
the benevolent will not do it.
Those of great benevolence
love the near and extend to the distant;
when faced with incompatibility,
they sacrifice minor benevolence to achieve major benevolence.
Great benevolence
extends kindness throughout the world;
minor benevolence
stops with wife and children.
Those concerned with wife and children
use their wisdom to seek profit,
comforting them with a woman's kindness,
disguising their true feelings,
embellishing their falsehoods.
Who knows they are not genuine?
Though they may gain honor at the time,
gentlemen consider this a great disgrace.
Thus Gònggōng, Huāndōu, Fúlǐ, and Dèng Xī
were not without knowledge,
yet they were executed by sage kings
because they were virtueless and pursued profit recklessly.
Shù Diāo and Yì Yá mutilated themselves and killed their sons to seek advantage,
ultimately becoming traitors in Qí.
Therefore, if ministers are not benevolent,
usurpation and regicide arise;
if ministers are benevolent,
the state is well-governed and the ruler honored.
When enlightened rulers understand this,
the ancestral temple enjoys great peace.
If even ministers should value benevolence,
how much more should rulers?
Thus Jié and Zhòu lost the world through lack of benevolence,
while Tāng and Wǔ possessed the realm through accumulated virtue.
Therefore, sage kings value virtue and diligently practice it.
The Mèngzǐ says:
"Extending kindness can reach throughout the world;
failing to extend kindness cannot protect even wife and children.
The reason the ancients greatly surpassed others was nothing else
but their skill in extending what they possessed."
5.8 Yànzǐ was serving wine to Duke Jǐng,
and ordered that all vessels must be new.
The steward said:
"Our resources are insufficient,
may we collect from the people?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Stop!
Joy should be shared by high and low alike.
Thus the Son of Heaven shares with all under heaven,
feudal lords share within their domains,
and from ministers down, each shares with their colleagues.
There should be no solitary enjoyment.
Now if those above enjoy their pleasure
while those below suffer the expense,
this is solitary enjoyment.
It cannot be done."
5.9 Duke Huán of Qí went north to attack the Shānróng tribe,
passing through Yān on his way.
The ruler of Yān came to meet him beyond his borders.
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"According to ritual, when feudal lords meet each other,
should they necessarily go beyond borders?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Only for the Son of Heaven should one go beyond borders."
Duke Huán said:
"Then the ruler of Yān, in his awe, has breached ritual,
and I, being unprincipled,
have caused the ruler of Yān to breach ritual."
Thereupon he cut off the territory where the ruler of Yān had reached
and gave it to Yān.
When the feudal lords heard of this,
they all came to pay homage to Qí.
The Shī says:
"Quietly reverent in your position,
loving this uprightness,
the spirits will hearken to you
and grant you great happiness."
This expresses that meaning.
5.10 Duke Jǐng touched a nestling,
and because the fledgling was weak,
he returned it.
Yànzǐ heard of this
and entered to see the Duke without waiting.
The Duke was sweating and apprehensive.
Yànzǐ said:
"What has Your Lordship done?"
Duke Jǐng said:
"I touched a nestling,
and because the fledgling was weak,
I returned it."
Yànzǐ hesitated, faced north, bowed twice, and congratulated him:
"Our lord possesses the way of a sage king!"
Duke Jǐng said:
"I touched a nestling,
and because the fledgling was weak,
I returned it.
How does this correspond to the way of a sage king?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"You touched a nestling,
and because the fledgling was weak,
you returned it.
This shows care for the young.
Our lord's benevolence and love
extends even to birds and beasts,
how much more to people?
This is the way of a sage king."
5.11 Duke Jǐng saw an infant begging on the road.
The Duke said:
"This child has no one to return to!"
Yànzǐ replied:
"While you live,
how can it have no one to return to?
Have an official care for it,
and this can be established and reported to you."
5.12 Duke Jǐng was traveling in the Shòu Palace,
when he saw an elderly wood-gatherer with a hungry appearance.
The Duke pitied him,
and sighing, ordered an official to care for him.
Yànzǐ said:
"I have heard that
delighting in the worthy and pitying the unworthy
is the foundation of preserving the state.
Now my lord loves the elderly,
and your kindness reaches everywhere.
This is the foundation of governing the state."
The Duke smiled,
with a pleased expression.
Yànzǐ said:
"Sage kings delight in the worthy when they see them,
and pity the unworthy when they see them.
Now let us seek out the elderly and weak who lack support,
widowers and widows who lack households,
assess their situations and provide for them."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Very well."
Thereupon the elderly and weak received care,
and widowers and widows had households.
5.18 Jì Kāngzǐ said to Zǐyóu:
"Does a benevolent person love others?"
Zǐyóu replied:
"Yes."
"Do others also love them?"
Zǐyóu said:
"Yes."
Kāngzǐ said:
"When Zǐ Chǎn died,
the people of Zhèng,
men discarded their jade pendants,
women removed their pearl earrings,
husbands and wives wept in the streets,
and for three months no music from reed pipes or zithers was heard.
When Zhòngní died,
I haven't heard that the people of Lǔ loved the Master,
why is that?"
Zǐyóu said:
"To compare Zǐ Chǎn with the Master,
is like comparing irrigation water with heavenly rain.
Where irrigation water reaches, things grow,
where it doesn't reach, they die.
But the life of these people,
must come from seasonal rain,
having given them life,
none feel grateful for its gift.
Therefore it is said:
to compare Zǐ Chǎn with the Master,
is like comparing irrigation water with heavenly rain?"
5.19 Zhōngháng Mùzǐ besieged Gǔ,
when some people of Gǔ offered to betray the city,
he refused.
His officers said:
"Our troops won't be wearied,
we can obtain the city,
why refuse?"
He replied:
"If someone were to betray my city,
I would deeply detest it,
if others bring their city to me,
why should I alone favor this?
To reward what I deeply detest,
is to err in rewarding,
what then of what I favor?
If I don't reward,
this is to break faith,
how could I show this to the people."
The people of Gǔ again requested to surrender,
he sent someone to observe them,
their people still had food,
so he didn't consent.
When the people of Gǔ reported their food exhausted and strength spent,
only then did he take it,
conquering Gǔ and returning,
without executing a single person.
5.20 When Confucius went to Chǔ,
a fisherman insistently offered him fish,
but Confucius declined.
The fish offerer said:
"The weather is hot and the market distant,
the fish won't sell,
I considered throwing them in the waste,
but thought it better to offer them to a gentleman."
Confucius bowed twice and accepted,
then had his disciples clean them for sacrifice.
A disciple said:
"That man was about to discard them,
yet you, Master, are about to sacrifice them,
why?"
Confucius said:
"I have heard that
those who devote themselves to giving without letting wealth rot
are sages.
Now having received a sage's gift,
how could I not sacrifice it?"
5.21 Zhèng attacked Sòng,
the people of Sòng prepared for battle.
Huà Yuán slaughtered sheep to feed his soldiers,
but his charioteer Yáng Zhēn wasn't included.
When battle came,
he said:
"Yesterday's mutton soup
was your affair,
today's matters
are my affair."
He drove Huà Yuán straight into the Zhèng army,
and the Sòng forces were defeated.
5.22 The King of Chǔ asked Zhuāng Xīn:
"What constitutes a gentleman's conduct?"
Zhuāng Xīn replied:
"Dwelling without building walls,
yet none can harm him;
traveling without armed escort,
yet none can assault him.
This is a gentleman's conduct."
The King of Chǔ asked again:
"What constitutes a gentleman's wealth?"
He replied:
"A gentleman's wealth
means lending to others
without expecting gratitude,
without demanding repayment;
feeding and watering others
without ordering them about,
without making them serve.
His relatives love him,
the multitude praises him,
the unworthy serve him,
all wishing him long life and happiness, unharmed by misfortune.
This is a gentleman's wealth."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Excellent."
5.23 Chancellor Xīpíng Hóu Yú Dìngguó
was from Xiàpī in Dōnghǎi.
His father was called Yú Gōng,
serving as county jailer and legal secretary,
judging cases and applying laws fairly,
never causing any injustice.
Those in the commandery involved in legal disputes,
when judged by Yú Gōng,
dared not conceal the truth.
The people of Dōnghǎi commandery built a temple for Yú Gōng during his lifetime,
naming it Yú Gōng Temple.
In Dōnghǎi there was a filial daughter-in-law,
childless,
widowed young,
who cared for her mother-in-law very diligently.
Her mother-in-law wanted her to remarry,
but she steadfastly refused.
Her mother-in-law told the neighbors:
"My daughter-in-law cares for me very diligently,
I pity her childlessness and long widowhood,
I am old,
burdening someone in her prime,
what can be done?"
Later the mother hanged herself,
and her daughter reported to the officials:
"The daughter-in-law killed my mother."
The officials arrested the filial daughter-in-law,
but she denied killing her mother-in-law.
When the officials threatened torture,
she falsely confessed.
When the case documents were sent to the prefecture,
Yú Gōng argued that she had cared for her mother-in-law for ten years and was known for filial piety,
so she wouldn't have killed her.
The governor wouldn't listen,
and after repeated protests failed,
Yú Gōng resigned pleading illness.
The governor ultimately executed the filial daughter-in-law.
The commandery then suffered drought for three years.
When a new governor arrived,
he divined to find the cause,
Yú Gōng said:
"The filial daughter-in-law didn't deserve death,
the former governor forcibly killed her,
the fault must lie here."
They then slaughtered an ox and sacrificed at the filial daughter-in-law's grave,
with the governor and all officials attending personally.
Heaven immediately sent heavy rain,
the harvest was abundant,
and the commandery thereby respected Yú Gōng even more.
When Yú Gōng built his house,
he told the craftsmen:
"Make my gate high,
for in judging cases I've never caused injustice,
my descendants will surely be enfeoffed as marquises,
so it must accommodate a high-canopied four-horse carriage."
When it came to his son,
he was enfeoffed as Xīpíng Hóu.
5.24 When Mèng Jiǎnzǐ was prime minister of Liáng,
and annexed Wèi,
he committed a crime and fled to Qí.
Guǎn Zhòng greeted him and asked:
"When you, sir, were prime minister of Liáng and annexed Wèi,
how many followers did you have under your command?"
Mèng Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I had over three thousand followers."
Guǎn Zhòng asked:
"How many have come with you now?"
He replied:
"I have come with only three men."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"One man's father died with no means for burial,
I buried him;
another's mother died with no means for burial,
I also buried her;
another's elder brother was imprisoned,
I secured his release.
That is why I have these three men with me."
Guǎn Zhòng mounted his carriage and said:
"Alas!
I am surely destined for hardship,
for I have not been able to nurture people with the spring breeze,
nor to moisten people with the summer rain.
I am surely destined for hardship!"
5.25 In human nature generally,
none do not wish to perfect their virtue;
yet those who cannot achieve virtuous conduct
are led astray by profit.
Thus the gentleman is ashamed to speak of profit and fame;
if speaking of profit and fame is still shameful,
how much more so is residing in position while seeking profit?
When the Zhōu Son of Heaven sent Jiǎfǔ Máobó to seek chariots and gold from the feudal lords,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" criticized it.
Thus if the Son of Heaven favors profit, the feudal lords become greedy;
if the feudal lords are greedy, the great officers become base;
if the great officers are base, the common people become thieves.
The transformation from above to below
is like the wind bending the grass.
Therefore, for one who serves as ruler,
to make clear the valuing of virtue and disdain for profit in guiding subordinates—
even then the wrongdoing of subordinates
still cannot be stopped.
Now Duke Yīn, greedy for profit, personally fished at the Jì River,
and performed the eight-row dance,
thereby influencing the people of the state.
How could the people not then become lax in righteousness?
Being lax in righteousness and indulging their desires,
then disasters arise and ministers become depraved.
Thus in his fifth year it was first recorded "caterpillars,"
indicating disasters would arise,
and the state would fall into disorder, it is said.
5.26 Xúnzǐ said:
"Those who fight
forget their own persons,
forget their parents,
forget their rulers.
Acting on momentary anger to fight,
bringing lifelong calamity—
yet still doing it,
this is forgetting one's own person;
households scattered and separated,
relatives slain,
yet still doing it,
this is forgetting one's parents;
what the ruler deeply detests,
what penalties and laws strictly prohibit,
yet still violating them,
this is forgetting one's ruler.
Now even birds and beasts know to stay close to their parents,
not forgetting their kin.
For a person to forget their own person,
inwardly forget their parents,
above forget their ruler—
this makes them inferior to the benevolence of birds and beasts.
All who fight
consider themselves right,
and others wrong.
If one is truly right,
and others truly wrong,
then one is the gentleman and they are petty men.
For a gentleman to harm petty men—
this is what people call using fox fur to mend dog and sheep skins,
smearing oneself with charcoal—
is that not extremely mistaken?
To consider it wise?
Then no folly is greater;
to consider it profitable?
Then no harm is greater;
to consider it honorable?
Then no disgrace is greater.
Why do people fight?
What is the reason?
To compare it to madness or delusion sickness?
That cannot be,
for in appearance they are human and their likes and dislikes are largely similar.
Human fighting
truly stems from folly, delusion, and loss of the Way."
The "Book of Songs" says:
"They shout and they yell,
making the day into night."
This describes fighting behavior.
5.27 Zǐlù held a sword.
Confucius asked him:
"Yóu,
what need have you for this?"
Zǐlù said:
"For those who treat me well,
I will naturally treat them well;
for those who treat me ill,
I will use it for self-defense."
Confucius said:
"The gentleman takes loyalty as his substance,
and benevolence as his defense.
Without leaving his humble dwelling's walls,
he is known a thousand miles away.
For the ill-disposed, he transforms them with loyalty;
for invaders and violence, he surrounds them with benevolence.
Why must you hold a sword?"
Zǐlù said:
"I, Yóu,
ask to tuck in my robe and serve you, Master."
5.28 Yuè Yáng served as general for Marquis Wén of Wèi,
attacking Zhōngshān.
His son was in Zhōngshān at the time,
and Zhōngshān hung his son up to show Yuè Yáng.
Yuè Yáng's resolve did not weaken;
he attacked more fiercely.
Zhōngshān then cooked his son and sent the broth to him;
Yuè Yáng ate a full cup of it.
Zhōngshān, seeing his determination,
could not bear to fight him,
and indeed surrendered to him.
Thus he expanded territory for Marquis Wén.
Marquis Wén rewarded his achievement but doubted his heart.
Mèngsūn hunted and captured a fawn,
ordering Qín Xībā to carry it back.
Its mother followed, crying.
Qín Xībā could not bear it,
and released the fawn to her.
Mèngsūn, angry, banished Qín Xībā.
After one year,
he summoned him back to be his son's tutor.
His attendants said:
"Qín Xībā offended you,
yet now you make him the young master's tutor—
why?"
Mèngsūn said:
"If he could not bear to harm a fawn,
how could he bear to harm my son?"
Thus it is said:
Cunning artifice is inferior to simple sincerity.
Yuè Yáng, though achieving merit, was doubted;
Qín Xībā, though offending, gained greater trust—
this stems from benevolence and the lack thereof.
5.29 When Zhì Bó returned from Wèi,
the three ministers feasted at Lántái.
Zhì Xiāngzǐ teased Hán Kāngzǐ and insulted Duàn Guī.
Zhì Guǒ heard of this,
and admonished, saying:
"If my lord does not prepare for calamity,
calamity is sure to arrive."
(Zhì Bó) said:
"Calamity will come from me;
if I do not create calamity,
who would dare to raise it!"
(Zhì Guǒ) replied:
"It is different from this.
The Xì family had the calamity of the chariot shaft,
the Zhào family had the slander of Mèng Jī,
the Luán family had the accusations of Shū Qí,
the Fàn and Zhōngháng families had the calamity of Hán Yě—
all of these are known to my lord.
The 'Book of Xià' says:
'When one person has three faults,
can resentment only lie in what is obvious?
Plan for what is not yet seen.'
The 'Book of Zhōu' says:
'Resentment is not necessarily in great matters,
nor is it only in small ones.'
The gentleman can attend diligently to small matters,
therefore he has no great disasters.
Now with one scheme my lord has shamed the ruler and minister,
and still does not prepare,
saying:
'They dare not raise calamity'—
is this not unacceptable?
Alas!
One cannot but fear;
gnats, ants, bees, and scorpions
can all harm people,
how much more so a ruler and his minister?"
(Zhì Bó) did not listen.
Five years from then,
the disaster of Jìnyáng occurred,
Duàn Guǐ turned around and killed Zhì Bó in the army,
thus annihilating the Zhì clan.
5.30 When Zhì Xiāngzǐ built a magnificent house,
Shì Zhuó visited in the evening.
Zhì Bó said:
"The house is magnificent, is it not!"
(Shì Zhuó) replied:
"Magnificent it is indeed,
but your servant also has fears."
Zhì Bó said:
"What fears?"
(Shì Zhuó) replied:
"Your servant serves you with the writing brush.
The records say:
'High mountains and deep springs
do not produce grasses and trees;
where pines and cypresses grow,
the soil is not fertile.'
Now the timber and earth surpass the human,
your servant fears it will not bring peace to people."
Three years after the house was completed,
the Zhì clan perished.
6.1 Confucius said:
"Virtue is not left to stand alone;
he who practices it will have neighbors."
Those who bestow virtue value not claiming it as a favor;
those who receive kindness honor the necessity of repaying it.
Therefore, ministers labor diligently for their lord without seeking reward;
the lord holds forth kindness to govern his subjects without claiming it as a favor.
Thus the 'Yì Jīng' says:
"Toil without resentment,
achieve merit without claiming virtue,
this is the height of generosity."
When lord and minister interact,
they connect as in market dealings:
the lord suspends emoluments to await service,
the minister exhausts his strength to repay it.
When a minister achieves unforeseen merit,
the lord rewards him heavily;
if the lord shows extraordinary kindness,
the minister will surely die to repay it.
Confucius said:
"In the north there is an animal,
