its name is Jué,
with front legs like a rat's,
and hind legs like a rabbit's.
This animal
greatly loves the Qióngqióng and Jùxū;
when it finds sweet grass,
it always bites some to give to the Qióngqióng and Jùxū.
When the Qióngqióng and Jùxū see someone approaching,
they always carry the Jué on their backs and flee.
The Jué does not inherently love the Qióngqióng and Jùxū;
it is for the sake of borrowing their feet;
the two animals
also do not inherently love the Jué;
it is because it gives them sweet grass.
Even birds, beasts, and insects know to rely on each other and reciprocate kindness,
how much more should gentlemen who wish to promote fame and benefit in the world?"
If ministers do not repay their lord's kindness,
but instead seek only their private gain,
this is the source of disaster.
If the lord cannot reward his ministers' merits,
but is reluctant to bestow rewards,
this is also the foundation of chaos.
The source of disaster and chaos
arises from failing to repay kindness.
6.2 When Zhào Xiāngzǐ was besieged at Jìnyáng,
after the siege was lifted,
he rewarded five ministers who had merit.
Gāo Hè, who had no merit, received the highest reward,
and the five were all angry.
Zhāng Mèngtán said to Xiāngzǐ:
"During the siege of Jìnyáng,
Hè had no great merit;
why now give him the highest reward?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"When I was in constrained circumstances,
the one who did not neglect the rites between lord and minister
was only Hè.
You others, though you had merit,
were all arrogant.
Is it not appropriate that I give Hè the highest reward?"
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"Zhào Xiāngzǐ may be called skilled at rewarding his officers indeed!
By rewarding one man,
all under heaven who serve as ministers
dare not neglect the rites between lord and subject."
6.3 When Jìn Wéngōng was in exile,
Táo Shūhú followed him.
When Wéngōng returned to his state,
after three rounds of rewards, Táo Shūhú had not been included.
Táo Shūhú went to see Jiù Fàn and said:
"I followed my lord into exile for thirteen years,
my face became swarthy,
my hands and feet calloused.
Now my lord has returned to the state,
and after three rounds of rewards I have not been included.
Does my lord intend to forget me?
Or have I committed some great fault?
Please try to speak of this to our lord for me."
Jiù Fàn spoke of it to Wéngōng,
and Wéngōng said:
"Alas,
how could I forget this man!
Those of supreme wisdom and worthiness,
of complete virtue and sincere conduct,
who guide me with the Way,
delight me with benevolence,
cleanse my actions,
and make my name illustrious,
enabling me to become a complete man—
these I consider worthy of the highest reward.
Those who guard me with ritual,
admonish me with righteousness,
support and aid me,
keeping me from wrongdoing,
and repeatedly lead me to the gates of worthy men—
these I consider worthy of the next reward.
Those of brave and strong defense,
who stand in front when danger is ahead,
and behind when danger is behind,
saving me from perilous situations—
these I also consider worthy of the next reward.
And have you not heard?
Saving a man's life is better than mourning the dead;
preserving a man's state is better than witnessing its loss.
After three rounds of rewards,
then come the toiling and laboring officers.
Among the toiling and laboring officers,
this man certainly comes first.
How could I dare forget him?"
Zhōu's internal historian Shū Xīng heard of this and said:
"Wéngōng is fit to be a hegemon indeed!
The sage kings of old put virtue before force;
Wéngōng matches this description!"
The 'Book of Odes' says:
"Following ritual without transgression."
This expresses it.
6.9 After Lord Píngyuán returned to Zhào,
the Chǔ state sent Lord Chūnshēn to lead troops to rescue Zhào,
and Lord Xìnlíng of Wèi also seized Jìn Bǐ's army by deceit to go rescue Zhào,
but none had arrived yet.
Qín urgently besieged Hándān,
and Hándān, in dire straits, was about to surrender.
Lord Píngyuán was deeply worried about this.
Lǐ Tán, son of an official at a Hándān relay station, said to Lord Píngyuán:
"My lord, are you not worried about Zhào's destruction?"
Lord Píngyuán replied:
"If Zhào perishes, I would become a captive—
how could I not be worried?"
Lǐ Tán said:
"The people of Hándān,
burning bones for fuel and exchanging children to eat,
can be said to be in extreme hardship.
Yet in your rear palaces, you have hundreds of women,
with wives and concubines draped in fine silks,
and the kitchens have leftover fine grains and meat.
The people are exhausted, weapons depleted,
some whittling wood into spears and halberds,
while your vessels, bells, and chimes remain as they are.
If Qín destroys Zhào,
how could you keep these?
If Zhào is preserved,
why worry about not having them?
If you could have your ladies and below join the ranks of the soldiers,
sharing the labor and duties,
and distribute all your household's possessions to feast the troops—
in this time of crisis and suffering,
it would be easy to earn their gratitude."
Thereupon, Lord Píngyuán followed his plan,
and three thousand courageous men,
all willing to die,
followed Lǐ Tán to charge the Qín army.
The Qín army retreated thirty lǐ.
It so happened that rescue forces from Chǔ and Wèi arrived,
and the Qín army then withdrew.
Lǐ Tán died,
and his father was enfeoffed as Lord Lǐ.
6.10 Duke Mù of Qín once went out and lost his fine horse.
He went himself to search for it,
and found people had already killed his horse
and were just eating its meat.
Duke Mù said to them:
"This is my fine horse."
The men all stood up in fear,
but Duke Mù said:
"I've heard that eating fine horse meat without drinking wine
can kill a person."
He then gave them wine to drink in turn,
and the horse killers left in shame.
Three years later,
Jìn attacked Duke Mù of Qín
and surrounded him.
Those who had eaten the horse meat said to each other:
"We can now risk death
to repay the kindness of getting wine after eating the horse."
They then broke the encirclement,
and Duke Mù was ultimately able to escape the crisis,
defeat Jìn,
and capture Duke Huì to return.
This is virtue going out and blessing returning.
6.11 King Zhuāng of Chǔ feasted his ministers with wine.
As dusk fell and they were merrily drunk,
the lamps and candles went out,
and someone tugged at the clothes of a beauty.
The beauty snatched off the man's hat tassel,
and told the king:
"Just now when the candles went out,
someone tugged at my clothes.
I've snatched his hat tassel and hold it.
Bring a light quickly,
and we'll see whose tassel is broken."
The king said:
"I gave them wine,
causing them to get drunk and lose propriety.
Why should I disgrace a gentleman to display a woman's chastity?"
He then ordered his attendants:
"Today, those who drink with me
must break their hat tassels or the revelry stops."
Over a hundred ministers
all broke off their hat tassels before the lights were lit,
and the feast ended in full merriment.
Two years later,
Jìn and Chǔ fought a battle,
and one minister was always at the front,
engaging five times, taking five heads, and repelling the enemy,
ultimately securing victory.
King Zhuāng, surprised, asked him:
"My virtue is meager,
and I've never treated you specially.
Why do you risk death without hesitation like this?"
He replied:
"I deserve death.
In the past, I was drunk and lost propriety,
but you tolerated it and did not expose or punish me.
I have never dared to forget this hidden kindness
and not repay you openly.
I have long wished to spill my liver and brains on the ground,
and long to drench the enemy with the blood from my neck.
I am the one whose tassel was broken that night."
He then repelled the Jìn army,
and Chǔ thereby became strong.
This shows that those who accumulate hidden virtue will surely receive open reward.
6.12 Zhào Xuānmèng was going to Jiàng from the capital
when he saw a starving man lying under a mulberry tree, unable to move.
Xuānmèng stopped his carriage, got down, and prepared a meal for him,
feeding him with his own hands.
The starving man swallowed twice before he could see.
Xuānmèng asked:
"Why are you so hungry like this?"
He replied:
"I served as an official in Jiàng,
and on my return, my food ran out.
Ashamed to beg and loath to steal,
I ended up in this state."
Xuānmèng gave him a pot of food and two pieces of dried meat.
The man bowed twice, kowtowed, and accepted them,
but did not dare eat.
Asked why,
he replied:
"The food just now was delicious.
I have an old mother,
and I wish to offer it to her."
Xuānmèng said:
"You eat this now,
and I will give you more."
He then prepared another basket of food for him,
along with two bundles of dried meat and a hundred coins,
and sent him on his way to Jiàng.
Three years later,
Duke Líng of Jìn wanted to kill Xuānmèng.
He set ambushing soldiers in a room
and invited Xuānmèng to drink.
Xuānmèng realized this,
and left midway through the drinking.
Duke Líng ordered the soldiers in the room to quickly pursue and kill him.
One pursuer was very fast
and caught up with Xuānmèng first.
Upon seeing Xuānmèng's face,
he said:
"Alas,
it is you, my lord!
Please let me turn back and die for you."
Xuānmèng asked:
"What is your name?"
The man turned to run back,
and as he went, replied:
"Why ask for a name?
I am the starving man under the mulberry tree."
He returned to fight and died.
Xuānmèng thus survived.
This is what is called the power of virtue and kindness.
Therefore, bestow kindness on a gentleman,
and the gentleman will bring you blessings;
bestow kindness on a common man,
and the common man will exert his strength for you.
By showing virtue to one person, one saves one's own life—
how much more if kindness is extended to ten thousand people?
Hence it is said:
"No act of virtue is too small,
no grievance is too minor."
How can one not cultivate virtue and eliminate resentment,
striving to benefit others?
Where benefit goes out, blessings return;
where grievances go forth, calamity comes.
What is shaped within is answered without—
one cannot but be cautious.
This is what the *Book of Documents* means by "no virtue is too small."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Valiant are the warriors,
bulwark of the lords."
"With many scholars gathered,
King Wén found peace."
How can a ruler not strive to love his scholars?
6.18 Jìn's Zhào Dùn recommended Hán Jué,
and the Jìn ruler appointed him as Central Army Commandant.
After Zhào Dùn died,
his son Shuò succeeded him as a high minister.
By the third year of Lord Jǐng's reign,
Zhào Shuò served as a general of Jìn.
Shuò married the elder sister of Lord Chéng as his wife.
The senior official Tú'àn Gǔ wanted to exterminate the Zhào clan.
Earlier,
when Zhào Dùn was alive,
he dreamed of Shū Dài holding his waist and weeping,
very sorrowfully;
then laughing,
clapping hands and singing.
Dùn had this divined,
and the omen showed catastrophe followed by recovery.
Zhào's historian Yuán interpreted it:
"This is very ominous,
though not affecting you personally,
it will reach your son,
yet it still stems from your fault.
By your son Zhào Shuò's generation, the decline will worsen."
Tú'àn Gǔ
first gained favor under Lord Líng,
and by Lord Jǐng's time, Gǔ became Minister of Justice.
Planning to incite trouble,
he prosecuted Lord Líng's assassination to implicate Zhào Dùn,
announcing to all generals:
"Zhào Chuān murdered Lord Líng;
though Dùn didn't know,
he remains the chief culprit.
When a subject kills his lord,
and his descendants remain at court,
how can we punish the crime?
I request their execution."
Hán Jué said:
"When Lord Líng was killed,
Zhào Dùn was abroad;
our former lord deemed him innocent,
hence didn't punish him.
Now you wish to execute his posterity—
this contradicts our former lord's intent and constitutes reckless killing.
Reckless killing is called chaos.
For ministers to undertake major affairs without the ruler's knowledge
is to deny the ruler's authority."
Tú'àn Gǔ didn't listen.
Jué urged Zhào Shuò to flee.
Shuò refused,
saying:
"If you ensure the Zhào lineage continues,
I'll die without regret."
Hán Jué promised,
and feigned illness, staying home.
Gǔ, without seeking approval, joined generals attacking the Zhàos at Xiàgōng,
killing Zhào Shuò, Zhào Tóng, Zhào Kuò, Zhào Yīngqí,
exterminating their clan.
Shuò's wife (Lord Chéng's sister),
pregnant,
fled to the ducal palace to hide.
She later bore a son,
whom she nursed.
Shuò's retainer Chéng Yīng carried him away to hide in the mountains.
They stayed fifteen years.
When Lord Jǐng of Jìn fell ill,
divination indicated,
saying:
"The specter is a failed descendant of Dà Yè."
Lord Jǐng asked Hán Jué,
who knew the Zhào orphan lived,
thus said:
"In Jìn, whose lineage from Dà Yè was cut off?
Isn't it the Zhào clan?
Since Zhòng Yǎn, all were of the Yíng surname.
Zhòng Yǎn had a human face and bird's beak,
descended to assist Emperor Dà Wù of Yīn,
and up to the Zhōu kings,
all had illustrious virtue.
Down to the tyrannical Yōu and Lì,
Shū Dài left Zhōu for Jìn,
serving former lord Wén Hóu,
until Lord Chéng's time,
each generation achieved merits,
never losing their sacrifices.
Now only in your reign was the Zhào clan destroyed,
and the people grieve for them,
hence it appears in the turtle and stalks.
I beg you to consider this."
Lord Jǐng asked:
"Does Zhào still have surviving descendants?"
Hán Jué fully disclosed the truth.
Thereupon, Lord Jǐng conspired with Jué to install the Zhào orphan,
summoning and hiding him in the palace.
When the generals entered to inquire about his illness,
Lord Jǐng used Jué's men to compel them to see the Zhào orphan,
named Wǔ.
The generals had no choice,
and said:
"The former Xiàgōng disaster
was Tú'àn Gǔ's doing,
falsely using your order
to command the ministers.
Otherwise,
who would dare rebel!
Had you not fallen ill,
we'd have requested to restore Zhào's heir.
Now your command
is our wish."
Then they summoned Zhào Wǔ and Chéng Yīng to bow to all generals,
who then turned to join Chéng Yīng and Zhào Wǔ attacking Tú'àn Gǔ,
exterminating his clan.
They restored Zhào Wǔ's lands and towns as before.
Thus, how can one be without gratitude?
For those who received kindness here,
attacked in return there—
without Chéng Yīng, the Zhào orphan wouldn't have survived;
without Hán Jué, the Zhào line wouldn't have been restored.
Hán Jué can be said not to forget kindness.
6.19 Qú Bóyù offended the ruler of Wèi,
and fled to Jìn.
A Jìn senior official, Mùmén Zǐgāo,
hosted Qú Bóyù in his home.
After two years,
the Wèi ruler pardoned him and recalled him.
Mùmén Zǐgāo sent his son to escort him to the border,
where Qú Bóyù said:
"This rustic's son may return now."
Later, Mùmén Zǐgāo offended the Jìn ruler,
and sought refuge with Qú Bóyù.
Bóyù spoke to the Wèi ruler:
"Jìn's worthy senior official Mùmén Zǐgāo has offended the Jìn ruler;
I hope you'll treat him with courtesy."
Thereupon, the Wèi ruler welcomed him at the suburbs,
and eventually made him a high minister.
6.20 Běiguō Sāo visited Yànzǐ at his gate, saying:
"I privately admire your righteousness, sir,
and beg for means to support my mother."
Yànzǐ had granary grain and treasury gold brought to give him,
but he declined the gold and accepted the grain.
Some time later,
Yànzǐ fell under suspicion by Lord Jǐng,
and fled.
Běiguōzǐ called his friend and said:
"I admired Yànzǐ's righteousness,
and once begged from him to support my mother.
I've heard it said:
'Those who care for one's parents
should endure hardship for them.'
Now Yànzǐ is suspected;
I'll stake my life to clear him."
He went to the court,
requesting an audience:
"Yànzǐ
is a worthy of the world.
If he leaves Qí,
Qí will surely be invaded.
Rather than see the state invaded,
I'd rather die first—
I beg to cut my throat to vindicate Yànzǐ."
He retreated slowly,
and killed himself.
The lord heard of it,
greatly shocked,
mounted a carriage and personally pursued Yànzǐ,
reaching the state's outskirts,
where he begged him to return.
Yànzǐ, compelled, returned,
and learned Běiguōzǐ had died to clear him.
He sighed deeply:
"I, Yīng, am unworthy,
my faults deserved this,
yet a scholar died to prove my innocence—
how sorrowful!"
6.21 Wú Chìshì was sent as an envoy to the Zhì family,
passing through Wèi.
Nìng Wénzǐ prepared three hundred sets of ramie and fine linen clothing,
intending to present them to him.
Minister Bào said:
"Although Wú is a large state,
we share no border,
and allowing them passage
is already respectful enough.
Why offer additional courtesies?"
Nìng Wénzǐ did not listen,
and proceeded to give the gifts.
When Wú Chìshì reached the Zhì family,
after completing his mission,
he prepared to return to Wú.
Earl Zhì ordered boats to be joined to form a pontoon bridge.
Wú Chìshì said:
"I have heard that
when the Son of Heaven crosses waters,
boats are joined to form a bridge;
when feudal lords cross, boats are linked in rows;
while senior officials use paired boats.
Paired boats
are appropriate for my rank.
Moreover, such excessive respect
must have a reason."
He sent someone to investigate,
and found troops positioned behind,
planning to attack Wèi.
Wú Chìshì said:
"Wèi allowed me passage,
and generously gifted me.
If I see danger and do not warn them,
I would be conspiring with the attackers."
He claimed illness and delayed his departure,
sending word to warn Wèi.
The people of Wèi went on alert,
and when Earl Zhì heard of this,
he stopped the plan.
6.22 Chǔ and Wèi met at Jìnyáng,
planning to attack Qí.
The King of Qí was troubled by this,
and sent for Chúnyú Kūn, saying:
"Chǔ and Wèi are plotting to attack Qí.
I hope you will share this concern with me."
Chúnyú Kūn laughed heartily but did not respond.
The king asked again,
and again he laughed without responding.
After three questions met with three laughs and no response,
the king flushed with anger and said:
"Does my state amuse you?"
Chúnyú Kūn replied:
"I dare not make light of your kingdom.
I was laughing at my neighbor's field sacrifice,
where he offered a box of rice and one crucian carp,
yet prayed:
'May my low-lying, waterlogged fields
yield a hundred cartloads of grain,
and my crab-hills produce abundant crops.'
I laughed because his offering was meager,
yet his demands were great."
The king said:
"Well said."
He rewarded him with a thousand pieces of gold,
a hundred chariots,
and appointed him chief minister.
6.23 Yáng Hǔ, having offended Wèi,
went north to see Jiǎnzǐ and said:
"From now on,
I will never again cultivate people."
Jiǎnzǐ asked:
"Why is that?"
Yáng Hǔ replied:
"Of those in the main hall,
over half were cultivated by me;
of the court officials,
those I established
also number over half;
and of the border officers,
those I appointed
also exceed half.
Yet now those in the main hall
personally urged the ruler to reject me;
the court officials
personally endangered me through legal means;
and the border officers
personally threatened me with arms."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Only the worthy can repay kindness;
the unworthy cannot.
Those who plant peaches and plums
can rest in their shade in summer,
and eat their fruit in autumn;
those who plant thistles and thorns
get no shade in summer,
and are pricked by their thorns in autumn.
Those you cultivated
are thistles and thorns,
not peaches and plums.
From now on,
be selective in whom you cultivate,
rather than cultivating first and selecting later."
6.24 Dōnglúzǐ once enjoyed wealth and status but later became a beggar.
Someone asked him,
saying:
"How did you come to this?"
He replied:
"I know that while I served as prime minister for six or seven years,
I never elevated anyone;
and though I twice possessed thirty million in wealth,
I never enriched anyone.
I realize this was the fault of not recognizing worthy men."
Confucius said:
"Things are difficult indeed.
Whether small or large, many or few,
all incur resentment and dislike—
this is the principle of fate.
If one obtains them,
it is through external borrowing."
6.25 Wèi Wénhóu was conversing with Tián Zǐfāng
while two children dressed in blue and white attended before the ruler.
Zǐfāng asked:
"Are these your favored sons?"
Wénhóu replied:
"No.
Their fathers died in battle,
and these are their young orphans
whom I have taken in."
Zǐfāng said:
"I thought your heart for vengeance was sufficient,
but now it grows stronger.
Since you favor these children,
whose father will you have killed next?"
Wénhóu looked dismayed and said:
"I accept your instruction."
From then on,
he ceased employing arms.
6.26 Wú Qǐ, as a general of Wèi,
attacked Zhōngshān.
A soldier developed a ulcer,
and Wú Qǐ personally sucked out the pus,
making the soldier's mother weep.
Someone asked:
"The general treats your son like this;
why are you weeping?"
She replied:
"Lord Wú sucked this boy's father's wound
and got him killed in the battle of Zhùshuǐ,
where he fell fighting without retreating.
Now he sucks this one's wound—
who knows in which battle this son will die?
That is why I weep."
6.27 When Duke Yì of Qí was still a prince,
he contended for land with Bǐng Chù's father and lost.
After ascending the throne,
he had the father's corpse exhumed and mutilated,
then made Chù his charioteer;
he also took away Yōng Zhī's wife,
and made Zhī his chariot guard.
While the duke was touring Shēn Pond,
the two men were bathing in the pond,
and Chù struck Zhī with a whip,
angering Zhī.
Chù said:
"Someone took your wife, yet you dared not be angry;
one lash from me—
what harm is there?"
Zhī said:
"How does that compare with mutilating one's father without feeling distress?"
They then plotted to kill the duke
and hid his body in a bamboo grove.
6.28 A man from Chǔ presented a giant soft-shelled turtle to Duke Líng of Zhèng.
Prince Jiā saw it.
Prince Sòng's index finger twitched,
and he said to Prince Jiā:
"Whenever my finger twitches like this before,
I am sure to taste some extraordinary delicacy."
When the duke invited his ministers to feast on the turtle,
he summoned Prince Sòng but did not give him any.
Prince Sòng grew angry,
dipped his finger into the cauldron,
tasted it, and left.
The duke was enraged
and wanted to have him killed.
Prince Sòng then conspired with Prince Jiā to strike first,
and they assassinated Duke Líng.
Zǐxià said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals records instances of rulers not acting as rulers,
ministers not as ministers,
fathers not as fathers,
and sons not as sons.
These are not matters of a single day
but have developed gradually to reach such a state."
7.1 Governance has three grades:
the governance of a true king transforms the people;
it transforms them.
The governance of a hegemon intimidates the people;
it intimidates them.
The governance of a mere powerful state coerces the people;
it coerces them.
These three each have their application,
but transformation is the most noble.
When transformation fails to bring change, then intimidation is used;
when intimidation fails to bring change, then coercion is used;
when coercion fails to bring change, then punishment is applied.
As for reaching the point of punishment,
it is not what a true king values.
Therefore, the sage kings prioritize moral education and only then apply penalties,
establishing honor and shame to clearly set up defenses and prohibitions,
exalting the rules of ritual and righteousness to demonstrate them,
and debasing the harms of material profit to change the people.
By cultivating what is near and putting internal affairs in order,
rectifying the rituals of key mechanisms,
and unifying the relationships between spouses,
then those below will all admire the glory of righteousness and ritual
and detest the shame of greed and disorder.
The means by which this is achieved
is through transformation.
7.2 Jìsūn asked Confucius:
"What if one were to kill those without virtue
to get closer to those with virtue?
What would you say?"
Confucius said:
"In your governance,
why use killing?
If you desire goodness, the people will be good.
The virtue of a gentleman is like the wind;
the virtue of a petty person is like grass.
When the wind blows over the grass, it must bend."
This speaks of making transformation clear.
7.3 Governing a state has two key mechanisms:
punishment and virtue.
A true king emphasizes virtue and seldom uses punishment;
a hegemon combines punishment and virtue;
a powerful state uses punishment first and virtue later.
Punishment and virtue
are the means by which transformation arises.
Virtue
nurtures goodness and promotes the remedying of shortcomings;
punishment
chastises evil and prevents future wrongdoing.
Thus, the highest form of virtuous transformation leads to rewards,
while the severest form of punishment leads to execution.
Execution and rewards
are used to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy,
and to rank the meritorious and the unmeritorious.
Therefore, execution and rewards must not be erroneous,
for if they are, good and evil become confused.
If there is merit but no reward, then goodness is not encouraged;
if there is fault but no punishment, then evil is not feared.
I have never heard of anyone who could transform the world through action
without encouraging goodness and making evil fearful.
The Book of Documents says:
"Exert full effort in rewards and punishments."
This is what it means.
7.4 When water is turbid, the fish are in distress;
when decrees are harsh, the people are in turmoil;
when city walls are steep, they will surely collapse;
when riverbanks are high, they will surely crumble.
Therefore, governing a state is like tuning a zither:
if the large strings are too tight, the small strings will snap.
Hence it is said:
"One who pulls the reins too tightly
is not a driver for a thousand-mile journey."
The sound that has a voice
does not carry beyond a hundred miles;
the sound without a voice
reaches to the four seas.
Thus, when emoluments exceed one's merit, they are reduced;
when reputation exceeds reality, it is diminished.
When one's conduct matches one's true nature and reputation corresponds to it,
then fortune and misfortune do not come in vain.
The Book of Songs says:
"Why does he stay?
He must have a reason.
Why does he linger?
He must have a cause."
This is what it means.
7.5 Gōngshū Wénzǐ served as the Lìngyǐn of Chǔ.
After three years,
no one dared to come to the court.
Gōngshūzǐ visited and said:
"It is too severe."
Wénzǐ said:
"If the court is severe,
how could it harm the governance of the state?"
Gōngshūzǐ replied:
"Severity silences those below;
when those below are silent, those above are deaf.
Deafness and silence cannot communicate;
how can the state be governed?
I have heard that
following the needle and thread completes a curtain,
combining pints and bushels fills the granary,
and uniting small streams forms rivers and seas.
An enlightened ruler
may receive commands and not act on them,
but there has never been one who does not receive them at all."
7.6 Duke Líng of Wèi said to Confucius:
"Someone told me
that if one who governs a state is cautious in the temple and court,
then the state will be well-governed.
Is this possible?"
Confucius said:
"It is possible.
Those who love others will be loved by them;
those who hate others will be hated by them.
Those who understand that they can gain from themselves
also understand that others can gain from them.
This is what is called knowing the world without leaving one's humble room,
by reflecting on oneself."
7.7 Zǐgòng asked Confucius about governing the people,
and Confucius said:
"Be as cautious as if driving a galloping horse with a rotten rein."
Zǐgòng said:
"Why so fearful?"
Confucius said:
"In a prosperous state, all are people.
If guided by the Way, they are like my livestock;
if not guided by the Way, they become my enemies.
How can one not be fearful?"
7.8 Duke Huán of Qí said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I wish to undertake affairs in the state
as clearly as the sun and moon,
so that even every simple man and woman says it is good.
Is this possible?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It is possible,
but it is not the way of a sage."
Duke Huán said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"A short rope cannot draw water from a deep well, and limited knowledge cannot grasp the words of a sage.
With a benevolent scholar, one can discuss things;
with a wise scholar, one can discuss the boundless;
with a sage, one can discuss the divine and enlightened.
What a sage does
is beyond the reach of ordinary people.
If the people know ten times more than you, they will still contend with you,
saying:
'You are not as good as I am.'
If a hundred times more, they will find fault with your errors;
if a thousand times more, they will not believe you at all.
Therefore, the people cannot be controlled by slight means,
but can be gathered and guided;
they cannot be violently suppressed,
but can be directed and led;
the masses cannot be persuaded household by household,
but can be shown by example."
7.9 Duke Líng of Wèi asked Shǐ Qiū, saying:
"In governance, what is the most urgent matter?"
Shǐ Qiū replied:
"The administration of justice is the most urgent.
If judgments in hearing lawsuits are unjust,
the dead cannot be brought back to life,
and the severed cannot be rejoined.
Therefore it is said:
The administration of justice is the most urgent."
A little later,
Zǐlù appeared before the duke.
The duke told him what Shǐ Qiū had said,
Zǐlù said:
"The duties of the Minister of War are the most urgent.
When two states face conflict,
and two armies confront each other,
the Minister of War takes up the drumstick to direct the battle.
If one engagement is mishandled,
tens of thousands may die.
Though killing people is considered wrong,
in this case the number of people killed can be enormous.
Therefore it is said:
The duties of the Minister of War are the most urgent."
A little later,
Zǐgòng entered for an audience.
The duke told him what the two men had said,
Zǐgòng said:
"How ignorant they are!
Long ago, Yǔ battled with the Yǒuhù clan,
and after three engagements they still would not submit.
Yǔ then cultivated education for a year,
and the Yǒuhù clan requested to submit.
Therefore it is said:
Remove what the people contend over,
then what lawsuits are there to hear?
If weapons and armor are not arrayed,
then what drums are there to beat?
Therefore it is said:
Education is the most urgent matter."
7.10 Duke Huán of Qí went out hunting,
chased a deer and followed it into a mountain valley,
where he saw an old man and asked him,
saying:
"What valley is this?"
The old man replied:
"It is called Foolish Old Man's Valley."
Duke Huán said:
"Why is it called that?"
He replied:
"It is named after me."
Duke Huán said:
"Now looking at your appearance and demeanor,
you do not seem to be a foolish man.
Why is it named after you?"
He replied:
"Allow me to explain.
I used to keep a母牛,
which bore a calf that grew large,
so I sold it and bought a colt.
A young man said:
'A cow cannot give birth to a horse.'
Then he took the colt away.
My neighbors heard about this,
and considered me foolish,
hence they named this valley Foolish Old Man's Valley."
Duke Huán said:
"You certainly were foolish!
Why did you give it to him?"
Duke Huán then returned.
The next day at court,
he told Guǎn Zhòng about it.
Guǎn Zhòng straightened his lapels, bowed twice, and said:
"This reveals my foolishness.
If Yáo were on the throne,
and Gāo Yáo were administering justice,
how could there be anyone who would take another's colt?
If this old man had encountered such violence,
he certainly would not have given it to him.
This old man knew that litigation was unjust,
so he gave it to him.
I request to retire and improve the governance."
Confucius said:
"Disciples, remember this.
Duke Huán
was a hegemon lord;
Guǎn Zhòng
was a worthy minister.
Yet even they could mistake wisdom for foolishness,
how much more those who are inferior to Duke Huán and Guǎn Zhòng!"
7.11 In Lǔ, there was a case of a father and son suing each other.
Kāngzǐ said:
"Execute them."
Confucius said:
"They should not be executed.
The people have long been unaware that father and son litigating is wrong!
This is the fault of those above.
If those above govern rightly,
such people would not exist."
Kāngzǐ said:
"Governing the people is based on filial piety.
Now by executing one person to punish unfilial conduct,
is that not acceptable?"
Confucius said:
To execute someone for being unfilial
is to cruelly kill the innocent.
When the three armies suffer a great defeat,
you cannot punish all;
when lawsuits are not properly managed,
you cannot apply punishments.
If those above display the teachings and first practice them themselves,
then the common people will follow like the wind.
If personal example is not followed,
and only then punishments are applied,
then the people will know their offense.
A wall of seven feet,
people cannot climb over;
a mountain of seven hundred feet,
children can ascend and play on it—
because it slopes gradually.
Now the gradual decline of benevolence and righteousness has been long!
Can you say the people will not transgress?
The Book of Songs says:
'Make the people not go astray.'
In the past,
the gentleman guided his people and did not let them go astray,
therefore intimidation and severity were unnecessary,
and punishments were set aside and not used."
When the litigants heard this,
they requested to withdraw their lawsuit.
7.12 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius about governance.
Confucius replied:
"Good governance makes the people wealthy and long-lived."
Duke Āi said:
"What does that mean?"
Confucius said:
"Light taxes make the people wealthy;
avoiding unnecessary tasks keeps them from crime;
staying away from crime makes the people long-lived."
The duke said:
"If so, then I would become poor."
Confucius said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'Kindly and gentle君子,
the parent of the people.'
Never has there been a case where the child is wealthy and the parent poor."
7.13 King Wén asked Lǚ Wàng:
"How should one rule the world?"
Lǚ Wàng replied:
"A kingly state enriches the people;
a hegemonic state enriches the scholars;
a barely surviving state enriches the high officials;
a state without the Way enriches the storehouses and treasuries.
This is called the top overflowing while the bottom leaks."
King Wén said:
"Good."
Lǚ Wàng replied:
"It is inauspicious to delay good actions."
That very day,
he opened the storehouses and treasuries to relieve the widowers, widows, orphans, and childless.
7.14 King Wǔ asked Tàigōng:
"What is the way to govern a state?"
Tàigōng replied:
"The way to govern a state
is simply to love the people."
King Wǔ said:
"How does one love the people?"
Tàigōng said:
"Benefit them and do not harm them;
help them succeed and do not cause them to fail;
let them live and do not kill them;
give to them and do not take from them;
make them happy and do not make them suffer;
delight them and do not anger them—
this is the way to govern a state,
the principle of guiding the people,
simply to love them.
If the people lose their occupations,
that harms them;
if farmers miss their seasons,
that causes them to fail;
if the guilty are heavily punished,
that kills them;
if taxes are heavy,
that takes from them;
if there are many corvée duties exhausting the people's strength,
that makes them suffer;
if they are wearied and harassed,
that angers them.
Therefore, those skilled in governing a state
treat the people as parents love their children,
as elder brothers love their younger brothers.
They grieve to hear of their hunger and cold,
and pity to see their toil and hardship."
7.15 King Wǔ asked of Tàigōng:
"How does a worthy ruler govern the state?"
He replied:
"When a worthy ruler governs the state,
his administration is equitable,
his officials are not harsh,
his tax collections are moderate,
his personal maintenance is frugal,
and he does not let private favors harm public law.
Rewards are not bestowed on the meritless,
punishments are not inflicted on the innocent;
he does not reward out of personal pleasure,
nor execute out of personal anger;
those who harm the people are deemed guilty,
those who recommend the worthy and point out faults are rewarded.
The inner palace is not neglected,
petitions from women are not heeded;
those above do not indulge in debauchery,
those below do not secretly harm others;
he does not lavish palaces to waste wealth,
nor multiply sightseeing towers and ponds to exhaust the people,
nor carve patterns and engravings to please the eyes and ears.
The government stores are not rotten or worm-eaten,
the state has no wandering or starving people.
This is how a worthy ruler governs the state."
King Wǔ said:
"Excellent!"
7.16 King Wǔ asked of Tàigōng:
"Why is it that those who govern states frequently change laws and orders?"
Tàigōng said:
"Those who govern states and frequently change laws and orders
do not take law as law,
but make law according to what they personally prefer.
Thus when orders are issued, chaos ensues,
and when chaos ensues, they change the laws again,
hence their laws and orders are frequently changed."
7.17 King Chéng asked about governance from Yǐn Yì:
"What virtue must I practice
for the people to be close to their superiors?"
He replied:
"Employ them seasonally and respectfully comply with them,
be loyal and love them,
issue orders credibly and do not go back on your word."
The King said:
"To what extent should this caution reach?"
He replied:
"As if facing a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice."
The King said:[54"Terrifying!"
He replied:
"Between heaven and earth,
within the four seas,
if treated well they are our charge,
if treated poorly they become our enemies.
In former times, the ministers of Xià and Yīn
turned against Jié and Zhòu to become ministers to Tāng and Wǔ;
the people of Sùshā
attacked their own lord and returned to Shénnóngshì.
This is well known to you, my lord,
so how can you not be fearful?"
7.18 Zhòngní visited the Lord of Sòng,
the Lord of Sòng asked Zhòngní:
"I wish to long possess the state;
I wish to obtain the allegiance of all cities;
I wish to make the people tranquil and unconfused;
I wish to make the officers exhaust their efforts;
I wish to make the sun and moon appear at proper times;
I wish to make the sages come of themselves;
I wish to make the government offices well-governed.
How can this be done?"
Zhòngní replied:
"Lords of a thousand chariots,
rulers of ten thousand chariots,
many have questioned Qiū,
none have asked Qiū about methods like you, my lord, have,
yet all can be obtained.
Qiū has heard that
when two rulers are close, then the state is long possessed;
when the ruler is benevolent and the ministers loyal, then all cities are obtained;
do not kill the innocent,
do not release the guilty,
then the people will not be confused;
increase the officers' emoluments and rewards, then they will exhaust their efforts;
revere heaven and respect spirits, then the sun and moon will appear at proper times;
be good at punishments, then the sages will come of themselves;
honor the worthy and employ the capable, then the government offices will be well-governed."
The Lord of Sòng said:
"How could it be otherwise!"
7.19 Zǐgòng said:
"Duke Yè asked the Master about governance,
the Master said:
'Governance lies in attracting those nearby and drawing those from afar.'
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked the Master about governance,
the Master said:
'Governance lies in instructing the ministers.'
Duke Jǐng of Qí asked the Master about governance,
the Master said:
'Governance lies in economizing expenditures.'
Three lords asked the Master about governance,
the Master answered them differently,
so then is governance different?"
Confucius said:
"The land of Jīng was vast but its capital narrow,
the people had intentions to leave,
therefore it was said:
'Governance lies in attracting those nearby and drawing those from afar.'
Duke Āi had three ministers,
who internally colluded to delude their lord,
externally blocked the feudal lords and guests,
to obscure his clarity,
therefore it was said:
'Governance lies in instructing the ministers.'
Duke Jǐng of Qí was extravagant with towers and pavilions,
excessive with parks and preserves,
the music of the five offices never ceased,
once he bestowed the rank of hundred-chariot households three times in a single morning,
therefore it was said:
'Governance lies in economizing expenditures.'
These three things
are all governance.
Does the Book of Songs not say,
'With disorder and separation comes this distress,
where then is the fitting place to return?'
This laments separation and dispersion leading to disorder;
'Not that they cease their duties,
but they become the king's burden.'
This laments treacherous ministers obscuring the lord leading to disorder;
'Bringing disorder, destroying resources,
they have never benefitted our multitude.'
This laments extravagance and lack of restraint leading to disorder.
Examining what these three desired,
could governance be the same for them!"
7.20 Gōngyí Xiū was minister of Lǔ,
when the Lord of Lǔ died,
his attendants requested to close the gates.
Gōngyí Xiū said:
"Stop!
I taxed not the pools and deeps,
I levied not on Méng Mountain,
I promulgated no harsh orders,
I have already closed my heart,
why close the gates!"
7.21 Zǐchǎn was minister of Zhèng,
Duke Jiǎn said to Zǐchǎn:
"Internal affairs should not go out,
external affairs should not come in.
If robes and furs are not beautiful,
if chariots and horses are not adorned,
if sons and daughters are not pure,
that is my disgrace.
If the state is not well-governed,
if the borders are not properly maintained,
that is your disgrace."
Zǐchǎn served as minister of Zhèng,
throughout Duke Jiǎn's lifetime,
there was no disorder within the state,
and no trouble from the feudal lords without.
When Zǐchǎn conducted government,
he selected the capable and employed them.
Féng Jiǎnzǐ was good at deciding matters.
Zǐ Tàishū was good at decisions and was cultivated.
Gōngsūn Huī knew the affairs of the four states,
and could distinguish the clan names of their great officers,
could quickly respond as situations arose,
and was also good at diplomatic language.
Pí Chén was good at planning,
when planning in the wild he succeeded,
when planning in the city he did not.
When there was business, they would carry Pí Chén
and go with him to the wild,
have him plan what was feasible,
then tell Féng Jiǎnzǐ to decide it,
have Gōngsūn Huī compose the diplomatic language,
when completed,
it would be given to Zǐ Tàishū to implement,
to respond to guests,
thus they rarely had failed affairs.
7.22 Dǒng Ānyú was governing Jìnyáng,
and he asked about governance from an elder of Jiǎn,
who said:
"It is about loyalty,
about trustworthiness,
about courage."
Dǒng Ānyú asked:
"How should I be loyal?"
The reply was:
"Be loyal to your lord."
He asked:
"How should I be trustworthy?"
The reply was:
"Be trustworthy in carrying out orders."
He asked:
"How should I be courageous?"
The reply was:
"Be courageous in dealing with wicked people."
Dǒng Ānyú said:
"These three principles are sufficient!"
7.23 Marquis Wén of Wèi sent Xīmén Bào to govern Yè,
instructing him:
"You must achieve complete success, establish a reputation, and spread righteousness."
Bào asked:
"May I ask how to achieve complete success, establish a reputation, and spread righteousness,
and what should be done to accomplish this?"
Marquis Wén said:
"As you go there,
know that there is no town without worthy and eminent people, or those skilled in debate and broad learning;
and no town without those who enjoy exposing others' faults and concealing others' virtues.
When you arrive, be sure to consult the eminent and worthy,
and thereby draw close to them;
as for those skilled in debate and broad learning,
take them as teachers;
and regarding those who enjoy exposing others' faults,
or concealing others' virtues,
observe them carefully.
Do not act solely based on what you hear.
For hearing about something
is not as good as seeing it with your own eyes;
seeing it with your own eyes
is not as good as stepping onto it with your feet;
stepping onto it with your feet
is not as good as discerning it with your hands.
When one first enters office,
it is like entering a dark room;
over time, it becomes brighter,
and with brightness comes good governance,
and with good governance, actions can be carried out."
7.24 Fú Zǐjiàn governed Dānfù,
playing his melodious zither,
without ever leaving his hall,
yet Dānfù was well-governed.
Wū Mǎqī also governed Dānfù,
leaving at starlight,
returning by starlight,
without rest day or night,
personally involved in everything,
and Dānfù was also well-governed.
Wū Mǎqī asked Fú Zǐjiàn the reason for this,
and Fú Zǐjiàn said:
"My method is called employing people,
yours is called employing effort.
Employing effort inevitably toils,
employing people naturally rests."
People said:
"Fú Zǐjiàn is indeed a gentleman,
resting his limbs,
preserving his senses,
calming his mind and energy, yet all officials are well-governed,
simply by applying his methods.
Wū Mǎqī, however, is not so;
he exhausts his nature with affairs,
laboring and troubling with instructions,
and though he governs well,
he has not yet reached the ultimate."
7.25 Confucius said to Fú Zǐjiàn:
"You govern Dānfù and the people are pleased;
tell me how you achieve this."
He replied:
"I treat their fathers as my father,
their sons as my sons,
sympathize with the orphans, and grieve in funeral matters."
Confucius said:
"Good,
but these are minor virtues;
the common people are attached,
yet it is still not enough."
He said:
treat three men as fathers,
five men as elder brothers,
and befriend eleven others."
Confucius said:
"Treating three as fathers
can teach filial piety;
treating five as elder brothers
can teach fraternal respect;
befriending eleven
can teach learning.
These are moderate virtues;
the average people are attached,
yet it is still not enough."
He said:
"Among the people here, there are five more worthy than I,
whom I serve,
and they all teach me the methods of governance."
Confucius said:
"The greater aim
lies precisely in this.
In the past, Yáo and Shùn humbled themselves,
to observe and listen to the world,
striving to attract worthy men.
For promoting the worthy
is the source of all blessings,
and the master of spiritual intelligence.
Alas!
That what Fú Zǐjiàn governs is small;
if what he governed were great,
he would succeed Yáo and Shùn."
7.26 Fú Zǐjiàn was to become magistrate of Dānfù,
and took leave of the Master.
The Master said:
"Do not reject others as they approach,
nor consent at a glance.
Consenting easily loses your stance,
rejecting blocks communication,
like a high mountain or deep abyss,
looking up, its summit cannot be reached,
measuring, its depth cannot be fathomed."
Zǐjiàn said:
"Well said,
how dare I not accept your instruction!"
7.27 Fú Zǐjiàn was to become magistrate of Dānfù,
and visited Yáng Zhòu,
saying:
"Do you have any advice to send me off with?"
Yáng Zhòu said:
"I was of low status in youth,
and do not know the art of governing people,
but I have two principles of fishing,
which I offer to you."
Zǐjiàn said:
"What are the principles of fishing?"
Yáng Zhòu said:
"When you cast the line and bait,
those that rush to bite are the yángqiáo fish,
which are meager and not tasty;
those that seem interested yet not,
nibbling but not biting, are the bream,
which are plump and richly flavored."
Fú Zǐjiàn said:
"Excellent."
Then, before reaching Dānfù,
those in official carriages and canopies welcoming him
crowded the roads.
Zǐjiàn said:
"Drive on,
drive on,
these are the so-called yángqiáo that Yáng Zhòu mentioned."
Upon arriving in Dānfù,
he invited the respected elders and worthy sages to join him in governing Dānfù.
7.28 Confucius had a nephew named Kǒng Miè
who held office along with Fú Zǐjiàn.
Confucius visited Kǒng Miè and asked him:
"Since you assumed office,
what have you gained and what have you lost?"
Kǒng Miè replied:
"Since I took office, I've gained nothing
but lost three things.
They are:
Official duties are overwhelming,
leaving no time to practice my studies,
thus my learning fails to improve —
this is the first loss;
my salary is meager,
insufficient to provide porridge for my relatives,
so they've grown more distant —
this is the second loss;
public affairs are often urgent,
leaving no time to console mourners or visit the sick,
thus my friends have become more distant —
this is the third loss."
Confucius was displeased
and went to see Zǐjiàn, asking:
"Since you assumed office,
what have you gained and what have you lost?"
Zǐjiàn said:
"Since I took office,
I've lost nothing
but gained three things:
the texts I once memorized,
I now practice and implement,
so my learning grows clearer daily —
this is the first gain;
though my salary is small,
it provides enough porridge for my relatives,
so they've grown closer —
this is the second gain;
though public affairs are urgent,
I visit mourners and the sick diligently at night,
so my friends have become closer —
this is the third gain."
Confucius said to Zǐjiàn:
"A noble person indeed is this man!
A noble person indeed is this man!
If Lǔ lacked noble persons,
where would he have learned this!"
7.29 Yànzǐ governed Dōng'ē
for three years.
Duke Jǐng summoned and reproached him:
"I thought you capable
and put you in charge of Dōng'ē,
yet now you've governed it into chaos.
Withdraw and examine yourself,
for I shall impose severe punishment on you."
Yànzǐ replied:
"I request to change my methods and govern Dōng'ē differently.
If in three years I fail to govern it well,
I beg to die for it."
Duke Jǐng agreed.
The following year during the financial report,
the Duke welcomed him joyfully:
"Excellent indeed!
Your governance of Dōng'ē!"
Yànzǐ responded:
"When I previously governed Dōng'ē,
I refused special requests,
accepted no bribes,
and used fish from ponds
to benefit the poor.
At that time,
no one went hungry,
yet you faulted me.
Now that I govern Dōng'ē again,
I allow special requests,
accept bribes,
increase taxes excessively,
reduce treasury deposits,
curry favor with your attendants,
and let fish from ponds
go to powerful families.
Now,
over half the people starve,
yet you welcome and praise me.
I am too foolish to govern Dōng'ē further,
I wish to retire
and make way for worthy men."
He bowed twice and withdrew.
Duke Jǐng left his mat and apologized:
"Please resume governing Dōng'ē.
Let Dōng'ē
be your Dōng'ē —
I will not interfere again."
7.30 Zǐlù was to govern Pú.
He visited Confucius and said:
"I wish to receive your instruction."
Confucius said:
"Pú has many strong warriors,
making it hard to govern.
But I tell you:
Be reverent and respectful
to restrain the brave;
be broad-minded and upright
to embrace the multitude;
be respectful and pure
to draw close to superiors."
7.31 Zǐgòng was appointed magistrate of Xìnyáng.
He took leave of Confucius,
who said:
"Exert effort appropriately,
follow heaven's timing,
neither rob nor attack,
neither tyrannize nor steal."
Zǐgòng asked:
"Since youth I've served you, noble sir.
Can a noble man actually steal?"
Confucius replied:
"When the unworthy attack the worthy,
that is robbery.
When the worthy attack the unworthy,
that is aggression.
To enforce laws laxly
but punish harshly
is tyranny.
To claim others' merits as your own
is theft.
The noble man's theft
needn't involve money.
I have heard:
Those who know governance
uphold laws to benefit the people;
those who don't
twist laws to oppress them,
which breeds resentment.
In office, nothing equals impartiality;
with wealth, nothing equals integrity.
Guarding integrity and impartiality
makes one unassailable.
To conceal others' goodness
is to obscure the worthy;
to publicize others' faults
is petty.
Not teaching internally but slandering externally
shows untrustworthiness.
Speaking of others' merits
brings gain without loss or harm;
speaking of others' faults
brings no gain but harm.
Thus the noble man is cautious in speech,
not putting self before others,
choosing words carefully,
making mouth and ear alike."
7.32 Yáng Zhū visited King of Liáng,
saying governing the world was like moving something in his palm.
The King said:
"You can't manage one wife and one concubine,
nor tend a three-acre garden,
yet claim governing the world is palm-moving.
Why?"
Yáng Zhū replied:
"I have my reasons.
Haven't you seen shepherds?
A hundred sheep in a flock
can be led by a child with a stick
east or west
as he wishes.
But if you make Yáo lead one sheep
and Shùn follow with a stick,
chaos begins.
I've heard:
The fish that swallows boats doesn't swim in shallows;
the swan flying high avoids filthy ponds.
Why?
Their aims are extremely far.
The huángzhōng and dàlǚ tones
can't accompany intricate dances.
Why?
Their notes are sparse.
Those governing great things don't bother with small;
achieving great deeds doesn't require petty scrutiny.
This illustrates it."
7.33 Jǐng Chā was minister of Zhèng.
A man of Zhèng waded winter waters
and emerged with chilled legs.
Later, Jǐng Chā passed by,
descended his carriage to take him in,
and covered him with his robe.
Shū Xiàng heard of it and said:
"As minister of a state,
Jǐngzǐ is surely incompetent!
I hear good officials,
within three months repair ditches and canals,
within ten months complete bridges and ferries,
so even livestock don't wet their feet,
let alone people!"
7.34 Wèi Wénhóu asked Lǐ Kè:
"How should a state be governed?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that the way to govern a state
is to provide food to those who labor and stipends to those with merit,
employ the capable and ensure rewards are carried out,
and punishments are justly applied."
Wénhóu said:
"My rewards and punishments are all just, yet the people do not support me.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"Could it be that the state has profligate people?
Your servant has heard it said:
'Take away the stipends from the profligate,
to attract scholars from all directions.'
Their fathers had merit and received stipends,
but their sons consume without merit.
When they go out, they ride in carriages and horses,
wear fine furs,
considering it glorious;
when they come in, they cultivate the sounds of zithers and stone chimes,
and indulge in the pleasures of their children,
thereby corrupting the teachings of the local communities.
For such people, take away their stipends to attract scholars from all directions.
This is what is called taking from the profligate."
7.35 Qí Huángōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What should a state fear in governance?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"The fear is the shrine rats."
Huángōng said:
"What does that mean?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"The shrine is built of bundled wood and plastered with clay,
and rats take refuge there.
If you smoke them out, you fear burning the wood;
if you flood them out, you fear ruining the plaster.
The reason these rats cannot be killed
is because of the shrine.
The state also has its shrine rats,
and they are the ruler's attendants.
Internally, they conceal good and evil from the ruler;
externally, they sell authority and influence to the common people.
If not punished, they cause chaos;
if punished, they are protected and upheld by the ruler,
who shelters and favors them.
These are the state's shrine rats.
There was a wine seller
who kept his vessels very clean,
and his shop sign was very prominent,
yet his wine turned sour and did not sell.
He asked his neighbors the reason,
and they said:
'Your dog is fierce;
when people bring their vessels
and come to buy your wine,
the dog rushes to bite them.
This is why your wine sours and does not sell.'
The state also has its fierce dogs,
and they are the officials in power.
When scholars with wisdom and methods
wish to enlighten the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
the officials in power rush to slander them.
These are the state's fierce dogs.
If attendants are shrine rats
and officials in power are fierce dogs,
then scholars with wisdom and methods cannot be employed.
This is what a state should fear in governance."
7.36 The Marquis of Qí asked Yànzǐ:
"What should governance fear?"
He replied:
"The fear is not distinguishing good from evil."
The Marquis said:
"How can one discern this?"
He replied:
"Carefully select your attendants.
If your attendants are good, then all officials will find their proper places,
and good and evil will be distinguished."
Confucius heard this and said:
"These words are indeed true!
If good words are advanced,
then bad ones have no way to enter;
if good words are not advanced,
then good ones have no way to enter."
7.37 The ruler of Fùgǎo visited Qí in court,
and Huángōng asked him about governing the people.
The ruler of Fùgǎo did not reply,
but instead touched his mouth,
pulled his lapel,
and pressed his heart.
Huángōng said:
"Share the sweet and bitter, hunger and cold with the people!
He considers me a sage,
thus conveying without words."
Thereupon, he honored him with a thousand in gold.
7.38 During the time of Jìn Wéngōng,
a man from Dí presented furs of large foxes and patterned leopards.
Wéngōng sighed and lamented:
"What crime have the large foxes and patterned leopards committed!
Their crime is their fur."
Grand Officer Luán Zhī said:
"If the land is vast but not leveled,
and wealth is amassed but not distributed,
is that not the crime of the foxes and leopards?"
Wéngōng said:
"Well said!
Explain it."
Luán Zhī said:
"If the land is vast but not leveled,
people will level it;
if wealth is amassed but not distributed,
people will contend for it."
Thereupon, he allotted land to divide among the people
and distributed wealth to relieve the poor.
7.39 Jìn Wénhóu asked Jiù Fàn about governance,
and Jiù Fàn replied:
"Sharing cooked food is not as good as sharing raw meat;
sharing raw meat is not as good as sharing land.
Dividing it to distribute among the people and increasing their ranks and stipends
is how the ruler gains land and the people know wealth,
and the ruler loses land and the people know poverty.
What ancient times called inciting the army to fight
refers to this very idea."
7.40 The Marquis of Jìn asked Shì Wénbó:
"On the first day of the third month,
there was a solar eclipse.
I am confused in my learning;
the Odes say, 'That sun is eclipsed,
how inauspicious it is'—
what does this mean?"
He replied:
"It refers to poor governance.
If the state lacks proper governance,
and does not employ the good,
then it brings censure upon itself through the disasters of the sun and moon,
so governance must be handled with care.
There are three aspects to governance.
First:
follow the people;
second:
select the right persons;
third:
accord with the times."
7.41 Yánlíng Jìzǐ traveled to Jìn.
Entering its borders,
he said:
"Alas,
how oppressive this state is!"
Entering its capital,
he said:
"Alas,
how exhausted its people's strength is!"
Standing in its court,
he said:
"Alas,
how chaotic this state is!"
His followers said:
"Master, you have not been long in Jìn's borders;
how can you be so certain in your judgments?"
Yánlíng Jìzǐ said:
"Indeed,
I entered its borders
and saw the fields overgrown and uncultivated,
with weeds growing tall,
so I knew the state's oppression.
I entered its capital
and saw new houses shabby while old ones fine,
new walls low while old ones high,
so I knew its people's strength is exhausted.
I stood in its court
and saw the ruler able to observe but not inquiring of his subordinates,
and his ministers skilled in boasting but not remonstrating with their superior,
so I knew the state's chaos."
7.42 The reason why Qí fell short of Lǔ was that
Tàigōng's worthiness
did not match that of Bóqín.
Bóqín and Tàigōng both received their fiefs and went to their respective states.
After three years,
Tàigōng came to court,
and Zhōugōng asked him:
"How have you governed so swiftly?"
He replied:
"By honoring the worthy,
putting the distant before the close,
and righteousness before benevolence."
This is the way of a hegemon.
Zhōugōng said:
"Tàigōng's influence will last for five generations."
After five years,
Bóqín came to court,
and Zhōugōng asked him:
"Why has your governance been so difficult?"
He replied:
"By cherishing the close,
putting the inner before the outer,
and benevolence before righteousness."
This is the way of a true king.
Zhōugōng said:
"Lǔ's influence will last for ten generations."
Thus, Lǔ possessed the traces of kingship
due to its benevolence and generosity;
Qí had the traces of hegemony
due to its martial governance.
The reason why Qí fell short of Lǔ,
was that Tàigōng's worthiness,
did not match that of Bóqín.
7.43 Duke Jǐng favored women dressing in men's attire,
and all the people in the state followed suit.
The duke ordered officials to prohibit it,
saying:
"Any woman dressed as a man
shall have her clothes torn
and her belt severed."
Torn clothes and severed belts were seen everywhere, yet the practice did not stop.
Yànzǐ had an audience,
and the duke said:
"I ordered officials to prohibit women from dressing as men,
tearing their clothes,
and severing their belts,
yet it is seen everywhere and does not stop.
Why is that?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Your Highness allows it within the palace,
yet prohibits it outside;
it is like hanging a cow's head at the gate
while trying to sell horse meat.
Why not forbid it inside the palace,
then none outside would dare to do it."
The duke said:
"Well said."
He forbade it inside the palace,
and within less than a month,
no one in the state did it anymore.
7.44 The people of Qí greatly enjoyed bumping carriage hubs against each other for fun,
and prohibitions could not stop it.
Yànzǐ was troubled by this,
so he prepared a new carriage and fine horses,
went out and bumped hubs with others,
saying:
"Bumping hubs is inauspicious;
could it be that my sacrifices were improper,
or my daily conduct disrespectful?"
He then alighted,
abandoned the carriage, and left.
After that, the people of the state ceased the practice.
Hence it is said:
"To prohibit by decree
without setting an example oneself,
the people will not stop.
Thus, to transform their hearts, nothing is better than teaching."
7.45 According to the law of the state of Lǔ,
if any person from Lǔ ransomed servants or concubines from other feudal lords,
they could receive payment from the treasury.
Zǐgòng ransomed someone from another state but returned the payment.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"Cì missed the point!
When a sage acts,
it should be to change customs and practices,
and his teachings should be applicable to the common people,
not just suit his own conduct.
Now in Lǔ, the rich are few and the poor many;
if accepting payment for ransoming
is deemed corrupt,
but not accepting it
means no one will ransom again.
From now on,
people of Lǔ will no longer ransom others."
Confucius can be said to have understood transformation.
Therefore, Lǎozǐ said:
"Perceiving the small is called clarity."
7.46 Confucius visited Jì Kāngzǐ,
but Kāngzǐ was not pleased,
so Confucius visited him again.
Zǎi Yǔ said:
"I have heard our Master say:
'If kings and dukes do not invite,
one does not act.'
Now you have visited the Minister of Justice quite a few times."
Confucius said:
"In Lǔ, the multitude oppresses each other,
and armed violence prevails;
this has lasted long,
yet the authorities do not govern.
What invitation could be greater than this!"
The people of Lǔ heard this and said:
"The sage is about to bring order;
should we not first impose punishments on ourselves?"
From then on,
there were no more conflicts in the state.
Confucius said to his disciples:
"Ten lǐ from the mountain,
the sound of cicadas
can still be heard;
governance is no different—it must be close and attentive."
7.47 In ancient customs of Lǔ,
the village of Túlǐ,
the nets of Luómén,
and the fishing of Xuànmén,
all uniquely adhered to propriety.
Therefore, Confucius praised them.
In the village of Túlǐ,
the wealthy provided for the poor;
in the nets of Luómén,
those with kin took more,
those without took less;
in the fishing of Xuànmén,
those with kin took the large catch,
those without took the small.
7.48 The *Spring and Autumn Annals* say:
"When the four classes are balanced, the kingly way flourishes and the people are at peace."
The so-called four classes
are scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
7.49 If the way of marriage is abandoned,
then the proper relations between men and women are disrupted,
and the path to licentiousness arises.
8.1 A ruler who wishes to bring peace and order to the world and leave a glorious name
must honor the worthy and defer to scholars.
The *Yìjīng* says:
"From above, descending to those below,
the way is greatly illuminated."
It also says:
"The noble deferring to the humble
greatly wins the people."
When an enlightened king bestows virtue and humbles himself to the lowly,
he embraces the distant and draws the near.
If the court lacks worthy men,
it is like a swan without wings;
even with a thousand-mile ambition,
it cannot reach where it desires to go.
Thus, those who traverse rivers and seas rely on boats,
those who journey far rely on carriages,
and those who seek hegemony or kingship rely on the worthy.
Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Shàng, Guǎn Yíwú, and Bǎilǐ Xī
are the boats and carriages for hegemons and kings.
To set aside one's own kin and descendants
is not to neglect them;
to employ cooks, fishermen, enemies, and slaves
is not to flatter them.
The way to uphold the state and achieve merit and fame
requires nothing less.
It is like a master builder constructing a palace:
he measures the size and knows the timber needed,
assesses the work and knows the men required.
Thus, when Lǚ Shàng was employed, the world knew Shāng would fall and Zhōu would reign;
when Guǎn Yíwú and Bǎilǐ Xī were appointed, the world knew Qí and Qín would surely become hegemons.
How could they be merely boats and carriages!
Indeed, achieving kingship or hegemony depends on having the right men,
and ruining states and destroying families also depends on having the wrong men.
Jié employed Yǒushēn,
Zhòu employed Èlái,
Sòng employed Táng Yāng,
Qí employed Sū Qín,
Qín employed Zhào Gāo,
and the world knew they would fall.
To seek achievement without the right men
is like hoping for long nights on the summer solstice,
or shooting at fish while pointing at the sky and expecting to hit the mark.
Even Shùn and Yǔ would be hard-pressed,
let alone an ordinary ruler!
8.2 During the Spring and Autumn period,
the Son of Heaven was weak and insignificant,
the feudal lords governed by force,
all rebelled and did not attend court;
the many oppressed the few,
the strong plundered the weak;
the southern Yí and northern Dí tribes invaded alternately,
and the Central States hung by a thread, nearly severed.
Duke Huán then employed Guǎn Zhòng, Bào Shū, Xí Péng, Bīn Xūwú, and Nìng Qī,
three times restored states from extinction,
once continued a severed lineage,
saved the Central States,
repelled the Róng and Dí tribes,
finally intimidated Jīng and the Mán,
thereby honoring the Zhōu court,
and became hegemon over the feudal lords.
Duke Wén of Jìn employed Jiù Fàn, Xiān Zhěn, and Yáng Chǔfǔ,
strengthened the Central States,
defeated powerful Chǔ,
assembled the feudal lords,
attended the Son of Heaven's court,
and brought glory to the Zhōu court.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ employed Sūn Shū'áo, Minister of War Zǐ Fǎn, and General Zǐ Zhòng,
subjugated Chén and won over Zhèng,
defeated powerful Jìn,
and had no rival in the world.
Duke Mù of Qín employed Bǎilǐ Zǐ, Jiǎn Shū Zǐ, Wángzǐ Liào, and Yóu Yú,
occupied and held Yōngzhōu,
repelled and defeated the western Róng.
Wú employed Yánzhōulái Jìzǐ,
annexed Jìzhōu,
and displayed might at Jīfǔ.
Duke Xī of Zhèng, though wealthy with a state of a thousand chariots,
and noble as a feudal lord,
governed with righteousness that did not accord with the people's hearts,
and was assassinated by his ministers—
because he did not first obtain worthy men.
Later, Duke Jiǎn employed Zǐ Chǎn, Pí Chén, Shì Shū, and Diplomat Zǐ Yǔ,
treacherous ministers were removed,
upright ministers advanced,
kept strong Chǔ at bay,
united with the Central States,
the state and clan were peaceful and stable,
for over twenty years,
without the threat of strong Chǔ.
Thus, Yú had Gōng Zhīqí,
and Duke Xiàn of Jìn because of him could not sleep all night.
Chǔ had Zǐ Yù and Dé Chén,
and Duke Wén because of them sat on the edge of his mat.
Far-reaching is how the worthy can avert difficulties and repulse the enemy!
Now Duke Xiāng of Sòng did not heed the words of Prince Mùyí,
and was greatly humiliated by Chǔ.
Cáo did not adopt the remonstrance of Xī Fùjī,
and was defeated and died at the hands of the Róng.
Therefore, to uphold the essentials of the five beginnings,
the origins of order and chaos,
lie in examining oneself and employing the worthy.
When a state employs the worthy, it is auspicious;
when it employs the unworthy, it is inauspicious.
Examining past ages and observing past events,
this inevitability is like matching tally tokens.
This is why the ruler of men cannot but be cautious.
When a state is benighted and chaotic, good ministers appear.
The state of Lǔ was in great chaos,
and the worthiness of Jì Yǒu became apparent.
When Duke Xī ascended the throne and appointed Jìzǐ,
Lǔ was peaceful and stable,
with no worries internally or externally,
and he administered governance for twenty-one years.
After Jìzǐ's death,
Zhū attacked from the south,
Qí invaded from the north,
Lǔ could not withstand its troubles,
and was about to beg for troops from Chǔ,
merely to preserve itself.
Therefore, the Commentary says:
"The rise of trouble
must begin from this."
Prince Mǎi could not be sent to guard Wèi,
Prince Suì disobeyed the ruler's command and arbitrarily went to Jìn,
internally encroached upon by ministers,
externally beset by military chaos—
such is the trouble of weakness.
Duke Xī's nature
was not consistently worthy for the first twenty-one years,
and then later gradually changed to unworthiness;
this shows the benefit of Jìzǐ's presence,
and the loss from his absence.
Gaining or losing the worthy—
the evidence of its benefit and loss is like this.
Yet rulers are negligent in their employment,
which is deeply painful.
If one's wisdom is insufficient to recognize the worthy,
there is no help for it;
but if one has the wisdom to see them yet forcefully cannot decide,
hesitates and does not employ them,
then in major cases it leads to death and ruin,
in minor cases to chaos and overthrow—
this is deeply lamentable.
Did Duke Shāng of Sòng not know of Kǒng Fù's worthiness?
How did he know that when Kǒng Fù died, he himself would surely die,
and rushed to save him?
Rushing to save him
shows he knew of his worthiness.
Did Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ not know of Jìzǐ's worthiness?
How did he know, when ill and near death, to summon Jìzǐ and entrust him with the state's governance?
Entrusting him with the state's governance
shows he knew of his worthiness.
These two rulers had the wisdom to recognize worthies but both failed to employ them,
hence Duke Shāng of Sòng was killed,
and Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ had a villain as his successor.
Had Duke Shāng of Sòng early on appointed Kǒng Fù,
and Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ consistently employed Jìzǐ,
they would have pacified neighboring states,
let alone preserved themselves!
8.3 Zōu Zǐ persuaded King of Liáng, saying:
"Yī Yǐn was originally a serving retainer of the Yǒushēn clan,
yet Tāng appointed him as one of the Three Dukes,
and the world was governed in great peace.
Guǎn Zhòng was originally a petty thief from Chéngyīn,
a common man of the world,
yet Duke Huán of Qí obtained him and made him Zhòngfù.
Bǎilǐ Xī begged for food on the road,
was traded for the price of five sheepskins,
yet Duke Mù of Qín entrusted him with governance.
Nìng Qī was originally a cart driver,
who tapped the carriage rail and sang as he walked on the road to Kāng,
yet Duke Huán entrusted him with the state.
Sīmǎ Xǐ had his kneecaps removed in Sòng,
yet eventually became chancellor of Zhōngshān.
Fàn Jū had his ribs broken and teeth pulled out in Wèi,
yet later became Marquis of Yìng.
Tàigōng Wàng was originally an expelled husband by an old woman,
a butcher's assistant in Zhāogē,
an innkeeper at Jíjīn,
yet at seventy became chancellor of Zhōu,
and at ninety was enfeoffed in Qí.
Therefore, the Odes say:
'The sprawling kudzu vine,
in the open wilds;
if a skilled craftsman finds it,
he makes fine linen and hemp cloth;
if no skilled craftsman finds it,
it withers and dies in the wild.'
Had these seven men not encountered enlightened rulers and sage sovereigns,
they would nearly have been beggars,
withering and dying in the wilderness,
just like the sprawling kudzu vine."
8.4 The subtleties of the eyebrows and eyelashes,
when observed, take form in the countenance;
the influence of sounds and voices,
when felt, stir the heart.
Nìng Qī struck the ox's horn and sang a merchant's song,
Duke Huán heard it and raised him up;
Bào Lóng knelt on stones and climbed a steep peak,
and Confucius descended from his carriage for him.
When Yáo and Shùn met,
it did not take longer than the shade of a mulberry tree to move;
King Wén raised Tàigōng,
not requiring long days.
Thus, when worthies and sages meet,
they do not need long to become close;
when capable men meet,
they do not need trials to know each other.
Therefore, in interacting with scholars,
one need not necessarily share wealth and divide goods with them to know their integrity;
nor necessarily face difficulties and dangers with them to know their courage.
How they handle affairs and make decisions—
this is how one knows their courage;
how they take and give with deference—
this is how one knows their integrity.
Thus, seeing a tiger's tail, one knows it is larger than a wildcat;
seeing an elephant's tusk, one knows it is larger than an ox.
One segment seen reveals all segments.
From this perspective,
by what is seen, one can predict the undeveloped;
observing the small details,
surely suffices to know the greater whole.
8.5 Yǔ established the Xià dynasty's rule,
while Jié led to its downfall;
Tāng established the Yīn dynasty's rule,
while Zhòu led to its demise.
Hé Lǘ made Wú victorious and unmatched in the world,
yet Fū Chāi was captured by Yuè;
Duke Wén made Jìn a hegemon, while Duke Lì was assassinated in the Jù Lì palace;
King Wēi made Qí powerful in the world, yet King Mǐn was killed at the temple beam;
Duke Mù made Qín renowned and honored, yet the Second Emperor was seized at Wàng Yí.
The reason they all became rulers was the same,
yet their achievements were unequal;
it was due to whom they appointed.
Thus, King Chéng, while still in swaddling clothes, received homage from the feudal lords,
because the Duke of Zhōu was in charge;
King Wǔ Líng of Zhào, at fifty, starved at Shā Qiū,
because he appointed Lì Duì.
Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
convened the feudal lords nine times,
and unified the world;
after losing Guǎn Zhòng,
he appointed Shù Diāo and Yì Yá,
resulting in his death without a proper burial,
becoming a laughingstock of the world.
In one person's life,
both honor and disgrace can occur,
depending on whom they appoint.
Thus, Wèi had Lord Wú Jì and regained lost territory.
Zhào appointed Lìn Xiàng Rú, and Qín's troops dared not advance.
Yān Líng appointed Táng Jū, and the state stood alone and independent.
Chǔ had Shēn Bāo Xū, and King Zhāo was restored to the throne.
Qí had Tián Dān,
and King Xiāng regained the state.
From this, it is clear that
no state without wise assistants and outstanding men has ever achieved success, established fame, ensured safety, or continued a severed line.
Therefore, a state should not strive for size but for winning the people's hearts;
assistants should not be numerous but should be virtuous and talented.
Those who win the people's hearts will have the people flock to them;
those with wise assistants will have scholars return to them.
King Wén requested the abolition of the pào luò punishment, and the people of Yīn followed;
Tāng removed three sides of the hunting net, and the people of Xià followed;
the King of Yuè did not destroy old graves, and the people of Wú submitted,
because their actions aligned with the people's hearts.
Thus, when voices are the same, even in different places, they respond to each other;
when virtues match, even without meeting, they feel close.
When the virtuous serve in the court,
the heroes of the world
will lead one another to come.
How do we know this is so?
It is said:
Guǎn Zhòng
was Duke Huán's enemy,
yet Bào Shū considered him more virtuous than himself and recommended him as chancellor;
after seventy persuasions, his advice was heeded,
leading Duke Huán to abandon his desire for revenge and entrust him with state affairs.
Duke Huán ruled effortlessly and received homage from the feudal lords,
all due to Bào Shū's efforts.
The reason Guǎn Zhòng could flee north to Duke Huán without fear for his safety
was because he shared the same voice as Bào Shū.
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐ Gān, and Jī Zǐ let his hair down and feigned madness;
Duke Líng of Chén killed Xiè Yě, and Dèng Yuán left Chén,
taking his clan with him;
after this,
Yīn was annexed by Zhōu,
and Chén perished under Chǔ,
because they killed Bǐ Gān and Xiè Yě and lost Jī Zǐ and Dèng Yuán.
King Zhāo of Yān obtained Guō Wěi,
and Zōu Yǎn and Yuè Yì came from Qí and Zhào,
Sū Zǐ and Qū Jǐng came from Zhōu and Chǔ;
then he raised an army to attack Qí,
and confined King Mǐn in Jǔ.
Yān measured its land and counted its people,
finding them not equal to Qí,
yet they could achieve their will to this extent
because they obtained scholars.
Thus, there is no perpetually stable state,
no eternally governed people;
with the virtuous, there is safety and prosperity;
without them, there is danger and ruin.
From ancient times to the present,
this has never been otherwise.
A clear mirror is for reflecting form;
the past is for understanding the present.
To know the causes of danger and ruin in the past
but not strive to follow the path of safety and prosperity
is no different from running backward while trying to catch up with those ahead.
Tài Gōng understood this,
so he promoted the descendants of Wēi Zǐ
and built a tomb for Bǐ Gān.
If sages treat the dead
with such reverence,
how much more should they treat the living in the present?
Then it is clear that they should not be lost.
8.6 Duke Jǐng of Qí asked Confucius:
"Duke Mù of Qín, his state was small and remote, yet he became a hegemon;
why?"
Confucius replied:
"His state was small, but his ambition was great;
though remote, his governance was just;
his actions were decisive,
his plans harmonious,
his decrees not negligent.
He personally elevated the Five Rams Minister from the bonds of imprisonment,
spoke with him,
and after three days entrusted him with governance.
With this approach,
he could have been a king;
being a hegemon is minor."
8.7 Some say:
Can Duke Huán be called benevolent and righteous?
He killed his elder brother and took the throne,
which is not benevolent or righteous.
Can Duke Huán be called respectful and frugal?
He rode in the same carriage with women,
galloping through the city,
which is not respectful or frugal.
Can Duke Huán be called pure?
Within his household,
there were no women left to marry out,
which is not pure.
These three traits
are the behaviors of a ruined state and a failed ruler,
yet Duke Huán possessed them all.
By obtaining Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng,
he convened the feudal lords nine times,
unified the world,
brought all to pay homage to the Zhōu court,
and became the chief of the Five Hegemons,
all because he obtained wise assistants.
After losing Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng,
he appointed Shù Diāo and Yì Yá,
died without burial,
with worms flowing out the door.
In one person's life,
how can both honor and disgrace occur?
It depends on whom he appoints.
From this, it is clear
that the appointment of assistants is crucial.
8.8 The Duke of Zhōu Dàn humbled himself before scholars in humble dwellings,
bowing to seventy men,
and the scholars of the world came.
