Yàn Zǐ shared food and clothing with a hundred men,
and the scholars of the world also came.
Zhòng Ní cultivated the Way and practiced virtue,
organized literature,
and the scholars of the world came as well.
Bó Yá Zǐ played the qin,
and his friend Zhōng Zǐ Qī listened.
When he played with his mind on Tài Shān,
Zhōng Zǐ Qī said:
"How excellently you play the qin!
As majestic as Tài Shān."
A short while later,
when his mind was on flowing water,
Zhōng Zǐ Qī again said:
"How excellently you play the qin!
As vast as flowing water."
After Zhōng Zǐ Qī died,
Bó Yá broke his qin and severed the strings,
never playing again in his life,
believing there was no one in the world worth playing for.
Not only the qin is like this;
the virtuous are the same.
Even if there are virtuous people, without someone to connect with them,
how can the virtuous give their full loyalty?
A steed does not become a thousand-mile runner on its own;
it waits for Bó Lè to make it so.
8.9 Duke Wēi of Zhōu asked Nìngzǐ:
"Is there a way to attract scholars?"
He replied:
"Yes.
Elevate those in poverty,
restore those who have lost their positions,
then scholars from all directions will come from everywhere.
If the impoverished are not elevated,
the displaced are not restored,
the dismissed are not revived,
then scholars from all directions will turn away.
Even the strongest walls cannot defend themselves,
the sharpest weapons cannot protect themselves -
if you gain scholars but lose them,
there must be a reason.
revive those who have been dismissed,
without scholars, the ruler is humbled."
Duke Wēi of Zhōu said:
"Are scholars really so important?"
He replied:
"Have you not heard about Chǔ?
The king had scholars named Chǔ Xīxū and Qiū Fùkè,
whom he intended to execute,
so they fled to Jìn,
where the Jìn people employed them -
this led to the Battle of Chéngpú.
There was another scholar named Miáo Bēnhuáng,
whom the king intended to execute,
so he fled to Jìn,
where the Jìn people employed him -
this led to the Battle of Yānlíng.
There was another scholar named Shàng Xiěyú,
whom the king intended to execute,
so he fled to Jìn,
where the Jìn people employed him -
this led to the Battle of Liǎngtáng.
There was another scholar named Wǔ Zǐxū,
whose father and brother the king had killed,
so he fled to Wú,
where Hé Lǘ employed him,
and then raised an army to attack Yǐng.
Thus, even when Chǔ greatly offended the rulers of Liáng, Zhèng, Sòng, and Wèi,
it never came to this extent.
But these four offenses against its scholars
resulted in three times exposing the bones of its people in battle,
and once in the loss of the state.
From this we can see:
with scholars, the state survives;
without scholars, the state perishes.
Wǔ Zǐxū in anger destroyed it,
while Shēn Bāoxū in anger preserved it -
how can scholars not be valued!"
8.10 Duke Āi asked Confucius:
"What kind of person is worth selecting?"
Confucius replied:
"Do not select the obstructive,
do not select the aggressive,
do not select the glib-tongued."
Duke Āi said:
"What do you mean?"
Confucius said:
"The obstructive are too sharp-tongued
and cannot be fully employed;
the aggressive always want to surpass others
and cannot be taken as models;
the glib-tongued are full of empty talk with little sincerity,
and their words later prove unreliable.
The bow and arrow must be well-tuned before seeking accuracy;
horses must be honest and obedient before seeking their quality;
people must be loyal, trustworthy, and substantial
before seeking their wisdom and ability.
If someone lacks loyalty, trustworthiness and substance but has much wisdom and ability,
such a person is like a wolf or jackal -
one cannot approach them.
Therefore, first find those with genuine benevolence and trustworthiness,
then become close to them.
Among these,
then appoint those with wisdom and ability.
Thus it is said:
'Be close to the benevolent and employ the capable.'
The method of selecting people
is to observe their words and examine their actions.
Words
are how people express their thoughts and feelings.
Those capable of action
will certainly be capable of speech.
Therefore, first observe their words and measure them against their actions.
Using words to measure actions,
even treacherous people
cannot hide their true nature."
Duke Āi said:
"Excellent."
8.11 When the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent for seven years,
he received commoner scholars,
ten whom he met as teacher with gifts,
twelve whom he met as friends,
forty-nine poor scholars from humble dwellings whom he received first,
hundreds who offered good advice from time to time,
thousands whom he instructed,
and tens of thousands who served at court.
At that time,
if the Duke of Zhōu had been arrogant and stingy,
few worthy scholars would have come.
And if any had come,
they would have been greedy officials drawing salaries without working.
Officials who draw salaries without working
cannot preserve their ruler.
8.12 Duke Huán of Qí set up courtyard torches for scholars wishing to visit him,
but after a year no scholars came.
Then a rustic from the eastern wilds came to see him with his skill in multiplication tables,
and Duke Huán said:
"Is multiplication table skill sufficient for an audience?"
The rustic replied:
"I don't think multiplication tables are sufficient for an audience,
but I heard you set up courtyard torches to receive scholars,
yet after a year no scholars have come.
The reason scholars haven't come
is that you,
being a worthy ruler of the realm,
make scholars from all directions feel their arguments cannot match yours,
so they don't come.
Multiplication tables are a minor skill,
yet you still treat me with courtesy -
how much more would you treat those more worthy than multiplication table experts?
Mount Tài doesn't refuse soil and stones,
rivers and seas don't reject small streams -
that's how they achieve greatness.
The Book of Songs says:
'The ancients had a saying:
Consult even grass and firewood gatherers.'
This means seeking broad counsel."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent."
He then treated him with courtesy,
and within a month,
scholars from all directions came hand in hand.
The Book of Songs says:
"From the hall to the foundation,
from the sheep to the oxen."
This means proceeding from inner to outer,
from small to large.
8.13 Duke Jǐng of Qí attacked Sòng,
reaching atop Qí Dī,
where he climbed high to look around
and sighed deeply:
"Previously, my ancestor Duke Huán had eight hundred war chariots and dominated the feudal lords.
Now I have three thousand war chariots yet dare not remain long here -
is it because I lack a Guǎn Zhòng?"
Xián Zhāng replied:
"I have heard that
wide waters produce big fish,
enlightened rulers produce loyal ministers;
previously there was Duke Huán,
therefore there was Guǎn Zhòng.
If Duke Huán were here now,
then all the ministers below your carriage
would be Guǎn Zhòngs."
8.14 Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào was enjoying himself traveling on the Western River
and sighed:
"How can I get worthy scholars to stay with me?"
The boatman Gǔsāng knelt and replied:
"Pearls and jade have no feet,
yet can come from thousands of miles away -
because people desire them.
is this because our lord doesn't desire them?"
Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào said:
"I have a thousand retainers at my gate;
if morning meals are insufficient,
I collect market taxes by evening;
if evening meals are insufficient,
I collect market taxes by morning.
Can I still be said to not desire scholars?"
The boatman Gǔsāng replied:
"Swans fly high and far,
relying on their six main wing feathers.
The fur on their backs,
the down on their bellies -
even if you gather a handful,
removing it
doesn't make them fly lower;
adding a handful
doesn't make them fly higher.
I wonder if your thousand retainers
serve as the six main feathers,
or are just all down and fur?"
8.15 King Xuān of Qí was seated,
with Chúnyú Kūn in attendance.
King Xuān said,
"What do you, sir, say are my preferences?"
Chúnyú Kūn replied,
"The ancients had four preferences,
but you, great king, have only three."
King Xuān said,
"How do the preferences of the ancients
compare with mine?"
Chúnyú Kūn said,
"The ancients prized fine horses,
and you, great king, also prize fine horses;
the ancients prized fine flavors,
and you, great king, also prize fine flavors;
the ancients prized beauty,
and you, great king, also prize beauty;
the ancients prized scholars,
but you, great king, alone do not prize scholars."
King Xuān said,
"It is only that the state lacks scholars;
if there were any, I would delight in them too."
Chúnyú Kūn said,
"In ancient times, there were Huáliú and Qíjì horses,
but now there are none,
yet you select from among the multitude,
so you prize horses.
In ancient times, there were leopard and elephant fetuses,
but now there are none,
yet you select from among the multitude,
so you prize flavors.
In ancient times, there were Máoqiáng and Xīshī beauties,
but now there are none,
yet you select from among the multitude,
so you prize beauty.
If you, great king, must wait for scholars like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng before prizing them,
then scholars of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng's caliber
would not prize you either."
King Xuān fell silent and had no reply.
8.16 The ruler of Wèi asked Tián Ràng,
"I have enfeoffed nobles with territories spanning a thousand lǐ;
I have bestowed rewards with all the silks from the imperial treasury,
yet scholars do not come.
Why is this?"
Tián Ràng replied,
"Your rewards
cannot be attained through merit;
your punishments
cannot be avoided through reason.
It is like raising a stick to call a dog,
or drawing a bow to beckon a chicken!
Even with fragrant bait, they cannot be attracted,
for harm is certain."
8.17 Zōng Wèi served as chancellor of Qí,
but encountered dismissal,
and returned home.
He summoned his gate captain Tián Ráo and twenty-six others, asking them,
"Is there any gentleman among you who will accompany me to serve another lord?"
Tián Ráo and the others all prostrated themselves and did not respond.
Zōng Wèi said,
"Why is it that gentlemen are easy to obtain but hard to employ?"
Tián Ráo replied,
"It is not that gentlemen are hard to employ,
but that you, my lord, cannot employ them."
Zōng Wèi said,
"What do you mean by my inability to employ gentlemen?"
Tián Ráo replied,
"If the kitchen has spoiled meat,
then the gate will have no devoted scholars.
Now, three shēng of millet is insufficient for your scholars,
yet your geese and ducks have surplus grain;
fine silks and embroideries,
extravagant hall decorations,
wear out with wind and rain while scholars cannot even use them to edge their garments;
the pears and chestnuts from your orchards,
the women of the rear palace gather and toss to each other, yet scholars never get to taste one.
Moreover, wealth is
what you, my lord, treat lightly;
death is
what scholars treat heavily.
If you, my lord, cannot use the wealth you treat lightly
to make scholars devote what they treat heavily—their lives,
is that not indeed difficult?"
Thereupon, Zōng Wèi showed a ashamed expression,
hesitated, rose from his mat, and apologized,
"This is Wèi's fault."
8.18 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius,
"Among the gentlemen of the present time, who is worthy?"
Confucius replied,
"Duke Líng of Wèi."
The duke said,
"I have heard that
within his inner chambers,
there is no distinction between his aunts and sisters."
Confucius replied,
"I observe the court,
not the private halls.
Duke Líng's younger brother is called Prince Qúmóu;
his wisdom is sufficient to govern a state of a thousand chariots,
his integrity sufficient to preserve it,
and Duke Líng cherishes him.
There is also a scholar named Wáng Lín;
whenever the state has a worthy man,
he invariably recommends and employs him,
and none fails to attain office;
if one cannot attain office,
he withdraws and shares his own emolument with him,
and Duke Líng honors him.
There is another scholar named Qìng Zú;
whenever the state has a great affair, he steps forward to manage it,
and none fails to be accomplished,
and Duke Líng delights in him.
When Shǐ Qiū left Wèi,
Duke Líng stayed at a lodge for three months,
not playing his zithers,
waiting for Shǐ Qiū to return before he would enter the palace.
Therefore, I know his worthiness."
8.19 Jièzǐtuī attained the age of fifteen and became chancellor of Jīng.
Confucius heard of this
and sent someone to observe.
Upon returning,
the messenger said,
"There are twenty-five outstanding scholars in the corridors,
and twenty-five elders in the hall."
Confucius said,
"Combining the wisdom of twenty-five men,
their wisdom surpasses that of Tāng and Wǔ;
uniting the strength of twenty-five men,
their strength surpasses that of Péng Zǔ.
To govern the world with these,
would it not surely be secured?"
8.20 Confucius was at leisure in his residence,
when he sighed deeply and said,
"If Tóngdī Bóhuá were not to die,
the world would surely be settled!"
Zǐlù said,
"I would like to hear what kind of man he was."
Confucius said,
"In his youth,
he was quick-witted and loved learning;
in his prime,
he was courageous and unyielding;
in his old age,
he possessed the Way and could humble himself before others."
Zǐlù said,
"That in his youth,
he was quick-witted and loved learning is acceptable;
that in his prime,
he was courageous and unyielding is acceptable.
But having the Way, whom would he humble himself before?"
Confucius said,
"Yóu, you do not understand.
I have heard that
using the many to attack the few, none will not be dissolved;
using the noble to humble before the lowly, none will not be obtained.
In ancient times,
the Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, regulated the governance of the world,
yet humbled himself before seventy scholars.
Was it because he lacked the Way?
It was because he desired to obtain scholars.
To possess the Way and yet be able to humble oneself before the scholars of the world,
is that not a true gentleman?"
8.21 When Marquis Wén of Wèi hurried from Zhōngshān to Ānyì,
Tián Zǐfāng was lagging behind.
The crown prince Jī encountered him,
descended from his carriage and hastened forward,
but Zǐfāng remained seated in his carriage as before.
He announced to the crown prince:
"Request the ruler on my behalf to await me at Zhāogē."
The crown prince was displeased,
and thus said to Zǐfāng:
"I wonder, is it the poor who are arrogant towards others,
or the rich and noble who are arrogant towards others?"
Zǐfāng said:
"It is the poor who are arrogant towards others;
how dare the rich and noble be arrogant towards others?
If a ruler is arrogant towards others, he will lose his state—
I have never seen anyone preserving a state awaiting its loss;
if a high official is arrogant towards others, he will lose his family—
I have never seen anyone preserving a family awaiting its loss.
If the poor are dissatisfied,
they can pack their shoes and leave.
Where could they go and not find poverty?
Thus, the poor can be arrogant towards others;
how dare the rich and noble be arrogant towards others?"
When the crown prince reached Marquis Wén,
he recounted Tián Zǐfāng's words.
Marquis Wén sighed and said:
"If not for your sake,
how could I have heard the words of a worthy person!
I humble myself before Zǐfāng in conduct,
gaining him as a friend.
Since I befriended Zǐfāng,
the ruler and ministers have grown closer,
the common people have become more attached,
thus I have achieved the benefit of befriending a scholar.
I wished to attack Zhōngshān,
so I humbled myself militarily before Yuè Yáng,
and in three years, Zhōngshān was presented to me.
Thus I achieved the benefit of befriending a military man.
The reason I have not advanced further than this
is that I have not yet encountered anyone who could pride themselves on their wisdom before me.
If I could meet someone who prides themselves on their wisdom before me,
would I not then match the ancients?"
8.22 Marquis Wén of Jìn was walking over land and ascending a slope,
all the high officials supported him,
but Suí Huì did not support him.
Marquis Wén said:
"Huì,
for a minister to be cruel to his ruler,
what is the crime like?"
He replied:
"The crime is double death."
Marquis Wén said:
"What is meant by double death?"
He replied:
"He himself dies,
and his wife and children are executed."
Suí Huì then said:
"Why does my lord only ask about ministers who are cruel to their rulers,
and not ask about rulers who are cruel to their ministers?"
Marquis Wén said:
"For a ruler to be cruel to his ministers,
what is the crime like?"
Suí Huì replied:
"If a ruler is cruel to his ministers,
then the wise will not plan for him,
the eloquent will not speak for him,
the benevolent will not act for him,
the brave will not die for him."
Marquis Wén grasped the carriage strap and descended,
apologizing to the high officials, saying:
"I have an ailment in my waist and thighs,
I hope the high officials will not blame me."
8.23 When the Qí general Tián Kuì set out to command troops,
a certain Mr. Zhāng saw him off at the outskirts and said:
"In ancient times, Yáo offered the world to Xǔ Yóu,
who washed his ears and would not accept it—
does the general know of this?"
He said:
"Yes,
indeed,
I know it."
"Bóyí and Shūqí declined the position of feudal lords and would not take it—
does the general know of this?"
He said:
"Yes,
indeed,
I know it."
"Yúlíng Zhòngzǐ declined the position of one of the three highest ministers and hired himself out,
watering gardens for others—
does the general know of this?"
He said:
"Yes,
indeed,
I know it."
"Zhìguǎng left his lord's younger brother,
changed his name,
and escaped to become a commoner—
does the general know of this?"
He said:
"Yes,
indeed,
I know it."
"Sūn Shū'áo three times left the position of chancellor without regret—
does the general know of this?"
He said:
"Yes,
indeed,
I know it."
"These five great men
nominally declined but were actually ashamed of such positions.
Now you, general, are just swallowing the power of an entire state,
grasping the drum and bearing the flags,
clad in armor and holding sharp weapons,
maneuvering a host of a hundred thousand troops,
wielding the authority of execution with axe and yue—
take care not to pride yourself before scholars with what scholars find shameful."
Tián Kuì said:
"Today, all you gentlemen have come to bid me farewell,
with wine and dried meat,
but you, sir, alone instruct me with the great way of the sages—
I respectfully heed your command."
8.24 When Marquis Wén of Wèi went to see Duàngān Mù,
he stood until weary but dared not rest;
but when he saw Zhái Huáng,
he sat sprawled in the hall and spoke with him.
Zhái Huáng was displeased.
Marquis Wén said:
"Duàngān Mù—if I offer him office, he is unwilling;
if I offer him salary, he does not accept.
Now you—if you desire office, the chancellorship is yours;
if you desire salary, the position of high minister is yours.
Having already received my rewards,
yet you demand from me ritual respect—
is that not rather difficult?"
8.25 When Confucius went to Tán,
he met a certain Mr. Chéng on the road,
and they talked all day with their carriage canopies tilted together.
After a while,
he turned to Zǐlù and said:
"Fetch a bundle of silk,
to present to this gentleman."
Zǐlù did not respond.
After another while,
he again turned and said:
"Fetch a bundle of silk,
to present to this gentleman."
Zǐlù reluctantly replied:
"I have heard that
for a scholar to present himself without proper introduction,
or a girl to marry without a matchmaker,
is what a gentleman does not do."
Confucius said:
"Yóu,
does the Book of Songs not say?
'In the wilds there is creeping grass,
thick with falling dew;
there is a beautiful one,
with clear eyes and lovely brows;
we meet by chance,
and she suits my wish.'
Now Mr. Chéng is a worthy scholar of the world;
if I do not present this gift now,
I may never see him again in my lifetime.
In great virtue, do not overstep the bounds;
in small virtues, it is permissible to come and go."
8.26 Duke Huán of Qí appointed Guǎn Zhòng to govern the state,
and Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"The lowly cannot oversee the noble."
Duke Huán made him high minister,
yet the state was not well governed.
Duke Huán said:
"What is the reason?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"The poor cannot command the rich."
Duke Huán granted him a year's market taxes from the state of Qí,
yet the state was not well governed.
Duke Huán said:
"What is the reason?"
He replied:
"The distant cannot control the close."
Duke Huán then established him as 'Uncle Zhòng'.
Thereupon, the state of Qí became greatly peaceful and went on to dominate the world.
Confucius said:
"Even with Guǎn Zhòng's worth,
if he had not obtained these three authorities,
he could not have made his ruler face south and become hegemon."
8.27 Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"If I let wine spoil in the vessels,
and meat rot on the stands,
would it harm my hegemony?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"This is merely not what is most noble,
but it does not harm hegemony."
Duke Huán said:
"Then what would harm hegemony?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Not recognizing the worthy,
harms hegemony;
recognizing but not employing them,
harms hegemony;
employing but not entrusting them,
harms hegemony;
entrusting but not trusting them,
harms hegemony;
trusting them yet allowing petty men to interfere,
harms hegemony."
Duke Huán said:
"Well said."
8.28 The people of Lǔ attacked Bì.
Zēngzǐ took leave of the lord of Bì, saying:
"I beg to depart,
and return after the invaders have withdrawn.
I ask that you temporarily prevent dogs and pigs from entering my house."
The lord of Bì said:
"My relationship with you, sir,
is known to all.
Now when the people of Lǔ attack me, you leave me—
why should I guard your house?"
The people of Lǔ indeed attacked Bì and listed ten crimes,
nine of which were matters Zēngzǐ had contested.
When the Lǔ army withdrew,
the lord of Bì repaired Zēngzǐ's house before welcoming him back.
8.29 Sīchéng Zǐhǎn of Sòng honored Zǐ Wéi,
sharing meals with him indoors,
and clothing outdoors.
When Zǐhǎn was exiled,
Zǐ Wéi did not follow.
When Zǐhǎn returned,
he summoned Zǐ Wéi again and honored him.
His attendants said:
"You were so good to Zǐ Wéi,
yet he did not follow you in exile,
and now you honor him again upon return—
do you not feel ashamed before your loyal ministers?"
Zǐhǎn said:
"It was precisely because I did not employ Zǐ Wéi that I was exiled.
That I can return now
is still due to Zǐ Wéi's remaining virtue and teachings,
hence I honor him.
Moreover, when I was exiled,
what good did my ministers who erased their tracks and uprooted trees to follow me do for my exile?"
8.30 Yáng Yīn visited Lord Jiǎn of Zhào, saying:
"I was driven out three times in my village,
and left five rulers I served.
Hearing of your fondness for scholars,
I have come to see you."
Lord Jiǎn heard this,
stopped eating and sighed,
then rose to his knees and moved forward.
His attendants advised:
"Being driven out three times in his village
means he was not accepted by the crowd;
leaving five rulers he served
shows he was not loyal to his superiors.
Now you have seen this scholar's faults eightfold."
Lord Jiǎn said:
"You do not understand.
A beautiful woman
is the enemy of an ugly one;
a man of great virtue
is shunned in chaotic times;
upright conduct
is hated by the crooked."
Then he went out to meet him,
appointed him as chancellor,
and the state was greatly well-governed.
From this we see
that people, whether near or far,
must be carefully examined.
8.31 Marquess Yìng and Jiǎ Yúzǐ were sitting together
when they heard the sound of a zither.
Marquess Yìng said:
"Today's zither music
—why so sorrowful?"
Jiǎ Yúzǐ said:
"The strings are tight and the tuning low,
hence it sounds sorrowful!
Tight strings
indicate fine wood;
low tuning
signifies a low official rank.
To take fine wood and give it a low rank—
how can it not be sorrowful?"
Marquess Yìng said:
"Excellent!"
8.32 In the thirteenth year,
the feudal lords raised troops to attack Qí.
The King of Qí heard this,
trembled with fear,
summoned his ministers and officials, and said:
"Those with wisdom, use it for me."
Then Erudite Chúnyú Kūn looked up to the sky, laughed loudly, but did not respond.
The king asked again,
and he laughed again without responding;
asked a third time,
he laughed thrice without response.
The king flushed with anger and said displeased:
"Do you, sir, take my words as a joke?"
He replied:
"I dare not take Your Majesty's words as a joke.
I laugh at my neighbor's sacrifice to the field gods,
offering one box of rice, one pot of wine, and three crucian carp,
praying:
'May the high mounds yield grain,
the low wetlands a hundred carts,
passed down to later generations,
abundant and surplus.'
I laugh at his meager offering to the spirits yet extravagant requests."
Thereupon, the king made Chúnyú Kūn a high minister,
bestowed upon him a thousand pieces of gold,
a hundred chariots,
and tasked him with pacifying the feudal lords.
The feudal lords heard of this,
immediately withdrew their troops,
rested their soldiers,
and did not dare attack Qí.
Was this not due to Chúnyú Kūn's ability?
8.33 Tián Jì left Qí and fled to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ welcomed him at the suburbs to his residence,
and asked:
"Chǔ
is a state of ten thousand chariots;
Qí
is also a state of ten thousand chariots.
They often seek to annex each other—
what should be done?"
Tián Jì replied:
"Easy to know!
If Qí sends Shēn Rú as general,
then Chǔ should dispatch fifty thousand troops,
led by a supreme general,
and you'll return with the enemy general's head.
If Qí sends Tián Jū as general,
then Chǔ should dispatch two hundred thousand troops,
led by a supreme general,
resulting in a standoff with both sides withdrawing.
If Qí sends Miǎnzǐ as general,
then Chǔ must mobilize all within its borders,
with you, king, personally leading and me following,
the chancellor and supreme general as left and right commanders—
only then might you barely survive."
Later, Qí sent Shēn Rú as general,
Chǔ dispatched fifty thousand troops led by a supreme general,
and indeed returned with the enemy general's head.
Then the King of Qí, enraged,
replaced him with Miǎnzǐ as general.
Chǔ mobilized all within its borders,
the king personally led the army,
Tián Jì followed,
the chancellor and supreme general served as left and right commanders,
with nine additional chariots for the king,
and he barely escaped.
Back at the residence,
the king faced north, straightened his collar and sleeves,
and asked:
"How did you, sir, know this so early?"
Tián Jì said:
"Shēn Rú insults the worthy and despises the unworthy,
so neither the worthy nor unworthy will serve him,
hence his defeat.
Tián Jū honors the worthy and scorns the unworthy,
so the worthy take responsibility
while the unworthy withdraw,
leading to a standoff and withdrawal.
Miǎnzǐ honors the worthy and cares for the unworthy,
so both the worthy and unworthy take responsibility,
hence you barely survived."
8.34 Marquis Wén of Wèi held a banquet for his officials in Qǔyáng.
As the drinking reached its peak,
Marquis Wén sighed and lamented:
"Do I alone lack a Yù Ràng to serve as my minister?"
Jiǎn Zhòng raised his cup and stepped forward, saying:
"I request to toast you, my lord."
Marquis Wén asked:
"On what grounds?"
He replied:
"I have heard it said:
Parents who have fate,
do not recognize filial sons;
rulers who possess the Way,
do not recognize loyal ministers.
So what about Yù Ràng's lord?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Well said."
He accepted the toast and drank it,
draining the cup without declining,
and said:
"It is because I lack a Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū to serve as ministers,
that I have the achievement of Yù Ràng."
8.35 Jiǎn Zǐ of Zhào said:
"I wish to obtain the good ministers of the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans."
Shǐ Yǎn said:
"How would you use them?"
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Good ministers are what everyone desires,
why even ask?"
He replied:
"I believe it is because they had no good ministers.
Those who serve a ruler
remonstrate against his errors and recommend what is right,
promote goodness and replace the unworthy,
offer their abilities and advance the worthy,
reciting successes and failures morning and evening to present to him,
advancing if he listens, retreating if he does not.
Now, the so-called good ministers of the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans
could not correct and assist their lords,
allowing them to fall into distress,
exiled abroad,
and could not return;
when their lords perished, they abandoned them—
how can they be called good?
If they had not been abandoned,
how could you, my lord, obtain them?
A truly good minister would strive for his lord,
restoring him to his position,
and only cease upon death.
How can they be said to have come?
If they could not do this, they are not good."
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Well said."
8.36 Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"How does one govern a state well?"
Confucius said:
"It lies in honoring the worthy and despising the unworthy."
Zǐlù said:
"The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans honored the worthy and despised the unworthy,
so why did they perish?"
He replied:
"The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans honored the worthy but could not employ them,
despised the unworthy but could not remove them.
The worthy, knowing they were not used, resented them;
the unworthy, knowing they were despised, hated them.
With resentment and hatred confronting them together,
even if the Zhōngháng clan wished not to perish,
how could they avoid it?"
8.37 Jìn and Chǔ battled at Bì,
and the Jìn army was defeated.
Xún Línfǔ, who commanded, returned and requested death.
Duke Jǐng was about to grant it,
when Shì Zhēn bó said:
"You must not.
At the battle of Chéngpú,
when Jìn defeated Chǔ,
Duke Wén still looked worried,
saying:
'Zǐyù still lives; my worry is not over.
A cornered beast still fights, let alone a state minister?'
Only when Chǔ killed Zǐyù did the duke rejoice, saying:
'No one can harm me now.'
Now, perhaps Heaven is giving Jìn a great warning.
Xún Línfǔ in serving his lord
thinks of loyalty when advancing,
and of correcting faults when retreating;
he is a defender of the state.
To kill him now would only enhance Chǔ's victory."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Well said."
He then reinstated him as commander.
9.1 The Yìjīng says:
"The king's minister is steadfastly loyal, not for his own sake."
The reason a minister remains steadfast and finds it difficult to remonstrate with his lord
is not for personal gain,
but to correct the lord's errors and rectify his mistakes.
When a lord has faults,
it is the seed of peril and ruin.
To see the lord's faults and not remonstrate is to disregard his danger and downfall.
Disregarding the lord's peril is something a loyal minister cannot bear to do.
If after three remonstrations he is still not heeded, he should leave;
not leaving would risk his life,
which a benevolent person does not do.
Thus, there are five types of remonstrance:
first, direct remonstrance;
second, humble remonstrance;
third, loyal remonstrance;
fourth, blunt remonstrance;
fifth, indirect remonstrance.
Confucius said:
"I would follow indirect remonstrance!"
Not remonstrating endangers the lord,
but stubborn remonstrance endangers oneself.
Better to endanger oneself than the lord.
Yet if endangering oneself still yields no result, then remonstrance has been in vain.
The wise assess the lord and weigh the timing,
adjusting to urgency and acting appropriately,
so as not to endanger the lord above nor themselves below.
Thus, in the state, the state is not imperiled;
in the self, the self is not endangered.
Long ago, Lord Líng of Chén ignored Xiè Yě's remonstrance and killed him,
while Cáo Jī remonstrated three times with the lord of Cáo and left when not heeded.
The Spring and Autumn Annals, in narrating their righteousness, considers both worthy,
but Cáo Jī acted in accordance with ritual.
9.2 Duke Jǐng of Qí was enjoying himself traveling on the sea
and did not return for six months.
He ordered his attendants:
"Anyone who dares speak first of returning will be put to death without pardon!"
Yán Zhú hurried forward and admonished:
"If you enjoy governing the sea
but not governing the state,
and do not return for six months,
what if someone else governs the state?
How then could you, my lord, enjoy this sea?"
Duke Jǐng seized a halberd to strike him,
but Yán Zhú stepped forward,
straightened his clothes, and waited, saying:
"Why does my lord not strike?
Long ago, Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
In virtue, you are not like those two rulers;
in talent, I am not like those two men.
Why does my lord not strike?
To place me alongside those two—
would that not be fitting?"
Duke Jǐng was pleased
and thereupon returned.
On the way,
he heard that the people were plotting not to let him back in.
9.3 King Zhuāng of Chǔ was established as ruler,
but for three years he did not attend court audiences.
He then issued a decree to the state:
"I detest subjects who hastily admonish their ruler.
Now that I possess the state and family,
and have established the altars of soil and grain,
anyone who admonishes shall die without pardon!"
Sū Cóng said:
"Holding the high rank granted by the ruler,
and enjoying the generous salary provided by the ruler,
to cherish one's life and not admonish the ruler
is to be no loyal minister."
He then entered to admonish.
King Zhuāng stood between the bells and drums,
with the concubine Yáng Jī on his left,
and embracing the concubine Yuè Jī on his right,
wearing casual clothes on the left side,
and court attire on the right,
saying:
"I have no leisure even for my bells and drums,
how can I listen to admonitions!"
Sū Cóng said:
"Your servant has heard that
those who love the Way gain much support,
while those who love pleasure are often deluded;
those who love the Way have abundant provisions,
while those who love pleasure often perish.
The state of Jīng will perish any day now,
and I, a minister willing to die, dare to inform Your Majesty."
The king said:
"Excellent."
He took Sū Cóng's hand with his left,
drew a hidden blade with his right,
and cut down the hanging bells and drums.
The next day,
he appointed Sū Cóng as chancellor.
9.4 Duke Píng of Jìn loved music,
increased taxes and levies,
and neglected the repair of city walls,
saying:
"Whoever dares to admonish me shall die!"
The people of the state were worried.
There was a man named Jiù Fàn
who said to the gate officer:
"I have heard that our lord loves music,
so I wish to see him with music."
The gate officer entered and reported:
"A man of Jìn named Jiù Fàn
wishes to see you with music."
Duke Píng said:
"Admit him."
When he was seated in the hall,
the bells, chimes, panpipes, and zithers were brought out.
After sitting for a while,
Duke Píng said:
"May our guest perform some music."
Jiù Fàn replied:
"Your servant cannot perform music,
but I am skilled in riddles."
Duke Píng summoned twelve riddle masters.
Jiù Fàn said:
"Your humble servant secretly wishes to risk death to serve."
Duke Píng said:
"Very well."
Jiù Fàn extended his left arm and bent his five fingers.
Duke Píng asked the riddle officials:
"Interpret what this means?"
The riddle officials all said:
"We do not know."
Duke Píng said:
"Explain it."
Jiù Fàn then extended one finger and said:
"This first one means:
extensive travels deplete resources while city walls become steep and imposing;
the second:
pillars and beams are clothed in embroidery,
while scholars and commoners lack coarse clothing;
the third:
dwarfs have surplus wine while willing soldiers thirst;
the fourth:
the people have hungry faces while horses have grain rations;
the fifth:
close ministers dare not admonish,
and distant ministers cannot reach you."
Duke Píng said:
"Excellent."
He then put away the bells and drums,
removed the panpipes and zithers,
and subsequently governed the state together with Jiù Fàn.
9.5 Lord Mèngcháng was about to go west to Qín,
and his guests admonished him a hundred times,
but he would not listen.
He said:
"If you admonish me with human affairs,
I already know all about them;
but if you admonish me with ghostly ways,
I will kill you."
The usher entered and said:
"There is a guest who wishes to speak about ghostly ways."
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"Invite the guest in."
The guest said:
"As I was coming here,
I passed over the Zī River,
and saw a clay figurine speaking with a wooden figurine.
The wooden figurine said to the clay figurine:
'You were originally
earth,
molded into a figurine;
if heavy rain comes,
and floods arrive together,
you will certainly melt away.'
The clay figurine replied:
'If I melt, I simply return to my true form.
But you are a peach tree from the eastern garden,
carved into a human shape;
if heavy rain comes,
and floods arrive together,
you will certainly float away,
drifting aimlessly without knowing where you will stop.'
Now Qín is a state surrounded by natural barriers,
with the heart of a tiger or wolf,
and I fear you may suffer the fate of the wooden figurine."
Thereupon, Lord Mèngcháng hesitated, withdrew, and had no response,
and ultimately did not dare to go west to Qín.
9.6 The King of Wú wanted to attack Jīng,
and told his attendants:
"Whoever dares to admonish me shall die!"
There was a young page in the court
who wanted to admonish but did not dare,
so he carried pellets and a slingshot in his pocket,
and wandered in the back garden,
until dew soaked his clothes.
He did this for three mornings.
The King of Wú said:
"Come here!
Why do you torment yourself with dew soaking your clothes like this?"
The page replied:
"There is a tree in the garden,
and on it there is a cicada.
The cicada perches high, sings mournfully, and drinks dew,
unaware that a mantis is behind it.
The mantis bends its body and crouches, wanting to catch the cicada,
but does not know that a yellow bird is beside it.
The yellow bird stretches its neck, wanting to peck the mantis, but does not know that a pellet is below it.
These three all strive to gain their immediate advantage without considering the danger that lurks behind."
The King of Wú said:
"How true!"
He then called off the military campaign.
9.7 King Zhuāng of Chǔ wanted to attack Yángxià,
and the army had been stationed there for a long time without withdrawal.
The ministers wanted to admonish him but none dared.
When King Zhuāng was hunting at Yúnmèng,
Jiāo Jǔ came forward and admonished:
"The reason Your Majesty captures so much game
is because of your horses,
but if the kingdom perishes,
how could Your Majesty's horses still be available?"
King Zhuāng said:
"Well said.
I know that subduing powerful states can make one leader of the feudal lords,
and I know that gaining territory can bring wealth,
but I forgot that my people are not being used properly."
The next day,
he feasted all the high officials with wine,
and honored Jiāo Jǔ as the most esteemed guest.
He then withdrew the army from Yángxià.
9.8 The mother of Qín Shǐhuáng did not conduct herself prudently,
favoring the courtier Lào Ǎi,
whom she enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chángxìn,
and with whom she bore two sons.
Ǎi monopolized state affairs,
growing increasingly arrogant and extravagant,
gathering with the emperor's attendants and high-ranking ministers
to play board games,
drink alcohol,
and get drunk.
They argued and fought,
glaring fiercely and shouting loudly,
saying:
"I am the emperor's stepfather,
how dare you paupers oppose me!"
Those who fought with him fled,
went and reported to the emperor,
and the emperor was enraged.
Fearing execution,
Ǎi staged a rebellion,
battling at the Xiányáng Palace,
but was defeated.
The First Emperor then had Ǎi torn apart by four chariots;
he took his two half-brothers, stuffed them in sacks, and beat them to death;
he took the Empress Dowager and moved her to the Bèiyáng Palace.
He issued an order:
"Anyone who dares to remonstrate about the Empress Dowager
shall be executed,
with thorns piercing their back flesh, their limbs dried and piled beneath the palace gate."
Twenty-seven people died from remonstrating.
A visitor from Qí named Máo Jiāo then came forward,
presenting his petition:
"The visitor from Qí, Máo Jiāo, wishes to advise the emperor."
The emperor sent a messenger to ask:
"Is the visitor here to remonstrate about the Empress Dowager?"
Máo Jiāo said:
"Yes."
The messenger returned and reported:
"He is indeed here to remonstrate about the Empress Dowager."
The emperor said:
"Go and tell him,
does he not see the pile of corpses beneath the palace gate?"
The messenger asked Máo Jiāo,
who replied:
"I have heard that
heaven has twenty-eight constellations,
and now twenty-seven people have died.
The reason I have come
is to complete the number.
I am not afraid of death,
go and report this."
Those from Máo Jiāo's hometown who ate with him
all carried his belongings and fled.
The messenger went in and reported,
and the emperor said furiously:
"This man deliberately comes to violate my prohibition,
quickly heat the cauldron to boil him,
how can he be piled beneath the gate?
Summon him in at once!"
The emperor sat with his hand on his sword,
foam forming at his mouth.
The messenger summoned him in,
but Máo Jiāo refused to hurry,
walking only step by step.
The messenger urged him,
and Máo Jiāo said:
"Once I reach the front, I will die,
can you not grant me a moment?"
The messenger deeply pitied him.
When Máo Jiāo reached the front,
he bowed twice and rose,
stating:
"I have heard that
those who live should not avoid speaking of death,
those who rule a state should not avoid speaking of its fall;
avoiding death does not bring life,
avoiding talk of fall does not ensure survival.
Life, death, survival, and destruction
are what a wise ruler urgently wishes to hear about.
I wonder if Your Majesty wishes to hear it?"
The emperor said:
"What do you mean?"
Máo Jiāo replied:
"Your Majesty has committed reckless and perverse acts,
does Your Majesty not realize it?"
The emperor said:
"Like what?
I wish to hear."
Máo Jiāo replied:
"Your Majesty had your stepfather torn apart by chariots,
showing a jealous heart;
you killed your two half-brothers in sacks,
earning a reputation for lack of compassion;
you moved your mother to the Bèiyáng Palace,
committing an act of unfiliality;
you pierced remonstrators with thorns,
governing like Jié and Zhòu.
Now the world hears of this,
and all support for Qín disintegrates.
I fear for Qín's downfall,
and worry for Your Majesty.
My words are finished,
I beg to go to my execution."
He then removed his clothes and lay on the execution block.
The emperor descended from the dais,
supported him with his left hand,
and waved to his attendants with his right, saying:
"Pardon him,
sir, rise and put on your clothes,
I now wish to accept your counsel!"
He then appointed Máo Jiāo as his second father,
enfeoffing him as a high minister.
The emperor immediately prepared a carriage with a thousand chariots and ten thousand riders,
leaving the left seat empty,
and went personally to the Bèiyáng Palace to fetch the Empress Dowager,
returning with her to Xiányáng.
The Empress Dowager was overjoyed
and held a grand feast for Máo Jiāo.
During the feast,
she said:
"To rectify wrongs and make them right,
to turn failure into success,
to secure Qín's altars of state,
and to reunite me with my son—
all this is due to Máo Jiāo's efforts."
9.9 King Zhuāng of Chǔ built a multi-tiered tower,
transporting stones from a thousand lǐ away,
hauling soil from a hundred lǐ distant.
The laborers had to carry three months' rations with them.
Seventy-two ministers who remonstrated were all put to death.
There was one named Zhū Yùjǐ,
who farmed a hundred lǐ from Chǔ.
He said to his plowing partner:
"I shall go to see the king."
His partner said:
"With your person?
I have heard that
those who persuade rulers are all men of leisure,
yet they still ended up dying.
Now you are merely a man of the grasslands!"
Zhū Yùjǐ said:
"When plowing with you, we compare strength,
but when persuading a ruler, I won't compare wisdom with you."
He left his plowing and went to see King Zhuāng.
King Zhuāng said to him:
"Zhū Yùjǐ, you've come.
Are you going to remonstrate?"
Zhū Yùjǐ said:
"You, my lord, employ righteousness,
and practice laws.
Moreover, I have heard that
earth supported by water becomes level,
wood marked by a string becomes straight,
and a ruler who accepts remonstrance becomes sage.
You built a multi-tiered tower,
transporting stones from a thousand lǐ away,
hauling soil from a hundred lǐ distant.
The people's grievances and faults,
their blood forms streams on the roads,
yet none dared to remonstrate.
How would I dare to remonstrate?
But in my foolishness,
I privately heard that in the past, Yú did not employ Gōng Zhīqí and Jìn annexed it;
Chén did not employ Zǐjiā Jī and Chǔ annexed it;
Cáo did not employ Xī Fùjī and Sòng annexed it;
Lái did not employ Zǐ Měng and Qí annexed it;
Wú did not employ Zǐxū and Yuè annexed it;
Qín did not heed Jiǎn Shū's words and the Qín state was endangered;
Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng and Tāng obtained his throne;
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgàn and King Wǔ obtained his throne;
King Xuān killed Dù Bó and the Zhōu house declined.
These three sons of Heaven and six feudal lords all failed to honor the worthy and employ the words of persuaders,
hence they died and their states perished."
Then he hurried out.
The King of Chǔ quickly pursued him, saying:
"Jǐ,
come back!
I shall follow your advice.
Those who previously persuaded me,
their arguments
were insufficient to move my heart,
and they further endangered me,
so they all came to their death.
Now your argument
is sufficient to move my heart,
and does not endanger me,
therefore I shall follow your advice."
The next day,
he issued an order:
"Whoever can come and remonstrate,
I shall treat as a brother."
Then he dismantled the multi-tiered tower and relieved the people.
The people of Chǔ sang about it:
"Firewood ah, thorns ah!
Without Zhū Yùjǐ,
there would be no descendants ah!
Thorns ah, firewood ah!
Without Zhū Yùjǐ,
there would be no people ah!"
9.10 Duke Huán of Qí said to Bào Shū:
"I wish to cast a great bell
to make my name illustrious.
My conduct,
how could it be inferior to Yáo and Shùn?"
Bào Shū said:
"May I ask about your conduct?"
Duke Huán said:
"In the past, I besieged Tán for three years,
captured it but did not take it for myself—
this is benevolence.
I campaigned north against Gūzhú,
eradicated Lìngzhī and returned—
this is martial prowess.
I held the Kuíqiū assembly to cease the world's warfare—
this is civil virtue.
Nine states came bearing beautiful jade to pay court,
but I did not accept it—
this is righteousness.
Thus, civil and martial, benevolence and righteousness—
I possess them all.
My conduct,
how could it be inferior to Yáo and Shùn?"
Bào Shū said:
"You speak directly,
I shall respond directly.
In the past, Prince Jiǔ held high position but did not yield—
this was not benevolence.
You went against Tàigōng's words and invaded Lǔ's territory—
this was not righteousness.
On the altar platform, you yielded to a single sword—
this was not martial prowess.
Nieces and younger sisters never left your bosom—
this was not civil virtue.
Generally, those who do wrong everywhere without self-awareness,
if not visited by heaven's calamity, will surely suffer human harm.
Heaven resides very high,
but hears very low.
Aside from your mistaken words,
Heaven will also hear of them."
Duke Huán said:
"Have I faults?
Fortunately, you noted them—
this is the blessing of the state.
If you had not instructed me,
I might have committed great crimes to disgrace the state."
9.11 King Zhāo of Chǔ wished to travel to Jīngtái for pleasure.
Minister of War Zǐqí remonstrated, saying:
"The excursion to Jīngtái—
to the left lies the shore of Dòngtíng Lake,
to the right the waters of Pénglí,
southward one gazes upon Liè Mountain,
below overlooks Fāng Huái—
its pleasures make one forget old age and death.
Every ruler who traveled there lost his state.
I hope you will not go there for pleasure."
The king said:
"Jīngtái is my land.
Having the land, I travel there—
why do you stop my excursion?"
He angrily struck him.
Then Prime Minister Zǐxī harnessed a comfortable carriage with four horses and drove straight to the palace steps,
saying:
"Today's excursion to Jīngtái—
you must not miss seeing it."
The king mounted the carriage and patted his back, saying:
"The excursion to Jīngtái—
I shall enjoy it with you."
Zǐxī walked the horses for ten lǐ,
then pulled the reins and stopped, saying:
"I dare not dismount,
but wish to speak reason.
Will you listen, great king?"
The king said:
"Just speak."
Prime Minister Zǐxī said:
"I have heard that
a minister loyal to his ruler—
titles and emoluments are insufficient to reward him;
a minister who flatters his ruler—
punishments and penalties are insufficient to execute him.
As for Minister of War Zǐqí,
he is a loyal minister;
as for me,
I am a flattering minister.
I hope you will kill my body,
punish my family, and reward Minister of War Zǐqí."
The king said:
"If I can stop and listen,
you alone can forbid my excursion.
But later generations traveling there—
there will be no end to it.
What can be done?"
Prime Minister Zǐxī said:
"Wanting to forbid later generations is easy.
I hope that after your mountain mound collapses,
a tomb will be built at Jīngtái.
Never has there been one who, holding bells, drums, pipes, and strings,
enjoyed music upon his father's and grandfather's graves."
Thereupon the king turned his carriage around,
finally not traveling to Jīngtái,
and ordered the preliminary arrangements canceled.
Confucius, hearing of it from Lǔ, said:
"How admirable!
Prime Minister Zǐxī remonstrated ten lǐ ahead,
yet planned for a hundred generations thereafter."
9.12 King Wén of Jīng obtained a dog like the Rúhuáng breed,
and arrows with Jùnlù bamboo shafts,
with which he hunted in Yúnmèng,
not returning for three months;
he obtained the lady of Zhōu,
indulged in lust,
and for a full year did not attend court.
Bǎo Shēn remonstrated, saying:
"The former king divined and appointed me as guardian,
which was auspicious.
Now you, King, have obtained the dog like Rúhuáng,
arrows with Jùnlù bamboo shafts,
hunted in Yúnmèng,
not returning for three months,
and upon obtaining the lady of Zhōu,
indulged in lust,
for a full year not attending court.
Your crime deserves flogging."
He prostrated himself and was about to flog the King.
The King said:
"I left infancy behind,
and am entrusted among the feudal lords;
I wish to request reform instead of being flogged."
Bǎo Shēn said:
"I dare not disregard the command of the former king.
If you refuse the flogging,
it means discarding the former king's order.
I would rather offend you, King,
than fail the former king."
The King said:
"I respectfully comply."
Then he made the King sit on a mat,
and the King bowed down.
Bǎo Shēn tied fifty thin arrows together,
knelt and laid them on the King's back,
doing this twice,
then told the King to rise.
The King said:
"Since I bear the name of being flogged,
it's the same.
So carry it out properly."
Bǎo Shēn said:
"I have heard that
a gentleman feels shame,
a petty person feels pain.
If shame does not change one,
what good is pain?"
Bǎo Shēn hurried out,
intending to exile himself,
and asked the King for punishment.
The King said:
"This is my fault;
what crime have you, Guardian, committed?"
The King then changed his conduct, following Bǎo Shēn's advice,
killed the Rúhuáng-like dog,
broke the Jùnlù-shafted arrows,
expelled the lady of Zhōu,
and devoted himself to governing Jīng.
He annexed thirty states,
and that Jīng grew so vast to this extent
is due to Bǎo Shēn's courage in speaking forthrightly.
Xiāo Hé and Wáng Líng heard of this and said:
"A sage ruler who can uphold his ancestors' legacy and achieve success and fame—
surely that is only King Wén of Jīng!"
Hence the world praises him to this day,
and enlightened rulers, loyal ministers, and filial sons take him as a model.
9.13 Duke Píng of Jìn sent Shūxiàng on a mission to Wú,
where the people cleaned boats to welcome him,
with five hundred men on the left,
five hundred on the right,
some in embroidered clothes and leopard fur,
others in brocade and fox fur.
Shūxiàng returned and reported this to Duke Píng.
Duke Píng said:
"Is Wú about to perish?
Why such respect for boats?
Why such respect for the people?"
Shūxiàng replied:
"You, my lord, built the Chídǐ Terrace,
which can host a thousand troops above,
and display bells and drums below.
If the feudal lords hear of it, they too will say:
Why such respect for a terrace?
Why such respect for the people?
The objects of respect differ, that's all."
Thereupon, Duke Píng ceased the terrace construction.
9.14 Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào raised an army to attack Qí,
ordering that anyone in the army daring to remonstrate
would be guilty of a capital offense.
An armored soldier named Gōnglú
saw Jiǎnzǐ and laughed heartily.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Why do you laugh?"
He replied:
"I have an old joke to tell."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"If you can explain it, well;
if not, you die."
He replied:
"During the mulberry season,
my neighbor, a man, went to the fields with his wife.
He saw a woman among the mulberries,
and went after her,
but failed to catch her.
Returning home,
his wife was angry and left him.
I laugh at his folly."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Now I attack a state and may lose my own state;
that is my folly."
So he withdrew the army and returned.
9.15 Duke Jǐng built a terrace;
when it was completed,
he wanted to cast a bell.
Yànzǐ remonstrated:
"My lord, unable to curb your desires,
built the terrace;
now you wish to cast a bell.
This doubly burdens the people with taxes,
causing their distress.
To amuse oneself by taxing the people into distress
is inauspicious."
Duke Jǐng then stopped.
9.16 Duke Jǐng had a horse
that his groom killed.
The Duke was angry,
seized a spear and was about to strike him himself.
Yànzǐ said:
"He will die without knowing his crime;
allow me to enumerate it for you, my lord,
so he knows his crime before he is killed."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
Yànzǐ raised the spear and faced the groom, saying:
"You reared my lord's horse and killed it,
for which your crime deserves death;
you caused my lord to kill a groom over a horse,
for which your crime again deserves death;
you caused my lord to kill a man because of a horse,
and if this is heard by neighboring feudal lords,
your crime once more deserves death."
The Duke said:
"Sir, release him,
release him,
do not harm my benevolence."
9.17 Duke Jǐng enjoyed archery,
and had Zhúchú in charge of birds, but one escaped.
Duke Jǐng was angry and wanted to kill him.
Yànzǐ said:
"Zhúchú has three crimes;
let me list them before you kill him."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Very well."
So he summoned Zhúchú, and Yànzǐ enumerated before Duke Jǐng,
saying:
"You were in charge of my lord's birds and let one escape,
that is the first crime;
you caused my lord to kill a man over a bird,
that is the second crime;
you caused the feudal lords to hear of it,
making them think my lord values birds over men,
that is the third crime.
Having listed Zhúchú's crimes,
I request to kill him."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Stop.
Do not kill him."
And he apologized to him.
9.18 Duke Jǐng, at high noon with his hair untied,
mounted a six-horse carriage
and was driving his women out through the main palace gate
when the foot-amputee guard struck his horses and turned them back,
saying:
"You are not my lord."
The duke felt ashamed and did not hold court.
Yànzǐ saw Yuán Áo and asked:
"Why has our lord not held court?"
He replied:
"Previously, at high noon,
with his hair untied,
he mounted a six-horse carriage
and was driving his women out through the main palace gate
when the foot-amputee guard struck his horses and turned them back,
saying:
'You are not my lord.'
The duke felt ashamed and returned,
ultimately not going out,
and therefore has not held court."
Yànzǐ entered for an audience,
and the duke said:
"Previously, I was at fault,
with my hair untied,
mounted a six-horse carriage
to go out through the main palace gate,
when the foot-amputee guard struck my horses and turned them back,
saying:
'You are not my lord.'
Thanks to the assistance of you, my minister,
I have been able to lead the people and preserve the ancestral temple.
Now that I have been shamed by the foot-amputee guard,
bringing disgrace upon the state,
can I still stand equal with the feudal lords?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"My lord, do not resent this.
I have heard it said
that if those below lack straightforward words,
those above will have a ruler who hides his faults;
if the people are cautious in speech,
the ruler will have arrogant conduct.
In ancient times, when enlightened rulers were on the throne,
those below spoke straightforwardly;
when the ruler loved goodness,
the people did not guard their words.
Now that you have committed a fault in conduct,
and the foot-amputee guard has spoken straightforwardly,
this is your good fortune.
Therefore, I have come to congratulate you.
I request that you reward him
to show that our lord loves goodness;
honor him
to show that our lord accepts remonstrance."
The duke laughed and said:
"Is this permissible?"
Yànzǐ said:
"It is permissible."
Thereupon, he ordered the foot-amputee guard's resources to be doubled without levying taxes,
and for a time, court was held without incident.
9.19 Duke Jǐng was drinking
and, late at night,
moved the party to Yànzǐ's house.
The vanguard reported to the neighborhood gate:
"The lord has arrived!"
Yànzǐ, clad in black court robes,
stood at the gate and said:
"Could it be that the feudal lords have some trouble?
Or that the state has some trouble?
Why does our lord disgrace us with an untimely night visit?"
The duke said:
"The taste of fine wines,
the sound of bell and stone chimes—
I wished to enjoy them with you, Master."
Yànzǐ replied:
"As for spreading mats and arranging sacrificial vessels,
there are officials for that,
and I dare not participate."
The duke said:
"Move to Sīmǎ Rángjū's house."
The vanguard reported to the neighborhood gate:
"The lord has arrived!"
Sīmǎ Rángjū, in armor and helmet, holding a halberd, stood at the gate and said:
"Could it be that the feudal lords have troops [against us]?
Or that high officials have rebelled?
Why does our lord disgrace us with an untimely night visit?"
The duke said:
"The taste of fine wines,
the sound of bell and stone chimes—
I wished to enjoy them with you, Master."
He replied:
"As for spreading mats and arranging sacrificial vessels,
there are officials for that,
and I dare not participate."
The duke said:
"Move to Liángqiū Jù's house."
The vanguard reported to the neighborhood gate:
"The lord has arrived!"
Liángqiū Jù, holding a lute in his left hand
and a reed instrument in his right,
came forward singing.
The duke said:
"How joyful!
Tonight I shall drink.
Without those two gentlemen,
how could I govern my state?
Without this one minister,
how could I enjoy myself?"
Wise and sage rulers all have beneficial friends
and no ministers who indulge in pleasure.
Duke Jǐng could not attain this,
so he employed both types,
and barely managed to avoid ruin.
9.20 With the strategies of Wǔ Zǐxū and Sūn Wǔ, Wú
crushed the powerful Chǔ in the west,
intimidated Qí and Jìn in the north,
and attacked Yuè in the south.
Yuè King Gōu Jiàn counterattacked,
defeating Wú at Gūsū,
injuring Hé Lǘ's finger,
causing the army to retreat.
Hé Lǘ, afflicted by the wound, was near death
and said to Crown Prince Fū Chāi:
"Do you forget that Gōu Jiàn killed your father?"
Fū Chāi replied:
"I dare not forget."
That evening,
Hé Lǘ died.
After Fū Chāi ascended as king,
he appointed Bó Pǐ as Grand Steward
and practiced warfare and archery.
Two years later,
he attacked Yuè,
defeating it at Fú Jiāo.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè then took his remaining five thousand troops and retreated to Mount Kuàijī,
sending his minister Wén Zhǒng with rich gifts to Wú's Grand Steward Pǐ to sue for peace,
offering to submit his state as vassals.
The King of Wú was about to agree.
Wǔ Zǐxū admonished:
"King Gōu Jiàn is a man who endures hardship.
If you do not destroy him now,
you will surely regret it later."
The King of Wú did not listen,
adopting Grand Steward Pǐ's advice
to make peace with Yuè.
Five years later,
the King of Wú heard that Duke Jǐng of Qí had died and his ministers were contending for favor,
with the new ruler weak,
so he raised an army to attack Qí in the north.
Zǐxū admonished:
"This cannot be.
Gōu Jiàn eats plain food without variety,
mourns the dead and cares for the sick,
and moreover can employ men effectively.
If this man does not die,
he will surely become Wú's calamity.
Now Yuè is a disease in our vitals,
while Qí is but a skin rash.
Yet you do not deal with Yuè first,
but instead focus on attacking Qí.
Is this not mistaken?"
The King of Wú did not listen,
attacked Qí,
and greatly defeated the Qí army at Àilíng,
then met with the rulers of Zōu and Lǔ before returning,
growing even more distant from Zǐxū's counsel.
Four years later,
Wú was about to attack Qí again in the north.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè, following Zǐ Gòng's strategy,
led his troops to assist Wú
and presented precious treasures to Grand Steward Pǐ.
Since Grand Steward Pǐ had repeatedly accepted Yuè's bribes,
his affection and trust for Yuè were extreme,
and he spoke for them day and night to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú trusted and employed Pǐ's plans.
Wǔ Zǐxū admonished:
"Yuè
is a disease in our vitals.
Now you believe their deceptive words and falsehoods while coveting Qí.
This is like a stony field
that is of no use.
The 'Pán Gēng' says:
'Of old, there were those who were rebellious and disrespectful;
I cut them off and exterminated them,
leaving none to propagate,
not allowing them to spread their seed in this land.'
This is how Shāng rose.
I hope you will abandon Qí and deal with Yuè first;
if not,
you will regret it when it is too late."
The King of Wú did not listen,
sending Zǐxū to Qí.
Zǐxū said to his son:
"I admonished the king,
but he did not heed me.
Now I foresee Wú's destruction!
You and I will perish together,
there is nothing to be done."
He then entrusted his son to the Bào family of Qí and returned to report to the King of Wú.
Grand Steward Pǐ, having a grudge against Zǐxū,
slandered him:
"Zǐxū is by nature harsh, violent, and lacking in kindness.
His resentment and suspicion run deep,
and he can cause great harm.
Previously, when you wished to attack Qí,
Zǐxū said it could not be done,
yet you proceeded and achieved great success.
Zǐxū was ashamed that his advice was not used,
and thus became resentful.
Now you are again about to attack Qí,
and Zǐxū stubbornly and forcefully admonishes against it,
obstructing and undermining your plans,
hoping for Wú's defeat to prove his own strategies right.
Now you personally lead the campaign,
mobilizing all the military force in the state to attack Qí,
yet Zǐxū's advice is not followed,
so he feigns illness
and pretends to be too sick to go.
You must be prepared,
for he can easily cause trouble.
Moreover, I sent someone to spy on him,
and when he went to Qí,
he entrusted his son to the Bào family.
As a minister, dissatisfied internally,
he forms external alliances with feudal lords.
Considering himself the former king's strategist,
now unused,
he is constantly discontent.
I hope you will deal with him early."
The King of Wú said:
"Without your words,
I would still suspect him."
He then sent an envoy to present Zǐxū with the Dúlòu sword,
saying:
"You shall die by this."
Zǐxū said:
"Alas!
Slanderer Pǐ creates chaos,
yet the king instead executes me.
I made your father hegemon,
and when you were established,
with the various princes contending for the throne,
I risked death to plead for you before the former king,
almost failing to secure your position.
After you were established,
you wished to divide Wú with me,
but I dared not accept.
How then can you listen to a slanderer and kill an elder?"
Then he told his retainer:
"Be sure to plant catalpa trees on my grave,
so they can be made into instruments;
and gouge out my eyes and hang them on the eastern gate of Wú,
that I may see the Yuè invaders enter and destroy Wú."
Then he killed himself.
When the King of Wú heard this,
he was greatly angered,
took Zǐxū's corpse, stuffed it into a leather sack,
and cast it into the river.
The people of Wú pitied him,
and built a shrine for him by the river,
naming the place Xū Mountain.
More than ten years later,
Yuè attacked Wú.
The King of Wú returned to fight,
but was defeated.
He sent a minister to seek peace with Yuè,
but was refused.
The King of Wú, about to die, said:
"I have come to this because I did not heed Zǐxū's words.
If the dead have no consciousness, so be it;
but if the dead have consciousness,
what face have I to see Zǐxū?"
He then covered his face with a cloth and cut his own throat.
9.21 Duke Jiǎn of Qí had a minister named Zhū Yù Yāng,
who admonished the duke:
"Tián Cháng and Zǎi Yǔ
—these two men deeply hate each other.
I fear they will attack one another.
If they fight, it may lead to rebellion and endanger you.
This cannot be allowed.
I hope you will remove one of them."
Duke Jiǎn said:
"This is not something a petty person like you should discuss."
Not long after,
Tián Cháng indeed attacked Zǎi Yǔ in the court
and assassinated Duke Jiǎn in the audience hall.
Duke Jiǎn sighed deeply and said:
"I did not heed Yāng's words,
and thus have come to this disaster!"
Thus, the words of loyal ministers
cannot be ignored.
9.25 Confucius said:
"Good medicine is bitter to the taste but beneficial for the illness;
loyal advice is harsh to the ear but beneficial for conduct."
Thus King Wǔ thrived through having outspoken ministers,
while King Zhòu perished through keeping silent ones.
If a ruler has no outspoken ministers,
a father no outspoken sons,
an elder brother no outspoken younger brothers,
a husband no outspoken wife,
a scholar no outspoken friends,
their downfall can be expected to occur immediately.
Therefore it is said:
What the ruler loses,
the ministers gain;
what the father loses,
the sons gain;
what the elder brother loses,
the younger brothers gain;
what the husband loses,
the wife gains;
what the scholar loses,
his friends gain.
Hence there would be no destroyed states or ruined families,
no rebellious fathers or disorderly sons,
no estranged elder brothers or abandoned younger brothers,
no reckless husbands or licentious wives,
no severed relationships or failed friendships.
9.26 Yànzǐ reported to Duke Jǐng, saying:
"Is the court atmosphere severe?"
The Duke replied:
"If the court atmosphere is severe,
what harm does it do to governing the state?"
Yànzǐ responded:
"If the court atmosphere is severe, then subordinates will not speak;
if subordinates do not speak, then the ruler will not hear.
When subordinates do not speak, it is called mute;
when the ruler does not hear, it is called deaf.
Deaf and mute,
how could this not harm the governance of the state!
Moreover, grains of millet are gathered in small amounts to fill granaries;
thin threads are woven together to form curtains.
The height of Tài Shān
is not achieved with one stone;
it accumulates from low to high.
Those who govern the world
do not rely on one scholar's words.
There may be advice that is received but not used,
but how can there be refusal to even let it enter!"
10.1 Survival and destruction, fortune and misfortune,
their key lies in oneself.
The sage values warning,
respectfully cautious about what might be neglected.
The Doctrine of the Mean says:
"Nothing is more visible than the hidden,
nothing more apparent than the subtle.
Therefore the gentleman is careful when alone."
A proverb says:
"Through warning there is no shame,
through reflection no disgrace."
To preserve oneself and keep the state intact
without warning or reflection
is indeed difficult.
The Book of Songs says:
"Trembling with fear and caution,
as if approaching a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice."
This expresses it.
10.2 Formerly King Chéng enfeoffed the Duke of Zhōu,
but the Duke of Zhōu declined to accept.
Then he enfeoffed the Duke of Zhōu's son Bóqín in Lǔ.
As Bóqín was about to leave,
the Duke of Zhōu admonished him, saying:
"Go now,
but do not let the state of Lǔ make you arrogant toward scholars!
I am the son of King Wén,
the younger brother of King Wǔ,
the uncle of the present king,
and moreover serve as minister to the Son of Heaven.
My position in the world is not insignificant,
yet I have washed my hair and three times held it up to receive visitors,
eaten a meal and three times spat out food to receive guests,
still fearing to miss scholars from throughout the land.
I have heard it said:
'Those with vast virtue who maintain it with reverence
will be honored;
those with broad lands who maintain them with frugality
will be secure;
those with exalted rank who maintain it with humility
will be noble;
those with numerous people and strong armies who maintain them with caution
will be victorious;
those with intelligence and wisdom who maintain them with apparent foolishness
will gain more;
those with extensive learning and memory who maintain them with apparent shallowness
will broaden.'
These six preservations
are all virtues of humility.'
One honored as the Son of Heaven,
rich with all within the four seas,
if lacking humble virtue will lose the world
and perish himself,
as Jié and Zhòu did.
Can one not be cautious?
Thus the Yì Jīng has one way
that greatly can preserve the world,
moderately can preserve the state,
and minimally can preserve oneself -
this means humility.
The way of heaven reduces the full and increases the humble;
the way of earth changes the full and flows to the humble;
spirits and gods harm the full and bless the humble;
the human way dislikes the full and likes the humble.
Therefore when clothes are made, the lapel is cut;
when a palace is built, a corner is omitted;
when a house is completed, decorations are added -
showing incompletion is heaven's way.
The Yì Jīng says:
'The Qiān hexagram,
penetrating,
the gentleman has a good end,
auspicious.'
The Book of Songs says:
'Tāng descended without delay,
his sage reverence daily ascended.' Take warning!
Do not let the state of Lǔ make you arrogant toward scholars!"
10.3 When Confucius read the Yì Jīng and reached the sections on Decrease and Increase,
he sighed deeply.
Zǐxià left his mat and asked:
"Why does the Master sigh?"
Confucius said:
"Those who decrease themselves gain,
those who increase themselves lose,
therefore I sigh."
Zǐxià said:
"Then should learners not seek increase?"
Confucius said:
"No,
according to heaven's way,
the accomplished cannot long remain so.
Learners receive with emptiness,
therefore it is said:
they gain.
If one receives knowledge while holding to fullness,
then the world's good words cannot enter his ears.
Formerly Yáo occupied the Son of Heaven's position,
yet maintained it with sincere reverence,
remaining empty and calm to receive subordinates,
so after a hundred years he became even more flourishing,
and to this day grows more illustrious.
Kūnwú considered himself sufficient and was satisfied,
reaching great heights without decline,
so in his time he suffered defeat,
and to this day grows more despised.
Is this not evidence of decrease and increase?
Therefore I say:
humility
means achieving reverence to preserve one's position.
What is bright and active can become great,
but if great, it will diminish.
I take warning of this.
Therefore it is said:
the world's good words cannot enter his ears.
The sun at zenith must decline,
the full moon must wane;
heaven and earth wax and wane,
changing with the seasons.
Therefore the sage does not dare remain at peak,
descending from his carriage when meeting three people,
bowing at the crossbar when meeting two,
adjusting his fullness and emptiness,
thus able to endure long."
Zǐxià said:
"Excellent,
I shall recite this throughout my life."
10.4 Confucius was observing at the Zhōu temple,
where there was a tilting vessel.
Confucius asked the temple keeper,
"What kind of vessel is this?"
The keeper replied,
"It is probably the vessel placed on the right side of the seat."
Confucius said,
"I have heard of the vessel on the right side of the seat:
when full, it overturns;
when empty, it tilts;
when half-full, it stands upright.
Is this true?"
The keeper replied,
"Yes."
Confucius had Zǐlù fetch water to test it.
When full, it overturned.
When half-full, it stood upright.
When empty, it tilted.
Confucius sighed deeply and exclaimed,
"Alas!
How can anything full avoid overturning?"
Zǐlù asked,
"May I ask if there is a way to remain full?"
Confucius said,
"The way to remain full
is to draw from it and reduce it."
Zǐlù asked,
"Is there a way to reduce it?"
Confucius said,
"To be high yet able to lower oneself,
full yet able to be empty,
wealthy yet able to be frugal,
noble yet able to be humble,
wise yet able to appear foolish,
brave yet able to be cautious,
eloquent yet able to be reticent,
broad yet able to be shallow,
bright yet able to be obscure—
this is called reduction without extremity.
Only those of utmost virtue
can practice this way."
The Yì Jīng says:
'Not reducing it but benefiting it.'
Therefore, by reducing oneself, one ultimately gains benefit."
10.5 Cháng Chuāng was ill,
and Lǎozǐ went to inquire about him,
saying,
"Your illness is severe, sir.
Do you have any final teachings to impart to your disciples?"
Cháng Chuāng said,
"Even if you hadn't asked,
I would have told you."
Cháng Chuāng said,
"When passing through your hometown, you dismount from your carriage.
Do you know why?"
Lǎozǐ said,
"Is it not to show that one does not forget one's origins?"
Cháng Chuāng said,
"Ah!
That's it."
Cháng Chuāng said,
"When passing under tall trees, you quicken your pace.
Do you know why?"
Lǎozǐ said,
"Is it not to show respect for the aged?"
Cháng Chuāng said,
"Ah!
That's it."
Then he opened his mouth and showed it to Lǎozǐ, saying,
"Is my tongue still there?"
Lǎozǐ said,
"Yes."
"Are my teeth still there?"
Lǎozǐ said,
"No."
Cháng Chuāng said,
"Do you understand?"
Lǎozǐ said,
"The tongue remains
because it is soft, doesn't it?
The teeth are gone
because they are hard, isn't that so?"
Cháng Chuāng said,
"Ah!
That's it.
All under heaven is contained in this.
What more is there to tell you!"
10.6 Hán Píngzǐ asked Shū Xiàng,
"Which is stronger, hardness or softness?"
Shū Xiàng replied,
"I am eighty years old.
My teeth have fallen out twice, but my tongue remains.
Lǎo Dān once said:
'The softest things in the world
overcome the hardest things in the world.'
He also said:
'When a person is born, they are soft and weak;
when they die, they become stiff and hard.
All plants and trees are soft and pliable when alive,
but dry and brittle when dead.'
From this, we observe that
'softness and weakness are companions of life;
hardness and strength are companions of death.'
What is alive may be damaged but will recover,
while what is dead, once broken, is gone forever.
Therefore, I know that softness is stronger than hardness."
Píngzǐ said,
"Well said!
Then what do you practice?"
Shū Xiàng said,
"I practice softness.
Why should I use hardness?"
Píngzǐ said,
"But isn't softness fragile?"
Shū Xiàng said,
"Softness is pliable but does not break,
sharp but does not chip.
How can it be fragile?
The way of heaven
favors the subtle.
Thus, when two armies clash,
the softer one prevails;
when two rivals contend for gain,
the weaker one obtains it.
The Yì Jīng says:
'Heaven's way is to diminish the full and benefit the humble;
earth's way is to change the full and flow to the humble;
ghosts and spirits harm the full and bless the humble;
humanity's way hates the full and loves the humble.'
With humble and insufficient softness,
and the support of these four ways,
how can one not achieve one's aims?"
Píngzǐ said,
"Well said."
10.7 Duke Huán said,
"Metal that is hard breaks;
leather that is hard splits;
a ruler who is hard sees his state perish;
a minister who is hard loses his friends."
Hardness leads to lack of harmony,
and without harmony, nothing can be accomplished.
Thus, if four horses are not in harmony,
the journey will not be long;
if father and son are not in harmony,
their lineage will be destroyed;
if brothers are not in harmony,
they cannot long remain together;
if husband and wife are not in harmony,
the household will face great misfortune.
The Yì Jīng says:
"When two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal."
This is because they are not hard.
10.8 Lǎozǐ said,
"When you gain benefit,
you must consider the harm;
when you rejoice in success,
you must consider the potential for failure."
Those who do good
are rewarded with fortune by heaven;
those who do evil
are punished with misfortune by heaven.
Therefore, it is said:
"Misfortune is that upon which fortune depends;
fortune is that in which misfortune lurks."
Be cautious and careful.
If a gentleman does not strive,
how can he be prepared?
Those who understand heaven above do not miss opportunities;
those who understand earth below do not lose wealth;
those who are careful day and night will avoid disasters.
10.9 When Zēngzǐ was gravely ill,
Zēng Yuán held his head,
and Zēng Huá held his feet.
Zēngzǐ said:
"I do not possess the talent of Yán Huí,
so what can I tell you?
Though lacking ability,
a nobleman strives for self-improvement.
For blossoms that are plentiful but fruits that are few,
it is Heaven's doing;
for words that are many but deeds that are few,
it is man's doing.
Birds consider mountains low yet build layered nests on their peaks,
fish and turtles consider abysses shallow yet bore holes within them,
but the reason they are caught
is because of bait.
If a nobleman can avoid endangering himself for profit,
then how can disgrace come to him?
Official negligence arises from achieved position,
illness worsens when slightly relieved,
disaster springs from indolence,
filial piety declines because of wife and children.
Examine these four matters,
and be as cautious at the end as at the beginning."
The Book of Songs says:
"There is nothing without a beginning,
but few can bring things to an end."
10.10 Dān Kuài said:
"A state has five forms of coldness, and freezing ice is not among them.
First:
policies being externalized,
second:
women's dominance,
third:
leaked strategies,
fourth:
disrespect towards ministers leading to state collapse,
fifth:
inability to govern internally while pursuing external affairs.
If any one of these five appears,
even sacrifices bring no blessings,
averting disaster is certain,
but obtaining blessings is rare."
10.11 Confucius said:
"Survival and destruction, calamity and blessing,
all lie within oneself.
Even heavenly disasters and earthly portents cannot kill one.
In the time of King Dì Xīn of Yīn,
sparrows gave birth to crows at the city corner,
and the diviner interpreted it:
'When small things give birth to large ones,
the state will surely prosper,
and the king's fame will double.'
Dì Xīn delighted in the sparrows' virtue,
neglected state affairs,
became excessively tyrannical without limit,
until foreign invaders came,
and thus Yīn perished.
This is turning against Heaven's timing,
where deceitful blessings become calamities.
In the time of King Wǔ Dīng of Yīn,
the former kings' ways were deficient,
punishments were lax,
mulberry and grain trees grew together in the court,
reaching great thickness in seven days.
The diviner interpreted it:
'Mulberry and grain trees,
being wild plants,
growing in the court
suggest the court's demise?'
Wǔ Dīng was frightened,
reformed himself through moral conduct,
reflected on past kings' governance,
restored destroyed states,
continued extinct lineages,
promoted reclusive talents,
clarified the way of respecting the elderly.
After three years,
rulers from distant lands,
sixteen states in all, came to court through multiple translations.
This is welcoming Heaven's timing,
turning calamity into blessing.
Thus, strange phenomena
are Heaven's warnings to emperors and lords;
