nightmares
are warnings to officials.
So, strange phenomena cannot overcome good governance,
nor nightmares overcome good deeds.
At the peak of perfect order,
calamity turns into blessing."
Therefore, Tài Jiǎ said:
"Heaven-sent calamities
can still be avoided,
but self-made disasters
are inescapable."
10.12 Shí Chóu said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals record sudden events sufficient to cause ruin,
which rulers must be cautious about.
Having multiple consorts can lead to ruin,
royal families not being intimate can lead to ruin,
ministers not being trusted can lead to ruin,
state honors not being used can lead to ruin,
associating with flatterers and slanderers can lead to ruin,
undertaking affairs at inappropriate times can lead to ruin,
employing people without restraint can lead to ruin,
punishments not being appropriate can lead to ruin,
losing popular support internally can lead to ruin,
disrespecting major states externally can lead to ruin."
10.13 Blessings are born from hardship,
while calamities arise from complacency,
as exemplified by Qí Qǐnggōng.
Qí Qǐnggōng,
grandson of Huángōng,
with vast territory and numerous people,
strong army and wealthy state,
also inheriting a hegemon's prestige,
became arrogant and lazy,
unwilling to meet with other lords.
He raised troops to attack Lǔ,
instead defeated Wèi's army at Xīnzhù,
showing great contempt for small and large states alike.
Soon, Jìn and Lǔ sent envoys,
whom he mocked.
Both states angered,
sought allies for help,
gaining Wèi and Cáo,
forming a coalition of four states.
They met in battle at Ān,
where Qí's army was severely defeated,
Qǐnggōng captured,
Péng Chǒufù beheaded,
and then he was utterly terrified.
Relying on Péng Chǒufù's deception,
he managed to escape and return.
He mourned the dead and cared for the sick,
abstained from wine and meat for seven years,
kept away from music of strings and bamboo,
distanced himself from women's charms.
When attending meetings and alliances,
he humbled himself before other lords.
His state internally practiced righteousness,
and his reputation shook the feudal lords.
The lost territories
came back without seeking,
honor and favor obtained without military force,
demonstrating his ability to adapt through submission and change.
Thus, blessings are born from hardship,
while calamities arise from complacency,
this is the evidence of gain and loss.
10.14 The efficacy of great achievements
lies in employing the worthy and accumulating the Way,
which gradually becomes more illustrious and clear;
the fault of decline and destruction
lies in becoming complacent and negligent upon achieving success,
which gradually leads to obstruction and ruin.
Duke Wén of Jìn is evidence of this.
When Duke Wén of Jìn was in exile,
he cultivated the Way without cease,
and thus attained the rule of his state.
At the time of his rule,
above there was no enlightened Son of Heaven,
below there were no worthy feudal lords,
the powerful Chǔ presided over the meetings,
the feudal lords turned their backs and rebelled,
the Son of Heaven had lost the Way,
and had left to reside in Zhèng.
Duke Wén then pitied the decline of the Central States,
appointed Jiù Fàn, Xiān Zhěn, and Yáng Chǔfǔ,
cherished and loved the common people,
and trained and nurtured the warriors.
In the fourth year,
with internal governance settled,
he raised troops to attack Wèi,
captured the Earl of Cáo,
returned to defeat the powerful Chǔ,
and his might shook the world.
He illuminated the laws of the wise kings,
led the feudal lords to pay homage to the Son of Heaven,
and none dared not to listen;
the world was vast and peacefully settled,
and the Zhōu house was honored and exalted.
Therefore it is said:
The efficacy of great achievements
lies in employing the worthy and accumulating the Way,
which gradually becomes more illustrious and clear.
Duke Wén then established his hegemonic achievements,
and when his goals were reached and his will satisfied,
the hearts of Tāng and Wǔ arose, and he forgot his multitude.
Three times in one year he used his armies,
and did not rest,
then advanced to besiege Xǔ,
his troops quickly became exhausted,
and he could not subdue it,
dismissed the feudal lords and returned,
from then on he neglected governmental affairs,
for the Díquán alliance,
he did not attend in person,
his trustworthiness declined and his righteousness was lacking,
like a net that is not mended,
his might and power were thwarted and broken, and he was not trusted,
then the feudal lords did not pay homage,
Zhèng then rebelled,
the Yí and Dí invaded internally,
and Wèi moved to Shāngqiū.
Therefore it is said:
The fault of decline and destruction
lies in becoming complacent and negligent upon achieving success,
which gradually leads to obstruction and ruin.
10.15 Tián Zǐfāng was sitting in attendance on Marquis Wén of Wèi,
when Crown Prince Jí hurried in for an audience,
the guests and ministers all rose,
but Tián Zǐfāng alone did not rise.
Marquis Wén had a displeased expression,
and the Crown Prince was likewise.
Tián Zǐfāng declared:
"Should I rise for you?
There is nothing to be done about the rites!
Should I not rise for you?
There is nothing to be done about the offense!
Allow me to recite for you.
When King Gōng of Chǔ was Crown Prince,
he was about to go out to Yúnmèng,
when he met the Grand Master Gōng Yǐn,
Gōng Yǐn then hurried to avoid him inside the gate of a commoner's house,
the Crown Prince got off his carriage and followed him inside the gate of the commoner's house,
and said:
'You, Grand Master, why do you act like this?
I have heard that
one who respects the father does not include the son,
and one who includes the son,
there is no greater inauspiciousness.
You, Grand Master, why do you act like this?'
Gōng Yǐn said:
'Just now I saw your face,
from now on I will remember your heart.'
If it is truly so,
where will you go?'"
Marquis Wén said:
"Excellent."
Crown Prince Jí came forward,
recited King Gōng's words,
recited them three times and requested to learn them.
10.16 Zǐgòng was on his way to Chéng,
on the road,
he saw a man by the roadside wearing a worn headcloth and coarse cloth covering, clad in mourning garments,
his name was Zhōu Chuò,
Zǐgòng questioned him.
He said:
"How far is it from here to Chéng?"
Silently, he did not reply,
Zǐgòng said:
"When someone asks you a question and you do not respond,
why is that?"
He put aside his covering and said:
"To gaze upon and belittle others,
is that benevolent?
To see and not recognize,
is that wise?
To lightly insult others,
is that righteous?"
Zǐgòng got off his carriage and said:
"Cì is not benevolent,
having erred in three questions,
may I hear them again?"
He said:
"This is enough for you,
I will not tell you."
Thereupon, Zǐgòng would lean on the crossbar every third time he met someone,
and every fifth time he would dismount.
10.17 When Sūnshū Áo became the Prime Minister of Chǔ,
all the officials and people of the state came to congratulate him.
There was an old man wearing coarse clothes,
a white cap,
who came later to offer condolences.
Sūnshū Áo straightened his clothes and cap and went out to see him,
and said to the old man:
"The King of Chǔ does not know that I am unworthy,
and has made me receive the reproach of the officials and people;
everyone has come to congratulate me,
but you alone have come later to offer condolences,
surely you have something to say?"
The old man said:
"I have something to say:
one who, having become noble, is arrogant to others,
the people will leave him;
one who, having reached high position, monopolizes power,
the ruler will detest him;
one who, having ample salary, is not content,
disaster will reside with him."
Sūnshū Áo bowed twice and said:
"I respectfully receive your instruction,
and wish to hear your further teachings."
The old man said:
"The higher your position, the more humble your thoughts should be;
the greater your office, the more cautious your heart should be;
the more ample your salary, the more careful you should be not to take what is not yours.
If you, sir, carefully observe these three points,
you will be sufficient to govern Chǔ."
10.18 In the eleventh year of King Wèi Ān Xī,
King Qín Zhāo said to his attendants:
"At present, are Hán and Wèi stronger than Qín?"
They replied:
"They are not as strong as Qín."
The king said:
"Now, are Rú'ěr and Wèi Qí as worthy as Mèng Cháng and Máng Mǎo?"
They replied:
"They are not as worthy as Mèng Cháng and Máng Mǎo."
The king said:
"With the worthiness of Mèng Cháng and Máng Mǎo,
leading strong Hán and Wèi to attack Qín,
they still could do nothing to me.
Now with the incapable Rú'ěr and Wèi Qí leading weak Hán and Wèi to attack Qín,
their inability to harm me,
is even more evident!"
The attendants all said:
"Indeed."
Shēn Qí leaned on his sè and responded:
"Your Majesty's assessment of the world
is mistaken.
During the time of the six Jìn families,
the Zhì clan was the strongest,
destroying the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans.
Then leading the troops of Hán and Wèi, they besieged Zhào Xiāngzǐ in Jìnyáng,
diverting the Jìn River to flood Jìnyáng's walls,
leaving only three planks' height unsubmerged.
Zhì Bó inspected the waters,
with Wèi Xuānzǐ driving his chariot,
and Hán Kāngzǐ as his companion.
Zhì Bó said:
'I did not know before that water could destroy a state,
but now I understand.
The Fén River could flood Ānyì,
and the Jiàng River could flood Píngyáng.'
Wèi Xuānzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
and Kāngzǐ stepped on Xuānzǐ's foot.
Their elbows and feet connected on the chariot, and the Zhì clan was divided beneath Jìnyáng's walls,
their leader dead and state destroyed,
laughed at by the world.
Now though Qín is strong,
it does not surpass the Zhì clan,
and though Hán and Wèi are weak,
they are still more worthy than they were under Jìnyáng's walls.
This is precisely the time for elbows and feet to connect.
I hope Your Majesty will certainly not take this lightly!"
Then the king of Qín became fearful.
10.19 When Wèi Gōngzǐ Móu was traveling east,
Ránghóu saw him off, saying:
"You, sir, are leaving Rǎn for the lands east of the mountains;
do you not have a single word to instruct Rǎn?"
Wèi Gōngzǐ Móu said:
"Had you not mentioned it,
Móu would have nearly forgotten to speak to you.
Do you know that office does not await power, yet power comes of itself?
Power does not await wealth, yet wealth comes of itself?
Wealth does not await nobility, yet nobility comes of itself?
Nobility does not await arrogance, yet arrogance comes of itself?
Arrogance does not await crime, yet crime comes of itself?
Crime does not await death, yet death comes of itself?"
Ránghóu said:
"Excellent,
I respectfully receive your clear teaching."
10.20 Though highly placed and honoring the worthy,
do not be arrogant toward others;
though intelligent and sagely wise,
do not embarrass others;
though quick and resourceful,
do not strive to be first;
though resolute and brave,
do not seek to overpower others.
If you do not know, then ask;
if you cannot, then learn.
Though wise, always be sincere before arguing;
though capable, always be humble before acting.
Therefore, though a scholar may be intelligent and sagely wise,
he guards himself with simplicity;
though his achievements cover the world,
he guards himself with humility;
though his courage withstands the age,
he guards himself with caution;
though he possesses the wealth of the world,
he guards himself with frugality.
This is what is called being high without danger,
full without overflowing.
10.21 Duke Huán of Qí prepared wine for his ministers,
setting the time for noon.
Guǎn Zhòng arrived late,
and Duke Huán raised a cup for him to drink.
Guǎn Zhòng poured out half the wine,
and Duke Huán said:
"You arrive after the set time,
and pour out the wine when drinking;
is this according to ritual?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard that when wine enters the mouth, the tongue comes out;
when the tongue comes out, words go astray;
when words go astray, one loses one's life.
Considering that I would lose my life,
it is better to pour out the wine."
Duke Huán laughed and said:
"Rise, Father Zhòng,
and take your seat."
10.22 When King Gōng of Chǔ fought Duke Lì of Jìn at Yānlíng,
Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn, thirsty, asked for a drink,
and Shù Gǔyáng brought him wine.
Zǐfǎn said:
"Take it away,
it is wine."
Gǔyáng said:
"It is not wine."
Zǐfǎn again said:
"Take it away,
it is wine."
Gǔyáng again said:
"It is not wine."
Zǐfǎn accepted it and drank,
became drunk and fell asleep.
King Gōng wished to resume battle,
and sent someone to summon Zǐfǎn,
but Zǐfǎn pleaded heart illness.
Then King Gōng rode in his carriage to see him,
entered the tent,
and smelled the odor of wine.
He said:
"In today's battle,
our reliance was on the Sīmǎ,
yet the Sīmǎ is so drunk;
this is to destroy our state and have no care for our troops.
I have no means to continue the fight."
Thereupon he put Zǐfǎn to death as punishment,
and withdrew the army.
Now Gǔyáng's offering of wine
was not out of envy for Zǐfǎn,
but out of loyal affection, yet it precisely sufficed to kill him.
Therefore it is said:
Small loyalties
are the ruin of great loyalty;
small gains
are the destruction of great profit.
10.23 Ministers fond of war
must not go unexamined.
Shamed by small disgraces, they create great enmities;
greedy for small gains, they lose the multitudes.
The Spring and Autumn Annals contain such warnings,
as with Xiān Zhěn of Jìn.
Xiān Zhěn, wishing to achieve merit and gain fame,
because Qín did not request passage,
asked to intercept the Qín army.
Duke Xiāng said:
"It cannot be.
The earl of Qín and our former lord had a covenant;
if we raise troops to attack them the very day our former lord has died,
it would be I who betray our former lord,
破坏邻国之交,
and abandon the conduct of a filial son."
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Our former lord has died, and they do not come to mourn or offer condolences;
this shows no grief for our loss.
Raising an army and crossing our land without requesting passage;
this is to despise our orphaned state.
Moreover, the coffin is still in the humble chamber,
and they show no grief for our loss."
When raising the army,
the divination said:
"A great state's army is coming;
we request to attack them."
Then he heeded Xiān Zhěn and raised troops,
intercepting them at Xiáo,
and attacked them,
leaving not a single horse or chariot wheel intact.
Thus they deeply enraged and brought disaster upon Qín,
crossing blades and shedding blood,
corpses lying exposed,
the state thrown into turmoil
for over ten years,
until finally they lost their armies and multitudes,
disaster reaching the great officers,
and anxiety burdening later generations.
Therefore, ministers fond of war
must not go unexamined.
10.24 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius, saying:
"I have heard of those who are extremely forgetful,
moving and forgetting their wives.
Is there such a thing?"
Confucius replied:
"This is not the most extreme forgetfulness.
The most forgetful
forget themselves."
The Duke said:
"May I hear about this?"
He replied:
"In the past, Jié of Xià was noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich with all under heaven,
yet he did not cultivate the Way of Yǔ,
destroyed laws and regulations,
cut off the sacrifices of generations,
indulged excessively in pleasure,
and drowned himself in wine.
Among his ministers was one called Chùlóng of the Left Army,
who flattered incessantly.
When Tāng punished Jié,
Chùlóng of the Left Army
died with his four limbs not sharing the same altar in burial.
This is one who forgot himself."
The Duke, looking solemn and changing countenance, said:
"Well said."
10.25 Confucius went to Zhōu,
and visited the Great Temple.
In front of the right steps,
there was a bronze figure,
with three seals over its mouth,
and an inscription on its back reading:
"I am a careful speaker of ancient times.
Be warned,
be warned!
Do not speak much,
much speech brings much failure;
do not meddle much,
much meddling brings much trouble.
In joy and comfort, be cautious,
do not act to incur regret.
Do not say 'what harm can it do',
its disaster will be long.
Do not say 'what injury can it cause',
its disaster will be great.
Do not say 'how can it be cruel',
its disaster will indeed come.
Do not say 'no one will hear',
heavenly demons watch over men.
A spark unextinguished,
how can the blaze be quelled?
A trickle unblocked,
will become a river.
Threads unbroken,
will form a net.
Green growth uncut,
will require an axe handle.
If truly one cannot be cautious of it,
it is the root of disaster.
How does the mouth cause injury?
It is the gate of disaster.
The violent do not die a natural death,
the competitive will meet their match.
Thieves resent the owner,
the people harm their superiors.
The nobleman knows that the world cannot be covered up,
so he steps back and lowers himself,
making others admire him.
Holding to the soft and maintaining humility,
none can contend with him.
Others all rush there,
I alone hold fast here.
The crowd is confused and deluded,
I alone do not follow.
I keep my knowledge within,
and do not dispute skills with others.
Though I am honored and elevated,
none can harm me.
The rivers and seas are lords of a hundred valleys
because they lie lower.
The Way of Heaven has no favorites,
it constantly sides with the good.
Be warned,
be warned!"
Confucius turned to his disciples and said:
"Remember this.
These words, though plain, hit the truth of matters.
The Book of Songs says:
'Trembling with fear,
as if approaching a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice.'
If one conducts oneself thus,
how could they encounter disaster through speech!"
10.26 Duke Āi of Lǔ abandoned his state and fled to Qí.
The Marquis of Qí asked:
"Why are you so young yet have abandoned your state so early?"
Duke Āi of Lǔ replied:
"When I first became crown prince,
many advised me,
but I listened without heeding;
many loved me,
but I loved them without drawing close.
Thus, I had no insight within and no support without,
like an autumn tumbleweed,
ugly at the root but fair in branches and leaves.
Once the autumn wind rises,
the root will be plucked out."
10.27 Confucius was traveling on the road
when he heard the sound of someone weeping,
its tone very sorrowful.
Confucius said:
"Drive on!
Drive on!
Ahead is someone with an unusual voice."
A short way ahead,
they saw him—
it was Qiūwúzǐ,
holding a sickle, wearing a rope belt, and weeping.
Confucius stepped down from his carriage
and asked:
"You, sir, have no funeral,
why do you weep so sorrowfully?"
Qiūwúzǐ replied:
"I have three failures."
Confucius said:
"I wish to hear of these three failures."
Qiūwúzǐ said:
"In my youth, I loved learning,
traveled all under heaven,
and upon returning, my parents had died.
This is the first failure.
I served my lord with extravagance and arrogance,
and my remonstrance was not followed.
This is the second failure.
I formed deep friendships but later broke them off,
this is the third failure.
The tree desires stillness but the wind will not cease;
the son wishes to care for his parents, but they do not wait.
What goes and does not return
is the years;
what cannot be seen again
are one's parents.
I beg to take my leave from here."
Then he cut his throat and died.
Confucius said:
"Disciples, remember this.
This is sufficient to serve as a warning."
Thereupon, thirteen disciples bade farewell to return and care for their parents.
10.28 Confucius, discussing the Book of Songs,
came to the sixth chapter of 'Zhēng Yuè',
and said with alarm:
"The nobleman who meets not his time,
is he not in peril?
Following superiors and conforming to the world, he abandons the Way;
defying superiors and leaving customs, he endangers himself.
The world does not side with the good,
yet he alone follows it,
so they say he is either a demon or a monster.
Thus, Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
Therefore, the worthy who meet not their time
often fear they will not come to a natural end.
The Book of Songs says:
'I say heaven is so high,
yet I dare not not stoop;
I say earth is so thick,
yet I dare not not tread lightly.'
This refers to this situation."
10.29 Confucius saw a bird-catcher,
and all that he had caught were fledglings.
Confucius said:
"You've caught all the fledglings,
but not a single adult bird.
Why is that?"
The catcher replied:
"If the fledglings follow the adult bird, they cannot be caught;
if the adult bird follows the fledglings, it can be caught."
Confucius turned to his disciples and said:
"The nobleman is cautious about whom he follows.
If he does not find the right person,
then he faces the calamity of nets and snares."
10.30 To cultivate one's character and rectify one's conduct,
one must be cautious.
Desires cause flaws in behavior,
slander and flattery disrupt a righteous heart,
and public opinion can sway one's intentions.
Worries arise from negligence,
disasters start from minor details,
disgrace is hard to wash away,
and failure cannot be undone.
Without deep thought and long-term planning,
how great will the regret be!
For opportunism
is an axe that harms one's nature;
desires
are horses that chase disaster;
deceit and exaggeration
are the dwelling of shame and hardship;
oppressing others
is the path to calamity.
Therefore it is said:
Abandon opportunism,
practice loyalty and trustworthiness,
restrain desires,
do not oppress others,
and you will be called a noble person,
with a lasting reputation.
10.31 Resentment arises from lack of reciprocity,
disaster comes from excessive good fortune;
safety and danger depend on how one conducts oneself;
avoiding hardship lies in early preparation;
survival or demise rests on obtaining the right people;
being as cautious at the end as at the beginning,
ensures longevity.
Those who can practice these five things
can preserve themselves.
What you do not desire,
do not impose on others—
this is the essential way.
10.32 Yán Huí was about to travel west,
and asked Confucius:
"How should I conduct myself?"
Confucius said:
"Courtesy, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness
can guide your conduct.
Courtesy saves you from public criticism,
respect makes others love you,
loyalty makes others support you,
trustworthiness makes others rely on you.
Being loved,
supported,
and relied upon by others,
you will surely avoid calamity.
This can govern a state,
how much more for personal conduct?
So, not aligning with what is close but with what is distant,
is that not misguided?
Not cultivating inner virtue but focusing on appearances,
is that not contrary?
Not planning ahead,
only scheming when difficulty arises,
is that not too late?"
10.33 In governing oneself,
one must carefully uphold five fundamentals.
First:
Gentleness with benevolence;
second:
Sincerity with trustworthiness;
third:
Wealth and honor,
yet never arrogant toward others;
fourth:
Courtesy with respect;
fifth:
Broad-mindedness with calm.
Reflecting on these five,
one avoids misfortune.
It is said:
Cultivating reverence to align with heaven's timing,
misfortune will not come and disaster will stay away.
Respecting others
is not just respecting them,
but respecting oneself;
honoring others
is not just honoring them,
but honoring oneself.
In the past,
I have seen heaven rain metal, stones, and blood;
I have seen four suns appear together on the tenth day,
and chaos in the heavens;
I have seen high mountains collapse,
deep valleys blocked,
great capitals and royal palaces destroyed,
mighty states perish;
I have seen towering mountains crack,
deep abysses' sands dry up,
noble people torn apart by chariots;
I have seen dense forests without trees,
plains turned into ravines,
noble persons made servants;
I have seen rivers and streams dry into pits,
elm and mulberry gathered in midwinter,
snow and frost falling in midsummer,
rulers of a thousand chariots, lords of ten thousand chariots,
dying without burial.
Thus, the noble person uses reverence to achieve fame,
the common person uses reverence to avoid punishment—
how can one not be vigilant and carefully uphold the five fundamentals!
10.34 In Lǔ, there was a respectful scholar named Jī Sì,
aged seventy,
whose respect grew even greater.
In winter, he walked in the shade,
in summer, in the sun,
never failing to follow market order,
always accompanying others in threes,
sitting with caution,
rising three times during a single meal,
not ashamed to show respect to those in coarse clothing,
and bowing to them.
The ruler of Lǔ asked:
"Master Jī, you are very old,
can you not relax your respectfulness?"
Jī Sì replied:
"The noble person loves respect to build their reputation,
the common person learns respect to avoid punishment.
Sitting before a ruler,
is it not secure? Yet one may still stumble;
eating a meal,
is it not pleasant? Yet one may still choke.
Now, I, Sì, am what you call fortunate,
but surely cannot be certain.
Swans fly soaring to the sky,
is it not high? Yet arrows can still reach them;
tigers and leopards are fierce,
yet people still eat their flesh
and sit on their skins.
Those who praise are few,
those who criticize are many.
At seventy years of age,
I often fear the axe may fall upon me—
why should I abandon respectfulness!"
10.35 Chéng Huí studied under Zǐ Lù for three years,
and Huí remained ever respectful.
Zǐ Lù asked him the reason why.
Huí replied:
"I have heard that
a traveler is like a bird,
fearing hawks above
and nets below.
Those who do good are few,
those who slander are many.
As long as one lives,
how can one know that misfortune and blame will not befall?
At seventy years of age,
I often fear failing in my conduct.
Therefore, I use respectfulness to await my fate."
Zǐ Lù bowed and said:
"A noble person indeed!"
11.1 Xún Qīng said:
"The art of persuasion
requires dignity to establish it,
sincerity to approach it,
firmness to maintain it,
analogies to illustrate it,
distinctions to clarify it,
and enthusiasm to convey it;
treasure it, cherish it,
value it, and revere it.
If this is done, persuasion will rarely fail.
This is called being able to value what should be valued.
The Tradition says:
'Only the gentleman can value what should be valued.'"
The Book of Songs says:
"Do not take speech lightly,
do not say it is unimportant."
Guǐ Gǔ Zǐ said:
"It is difficult to correct what is bad in others.
When persuasion fails
and words are not followed,
it is because the argument is not clear.
If it is clear but still not followed,
it is because the maintenance is not firm.
If it is firm but still not followed,
it is because it has not hit upon what the heart finds good.
To argue it,
clarify it,
maintain it,
and firm it up,
while also hitting upon what the person finds good -
such words, divine and precious,
clear and distinct,
can enter people's hearts.
If persuasion still fails under such circumstances,
it has never been heard of in the world."
This is called skilled persuasion.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"The words one speaks and arguments one presents
determine personal success or failure,
and the safety or danger of the state."
The Book of Songs says:
"When words are harmonious,
the people are at peace."
Words are the means by which people communicate.
Zhǔ Fù Yǎn said:
"If a person lacks eloquence,
what use are they?"
In the past, Zǐ Chǎn cultivated his speech and Zhào Wǔ showed him respect;
Wáng Sūn Mǎn spoke clearly and King Chǔ Zhuāng felt ashamed;
Sū Qín practiced his persuasion and the six states were thereby secured;
Kuǎi Tōng presented his arguments and thereby preserved his life.
Words are indeed the means to honor the ruler and value oneself,
to secure the state and preserve one's nature.
Therefore, speech cannot be left uncultivated,
and persuasion cannot be left unperfected.
11.2 Zhào sent a messenger to tell the King of Wèi:
"Kill Fàn Cuó for me,
and I will offer you seventy li of land."
The King of Wèi said:
"Agreed."
He sent officials to arrest Cuó,
surrounding him but not yet killing him.
Cuó climbed onto the roof and, perched on the ridge, said to the messenger:
"Rather than trading dead Cuó,
better to trade living Cuó.
If I die,
and Zhào doesn't give the king the land,
what will the king do then?
So better to first settle the land transfer,
then kill me."
The King of Wèi said:
"Good."
Cuó then wrote to Lord Xìnlíng:
"I, Cuó,
am Wèi's former dismissed minister.
If Zhào uses land to have me killed and the King of Wèi complies,
what if powerful Qín similarly follows Zhào's desire -
what will you do then?"
Lord Xìnlíng spoke to the king and had him released.
11.3 When Wú invaded Jīng,
they summoned Duke Huái of Chén.
Duke Huái gathered the people and said:
"Those who side with Jīng go left,
those who side with Wú go right."
Féng Huá advanced directly toward the duke and said:
"Wú has no blessing,
Jīng has no disaster."
The duke said:
"Their state is defeated, their ruler exiled -
if that's not disaster, what is?"
He replied:
"When a small state has such, it still recovers,
how much more a large state?
Although Chǔ lacks virtue,
it does not slaughter its people.
Wú is daily exhausted by war,
bones exposed like thick grass,
showing no virtue.
Heaven may be properly instructing Jīng -
when disaster befalls Wú,
how long will it take!"
The Marquis of Chén followed his advice.
11.4 Duke Huán established Guǎn Zhòng as Zhòng Fù and addressed his ministers:
"Those who approve of me enter and go right,
those who disapprove enter and go left."
One man stood in the middle of the gateway.
Duke Huán asked him why,
and he replied:
"Guǎnzǐ's wisdom can plan for the world,
his strength can seize the world.
Do you rely on his trustworthiness,
entrusting internal affairs to him,
letting him decide external matters,
driving the people to follow him?
This too can be taken away."
Duke Huán said:
"Good."
He then told Guǎn Zhòng:
"Government shall ultimately rest with you.
Where government falls short,
only you shall correct it."
Guǎn Zhòng therefore built the Sānguī Terrace
to humble himself before the people.
11.5 King Xuān of Qí went hunting at Shè Mountain,
where thirteen village elders came to greet him.
The king said:
"Elders, you have suffered!"
He ordered his attendants to exempt the elders from land tax.
All the elders bowed except Lǘ Qiū Xiānshēng.
The king said:
"Do the elders consider this too little?"
He ordered his attendants to also exempt the elders from corvée labor.
All the elders bowed except Lǘ Qiū Xiānshēng again.
The king said:
"Those who bowed may leave;
he who didn't bow, come forward."
He said:
"I came today to inspect,
and you elders kindly greeted me,
so I exempted you from land tax -
all bowed except you, sir.
I thought it insufficient,
so I exempted you from corvée labor -
all bowed except you again.
Have I committed some fault?"
Lǘ Qiū Xiānshēng replied:
"I heard the great king was touring,
so I came to greet you,
hoping to gain longevity from the king,
hoping to gain wealth from the king,
hoping to gain honor from the king."
The king said:
"Heaven determines life and death -
this is beyond my control,
so I cannot grant you longevity;
though granaries are full,
they're for disasters,
so I cannot make you wealthy;
high offices have no vacancies,
low offices are humble,
so I cannot honor you."
Lǘ Qiū Xiānshēng replied:
"This is not what your servant dared hope for.
I wish the king would select virtuous sons of good families as officials,
equalizing laws and measures -
thus I could gain some longevity;
that in all seasons aid be timely distributed,
without harassing the people -
thus I could gain some wealth;
that the king issue orders
making the young respect their elders
and elders respect the aged -
thus I could gain some honor.
Now the king kindly exempts me from land tax,
but then granaries will be empty;
exempts me from corvée labor,
but then government will have no labor.
This is truly not what your servant dared hope for."
The King of Qí said:
"Excellent.
I wish to invite you, sir, to be my chancellor."
11.10 Chénzǐ persuaded King of Liáng,
and the King, though pleased, was skeptical,
saying:
"Why have you left the state of Lord Chén,
to instruct an orphan of a small state here?"
Chénzǐ replied:
"Virtue has its ways,
and encounters their timing.
In the past, Fù Yuè, clad in coarse cloth and rope belt, built at Bǐfù's wall,
and Wǔ Dīng dreamed at night and found him at dawn,
for it was the king's time.
Nìng Qì fed oxen on the broad road,
struck a cart spoke and sang,
was noticed,
and Duke Huán obtained him,
for it was the time of hegemony.
Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself for the price of five sheepskins,
became a captive of the Qín people,
and Duke Mù obtained him,
for it was the time of strength.
Judging by the conduct of these three men,
they could not be considered outstanding disciples of Confucius.
Now Confucius, in managing the world,
faced adversity in the south with Chén and Cài,
and in the north importuned Duke Jǐng,
sitting twice and standing five times,
never leaving his side.
Confucius's timing was not right,
and Duke Jǐng's moment was lax.
With Confucius's sageliness,
he could not use timely persuasion to overcome laxity;
what more could one do?"
11.11 Lín Jì, wearing leather garments, attended the court of Duke Jǐng of Qí,
and Duke Jǐng of Qí said:
"Is this the attire of a gentleman,
or that of a petty man?"
Lín Jì hesitated, then with a changed expression said:
"How can attire determine a scholar's conduct?
In the past, Jīng wore long swords and tall hats,
yet produced Chief Minister Zǐ Xī;
Qí had short coats and peaked caps,
yet produced Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng;
Yuè tattooed bodies and cut hair,
yet produced Fàn Lǐ and Grand Fū Zhǒng;
the Western Róng wore left-fastening robes and coiled hair,
yet produced Yóu Yú.
If it were as you say,
those in dog fur should bark,
and those in sheep fur should bleat.
Moreover, you wear fox fur to court;
might you then be expected to change?"
Duke Jǐng said:
"You are truly bold and fierce!
I have not yet witnessed your extraordinary eloquence;
is it that of a neighborhood brawl,
or of a victory with a thousand chariots?"
Lín Jì said:
"I do not know what you mean.
To climb heights and face danger without blinking,
and without stumbling,
is the bold fierceness of craftsmen;
to enter deep abysses,
stab at flood dragons,
and emerge clutching giant turtles,
is the bold fierceness of fishermen;
to enter deep mountains,
hunt tigers and leopards,
and emerge clutching bears and brown bears,
is the bold fierceness of hunters;
to not fear severed heads and torn bellies,
with bones exposed and blood flowing in the wilds,
is the bold fierceness of warriors.
Now I stand in this grand court,
with a stern expression and upright speech,
to provoke your lordship's anger;
though there may be rewards of carriages ahead,
I am not moved,
and though there may be the threat of axe and block behind,
I am not afraid.
This is why I am considered bold and fierce."
11.12 Marquis Wén of Wèi was drinking with his ministers,
and appointed Gōngchéng Bùrén as master of the feast,
saying:
"Those who do not drain their cups shall be fined a large goblet."
The Marquis drank but did not drain his cup,
so Gōngchéng Bùrén raised a large goblet to fine the lord,
who looked on without responding.
An attendant said:
"Bùrén, withdraw;
the lord is already drunk."
Gōngchéng Bùrén said:
"The 'Zhōu Shū' states:
'When the front cart overturns,
the rear cart takes warning.'
This speaks of peril;
it is not easy to be a minister,
nor is it easy to be a lord.
Now you have set a rule;
can it be disregarded?"
The lord said:
"Well said."
He raised the goblet and drank,
and after drinking said:
"Let Gōngchéng Bùrén be honored as a distinguished guest."
11.13 On the day of Lord Xiāngchéng's inaugural enfiefment,
he wore emerald robes,
belted with a jade clasp,
adorned with a jade sword,
and shod in white silk shoes,
standing by flowing water.
Ministers held bells and hammers suspended,
ordered to beat drums and call out,
asking who could ferry the king across.
The Chǔ minister Zhuāng Xīn passed by, admired him,
approached to pay respects,
rose and said:
"I wish to hold your hand;
may I?"
Lord Xiāngchéng flushed with anger and remained silent.
Zhuāng Xīn stepped back, clasped his hands, and declared:
"Have you not heard of Lord Èzǐ Xī boating on new waves?
He rode in a blue-feathered boat,
adorned with duckweed patterns,
under a green canopy,
and tapped a rhinoceros tail,
with splendid gowns and lapels;
when the bells and drums ceased,
a Yuè boatman held an oar and sang.
The lyrics said:
'Làn xī biàn cǎo làn yú,
chāng hù zé yú,
chāng zhōu zhōu,
shí zhōu yān hū,
qín xū xū,
màn yú hū,
zhāo chán qín yú,
shèn shì suí hé hú.'
Lord Èzǐ Xī said:
'I do not understand Yuè songs;
please interpret it in Chǔ speech for me.'
So he summoned a Yuè interpreter,
who rendered it in Chǔ speech:
'What night is this night,
that I drift midstream;
what day is this day,
that I share a boat with the prince.
Though shy, I am favored,
undaunted by shame.
My heart persists stubbornly,
knowing I've met the prince.
Mountains have trees, trees have branches,
my heart delights in you, but you do not know.'
Then Lord Èzǐ Xī, with long sleeves, stepped forward and embraced him,
raising an embroidered cover to shelter him.
Lord Èzǐ Xī was the full brother of the King of Chǔ's mother,
held the office of Chief Minister,
and the rank of Zhí Guī;
yet a mere Yuè boatman
could share joy and sincerity.
Now, how do you surpass Lord Èzǐ Xī,
and why am I less than that boatman,
that I wish to hold your hand,
and cannot?"
Lord Xiāngchéng then offered his hand and advanced, saying:
"In my youth,
I too was praised by elders for my looks,
but never encountered such abruptness.
From now on,
I will respectfully accept your guidance with the etiquette due to a young man."
11.14 Yōngmén Zǐzhōu came to see Mèngcháng Jūn with his zither.
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Master, when you play the zither,
can you also make Wén feel sorrow?"
Yōngmén Zǐzhōu replied:
"How could I alone make you feel sorrow!
Those whom I can make sorrowful
are those who were once noble but later became humble,
or who were once wealthy but later became poor.
Or those of outstanding talent
who unfortunately encounter tyrannical and unprincipled rulers,
and are wrongly accused of unfounded crimes;
or those in isolated positions,
cut off from neighbors,
bent and oppressed,
hiding in poor alleys,
with nowhere to plead their case;
or those deeply in love,
separated without grievance,
sent to distant lands,
with no hope of reunion;
or those who lost both parents young,
separated from siblings,
with insufficient family support,
and hearts full of sorrow.
At such times,
they cannot bear even the sound of birds or wind,
truly finding no joy in life.
For all such people,
when I tune my zither and sigh deeply,
tears soak my lapel.
But you, sir,
are a lord of a thousand chariots.
You dwell in vast mansions and deep rooms,
with silk curtains drawn,
welcoming cool breezes,
entertainers and dwarfs before you,
competing to flatter;
at banquets you play chess and watch Zhèng maidens dance,
enjoying stirring Chǔ melodies,
beautiful sights to delight your eyes,
flowing music to please your ears.
On water, you cruise with connected boats,
flying feathered banners,
with music over unfathomable depths;
in fields, you gallop and hunt across plains and vast parks,
fighting fierce beasts;
indoors, you strike bells and drums in deep palaces.
At such times,
you regard heaven and earth as less than a finger,
forgetting life and death—
even the best zither player
could never make you sorrowful."
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"No, no,
I truly don't think so."
Yōngmén Zǐzhōu said:
"Well,
there is one thing for which I sorrow for you.
You who rival emperors and trouble Qín,
it is you,
who formed the alliance of five states,
marching south to attack Chǔ—
again, it is you.
The world is never without events:
if not vertical, then horizontal alliances.
If vertical succeeds, Chǔ will king;
if horizontal succeeds, Qín will emperor.
Either would seek revenge on Xuē.
With Qín and Chǔ's strength
avenging on weak Xuē
is like sharpening an axe to cut morning mushrooms—
surely leaving no trace.
All insightful people under heaven
shiver and their noses sour for you.
After a thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
your ancestral temple will lack sacrifices.
Your high towers will crumble,
your winding ponds silt up,
your graves level,
overgrown with green.
Children and gatherers
will trample and sing above,
and passersby,
all saddened, will mourn for you,
saying:
'With Mèngcháng Jūn's nobility,
how could it come to this!'"
Then Mèngcháng Jūn welled up with tears,
glistening yet unfallen.
Yōngmén Zǐzhōu took his zither and played,
slowly moving through notes,
gently touching others,
until the melody ended.
Mèngcháng Jūn's tears flowed like sweat,
sobbing as he approached,
saying:
"Hearing your zither play,
I feel like one whose country and city have fallen."
11.15 Qú Bóyù, on a mission to Chǔ,
met Prince Xī by the Pú River.
Xī pulled grass while waiting,
saying:
"May I ask, honored envoy, where are you going?"
Qú Bóyù bowed in his carriage.
Prince Xī said:
"I've heard high scholars can be entrusted with expressions,
middle scholars with words,
low scholars with wealth.
Can one entrust oneself through these three?"
Qú Bóyù said:
"I heed your instruction."
Qú Bóyù met the King of Chǔ,
completed his mission,
and during conversation,
calmly turned to scholars.
The King asked:
"Which state has the most scholars?"
Qú Bóyù replied:
"Chǔ has the most scholars."
The King was delighted.
Qú Bóyù added:
"But Chǔ cannot use them."
The King startled:
"What do you mean?"
Qú Bóyù said:
"Wǔ Zǐxū was born in Chǔ,
fled to Wú,
where he became chancellor,
led troops against Chǔ,
desecrated King Píng's tomb—
born in Chǔ, but well-used by Wú.
Fèn Fēn Huáng, born in Chǔ,
went to Jìn,
governed seventy-two counties,
where nothing was lost on roads,
people took nothing undeserved,
city gates stayed open,
the state had no thieves—
born in Chǔ, but well-used by Jìn.
On my way here,
I met Prince Xī by the Pú River,
who said:
'High scholars can be entrusted with expressions,
middle scholars with words,
low scholars with wealth.
Can one entrust oneself through these three?'
I wonder what Prince Xī will accomplish."
Thereupon, the King sent a team of four,
with two secondary carriages,
to fetch Prince Xī from the Pú River.
Xī returned,
highly regarded in Chǔ,
thanks to Qú Bóyù's effort.
Thus the Odes say:
"Who will cook fish?
I'll clean the pot;
who goes west?
I'll send good news."
This illustrates it.
Things that complement each other
are indeed subtle.
11.16 Shū Xiàng's younger brother Yángshé Hǔ was friends with Yuè Dá.
Dá offended Jìn,
Jìn executed Yángshé Hǔ,
and Shū Xiàng was enslaved.
Then Qí Xī said:
"I've heard when petty men gain power,
not opposing injustice,
and when noble men worry,
not rescuing them is inauspicious."
He went to see Fàn Xuānzǐ and persuaded him,
saying:
"I hear those good at governing reward without excess and punish without abuse.
Excess rewards risk benefiting the wicked;
abuse of punishment risks harming noble men.
If misfortune must come,
rather err in rewarding the wicked
than err in punishing noble men.
Thus Yáo in punishment
executed Gǔn at Yǔshān yet employed Yǔ;
Zhōu in punishment
killed Guǎn and Cài yet employed the Duke of Zhōu—
this is not abuse of punishment."
Xuānzǐ then ordered Shū Xiàng's release.
Those who rescue others from trouble
undertake danger and hardship, undeterred by trouble or shame,
yet may not succeed;
but Qí Xī, citing ancient kings' virtue,
secured Shū Xiàng's release—
how can learning ever be enough!
11.17 Zhāng Lù, the sect leader, visited Mèngcháng Jūn and said:
"To have clothes that are always new and never old,
granaries that are full and never empty—
there is a way to achieve this.
Does my lord know of it?"
Mèngcháng Jūn replied:
"Clothes that are new and never old—
that would mean they are well-maintained;
granaries that are full and never empty—
that would mean wealth.
But how can this be done?
May I hear your explanation?"
Zhāng Lù said:
"I wish that when you are noble, you would promote the worthy;
when you are wealthy, you would relieve the poor.
If you do this, then your clothes will be new and never old,
and your granaries full and never empty."
Mèngcháng Jūn found his words reasonable,
was pleased with his ideas,
and admired his rhetoric.
The next day, he sent someone to present a hundred catties of gold
and a hundred bolts of patterned silk,
offering them to Master Zhāng.
But the master declined and did not accept.
Later, the master visited Mèngcháng Jūn again,
and Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Previously, you kindly instructed me, saying:
'Clothes that are new and never old,
granaries that are full and never empty.
There is a method to achieve this,
do you know of it?'
I privately appreciated your teaching,
so I sent someone to present a hundred catties of gold
and a hundred bolts of patterned silk,
offering them to you, sir,
to help those in need within your household.
Why did you decline and not accept?"
Zhāng Lù said:
"If you were to dig out your stored coins,
and open your granaries to aid the scholars,
then you would end up with worn clothes and torn shoes, unable to provide for yourself.
How would you have the leisure for clothes that are new and never old,
or granaries that are full and never empty?"
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Then what should be done?"
Zhāng Lù said:
"Now, Qín is a state surrounded by natural barriers,
a landlocked country,
and traveling officials cannot enter it.
I wish you would write a short letter for me,
addressed to the King of Qín.
If I go and am received,
it will surely be your introduction that gains me entry;
if I go and am not received,
even if others seek to intercede,
they certainly will not succeed on my behalf."
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"I respectfully heed your command."
Thereupon, he wrote the letter for him,
sending it to the King of Qín.
Zhāng Lù went and was greatly received,
and he said to the King of Qín:
"Since I, Lù, entered the borders of Your Majesty's realm,
the fields have become more cultivated,
and the officials and people are better governed.
However, there is one thing that Your Majesty lacks—
does Your Majesty know what it is?"
The king said:
"I do not know."
Zhāng Lù said:
"In Shāndōng, there is a chancellor,
the one called Mèngcháng Jūn.
This man is a worthy,
and when the world is not in crisis, all is well,
but when there is a crisis, he can gather the heroic and talented men of the world,
forming alliances and friendships with them.
I suspect he is unique in this.
So why does Your Majesty not make friends with him for me?"
The King of Qín said:
"I respectfully accept your advice."
He sent a thousand pieces of gold to Mèngcháng Jūn.
Mèngcháng Jūn stopped eating, pondered the matter, and realized:
"This is what Master Zhāng meant by clothes that are new and never old,
and granaries that are full and never empty."
11.18 Zhuāng Zhōu was in poverty
and went to borrow grain from Wèi Wénhóu.
Wénhóu said:
"Wait until the grain from my estate arrives, and I will give it to you."
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
"As I was coming here today,
I saw a carp in a cow's hoofprint by the roadside.
It sighed deeply and said to me:
'Can I still survive?'
I said:
'Wait for me to go south to see the King of Chǔ for you,
and have him divert the Jiāng and Huái rivers to irrigate you.'
The carp said:
'Now my life is in this puddle,
and you tell me you will see the King of Chǔ for me,
to divert the Jiāng and Huái rivers to irrigate me—
by then, you will be looking for me in the dried fish market.'
Now, I have come to borrow grain because of my poverty,
and you say to wait until the grain from your estate arrives to bestow it upon me.
By the time it comes, you will be seeking me in the hired laborers' market."
Wénhóu then issued a hundred zhōng of grain
and sent it to Zhuāng Zhōu's home.
11.19 Jìn Pínggōng asked Shū Xiàng:
"There is famine and plague among the people,
and the Dí people are attacking us.
What should I do?"
Shū Xiàng replied:
"In a year of famine,
the next year will see recovery;
the plague
will eventually cease;
the Dí people
are not a serious concern."
The duke said:
"Is there a greater worry than these?"
He replied:
"When high ministers value their salaries but do not remonstrate to the utmost,
when close officials fear punishment and dare not speak,
and when those around you are favored by petty officials without your knowledge,
these are truly the greatest worries."
The duke said:
"Well said."
Thereupon, he issued an order throughout the state:
"Those who wish to remonstrate may do so without concealment;
if those around me or state officials interfere,
they will be punished."
11.20 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ attacked Táo,
and two men were the first to scale the walls,
dying on top of the city.
Jiǎnzǐ wanted to retrieve their bodies,
but the Lord of Táo would not give them.
Chéng Pénjū said to the Lord of Táo:
"Jiǎnzǐ is going to dig up your ancestral tombs,
and bargain with your people, saying:
'Those who cross the city walls and scale the defenses will be pardoned;
those who do not—
I will dig up their graves,
scatter the ashes of the decayed,
and dismember the bodies of the undecayed.'"
The Lord of Táo grew fearful
and offered to hand over the two bodies to make peace.
11.21 Zǐgòng visited Grand Superintendent Pǐ,
and Grand Superintendent Pǐ asked:
"What is Confucius like?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"I am not capable of knowing."
Grand Superintendent Pǐ said:
"If you do not know,
how can you serve him?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"Precisely because I do not know,
I serve him.
My master is like a great mountain forest—
the common people each take what resources they need from it."
Grand Superintendent Pǐ said:
"Do you enhance your master?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"My master cannot be enhanced.
I, Cì, am like a clod of earth.
To add a clod of earth to a great mountain
does not increase its height
and only shows ignorance."
Grand Superintendent Pǐ said:
"Then do you have something to draw from?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"There is a great wine vessel in the world,
and yet you alone do not draw from it—
I do not know whose fault that is."
11.22 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Zǐgòng:
"What kind of person is Confucius?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"I, Cì, cannot comprehend him."
Jiǎnzǐ, displeased, said:
"You served Confucius for decades,
completed your studies, and then left him.
I ask you,
and you say:
'I cannot comprehend him.'
Why is that?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I am like a thirsty man drinking from the river or sea—
I know only when I am satisfied.
Confucius is like the river or sea;
how could I, Cì, be capable of comprehending him?"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Excellent are Zǐgòng's words."
11.23 Duke Jǐng of Qí said to Zǐgòng:
"Whom do you study under?"
He replied:
"Your servant studies under Zhòngní."
The Duke asked:
"Is Zhòngní worthy?"
He responded:
"Worthy."
The Duke said:
"How worthy is he?"
He answered:
"I do not know."
The Duke said:
"You know he is worthy,
but do not know how worthy he is,
is that acceptable?"
He replied:
"Now if we say the sky is high,
regardless of age or wisdom, all know it is high,
but how high it is,
all say they do not know.
Thus I know Zhòngní is worthy,
but do not know how worthy he is."
11.24 Zhào Xiāngzǐ said to Zhòngní:
"You, sir, have presented yourself to meet rulers,
seventy lords in total,
yet found no success.
Is it that the world lacks enlightened rulers?
Or is your Way fundamentally unsuccessful?"
Zhòngní did not respond.
Another day,
Xiāngzǐ saw Zǐlù and said:
"I once asked your master about the Way,
and he did not respond.
If he knows but doesn't answer, he is hiding it;
how can hiding be called benevolent?
If he truly doesn't know,
how can he be called sage?"
Zǐlù said:
"If you set up the world's loudest bell and strike it with a stick,
how could it possibly produce sound!
Your question to my master,
was it not like striking with a stick?"
11.25 General Wénzǐ of Wèi asked Zǐgòng:
"Jì Wénzǐ was three times impoverished and three times successful, why?"
Zǐgòng said:
"When impoverished, he served the worthy;
when successful, he promoted the poor;
when wealthy, he shared with the needy;
when noble, he respected the humble.
Being poor yet serving the worthy prevents humiliation;
being successful yet promoting the poor shows loyalty to friends;
being wealthy yet sharing with the needy makes the clan cherish him;
being noble yet respecting the humble makes the common people support him.
His gains were due to the proper Way,
his losses were fate."
He asked:
"What about those who lose and never regain?"
He replied:
"When poor, they don't serve the worthy;
when successful, they don't promote the poor;
when wealthy, they don't share with the needy;
when noble, they don't respect the humble.
Their gains are due to fate,
their losses are due to the proper Way."
11.26 Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"What kind of person was Guǎn Zhòng?"
The Master said:
"A great man."
Zǐlù said:
"Previously Guǎnzǐ advised Duke Xiāng,
but Duke Xiāng was not pleased - this shows lack of eloquence;
he wanted to establish Prince Jiū but failed - this shows incompetence;
his family suffered in Qí yet he showed no sorrow - this shows lack of compassion;
he was shackled in a prison cart without shame - this shows no remorse;
he served the lord he had shot at - this shows lack of integrity;
Zhào Hū died for his lord,
but Guǎn Zhòng did not die - this shows lack of benevolence.
Why do you, Master, consider him great?"
The Master said:
"When Guǎn Zhòng advised Duke Xiāng,
and Duke Xiāng was not pleased,
it wasn't that Guǎnzǐ lacked eloquence,
but that Duke Xiāng didn't understand persuasion;
wanting to establish Prince Jiū but failing,
wasn't incompetence,
but missing the right timing;
his family suffering in Qí yet showing no sorrow,
wasn't lack of compassion,
but understanding fate;
being shackled in a prison cart without shame,
wasn't lack of remorse,
but self-restraint;
serving the lord he had shot at,
wasn't lack of integrity,
but understanding expediency;
Zhào Hū dying for his lord,
while Guǎn Zhòng did not die,
wasn't lack of benevolence,
but weighing the relative importance.
Zhào Hū
had the talent of a minister;
if he hadn't died, he would have been captured by the three armies;
by dying,
he made his name known throughout the world -
why wouldn't he die?
As for Guǎnzǐ,
he was an assistant to the Son of Heaven,
a minister to the feudal lords;
had he died, he would have become rotting flesh in a ditch,
but by not dying, his achievements benefited the world -
why should he have died?
Yóu,
you do not understand."
11.27 Duke Píng of Jìn asked Shī Kuàng:
"Who is more worthy, Jiù Fàn or Zhào Cuī?"
He replied:
"Yáng Chǔfǔ wanted to serve Duke Wén as minister;
through Jiù Fàn, he waited three years without success;
through Zhào Cuī, he succeeded in three days.
If one has wisdom but doesn't know his own men,
he lacks wisdom;
if he knows but doesn't speak,
he lacks loyalty;
if he wants to speak but dares not,
he lacks courage;
if he speaks but isn't listened to,
he lacks worthiness."
11.28 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Chéng Tuán:
"I hear that Yáng Zhí is a worthy minister,
what is his conduct like?"
He replied:
"Your servant Tuán does not know."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I have heard
you are close friends with him,
yet you claim not to know him,
why is that?"
Tuán said:
"His character has changed several times.
At fifteen,
he was honest and did not conceal his faults;
at twenty,
he was benevolent and delighted in righteousness;
at thirty,
he became Central Army Commander of Jìn,
courageous and delighting in benevolence;
at fifty,
he became border city general,
reconciling with those who were distant.
Now I haven't seen him for five years,
and fear he may have changed again,
therefore I dare not claim to know him."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Truly a worthy minister indeed,
with each change he becomes even better."
12.1 The expressions in the Spring and Autumn Annals contain four apparent contradictions.
It states that ministers should not initiate actions arbitrarily,
meaning they must not create affairs on their own authority;
yet it also says that when beyond the borders, if they can secure the altars of soil and grain and benefit the state,
then they may exercise discretion.
It states that ministers go forth on the ruler's command,
yet their advance or retreat is determined by the ministers themselves;
and it also says that when going forth on the ruler's command,
upon hearing of mourning, they should proceed slowly but not turn back.
Why is this?
The answer is:
These principles each apply to their specific categories
and are not interchangeable.
"Must not initiate actions arbitrarily" refers to normal, routine matters;
"May exercise discretion" refers to rescuing from danger and eliminating calamities.
"Advance or retreat determined by the ministers" refers to generals employing troops;
"Proceed slowly but not turn back" refers to envoys on the road hearing of the mourning of their ruler or parents.
Gōngzǐ Jié initiated actions arbitrarily,
yet the Spring and Autumn Annals does not condemn him,
considering that he rescued Duke Zhuāng from danger;
Gōngzǐ Suì initiated actions arbitrarily,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals criticizes him,
considering that Duke Xī faced no dangerous situation.
Therefore, if the ruler is in danger and the minister does not exercise discretion to rescue him,
this is disloyalty;
if there is no danger yet the minister initiates actions arbitrarily,
this is failing in ministerial duty.
The Tradition says:
"The Book of Songs has no fixed interpretation,
the Book of Changes no fixed auspiciousness,
the Spring and Autumn Annals no fixed meaning."
This refers to such cases.
12.2 The King of Zhào sent an envoy to Chǔ.
While playing the sè, he dispatched him,
admonishing him:
"You must act exactly as I have said."
The envoy said:
"Your Majesty's playing of the sè has never been as sorrowful as this."
The King said:
"The gōng and shāng notes are indeed just in tune."
The envoy said:
"If they are in tune, then why not mark them on the bridges?"
The King said:
"The heavens have dryness and humidity,
the strings have slackness and tightness;
the shifts of gōng and shāng cannot be predetermined,
therefore they are not marked."
The envoy said:
"An enlightened ruler's dispatch of envoys
entrusts them with tasks
without constraining them with rigid words.
If they encounter good fortune, they congratulate;
if misfortune, they offer condolences.
Now, between Chǔ and Zhào, more than a thousand lǐ apart,
good or ill fortune, worries and troubles
cannot be foreknown,
just as the bridges cannot be marked."
The Book of Songs says:
"Numerous are the messengers on duty,
each bearing concerns lest they fail to fulfill their mission."
12.3 King Zhuāng of Chǔ raised an army to attack Sòng.
Sòng urgently sought help from Jìn.
Duke Jǐng of Jìn wished to send troops to rescue Sòng,
but Bó Zōng advised against it, saying:
"Heaven is currently favoring Chǔ;
it is not the time to attack."
So they sought a brave man
and found Xiè Yáng from Huò,
styled Zǐhǔ,
sending him to order Sòng not to surrender.
On the way, he passed through Zhèng,
which had recently allied with Chǔ,
so they seized Xiè Yáng and presented him to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ offered him rich rewards and made an agreement,
wanting him to reverse his message
and urge Sòng to hasten surrender,
but Xiè Yáng refused.
After three demands,
Xiè Yáng pretended to agree.
Thereupon, Chǔ had Xiè Yáng ascend a watchtower chariot,
ordering him to call out to Sòng to surrender;
but he betrayed the agreement with Chǔ
and conveyed his Jìn ruler's command, saying:
"Jìn is mobilizing all its national troops to rescue Sòng.
Though Sòng is hard-pressed,
take care not to surrender to Chǔ.
Jìn's army will arrive soon."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was greatly enraged
and was about to have him boiled alive.
Xiè Yáng said:
"A ruler's ability to issue commands constitutes righteousness;
a minister's ability to receive and carry out commands constitutes faithfulness.
Having received my ruler's command to go forth,
even death will not alter my loyalty."
The King said:
"You promised me,
then betrayed it;
where is your faithfulness?"
Xiè Yáng said:
"To promise the King, even unto death,
was intended to fulfill my ruler's command;
I have no regrets."
Turning, he said to the Chǔ army:
"Let no minister forget to be utterly loyal, even if it leads to death."
The King of Chǔ's brothers all advised the King to pardon him.
Thereupon, King Zhuāng finally pardoned Xiè Yáng and sent him back.
Jìn ennobled him as a high minister,
hence later generations speak of Huò Hǔ.
12.4 The King of Qín offered five hundred lǐ of land in exchange for Línglíng.
The Lord of Línglíng declined and did not accept,
sending Táng Jū to thank the King of Qín.
The King of Qín said:
"Qín has crushed Hán and destroyed Wèi;
the Lord of Línglíng alone survives with fifty lǐ of land.
Is it that I fear his power?
I merely admire his righteousness.
Now I offer him ten times the land in exchange,
yet the Lord of Línglíng declines and does not accept;
this is to despise me."
Táng Jū left his mat and replied:
"It is not so.
Línglíng is a place that does not act based on profit or harm.
The Lord of Línglíng received this land from his ancestors and guards it;
even a thousand lǐ more could not be equivalent,
let alone five hundred lǐ!"
The King of Qín, flushing with anger,
said furiously:
"Have you, sir, ever seen the anger of a Son of Heaven?"
Táng Jū said:
"Your servant has never seen it."
The King of Qín said:
"When the Son of Heaven is angry,
corpses fall by the millions,
blood flows for a thousand lǐ."
Táng Jū said:
"Has Your Majesty ever seen the anger of a scholar in cloth garments and leather girdle?"
The King of Qín said:
"The anger of a scholar in cloth garments and leather girdle—
he removes his cap, goes barefoot,
and knocks his head on the ground—
what is hard to know about that?"
Táng Jū said:
"This is the anger of an ordinary fool,
not the anger of a scholar in cloth garments and leather girdle.
When Zhuān Zhū assassinated King Liáo,
a comet swept the moon,
and shooting stars appeared by day;
when Yāo Lí assassinated Prince Qìngjì,
a gray falcon struck the terrace;
when Niè Zhèng assassinated the younger uncle of the King of Hán,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
These three men were all scholars in cloth garments and leather girdle who became angry;
with me, they make four.
When a scholar's anger is contained and not yet unleashed,
an ominous aura rises to heaven.
If a scholar is not angry, all is well;
once angry,
two corpses will fall,
blood will flow within five steps."
Then, pressing his dagger, he rose
and said to the King of Qín:
"It will happen now!"
The King of Qín, pale-faced, knelt upright and said:
"Sir, please resume your seat.
I understand now.
Qín crushed Hán and destroyed Wèi,
yet Línglíng alone survives with fifty lǐ of land—
solely because of you, sir."
12.5 When Qí attacked Lǔ,
Zǐgòng went to see Duke Āi,
requesting to seek help from Wú.
The Duke said:
"Why not use the treasures of our former lord first?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"If we make Wú demand our treasures in exchange for sending troops,
this is not something we can rely on."
Thereupon, they sent six bows made of yánggàn wood and hemp cords as gifts.
Zǐgòng said to the King of Wú:
"Qí is acting without principle,
wanting to cut off the sacrifices of the descendants of the Duke of Zhōu,
and Lǔ pays five hundred units of tribute,
Zhū pays three hundred units,
I don't know if using these to enrich Qí
would be beneficial to Wú or not?"
The King of Wú became apprehensive,
and then raised an army to rescue Lǔ.
The feudal lords said:
"Qí attacked the descendants of the Duke of Zhōu,
and Wú rescued them."
Thereupon they paid court to Wú.
12.6 Marquis Wén of Wèi enfeoffed his crown prince Jī in Zhōngshān,
for three years there was no communication between them,
his retainer Zhào Cāngtáng came forward and said:
"As a son, not hearing from one's father for three years
cannot be called filial;
as a father, not inquiring after one's son for three years,
cannot be called kind.
Why does my lord not send an envoy to the great state?"
The crown prince said:
"I have long wished to do so,
but have not found anyone suitable to send."
Cāngtáng said:
"I am willing to undertake the mission.
What are the Marquis's preferences?"
The crown prince said:
"The Marquis enjoys morning ducks,
and likes northern dogs."
Thereupon he sent Cāngtáng with a leashed northern dog,
presenting morning ducks,
to offer to Marquis Wén.
When Cāngtáng arrived,
he presented himself saying:
"The envoy of the unworthy son Jī,
dares not approach at the court of the high officials,
I beg to present in a private setting,
the morning ducks,
respectfully offered to the kitchen,
and the leashed northern dog,
respectfully presented to the attendants."
Marquis Wén was pleased and said:
"Jī loves me,
he knows what I enjoy,
he knows what I like."
He summoned Cāngtáng to see him and said:
"Is Jī well?"
Cāngtáng said:
"Yes,
yes."
This happened three times,
then he said:
"My lord sent out the crown prince and enfeoffed him in a state,
my lord named him,
this is not according to ritual."
Marquis Wén was startled and changed expression,
and asked:
"Is your lord well?"
Cāngtáng said:
"When I left,
he bowed in the courtyard sending off the letter."
Marquis Wén looked around at his attendants and said:
"Your lord,
how does he compare in stature to these men?"
Cāngtáng said:
"According to ritual, comparing people must be with their peers.
Feudal lords have no peers,
there is no one to compare him to."
He said:
"How does he compare in stature to me?"
Cāngtáng said:
"If my lord bestows a fur robe from the outer treasury,
he can wear it;
if bestowed a wide belt,
he would not need to have it altered."
Marquis Wén said:
"What does your lord study?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He studies the Book of Songs."
Marquis Wén said:
"What in the Book of Songs does he like?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He likes 'Morning Wind' and 'Millet Lush'."
Marquis Wén read aloud 'Morning Wind':
"Swift flies the morning wind,
Through the northern woods.
I have not seen my lord,
My heart is full of sorrow.
How, how can it be
That he forgets me so utterly?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Does your lord think I have forgotten him?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He would not dare think so,
only that you remember him at times."
Marquis Wén read aloud 'Millet Lush':
"The millet is lush,
The sorghum sprouts.
I walk slowly,
My heart swaying within.
Those who know me
Say my heart is grieved.
Those who do not know me
Say what is it I seek.
Oh, distant blue heaven,
Who is this man?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Your lord,
does he resent me?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He would not dare,
only remembers you at times."
Thereupon Marquis Wén sent Cāngtáng to bestow a set of clothes upon the crown prince,
ordering Cāngtáng to arrive at cockcrow.
The crown prince rose, bowed, and received the gift,
opened the box and saw the clothes were all inside out.
The crown prince said:
"Hurry and prepare the carriage early;
the lord is summoning Jī."
Cāngtáng said:
"When I came, I received no such order."
The crown prince said:
"The lord bestowed clothes upon Jī,
not because he is cold.
He wishes to summon Jī,
but has no one to consult with,
so he sent you with clothes,
ordering you to arrive at cockcrow.
The Book of Songs says:
'Before the east is bright,
I put on my clothes inside out.
Upside down and inside out,
It is because the duke summons me.'"
Thereupon he went west,
arrived,
and paid respects to Marquis Wén.
Marquis Wén was greatly pleased,
and set out wine, declaring:
"Keeping the worthy at a distance and favoring those one loves
is not a long-term strategy for the state."
Then he sent out his younger son Zhì,
enfeoffing him in Zhōngshān;
and restored crown prince Jī.
Therefore it is said:
To know the son,
look at his friends;
to know the ruler,
look at his envoys.
Zhào Cāngtáng's one mission
made Marquis Wén a kind father,
and Jī a filial son.
The crown prince then recited from the Book of Songs:
"The phoenixes fly about,
Their wings rustle,
They alight and rest.
The king has many good officers,
They are at the prince's command,
Loving the Son of Heaven."
This refers to the retainer.
12.7 King Zhuāng of Chǔ wanted to attack Jìn,
and sent Tún Yǐn to observe.
He returned and said:
"It cannot be attacked.
Their worries are with the superiors,
their joys with the inferiors,
and there are worthy ministers there,
named Shěn Jū."
The next year,
he again sent Tún Yǐn to observe.
He returned and said:
"It can be done now.
The worthy men from before have died,
flatterers are many in the ruler's court,
the ruler enjoys pleasures without ritual,
his inferiors live in peril and resent their superiors,
superiors and inferiors are of divided hearts.
Raise an army and attack them,
their people will surely revolt first."
King Zhuāng followed his advice,
and it turned out just as he had said.
12.8 King Liáng gathered his ministers to discuss his faults.
Rèn Zuò came forward to admonish, saying:
"Your Majesty's state is vast and expansive,
its people steadfast and numerous.
How is it that there are no worthy men or eloquent scholars in the state?"
The king said:
"My state is small and narrow,
its people weak and ministers few.
I alone govern it—
what need have I for worthy men or eloquent scholars?"
Rèn Zuò said:
"Not so.
In the past, Qí without reason raised troops to attack Lǔ.
The lord of Lǔ was troubled by this,
and summoned his chancellor, saying:
'What shall be done about this?'
The chancellor replied:
'Liǔxià Huì in his youth was fond of learning,
and in adulthood was praised for his wisdom.
My lord, try summoning him and sending him as an envoy to Qí.'
The lord of Lǔ said:
'I am the ruler of a thousand-chariot state.
If I personally go as envoy to Qí,
and Qí does not listen,
then Liǔxià Huì is but a scholar in cloth garments and leather girdle—
what good would sending him do?'
The chancellor replied:
'Your servant has heard that
if one fails to get fire by begging,
one cannot expect to roast with it.
Now if we send Liǔxià Huì to Qí,
even if he does not resolve the conflict with Qí's troops,
it would at least not worsen the attack on Lǔ.'
The lord of Lǔ then said:
'So be it!'
The chancellor immediately sent someone to summon Liǔxià Huì.
He came,
entered the gate, lifted his robes and did not hasten his steps.
The lord of Lǔ left his mat and stood, saying:
'What I have done is like seeking millet only when hungry,
or digging a well only when thirsty—
I have never been able to receive you with joy.
Now the affairs of state are urgent,
the common people are fearful.
I wish to rely on you, Sir, to go as envoy to Qí.'
Liǔxià Huì said:
'Very well.'
Thereupon he went east to see the Marquis of Qí.
The Marquis of Qí said:
'Is your lord of Lǔ afraid?'
Liǔxià Huì said:
'My lord is not afraid.'
The Marquis of Qí flared up in anger, saying:
'I look at your city of Lǔ—
it appears desolate like a lost, perished state.
The common people are tearing down houses and cutting trees to repair the city walls.
I regard your lord of Lǔ as similar to our state,
yet you say he is not afraid—
why is that?'
Liǔxià Huì said:
'The reason my lord is not afraid
is that his ancestors came out from Zhōu,
and were enfeoffed in Lǔ.
Your lordship's ancestors also came out from Zhōu,
and were enfeoffed in Qí.
Together they came out from the southern gate of Zhōu,
cut open a sheep and made a covenant, saying:
From now on, if any descendants dare attack each other,
may their crime be like this cut-open sheep!
Thus my lord firmly trusts in the cut-open sheep and is not afraid.
Otherwise,
the common people would indeed be anxious.'
Thereupon the Marquis of Qí withdrew his troops three hundred lǐ.
Now Liǔxià Huì was but a scholar in cloth garments and leather girdle,
yet he managed to resolve the difficulties between Qí and Lǔ.
How can you say there are no worthy scholars or sages!"
12.9 Lù Jiǎ followed Gāozǔ in pacifying the empire,
and was known as an eloquent scholar.
He stayed by the emperor's side,
and was often sent on missions to the various lords.
During Gāozǔ's time,
when the central plains were first stabilized,
Wèi Tuó pacified Nányuè,
and thereupon made himself its king.
Gāozǔ sent Lù Jiǎ to bestow upon Wèi Tuó the seal appointing him King of Nányuè.
When Master Lù arrived,
Wèi Tuó, with his hair in a mallet-shaped knot, sat sprawled out arrogantly to receive Master Lù.
Master Lù thereupon persuaded Tuó, saying:
"You, Sir, are a man of the central plains,
your relatives, brothers, and ancestral graves are in Zhēndìng.
Now you, Sir, have cast aside and rebelled against your innate nature,
discarded cap and girdle,
and wish to use this tiny Yuè to contend with the Son of Heaven as an enemy state.
Disaster will soon reach your person.
Moreover, when Qín lost its proper governance,
the various lords and heroes all rose up.
Only the King of Hàn first entered the passes,
and occupied Xiányáng.
Xiàng Jí broke the covenant,
set himself up as Hegemon King of Western Chǔ,
and all the various lords submitted to him—
he could be said to have reached the pinnacle of strength.
Yet the King of Hàn rose from Bā and Shǔ,
lashed the world into order,
subdued the various lords,
and thereupon executed Xiàng Yǔ and destroyed him.
Within five years,
the four seas were pacified and settled.
This was not by human power,
but was established by Heaven.
The Son of Heaven has heard that you, Great King, rule Nányuè,
yet do not help the world in punishing the violent and rebellious.
The generals and ministers wish to move troops to punish you, Great King.
But the Son of Heaven pities the people's recent toils and hardships,
and wishes to give them rest.
Therefore he sends me to confer upon you, Great King, the seal,
dividing the tally and opening diplomatic relations.
You, Great King, should have welcomed me at the outskirts,
facing north and declaring yourself a subject.
Instead, you wish to rely on this newly established, unconsolidated Yuè
to stubbornly resist here.
If Hàn truly hears of this,
they will dig up and burn the graves of your ancestors,
exterminate your clan and lineage,
and send one lieutenant general with a host of a hundred thousand to approach Yuè.
Then Yuè will kill you, Great King, to surrender to Hàn,
as easy as turning over one's hand."
Thereupon Wèi Tuó suddenly rose from his seat,
and apologized to Master Lù, saying:
"Having lived among the barbarians for so long,
I have greatly neglected ritual propriety."
Then he asked Master Lù:
"How do I compare in worthiness to Xiāo Hé, Cáo Cān, and Hán Xìn?"
Master Lù said:
"You, Great King, seem to be worthy."
He asked again:
"How do I compare in worthiness to the emperor?"
Master Lù said:
"The emperor rose from Fēng and Pèi,
campaigned against the violent Qín,
executed the strong Chǔ,
promoted benefits and eliminated harms for the world,
succeeded to the enterprises of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
and brought unified order to the central plains.
The people of the central plains number in the hundreds of millions,
the territory spans ten thousand lǐ,
occupying the most fertile land under heaven.
The population and chariots are numerous,
the ten thousand things are abundant and rich,
and governance issues from one house.
Since heaven and earth were separated,
such a thing has never been.
Now your host, Great King, numbers no more than several hundred thousand,
all barbarians,
perched in mountain and sea fastnesses,
comparable to but one commandery of Hàn.
How can you compare to the King of Hàn!"
Wèi Tuó laughed heartily and said:
"It is because I did not rise in the central plains
that I rule here.
Had I been in the central plains,
how would I necessarily be inferior to Hàn?"
Thereupon he was greatly pleased with Master Lù,
and kept him for several months of drinking.
He said:
"In Yuè there is no one worth talking with.
Since your arrival,
I daily hear what I have never heard before."
He bestowed upon Master Lù a bag of valuables worth a thousand pieces of gold,
and Tuó also gave him a thousand in farewell gifts.
Master Lù finally paid respects to Wèi Tuó as King of Nányuè,
ordering him to declare himself a subject and uphold the Hàn covenant.
Returning to report,
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased,
and appointed Jiǎ as Grand Master of the Palace.
12.10 The rulers of Jìn and Chǔ met for a friendly gathering on top of Wǎnqiū Hill.
Sòng sent a man there.
The great officers of Jìn and Chǔ said:
"Hurry and pay respects to our rulers with the ritual for seeing the Son of Heaven,
and we will arrange your audience."
The envoy said:
"Though a cap may be worn out,
it should still be placed on the head;
though shoes may be new,
they should still be placed beneath the feet.
Though the Zhōu house may be weak,
no feudal lord can replace it.
Even if troops ascended the walls of Sòng,
I would still not change my robes of minister."
He bowed and left them.
The various great officers were taken aback,
and thereupon received him with the ritual for feudal lords.
12.11 Yuè sent Zhū Fā holding a single plum branch to present to the King of Liáng.
A minister of the King of Liáng named Hánzǐ
looked to his attendants and said:
"How could one present a single plum branch to the ruler of a powerful state!
I shall put this man to shame for you all."
He went out and said to Zhū Fā:
"Our great king has commanded:
if a visitor wears a cap, he will be received with courtesy;
if he does not wear a cap, he will not."
Zhū Fā replied:
"That land of Yuè was also enfeoffed by the Son of Heaven,
yet we did not receive territories like Jì or Yǎn,
but dwell instead by the remote seas,
sheltered in the outer regions as our home,
where flood dragons compete with us for space.
Therefore we cut our hair and tattoo our bodies,
creating brilliant patterns,
to resemble the dragon's offspring -
this is to ward off water deities.
Now your great state has commanded
that only capped visitors receive courteous reception,
while uncapped ones do not.
Suppose an envoy from your great state
were to visit our humble city in due time,
and our humble city's ruler
similarly commanded:
'The visitor must cut his hair and tattoo his body,
only then may he be received.'
How would your great state respond?
If you find this acceptable,
I would gladly borrow a cap to be received;
if you find it unacceptable,
I hope you will not force us to change our state's customs."
When the King of Liáng heard this,
he threw on his robes and came out to receive Zhū Fā,
then ordered Hánzǐ expelled.
The Book of Songs says:
"Only the gentleman's envoy
pleases the Son of Heaven."
This describes such situations.
12.12 Yànzǐ was sent to Wú,
and the King of Wú told his protocol officer:
"I have heard Yàn Yīng is among the most eloquent and ritually proficient from the north."
He ordered his ushers to announce "The Son of Heaven requests your audience" when receiving the guest.
The next day,
when Yànzǐ had business,
the protocol officer said:
"The Son of Heaven requests your audience."
Yànzǐ looked uneasy three times,
then said:
"I have received orders from my humble city's ruler
to be sent to the court of the King of Wú.
Being unworthy and confused, I have mistakenly entered the court of the Son of Heaven -
may I ask where the King of Wú might be found?"
Thereafter the King of Wú said:
"Fūchāi requests your audience."
He received him with the rites due to a feudal lord.
12.13 Yànzǐ was sent to Wú,
and the King of Wú said:
"I, residing in this remote, rustic land of barbarians,
rarely receive instruction in gentlemanly conduct -
pray let me speak privately without offense."
Yànzǐ withdrew uneasily from his position.
The King of Wú said:
"I have heard the ruler of Qí is corrupt and arrogant,
crude and violent.
That you, sir, tolerate this -
how extreme!"
Yànzǐ hesitated before replying:
"I have heard that
those who cannot handle subtle matters
nor accomplish crude tasks
must labor;
