those who cannot achieve great things
nor perform small tasks
must be poor;
those who cannot attract people in great matters
nor reach others' gates in small matters
must be distressed.
This is why I take office.
As for someone like me,
how could I feed others through the Way!"
After Yànzǐ left,
the king laughed and said:
"Today my mocking of Yànzǐ
was like a naked man criticizing high collars."
12.14 Duke Jǐng sent Yànzǐ as envoy to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ offered oranges,
placing a peeling knife nearby,
but Yànzǐ ate them whole without peeling.
The King of Chǔ said:
"Oranges should be peeled."
Yànzǐ replied:
"I have heard that
before one's ruler,
melons and peaches are not peeled,
oranges and pomelos are not segmented.
Now the Ten-thousand Chariot state has given no instruction,
so I dare not segment them,
though it's not that I don't know how."
12.15 When Yànzǐ was about to be sent to Jīng,
the King of Jīng heard of it
and told his attendants:
"Yànzǐ
is a worthy man.
Now that he's coming,
I wish to humiliate him -
how should we proceed?"
The attendants replied:
"When he arrives,
let us bind a man
to pass before Your Majesty.
Your Majesty will ask:
'What has he done?'
We will reply:
'He is from Qí.'
Your Majesty will ask:
'What is his crime?'
We will say:
'The crime is theft.'"
Thus when the King of Jīng stood conversing with Yànzǐ,
a bound man passed before the king.
The king asked:
"What has he done?"
The reply came:
"He is from Qí."
The king asked:
"What is his crime?"
The answer:
"The crime is theft."
The king looked at Yànzǐ and said:
"Are people from Qí naturally skilled at theft?"
Yànzǐ turned and responded:
"I have heard that
south of the river there grows the orange tree.
When the King of Qí sent people to take and plant it north of the river,
it bore not oranges but trifoliate oranges.
Why did this happen?
The soil made it so.
Now when people from Qí dwell in Qí they don't steal,
but when they come to Jīng they steal -
could it be the soil makes them so?"
The King of Jīng said:
"I meant to wound you, sir,
but have instead wounded myself."
12.16 Yànzǐ was sent to Chǔ.
As Yànzǐ was short,
the people of Chǔ made a small gate beside the main gate to receive Yànzǐ.
Yànzǐ would not enter,
saying:
"Envoys to dog states
enter through dog gates.
Now I am envoy to Chǔ,
I should not enter through this gate."
The ushers then led him through the main gate
to see the King of Chǔ.
The king said:
"Has Qí no men?
That they send you as envoy."
Yànzǐ replied:
"Qí's Línzī has three hundred neighborhoods
where sleeves raised form curtains,
sweat waved forms rain,
people stand shoulder to shoulder and follow heel to heel -
how could we have no men?"
The king said:
"Then why send you?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Qí appoints envoys according to their assignments:
the worthy are sent to worthy rulers,
the unworthy to unworthy rulers.
I am the most unworthy,
so I was deemed suitable for Chǔ."
12.17 When Qín and Chǔ were at war,
the King of Qín sent an envoy to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ had someone jest with him, saying:
"Did you also consult the oracle before coming?"
The envoy replied:
"Indeed."
"What did the oracle say?"
He answered:
"Auspicious."
The man from Chǔ said:
"Alas,
how extreme!
Your state must lack a good tortoise shell for divination,
for our king is about to kill you to anoint the bells with blood,
so how can this be auspicious?"
The envoy said:
"Qín and Chǔ are at war,
my king sent me first to spy.
If I die and do not return,
then my king will know to be vigilant,
and prepare his troops against Chǔ.
This is what I call auspicious.
Moreover, if the dead have no consciousness,
what use is anointing bells with blood?
If the dead do have consciousness,
would I let Qín err and assist Chǔ?
I shall make Chǔ's bells and drums fall silent.
When bells and drums are silent,
you will have no means to marshal your troops and manage your sovereign's army.
Killing another's envoy,
thwarting another's plans,
is not the ancient way of proper conduct.
You, sir, should carefully consider this."
The envoy reported this to the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ pardoned him.
This is called forging one's own destiny.
12.18 Chǔ sent an envoy on a mission to Qí.
The King of Qí entertained him at the Wú Palace.
The envoy said:
"How grand this wú tree is!"
The king said:
"The fish in rivers and seas can swallow boats,
the trees of a great state must be vast in girth,
why should the envoy find it strange?"
The envoy said:
"Once Yān attacked Qí,
followed the Luò road,
crossed the Jì bridge,
burned the Yōng Gate,
struck Qí's left and emptied its right,
Wáng Chù died by a broken neck at Dù Shān,
Gōngsūn Chā fell at Lóng Mén,
watered horses at Zī and Shéng,
secured Lángyá,
the king and queen mother fled to Jǔ,
and hid in Chéngyáng's mountains.
At that time,
how big was this wú tree then?"
The king said:
"Let Mr. Chén answer him."
Mr. Chén said:
"I am not as good as Diāo Bó."
The king said:
"Let Mr. Diāo respond."
Diāo Bó said:
"Is the envoy asking about the wú tree's age?
Once King Píng of Jīng acted without virtue,
persecuted the Shēn clan,
killed Wǔ Zǐxū's father and brother,
Zǐxū fled with disheveled hair, begging in Wú,
Hélǚ made him general and minister,
after three years,
he led Wú's troops to take revenge on Chǔ,
triumphed at Bó Jǔ,
took countless heads,
Náng Wǎ fled to Zhèng,
the king sought refuge in Suí.
He led the army into Yǐng,
troops swarmed the capital like clouds,
Zǐxū personally shot arrows at the palace gate,
dug up King Píng's tomb,
whipped his grave,
enumerated his crimes,
saying:
'My ancestors were innocent, yet you killed them.'
The soldiers added a hundred lashes each,
then stopped.
At such a time,
this wú tree could have been used as a whip handle."
12.19 Cài sent Shī Qiáng and Wáng Jiān as envoys to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ heard of it and said:
"Many people have illustrious names,
why only name them Shī Qiáng and Wáng Jiān?
Summon them quickly,
without delay."
Seeing their appearance,
he doubted their names, despised their voices,
and detested their forms.
The King of Chǔ grew furious and said:
"Does Cài have no one else?
The state can be attacked;
does it have people but not send them?
The state can be attacked;
or is it deliberately using these men to insult me?
The state can be attacked."
Thus, by sending two envoys,
he saw three reasons for attack,
all concerning Cài.
12.20 Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào planned to attack Wèi,
and sent Shǐ Àn to scout it,
giving him a month's time.
He returned only after six months,
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Why so long?"
Àn said:
"Seeking gain but meeting harm,
stems from lack of observation.
Now Qú Bóyù is prime minister,
Shǐ Qiū assists him,
Kǒngzǐ is a guest,
and Zǐgòng gives commands before the lord, all heeded.
The Yì Jīng says:
'Dispersing the crowd,
greatly auspicious.'
Dispersing means
worthies;
crowd means
the multitude;
greatly means
the beginning of auspiciousness.
'Dispersing the crowd, greatly auspicious'
means its assistants are many worthies."
Jiǎnzǐ then halted his troops and did not move.
12.21 Marquis Wén of Wèi sent his attendant Wú Zé to present a swan to the Marquis of Qí.
On the journey, Wú Zé lost it,
and offered only an empty cage.
He appeared before the Marquis of Qí and said:
"My lord sent me, Wú Zé, to present a swan,
but on the way, it grew hungry and thirsty.
I let it out to feed and drink,
and it flew straight to the heavens,
never to return.
I considered that it was not for lack of money to buy another swan,
but how could I, as my lord's envoy,
lightly treat his gift?
I thought it not that I could not draw my sword and cut my throat,
leaving my rotting flesh and exposed bones in the wild,
for that would value the swan over the servant in my lord's eyes;
nor that I dared not flee to between Chén and Cài,
but I detest severing the envoys of two lords.
So I dared not cherish my life and flee death,
and have come to offer the empty cage,
awaiting your axe and block for execution."
The Marquis of Qí was greatly pleased and said:
"Today I have gained three such statements from you,
far more valuable than a swan.
I have a capital city,
with suburban lands a hundred lǐ square,
which I wish to offer you, sir, as a bathing fief."
Wú Zé replied:
"How can one, as his lord's envoy,
lightly treat his gift,
and yet profit from a feudal lord's land?"
Then he left and never returned.
13.1 When a sage king undertakes affairs,
he must first deliberate in planning,
then verify with milfoil and tortoise.
Scholars from humble huts,
all contribute to the planning;
even the lowly grass and firewood gatherers
exhaust their hearts in service.
Thus, myriad actions proceed without miscalculation or misstep.
The Zhuàn says:
"The wisdom of the multitude
can measure the heavens,
but integrating counsel and making solitary decisions
rests solely with one person."
This is the method of grand strategy.
Strategy has two foundations:
the superior strategist understands destiny,
the next understands affairs.
Those who understand destiny foresee the origins of survival and peril, fortune and misfortune,
knowing early the beginnings of prosperity and decline, abolition and rise.
They prevent matters before they sprout,
avoiding calamity while it is still formless.
Such individuals,
dwelling in chaotic times,
remain unharmed themselves;
in times of peace and order,
they inevitably attain authority over the realm.
Those who understand affairs are also esteemed;
they perceive matters and recognize the distinctions between gain and loss, success and failure,
and investigate their ultimate outcomes,
thus avoiding ruined enterprises and wasted efforts.
Confucius said:
"One may be capable of pursuing the Way,
but not necessarily capable of exercising discretion."
If not those who understand destiny and affairs,
who can practice the art of strategic discretion?
Now, strategic discretion can be upright or wicked;
the gentleman's strategic discretion is upright,
the petty person's strategic discretion is wicked.
The upright,
their strategic discretion is public-spirited,
hence their devotion to the people is sincere;
the wicked,
fond of selfishness and pursuing profit,
thus their service to the people is deceitful.
Deceit leads to chaos,
sincerity leads to peace.
Therefore, Yáo's nine ministers were sincere and flourished at court,
while his four ministers were deceitful and were executed in the wilderness.
The sincere are exalted unto later generations,
the deceitful perish in their very lifetimes.
Those who understand destiny and affairs and are capable in strategic discretion
must examine the roots of sincerity and deceit to guide their conduct;
this too is the art of strategic discretion.
The wise, when undertaking affairs,
at fullness consider overflow,
in calm consider danger,
in safety consider peril,
in crookedness consider straightness.
Through emphasizing preparation,
fearing only inadequacy,
thus numerous actions are undertaken without falling into traps.
13.2 Yáng Zǐ said:
"Affairs that can lead to poverty,
or can lead to wealth,
harm one's conduct;
affairs that can lead to life,
or can lead to death,
harm one's courage."
Pú Zǐ said:
"Yáng Zǐ is wise but does not understand destiny,
hence his wisdom is often doubtful."
The Analects say:
"Those who understand destiny are not perplexed."
Yàn Yīng was such a man.
13.3 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Jìn has Zé Míng and Dú Chōu,
Lǔ has Kǒng Qiū;
if I kill these three men,
then the realm can be schemed for."
Thereupon he summoned Zé Míng and Dú Chōu,
entrusted them with governance and then killed them.
He sent a messenger to invite Confucius from Lǔ,
Confucius reached the river,
approached the water and gazed, saying:
"How beautiful the water!
Vast and majestic!
That I do not cross here,
is destiny, alas!"
Zǐlù hurried forward and said:
"May I ask what you mean?"
Confucius said:
"Zé Míng and Dú Chōu
were worthy senior officials of Jìn;
when Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had not yet attained his ambition,
he shared knowledge and views with them.
When he attained his ambition,
he killed them and then assumed governance.
Thus I have heard:
if you cut open wombs and burn the young, the qílín will not come;
if you drain the marsh to fish, the jiāolóng will not swim;
if you overturn nests and destroy eggs, the fènghuáng will not soar.
I have heard:
the gentleman deeply grieves for his kind."
13.4 Confucius was sitting with Duke Jǐng of Qí,
when attendants reported:
"A messenger from Zhōu has come to report that a Zhōu temple has burned."
Duke Jǐng of Qí went out and asked:
"Which temple is it?"
Confucius said:
"It is King Lí's temple."
Duke Jǐng said:
"How do you know this?"
Confucius said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'August is the Lord on High,
His mandate is without error.
Heaven towards men,
must reward the virtuous.'
Calamity works the same way.
King Lí altered the institutions of King Wén and King Wǔ,
and built dark and yellow palaces,
with extravagant carriages and horses,
beyond redemption.
Thus Heaven brought disaster upon his temple;
this is how I know."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Why did Heaven not disaster his person,
but disaster his temple instead?"
The Master said:
"Heaven likely did so for King Wén's sake;
if it disastered his person,
then King Wén's sacrifices,
would they not be cut off?
Therefore, it disastered his temple
to manifest his faults."
The attendants entered and reported:
"It is King Lí of Zhōu's temple."
Duke Jǐng was greatly astonished,
rose and bowed twice, saying:
"Excellent!
The sage's wisdom,
is it not great indeed!"
13.5 Duke Huán of Qí and Guǎn Zhòng were planning to attack Jǔ.
Before the plan was put into action, it was already heard throughout the state.
Duke Huán found it strange
and asked Guǎn Zhòng about it.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"There must be a sage in the state."
Duke Huán sighed and said:
"Ah!
Among the laborers the other day,
there was one holding a mulberry pestle who looked upward—
could it be him?"
So he ordered the laborers to resume work,
without allowing substitutions.
After a short while,
Dōngguō Chuí arrived.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This must be the one."
He then ordered the usher to invite him in,
and he stood at his designated rank.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Was it you who spoke of attacking Jǔ?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ;
why did you mention it?"
He replied:
"I have heard that gentlemen are good at planning,
while commoners are good at intuiting.
I privately intuited it."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ;
how did you intuit it?"
He replied:
"I have heard that gentlemen have three expressions:
one of serene joy
is the expression of bells and drums;
one of solemn calm
is the expression of mourning garments;
one of vigorous intensity
is the expression of arms and armor.
The other day,
I saw you on the terrace,
filled with vigor—
this was the expression of arms and armor;
you were sighing without chanting,
and what you spoke of was Jǔ;
you raised your arm and pointed,
and what you aimed at was Jǔ.
I privately considered that among the small states not yet subdued,
was it not only Jǔ?
Thus I spoke of it."
The gentleman says:
Normally, the ear hears through sound,
but here, without hearing the sound,
and relying only on demeanor and arm movements,
Dōngguō Chuí heard without using his ears.
Though Duke Huán and Guǎn Zhòng were skilled in planning,
they could not conceal it.
Thus, the sage hears the soundless
and sees the formless;
Dōngguō Chuí possessed this ability.
Therefore, Duke Huán honored him with rank and treated him with respect.
13.6 Tú Yú, the Grand Historian of Jìn, seeing the disorder in the state of Jìn
and observing Duke Píng of Jìn's arrogance and lack of virtue and righteousness,
took its maps and laws and went to Zhōu.
Duke Wēi of Zhōu saw him and asked:
"Among the states under heaven, which will perish first?"
He replied:
"Jìn will perish first."
Duke Wēi asked for an explanation,
and he replied:
"When I was in Jìn, I dared not speak directly;
I showed Duke of Jìn the celestial portents,
that the movements of the sun, moon, and stars were often irregular,
and he said:
'What can these do!'
I showed him the injustices in human affairs,
and the many grievances of the people,
and he said:
'What harm can these cause.'
I also showed him that neighboring states were not submissive,
and that the worthy and virtuous were not promoted,
and he said:
'What danger can these pose.'
He did not understand the reasons for survival or perish,
so I say:
Jìn will perish first."
After three years,
Jìn indeed perished.
Duke Wēi again saw Tú Yú and asked:
"Which is next?"
He replied:
"Zhōngshān is next."
Duke Wēi asked the reason,
and he replied:
"Heaven gave birth to the people,
endowing them with distinctions.
Having distinctions
is the righteousness of humans,
what differentiates them from beasts and deer,
and the basis for establishing ruler and subject, superior and inferior.
The customs of Zhōngshān
treat day as night,
and continue night into day,
with men and women intimately mingling,
without rest,
indulging in wanton pleasure,
singing sorrowful songs,
and their ruler does not know to detest this.
This is the practice of a perishing state,
so I say:
Zhōngshān is next."
After two years,
Zhōngshān indeed perished.
Duke Wēi again saw Tú Yú and asked:
"Which is next?"
Tú Yú did not reply.
Duke Wēi pressed him,
and Tú Yú said:
"You are next."
Duke Wēi became fearful,
sought out the elders of the state,
honored Qí Chóu and Tián Yì with courtesy,
and also obtained Shǐ Lǐ and Zhào Xùn as remonstrating ministers,
abolishing thirty-nine harsh decrees,
and reported this to Tú Yú.
Tú Yú said:
"This may last only for your lifetime.
I have heard that when a state prospers,
Heaven sends it wise men
and those who offer utmost remonstrance;
when a state perishes,
Heaven gives it troublemakers and flatterers."
When Duke Wēi died,
his body lay for nine months without burial,
and Zhōu split into two.
Thus, the words of those who possess the Way
cannot but be valued.
13.7 The Marquis of Qí asked Yàn Zǐ:
"In the present time,
which among the feudal lords is in peril?"
He replied:
"Jǔ will likely perish first!"
The Duke said:
"What is the reason?"
He replied:
"Its territory is encroached by Qí,
and its resources exhausted by Jìn,
thus it will perish."
13.8 Zhì Bó led the armies of Hán and Wèi to attack Zhào,
besieging the city of Jìnyáng and flooding it,
until the walls were only three planks from being submerged.
Chī Cī said to Zhì Bó:
"The rulers of Hán and Wèi will surely rebel."
Zhì Bó said:
"How do you know?"
He replied:
"We agreed to divide Zhào's territory three ways upon victory.
Now the walls are only three planks from submersion,
mortars and stoves have frogs in them,
people and horses are eating each other,
and the city will surrender soon,
yet the rulers of Hán and Wèi show no joy but worried expressions.
If this is not rebellion, what is it?"
The next day,
Zhì Bó said to the rulers of Hán and Wèi:
"Chī Cī said you are about to rebel."
The rulers of Hán and Wèi said:
"We are certain to defeat Zhào and divide its land three ways.
Now the city is about to fall;
though we two may be foolish,
we would not abandon great profit and break the agreement
to undertake an impossible task.
The situation is clear;
this Chī Cī must be persuading you for Zhào's sake,
making you doubt our loyalty
and slacken the attack on Zhào.
Now you listen to a slandering minister
and estrange our alliance;
we regret this for your sake."
Zhì Bó left,
intending to kill Chī Cī.
Chī Cī fled,
and the rulers of Hán and Wèi indeed rebelled.
13.9 When the Gōngsuǒ family of Lǔ was about to perform a sacrifice, they lost their sacrificial animal.
Confucius heard about this and said:
"The Gōngsuǒ family will surely perish within three years."
One year later, they perished.
A disciple asked:
"Previously, when the Gōngsuǒ family lost their sacrificial animal, you, Master, said:
'They will surely perish within three years,'
yet they perished after only one year.
How did you, Master, know they would perish?"
Confucius said:
"The word 'sacrifice' (jì) relates to 'thorough search' (suǒ),
and 'thorough search'
means 'exhaustive effort,'
which is how a filial son exhausts himself in devotion to his parents.
If they lose the sacrificial animal during the ceremony,
then they must have lost many other things as well.
This is how I knew they would perish."
13.10 The Marquis of Cài, Duke of Sòng, and Count of Zhèng paid a court visit to Jìn.
The Marquis of Cài said to Shūxiàng:
"What do you have to say to me?"
He replied:
"Cài's territory is smaller and its population fewer
compared to Sòng and Zhèng,
yet its carriages, horses, and fur robes
are more extravagant than those two states.
Might the feudal lords have designs on Cài?"
After one year,
Chǔ attacked Cài and devastated it.
13.11 Bái Guī went to Zhōngshān,
and the King of Zhōngshān wanted to retain him,
but he firmly declined and left.
He then went to Qí,
and the King of Qí also wanted to retain him,
but he again declined and left.
Someone asked why he refused,
Bái Guī said:
"These two states are about to perish.
What I have learned is that a state has five exhaustions:
When no one is necessarily loyal,
then speech is exhausted;
when no one is necessarily praised,
then reputation is exhausted;
when no one is necessarily loved,
then kinship is exhausted;
when travelers have no provisions,
and residents have no food,
then wealth is exhausted;
when one cannot employ others,
nor use oneself effectively,
then achievement is exhausted.
A state with these five conditions
cannot escape ruin—
both Zhōngshān and Qí fit this description."
If the Kings of Zhōngshān and Qí had heard of the five exhaustions and reformed,
they surely would not have perished.
The problem was that they did not hear of it,
or even if they heard, they did not believe it.
Thus, the task of a ruler
lies solely in listening well.
13.12 The Wēi Gōng of Xiàcài shut his door and wept,
for three days and three nights,
until his tears dried and were followed by blood.
A neighbor peeped over the wall and asked him:
"Why are you weeping so sorrowfully?"
He replied:
"My state is about to perish."
The neighbor said:
"How do you know?"
He answered:
"I have heard that when a disease is fatal,
no good doctor can cure it;
when a state is about to perish,
no plans can save it.
I have repeatedly advised my lord,
but my lord does not heed me,
hence I know the state will perish."
Upon hearing this, the peeping neighbor
took his whole clan and left for Chǔ.
After several years,
the King of Chǔ indeed raised an army to attack Cài,
and the peeping neighbor became a Marshal,
leading troops there,
and captured many prisoners.
He asked:
"Are there any brothers or old acquaintances among you?"
He saw Wēi Gōng bound among the captives,
and asked:
"How did you come to this?"
Wēi Gōng replied:
"Why should I not have come to this?
Moreover, I have heard that
those who speak
are servants to those who act;
those who act
are masters to those who speak.
You can act,
I can speak;
you are the master,
I am the servant.
Why should I not have come to this?"
The peeping neighbor then spoke to the King of Chǔ on his behalf,
had his bonds removed,
and took him to Chǔ.
Hence it is said:
Those who can speak may not be able to act,
and those who can act may not be able to speak.
13.13 Guǎn Zhòng fell ill,
and Duke Huán went to see him,
saying:
"If you, Father Zhòng, abandon me,
can Shù Diāo be entrusted with governance?"
He replied:
"No.
Shù Diāo mutilated himself to gain access to his lord;
if he could be so cruel to his own body,
what would he not do to his lord?"
The Duke said:
"Then, is Yì Yá suitable?"
He replied:
"Yì Yá cooked his own son to feed his lord;
if he could be so cruel to his own son,
what would he not do to his lord?
If you employ him,
you will surely be laughed at by the feudal lords."
After Duke Huán died,
Shù Diāo and Yì Yá started a rebellion,
and when Duke Huán had been dead for sixty days,
maggots crawled out the door, yet his body remained unburied.
13.14 Shí Qǐ was sitting in attendance with Qū Jiàn,
and Qū Jiàn said:
"Is Bái Gōng going to rebel?"
Shí Qǐ said:
"What kind of talk is that!
Bái Gōng has no extravagant pursuits in his household,
he humbles himself before three scholars,
treats five men as his equals and ministers,
and shares food and clothing with a thousand people.
With such conduct from Bái Gōng,
why would he rebel?"
Qū Jiàn said:
"This is exactly what I call rebellion.
For a gentleman to act this way is acceptable,
but in a state, to exceed propriety in conduct makes the state suspicious.
Moreover, if he does not find it difficult to lower himself before his ministers,
he will surely not find it difficult to elevate himself above his lord.
This is why I know the Master will rebel."
Ten months later,
Bái Gōng indeed rebelled.
13.15 Hán Zhāohóu built a grand gate,
and Qū Yíjiù said:
"Zhāohóu will not pass through this gate."
Someone asked:
"Why?"
He said:
"The timing is wrong.
What I mean by wrong timing
is not about the date or hour,
but that people naturally have favorable and unfavorable times.
Zhāohóu once had favorable times,
yet he did not build a grand gate.
Last year, Qín captured Yìyáng,
and the next year, there was a great drought and the people starved.
Instead of relieving the people's distress at such a time,
he反倒 increased his extravagance.
This is what is called: good fortune does not come twice,
but calamity surely returns doubly."
When the grand gate was completed,
Zhāohóu died,
and indeed never passed through it.
13.16 Tián Zǐyán traveled from the main road to the city of Pínglíng,
where he saw sons and asked about their fathers,
and saw fathers and asked about their sons.
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"Is he going to rebel with Pínglíng?
I have heard that one acts inwardly before extending outwardly.
Zǐyán desires to win over the people intensely."
Later, he indeed rebelled with Pínglíng.
13.24 Zhì Bó requested land from Wèi Xuānzǐ,
but Xuānzǐ refused to give it.
Rén Zēng said:
"Why not give it?"
Xuānzǐ replied:
"He asked for land without reason,
so I therefore refused."
Rén Zēng said:
"When someone asks for land without reason,
and you give it to him without reason,
this encourages his insatiable greed.
He will be pleased,
and will surely request land from other lords as well.
When the other lords refuse,
he will surely become angry and attack them."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Well said."
He then gave the land.
Zhì Bó was pleased,
and then requested land from Zhào.
Zhào refused,
so Zhì Bó became angry
and besieged Jìnyáng.
Hán and Wèi joined forces with Zhào and turned against the Zhì clan,
and the Zhì clan was thus destroyed.
13.25 King Zhuāng of Chǔ fought with Jìn,
defeated them,
but feared that the other lords would be afraid of him.
So he built a platform five ren high,
and when the platform was completed, he feasted the lords,
who requested a covenant.
King Zhuāng said:
"I am a man of little virtue."
The lords requested a toast,
so he looked up and said:
"This lofty platform,
with its profound strategy;
if I speak inappropriately,
may the lords attack me."
Thereupon, those from afar came to pay homage,
and those nearby attended as guests.
13.26 King Fūchāi of Wú destroyed Yuè,
and was about to attack Chén.
The great officers of Chǔ were all afraid,
saying:
"In the past, Hélú was able to use his masses effectively,
so he defeated us at Bǎijǔ.
Now we hear that Fūchāi is even more formidable."
Zǐxī said:
"You gentlemen worry about not being harmonious with each other,
but have no fear of Wú.
In the past, Hélú did not eat two dishes at a meal,
did not use double mats when sitting,
and in his selections, he did not take what was extravagant.
In the state,
when there was a natural disaster,
he provided for his relatives when they were in need.
In the army,
he would only eat after half the soldiers had received cooked food.
Whatever delicacies he tasted,
his soldiers and charioteers would surely share in them.
Therefore, the people did not suffer from exhaustion,
and those who died knew they would not be forgotten.
Now Fūchāi has terraces and pavilions, ponds and pools for his lodgings,
and stays with consorts, concubines, and attendants.
On a single day's journey,
whatever he desires must be achieved,
his curios and favorites must follow him,
and rare treasures are gathered for him.
Fūchāi has already defeated himself first;
how can he defeat us?"
13.27 Yuè, having destroyed Wú,
requested troops from Chǔ to attack Jìn.
The King of Chǔ and his great officers were all afraid
and were about to consent.
The Left Historian Yǐ Xiāng said:
"This is probably because they fear we will attack them,
so they are showing us that they are not weak.
I request that we prepare a thousand long-chariots,
and thirty thousand soldiers,
to share in dividing the land of Wú with them."
King Zhuāng listened to him,
and thus took the eastern territories.
13.28 Yáng Hǔ caused trouble in Lǔ,
fled to Qí,
and requested troops to attack Lǔ.
The Marquis of Qí was about to consent.
Bào Wénzǐ said:
"This will not do.
Yáng Hǔ wants the Qí army to be defeated.
If the Qí army is defeated,
many of your great ministers will surely die,
and then he plans to vigorously implement his deceitful schemes.
Now, Hǔ was favored by the Jì family,
yet he tried to kill Jì Sūn,
seeking to harm the state of Lǔ and find acceptance for his own demands.
Now, you, my lord, are wealthier than the Jì family,
and your state is larger than Lǔ.
This is what Yáng Hǔ wishes to overthrow.
Lǔ has been spared his trouble, and now you, my lord, are taking him in;
would that not be harmful?"
The ruler of Qí then arrested him,
but he escaped and fled to Jìn.
13.29 Tāng wished to attack Jié.
Yī Yǐn said:
"I request that we halt the tribute payments,
to observe his reaction."
Jié became angry,
and raised an army from the Nine Yí to attack him.
Yī Yǐn said:
"Not yet.
He can still raise an army from the Nine Yí;
this means the fault lies with us."
Tāng then apologized and asked to submit,
and resumed paying tribute.
The following year,
he again withheld tribute.
Jié became angry and tried to raise an army from the Nine Yí,
but the Nine Yí did not provide troops.
Yī Yǐn said:
"It is possible now."
Tāng then raised an army,
attacked and devastated them,
and moved Jié to Náncháo.
13.30 King Wǔ attacked Zhòu.
At dawn, he raised torches,
passed through defiles and cut through embankments,
crossed rivers and broke his boats,
traversed valleys and destroyed bridges,
crossed mountains and burned the undergrowth,
showing the people he had no intention of turning back.
When they reached the defile of Yǒuróng,
a great wind broke the banner.
Sàn Yíshēng admonished:
"Is this an omen?"
King Wǔ said:
"No,
it is Heaven sending down troops."
When the wind ceased, they were met with heavy rain,
water leveling the ground and making it difficult to advance.
Sàn Yíshēng again admonished:
"Is this an omen?"
King Wǔ said:
"No,
it is Heaven washing the weapons."
When they divined, the turtle shell burned out.
Sàn Yíshēng again admonished:
"Is this an omen?"
King Wǔ said:
"It is unfavorable for prayer and sacrifice,
but favorable for attacking the multitude;
the burning out is thus."
Therefore, King Wǔ complied with Heaven and Earth,
confronted three omens and captured Zhòu at Mùyě,
for his unique insight was profound.
13.31 Duke Wén of Jìn battled the men of Jīng at Chéngpú.
The lord asked Jiù Fàn,
and Jiù Fàn replied:
"A lord who upholds righteousness
does not lack good faith;
a lord who engages in warfare
does not lack deceit.
You, my lord, should simply use deceit against him."
The lord asked Yōng Jì,
and Yōng Jì replied:
"To burn the forest for hunting,
though you catch many beasts,
there will be none next year;
to drain the pond for fishing,
though you catch many fish,
there will be none next year.
Deceit may steal temporary gain,
but later there will be no return."
They then engaged the Jīng army in battle,
and greatly defeated them.
When it came to rewards,
he put Yōng Jì first and Jiù Fàn later.
An attendant said:
"The battle of Chéngpú
was won by Jiù Fàn's strategy."
The lord said:
"Yōng Jì's words
are a plan for a hundred generations;
Jiù Fàn's words
were an expedient for the moment.
I have already acted upon this."
13.32 During the Battle of Chéngpú,
Duke Wén said to Jiù Fàn:
"I divined about the battle and the turtle shell cracked,
we face the auspicious year,
while they turn their backs to it;
a comet appears,
they hold its handle,
we hold its tail;
I also dreamed of wrestling with the King of Chǔ,
he was on top,
I was underneath.
I wish to avoid battle,
what do you think?"
Jiù Fàn replied:
"The cracked turtle shell in battle divination
indicates the Chǔ army's defeat;
we facing the auspicious year,
they turning their backs to it,
means they flee and we pursue them;
the comet's appearance,
with them holding its handle
and us holding its tail,
for sweeping they have the advantage,
but for striking we have the advantage;
Your Highness dreaming of wrestling with the King of Chǔ,
with him on top
and you underneath,
means you see Heaven while the King of Chǔ prostrates for his crimes.
Moreover, we have Sòng and Wèi as our main force,
with Qí and Qín assisting us,
we align with the Heavenly Way,
considering human affairs alone,
we are certain to defeat them."
Duke Wén followed his advice,
and the Chǔ army was severely defeated.
13.33 Yuè suffered famine,
Gōu Jiàn grew fearful,
Wén Zhǒng advised:
"This famine is Yuè's blessing,
and Wú's calamity.
The state of Wú is very wealthy with abundant resources,
its ruler loves reputation without considering future troubles,
if we use humble words and generous gifts to request grain from Wú,
Wú will surely give it to us,
and once they give it, Wú can be conquered."
The King of Yuè followed his advice,
and when Wú was about to grant it,
Wǔ Xū advised against it:
"This must not be.
Wú and Yuè share borders and adjacent territories,
with accessible routes and interconnected people,
we are rival states destined for conflict,
if Wú doesn't possess Yuè,
Yuè will surely possess Wú.
States like Qí and Jìn cannot cross the three rivers and five lakes to destroy Wú and Yuè,
it's better to attack them now,
this was how our former king Hé Lú achieved hegemony.
Besides, what is famine?
It's like an abyss,
matters of defeat and attack,
which state doesn't experience them?
If you don't attack but instead supply them with grain,
benefits will depart and misfortune arrive,
wealth will be exhausted and the people resentful,
regret will be too late."
The King of Wú said:
"I have heard that
righteous troops do not attack the submissive,
benevolent men do not attack others because of their hunger,
even if I could gain ten Yuès,
I would not do it."
So he provided the grain.
Three years later,
Wú also suffered famine,
and requested grain from Yuè.
The King of Yuè refused and instead attacked them,
thus conquering Wú.
13.34 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ sent Chéng Hé and Shè Tuō to form an alliance with Duke Líng of Wèi at Zhuānzé.
Before Duke Líng had smeared the blood of alliance on his lips,
Chéng Hé and Shè Tuō grabbed Duke Líng's hand and forced it down.
Duke Líng grew angry,
wanting to turn against Zhào,
Wángsūn Shāng said:
"If you wish to turn against Zhào,
it's better to make the people share your hatred of them."
The Duke asked:
"How?"
He replied:
"Please order me to announce to the state:
'Any family with unmarried women
must send one person as hostage to Zhào.'
The people will certainly resent this,
and you can then turn against them."
The Duke said:
"Good."
So he gave the order,
within three days they began conscripting,
in five days the order was fully implemented,
and the people wailed in the streets.
The Duke then summoned the senior officials to plan:
"Zhào is acting without principle,
is it acceptable to turn against them?"
The officials all said:
"Yes."
They then marched out the west gate,
closing the east gate,
when the Zhào clan heard of this,
they bound Shè Tuō and executed him,
to apologize to Wèi,
while Chéng Hé fled to Yān.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Wángsūn Shāng may be called skilled in strategy!
He could harm those he hated,
handle troubles when they arose,
and when wanting to use the people, could make them follow,
achieving three things with one move,
he may indeed be called skilled in strategy."
13.35 King Chéng of Chǔ humiliated the feudal lords,
making the Lord of Lǔ serve as charioteer,
the Lord of Lǔ gathered his ministers to discuss:
"Though we are small,
we are also a state established by Zhōu,
now King Chéng makes me his charioteer,
is this acceptable?"
The ministers all said:
"It is not."
Gōngyí Xiū said:
"No,
if we don't obey the King of Chǔ,
we will die and our state perish,
your ministers are what you possess,
as ruler of the people."
So the Lord of Lǔ became charioteer.
13.36 Duke Jǐng of Qí married his daughter to Hé Lú,
seeing her off to the outskirts,
he wept:
"I will die without seeing you again!"
Gāo Mèngzǐ said:
"Qí borders the sea and is shielded by mountains,
even if we cannot completely control all under heaven,
who would dare oppose our lord?
If you love her, don't let her go."
The Duke said:
"Though I have the security of Qí's state,
I cannot command the feudal lords,
nor can I make others listen,
this breeds disorder.
I have heard that
if one cannot command, it's better to obey.
Moreover, Wú
is like a hornet or scorpion,
if it doesn't inject its poison into others, it won't be quiet,
I fear it will inject its poison into me."
So he sent her off.
13.37 Qí wanted to marry a daughter to Prince Hū of Zhèng,
but Prince Hū declined.
When asked the reason,
the Prince said:
"Each person has their own match,
Qí is large,
not my proper match.
The Book of Songs says:
'Seek much blessing for yourself,'
it depends on myself alone."
Later, the Róng people attacked Qí,
Qí requested troops from Zhèng,
Prince Hū of Zhèng led troops to rescue Qí,
and severely defeated the Róng army.
Qí again wanted to marry a daughter to him,
but the Prince firmly declined.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"When I had no dealings with Qí,
I still didn't dare.
Now having followed my lord's command to rescue Qí in its emergency,
if I take a wife and return,
people will think I used troops for marriage."
He ultimately refused.
13.38 Confucius asked Qīdiāo Mǎrén, saying:
"You served Zāng Wénzhòng, Wǔzhòng, and Rúzǐ Róng.
Among these three great officers, who was the most worthy?"
Qīdiāo Mǎrén replied:
"The Zāng family possesses a turtle,
named Cài.
When Wénzhòng was in office,
he consulted it for one omen over three years;
when Wǔzhòng was in office,
he consulted it for two omens over three years;
when Rúzǐ Róng was in office,
he consulted it for three omens over three years.
I, Mǎrén, witnessed this,
but as for the worthiness or unworthiness of these three great officers,
I, Mǎrén, do not know."
Confucius said:
"How noble is
the son of the Qīdiāo family!
When speaking of others' merits,
he conceals yet reveals;
when speaking of others' faults,
he subtly yet clearly.
Thus, wisdom cannot reach it,
clarity cannot perceive it—
could it be that he relied on divination?"
13.39 Ānlíng Chán, due to his handsome and robust appearance, gained favor with King Gòng of Chǔ.
Jiāng Yǐ went to see Ānlíng Chán and said:
"Did your ancestors perhaps achieve military merit for the king?"
He replied:
"They did not."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Have you yourself perhaps achieved any?"
He replied:
"I have not."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"How then have you attained such high status?"
He replied:
"I do not know the reason."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"I have heard that
those who serve others with wealth
lose their connections when the wealth is exhausted;
those who serve others with looks
lose favor when their beauty fades.
Now your beauty will fade in time,
how will you maintain the king's favor without being dismissed?"
Ānlíng Chán said:
"I am young and foolish,
I wish to entrust my strategy to you, sir."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Simply vow to follow him in death."
Ānlíng Chán said:
"I respectfully heed your advice."
After Jiāng Yǐ left,
a year passed,
he met Ānlíng Chán and asked:
"Have you conveyed what I advised you previously
to the king?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
Another year passed,
Jiāng Yǐ again saw Ānlíng Chán and said:
"Have you not advised the king yet?"
Ānlíng Chán said:
"I have not found the right moment with the king."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"You go out with the king in the same carriage,
sit with him when inside,
for three years,
yet you say you haven't found the right moment—
you must think my advice is not feasible."
He left displeased.
That year,
King Gòng hunted in the wilderness by the river islets,
wildfires rose like clouds and rainbows,
the roars of tigers and wolves thundered,
a mad rhinoceros came from the south,
directly hitting the king's left team horse,
the king raised his banner and ordered skilled archers to shoot it,
with one shot,
the rhinoceros died beneath the carriage.
The king was greatly pleased,
clapping his hands and laughing,
then turned to Ānlíng Chán and said:
"After I pass away,
with whom will you share such joy?"
Ānlíng Chán then stepped back hesitantly,
tears wetting his collar,
embraced the king and said:
"After your majesty's passing,
I will follow you in death,
how would I know who enjoys this joy?"
Thereupon, King Gòng enfeoffed Ānlíng Chán with three hundred households at the foot of the carriage.
Thus it is said:
Jiāng Yǐ was skilled in strategy,
Ānlíng Chán knew the right timing.
13.40 Crown Prince Shāngchén bore a grudge against Lìngyǐn Zǐshàng.
Chǔ attacked Chén,
Jìn came to its rescue,
stationing troops on both sides of the Zhī River.
Yáng Chùfǔ, knowing of Shāngchén's grudge against Zǐshàng,
thus said to Zǐshàng:
"Retreat a bit,
and I will cross to join you."
Zǐshàng retreated,
so he ordered the Jìn army:
"Chǔ has fled."
He then sent someone to inform Shāngchén:
"Zǐshàng has taken bribes from Jìn and left."
Shāngchén reported this to King Chéng,
who then executed Zǐshàng.
13.41 Zhì Bó wanted to attack Wèi,
so he sent them chariot horses,
preceded by a jade disc.
The ruler of Wèi was greatly pleased,
poured wine,
and all the great officers were happy,
except for Nán Wénzǐ, who alone was not pleased,
wearing a worried expression.
The ruler of Wèi said:
"A great state shows courtesy to me,
so I pour wine for the great officers,
all are happy,
yet you alone are not pleased and look worried—why?"
Nán Wénzǐ said:
"Courtesy without reason,
rewards without merit,
are harbingers of disaster.
We have not given anything,
yet they send gifts;
this is why I worry."
Thereupon, the ruler of Wèi fortified bridges and ferries and prepared border cities,
Zhì Bó heard that Wèi troops were at the border,
and withdrew.
13.42 Zhì Bó wanted to attack Wèi,
so he pretended that his crown prince Yán had fled,
sending him to Wèi.
Nán Wénzǐ said:
"Crown Prince Yán is deeply loved
by his lord,
and has committed no great crime,
so his flight must have a reason.
However, to not accept a fugitive
is inauspicious."
He sent officials to meet him,
saying:
"If his convoy exceeds five chariots,
do not let him in."
Zhì Bó heard this,
and stopped the plan.
13.43 When Shū Xiàng caused the death of Cháng Hóng,
he frequently visited Cháng Hóng in Zhōu,
and pretended to drop a letter that said:
"Cháng Hóng told Shū Xiàng:
'Raise the army of Jìn to attack Zhōu,
and I will depose the Liú family and establish the Shàn family.'"
The Liú family pleaded with their lord:
"This is Cháng Hóng's doing."
So he was executed.
13.44 Chǔ's Prince Wǔ was sent as an envoy to Qín,
and Qín imprisoned him.
His younger brother offered three hundred jin of gold to Shū Xiàng.
Shū Xiàng said to Duke Píng:
"Why not fortify Húqiū?
If Qín and Chǔ are troubled by the fortification of Húqiū,
and if Qín, in fear, returns Prince Wǔ to stop our fortification,
you can then stop.
Without starting a conflict,
Chǔ will surely be grateful to you."
Duke Píng said:
"Good."
So they fortified it.
Qín grew fearful,
and returned Prince Wǔ,
sending him to Jìn,
whereupon Jìn halted the fortification,
and Chǔ presented Jìn with three hundred carts of tribute.
13.45 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ sent someone with six teams of pure white horses,
first presenting a jade disc,
as gifts to Wèi.
Wèi Shūwénzǐ said:
"Showing unexpected kindness can arouse suspicion,
this is how small states serve large ones.
Now before we have sent anything, Jiǎnzǐ has first sent gifts,
there must be a reason."
Thereupon they cleared forests and removed fortifications,
gathered and stored supplies,
and then dispatched an envoy.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"My move
was meant to be unpredictable,
now that they already know it,
I shall cease the encirclement of Wèi."
13.46 Duke Huán of Zhèng planned to attack Kuài,
first inquiring about Kuài's eloquent, wise, and courageous scholars,
writing down their names,
selected Kuài's good ministers and befriended them,
prepared official titles and ranks and recorded them,
then set up an altar outside the city gate and buried them,
smearing with blood as if for a covenant.
The lord of Kuài thought it was an internal revolt,
and executed all his good ministers.
Duke Huán then attacked,
and thus captured Kuài.
13.47 Duke Huán of Zhèng was going east to receive enfeoffment in Zhèng,
and stayed overnight at an inn east of Sòng.
An old man from the inn came from outside and said:
"Guest, where are you heading?"
He replied:
"To receive enfeoffment in Zhèng."
The old man from the inn said:
"I have heard that
opportunities are hard to gain but easy to lose.
Now you rest so peacefully,
I'm afraid you won't get the enfeoffment."
Duke Huán of Zhèng heard this,
took the reins and drove himself,
his servant cooked while traveling and carried him,
traveling ten days and ten nights until arrival,
and contended with Lí Hé for the enfeoffment.
Thus, with Duke Huán of Zhèng's virtue,
without the old innkeeper,
he would almost have missed the enfeoffment.
13.48 Duke Wén of Jìn attacked Wèi and entered its outer walls,
seated his soldiers and ordered them to eat, saying:
"Today we must scale the great wall."
Prince Lǚ looked down and laughed at him.
Duke Wén said:
"Why do you laugh?"
He replied:
"My wife was returning home,
I was seeing her off,
on my way back I saw a mulberry picker and helped her,
then I looked back at my wife,
and she also had someone seeing her off."
Duke Wén became fearful,
turned the army back and returned,
upon reaching his state,
the Mò people were attacking his land.
14.1 The "Shū" says:
"Unbiased and without faction,
the kingly way is vast."
This speaks of ultimate impartiality.
In ancient times, there was one who practiced great impartiality,
that was Emperor Yáo.
Noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing all under heaven,
he found Shùn and passed it to him,
not favoring his own descendants,
leaving the world as if discarding worn sandals.
If he was like this towards all under heaven,
how much more so in smaller matters!
If not Emperor Yáo, who could have done this?
Confucius said:
"How majestic!
Only heaven is great,
and only Yáo modeled himself after it."
The "Yì" says:
"Without a head,
auspicious."
This refers to the impartiality of a ruler.
To impartially give to the world,
his virtue is great indeed.
Applying it here,
and extending it there,
he is upheld by the myriad people,
and emulated by later generations.
As for the impartiality of ministers,
in handling official duties they do not seek private gain,
in public office they do not speak of profit,
in applying public law they do not favor relatives,
in recommending worthy men for public service they do not avoid enemies.
Loyal in serving the ruler,
benevolent in benefiting subordinates,
extending it with the way of reciprocity,
acting without factionalism,
such were Yī and Lǚ.
Thus their renowned names endure to this day,
this is called impartiality.
The "Shī" says:
"The Zhōu way is like a whetstone,
straight as an arrow,
trod by the noble man,
watched by the common people."
This refers to this.
Impartiality produces clarity,
bias produces obscurity,
uprightness produces understanding,
deceit produces obstruction,
sincerity produces divinity,
exaggeration produces confusion.
These six things,
the noble man is cautious about,
and they distinguish Yǔ from Jié.
The "Shī" says:
"Cruel and mighty God,
his commands are often perverse."
This speaks of partiality.
14.2 King Shòumèng of Wú had four sons,
the eldest named Yè,
the second Yú Zhài,
the third Yī Mèi,
the youngest Jì Zhá,
known as Yánlíng Jìzǐ,
the most virtuous,
which his three elder brothers all recognized.
When King Shòumèng died,
Yè yielded the throne to Jìzǐ,
but Jìzǐ firmly declined,
so Yè made an agreement:
"Jìzǐ is virtuous,
if the state can pass to Jìzǐ,
then Wú can prosper."
Thus the brothers succeeded each other,
and at meals would pray:
"May I die early,
so the state may pass to Jìzǐ."
Yè died,
Yú Zhài ascended;
Yú Zhài died,
Yī Mèi ascended;
Yī Mèi died,
and it was Jìzǐ's turn.
But Jìzǐ was away on a mission,
and not present,
so his half-brother Liáo said:
"I am also an elder brother."
And set himself up as King of Wú.
When Jìzǐ returned from his mission,
he served as before.
Yè's son Guāng said:
"According to my father's wish,
the state should go to Jìzǐ,
but by inheritance law,
I am the rightful heir,
I should be the ruling lord,
what right has Liáo?"
Thereupon he sent Zhuān Zhū to assassinate Liáo,
killing him,
and yielded the throne to Jìzǐ.
Jìzǐ said:
"You killed my lord,
if I accept the state from you,
then I am conspiring with you in usurpation.
You killed my brother,
if I kill you in turn,
then brothers and fathers and sons would kill each other endlessly."
He finally left for Yánlíng,
and never entered Wú again.
The noble man considers his refusal to kill as benevolence,
and his refusal to take the state as righteousness.
Not using the state for personal gain,
abandoning a thousand chariots without regret,
renouncing a noble position without resentment,
he nearly achieved perfection!
14.3 The principle for feudal lords is to die for the altars of soil and grain.
Yet the Great King abandoned his state and left—
why is that?
The sage does not wish for violence to oppress the common people,
hence he has feudal lords die for their states
to protect their people.
The Great King possessed the utmost benevolent grace;
he could not bear to see the people suffer in war.
Therefore, he served the Róng clan with dogs, horses, treasures, and silks,
yet the attacks did not cease.
When asked what they desired,
it was territory.
Thereupon, he gathered his ministers and elders and told them:
"Land
is that by which people are nourished.
A noble person does not allow that which nourishes to harm the nourished.
I shall leave this place."
So he dwelt at the foot of Mount Qí,
and the people of Bīn, carrying their young and supporting their elderly, followed him
as if returning to their parents.
After three relocations, the people increased fivefold from the start—
all because they were inspired by benevolence and righteousness to follow their superior.
A noble person defends the state and brings peace to the people;
it is not merely about battling troops or exhausting and killing the masses.
He does not act selfishly for himself;
he only ensures the people have enough.
Protecting the people—this is indeed the principle behind abandoning the state,
which is called the utmost impartiality.
14.4 Xīn Lì visited Duke Mù of Lǔ and said:
"The Duke of Zhōu was not as virtuous as Grand Duke Wàng."
Duke Mù asked:
"How do you reason that?"
Xīn Lì replied:
"The Duke of Zhōu chose a place and was enfeoffed at Qūfù,
while Grand Duke Wàng chose a place and was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū.
Their ranks and territories were equal,
yet his land was not as fine as Yíngqiū's,
and the people were not as numerous as Yíngqiū's.
Not only that,
but Yíngqiū also had natural fortifications."
Duke Mù felt ashamed in heart and could not respond.
Xīn Lì hurried out,
and Nángōng Biānzǐ entered.
Duke Mù relayed all of Xīn Lì's words to Nángōng Biānzǐ.
Nángōng Biānzǐ said:
"When King Chéng of Zhōu divined about dwelling in Chéngzhōu,
he addressed the tortoise shell saying:
'I alone possess all under heaven;
in governing and approaching the people,
how dare I be without the central land!'
'If I have committed offenses,
let the four quarters attack me—
it would not be hard to achieve.'
The Duke of Zhōu divined about dwelling at Qūfù,
and he addressed the tortoise shell saying:
'To build a city on the sunny side of the mountain—
if virtuous, it will flourish abundantly;
if not virtuous, it will quickly perish.'
Jìsūn Xíngfǔ admonished his son,
saying:
'I wish to build a house between the two altars of soil and grain,
so that if among my descendants there are those who cannot serve their superiors,
it will cause their replacement to come all the faster.'
Thus it is said:
'If virtuous, it will flourish abundantly;
if not virtuous, it will quickly perish.'
How can it lie in choosing a place for enfeoffment,
or in displaying natural fortifications!'
Xīn Lì's words
are those of a petty person;
do not speak of this again."
14.5 When Qín Shǐhuángdì had swallowed the world,
he summoned his ministers for discussion,
saying:
"In ancient times, the Five Emperors abdicated to the worthy,
while the Three Dynastic Kings passed it on hereditarily.
Which is right?
I shall act accordingly."
The seventy Erudites did not answer,
but Báo Báilìngzhī replied:
"When all under heaven is treated as public office, yielding to the worthy is right;
when all under heaven is treated as a family, hereditary succession is right.
Thus, the Five Emperors regarded all under heaven as public office,
while the Three Dynastic Kings regarded all under heaven as a family."
Qín Shǐhuángdì looked up to heaven and sighed, saying:
"My virtue surpasses that of the Five Emperors;
I shall make all under heaven public office.
Who can be made to succeed me?"
Báo Báilìngzhī replied:
"Your Majesty practices the ways of Jié and Zhòu,
yet wishes to perform the abdication of the Five Emperors—
this is not something Your Majesty can accomplish."
Qín Shǐhuángdì was greatly enraged and said:
"Step forward!
How dare you say I practice the ways of Jié and Zhòu?
Explain quickly—
if your explanation is unclear, you die."
Lìngzhī replied:
"I beg to explain.
Your Majesty builds towers that reach the clouds,
palaces spanning five lǐ.
You cast bells of a thousand shí,
erect bell stands of ten thousand shí.
You have hundreds of women in succession,
thousands of actors and musicians accumulated.
You construct palaces at Mount Lí,
extending to Yōng without cease.
That with which you serve yourself
exhausts all under heaven,
depletes the people's strength.
You are biased and selfish,
unable to extend to others.
Your Majesty is what is called a ruler who only preserves himself;
how could you have leisure to compare your virtue to the Five Emperors,
wishing to make all under heaven public office?"
The First Emperor fell silent, having no reply;
his face showed shame.
After a long time,
he said:
"Lìngzhī's words
have made the multitude despise me."
Thereupon, he abandoned the plan,
with no intention to abdicate.
14.6 Duke Jǐng of Qí's rewards and gifts extended to the inner palace;
embroidered silks draped his terraces and pavilions,
beans and grains fed his ducks and geese.
Going out, he saw a starved corpse and
said to Yànzǐ:
"Why did this person die?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"This one died of starvation."
The Duke said:
"Alas!
My lack of virtue
is extreme indeed!"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Your Lordship's virtue is evident and clear—
why say you have no virtue?"
Duke Jǐng said:
"What do you mean?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Your Lordship's virtue extends to the inner palace and the terraces;
your playthings
are clothed in embroidered silks;
your ducks and geese
are fed with beans and grains;
your efforts within to please yourself
extend even to the clans of the inner palace.
How can you say you have no virtue!
However, I wish to make a request of you:
from your intent,
from your heart that seeks self-pleasure,
extend it and share it with the common people—
then how could there be any starved corpses!
If you do not extend this,
but only strive within for your own preferences and selfishness,
causing wealth and goods to accumulate disproportionately,
with beans, grains, coins, and silks rotting in granaries and treasuries,
kindness not universally bestowed upon the people,
and public-mindedness not encompassing all states,
then this is the reason Jié and Zhòu perished.
The reason scholars and people rebel
is due to such bias.
If you consider my words, Yīng's,
and extend your abundant virtue,
imparting it publicly to all under heaven,
then the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ can be achieved,
and one starved corpse is hardly worth grieving over!"
14.7 King Gòng of Chǔ went out hunting and lost his bow.
His attendants asked to search for it,
but King Gòng said:
"Stop.
A person of Chǔ lost the bow,
and a person of Chǔ will get it.
What need is there to search?"
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"It's a pity his perspective is not broader.
He should have said:
'A person lost the bow,
and a person will get it.'
Why must it be a person of Chǔ?"
This is what Zhòngní called great impartiality.
14.8 Wàn Zhāng asked:
"When Confucius was in Wèi, did he stay with Yōng Jū,
and when in Qí, with the eunuch Jǐ Huán?
Is this true?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"No,
it is not so.
This was fabricated by busybodies.
In Wèi, he stayed with Yán Chóuyóu.
Mí Zǐ's wife and Zǐlù's wife
were sisters.
Mí Zǐ said to Zǐlù:
'If Confucius stays with me,
he can obtain the position of a minister of Wèi.'
Zǐlù reported this.
Confucius said:
'That depends on fate.'
Confucius advanced according to ritual,
and withdrew according to righteousness.
Whether obtaining a position or not,
he would say 'it depends on fate.'
But staying with Yōng Jū and the eunuch Jǐ Huán would have been against fate.
When Confucius was displeased in Lǔ and Wèi,
and was about to go to Sòng,
he encountered Minister Huán,
who intended to intercept and kill him,
so he passed through Sòng in disguise.
At this time, Confucius was in distress,
and stayed with Sīchéng Zhēnzǐ, who served as a minister to Lord Chén Zhōu.
I have heard that
one observes a local official by those he hosts,
and a visiting official by whom he stays with.
If Confucius had stayed with Yōng Jū and the eunuch Jǐ Huán,
how could he be Confucius?"
14.9 The Master traveled and advised seventy feudal lords without a fixed abode,
wishing to enable all the people under heaven to find their proper places,
but his Way was not implemented;
withdrawing, he compiled the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
recording even the smallest good deeds,
and condemning the slightest evils;
human affairs were thoroughly covered,
and the kingly way was fully set forth;
refining harmony with sage-like institutions,
it reached up to heaven, and a qilin appeared—
this was heaven's recognition of the Master.
Thereupon, he sighed deeply and said:
"Is it that heaven, in its utmost brightness, cannot be obscured?
Then why are there solar eclipses?
Is it that earth, in its utmost stability, cannot be shaken?
Then why are there earthquakes?
If even heaven and earth can be shaken and obscured,
it is no wonder that sages and worthies are thwarted in the world and cannot practice their Way,
hence disasters and anomalies occur together."
The Master said:
"I do not complain against heaven,
nor do I blame others.
I study what is below and comprehend what is above.
Is it heaven that knows me?"
14.10 Confucius was born in an age of chaos,
and none could tolerate him.
Thus, only when his words were heeded by the ruler,
and his beneficence reached the people,
would he take office;
if his words were not heeded by the ruler,
and his beneficence did not reach the people, he would remain in retirement.
Confucius, with a heart that embraced all under heaven,
and possessing the virtue of benevolence and sageliness,
lamented the corruption of the customs of the time,
grieved over the collapse of order and discipline,
shouldered heavy burdens and traveled far,
journeying everywhere in response to invitations,
hoping to fortunately impart his Way to the people,
yet none of the feudal lords of his time could employ him.
Thus, his virtue accumulated but was not displayed,
the great Way was constrained and could not extend,
the world did not receive his transformation,
and all living beings did not enjoy his kindness.
Therefore, he sighed deeply and said:
"If anyone would use me,
could I not make it an Eastern Zhōu?"
Hence, Confucius traveled and advocated,
not wishing to personally apply his virtue in just one city,
but aiming to spread it throughout the world,
and establish it among all living beings.
14.11 Qín and Jìn were at war,
engaged in battle,
when Qín sent a man to tell the Jìn general:
"The soldiers of our three armies have not yet rested,
tomorrow we request to battle again."
Yú Pián said:
"The envoy's eyes are shifting and his words are exaggerated,
he fears us,
and is about to flee.
If we press them to the river,
we are sure to defeat them."
Zhào Dùn said:
"To abandon the dead and wounded without collecting them
is not benevolent;
to not wait for the appointed time and force others into a perilous position
is not courageous.
Let us wait."
The Qín army fled that night.
14.12 Wǔ Zǐxū was about to go to Wú,
and bid farewell to his friend Shēn Bāoxū, saying:
"After three years,
if Chǔ is not destroyed,
I will not see you again."
Shēn Bāoxū said:
"Do your best,
I cannot assist you,
to assist you would be to attack our ancestral temple,
to stop you would be to fail as a friend.
Nevertheless,
if you destroy it,
I will preserve it."
Thus, they witnessed Chǔ both preserved and destroyed.
After three years,
the Wú army attacked Chǔ,
and King Zhāo fled.
Shēn Bāoxū, without orders,
went west to see the Earl of Qín, saying:
"Wú is without principle,
with strong soldiers and numerous people,
intending to conquer the world,
starting with Chǔ.
My lord has fled,
and is staying in Yúnmèng,
sending me to report the emergency."
Duke Āi said:
"Very well,
I will certainly consider it."
Shēn Bāoxū did not leave the court,
but stood in the Qín court,
weeping day and night,
for seven days and seven nights without ceasing.
Duke Āi said:
"With a minister like this,
how can we not rescue them?"
He raised an army to save Chǔ,
and the men of Wú, hearing of this,
withdrew their troops and returned.
King Zhāo returned,
and wished to enfeoff Shēn Bāoxū,
but Shēn Bāoxū declined, saying:
"Saving from destruction
is not for fame;
to receive a reward for achieving merit
is to sell one's courage."
He declined and did not accept,
then withdrew into seclusion,
and was never seen again for the rest of his life.
The "Book of Songs" says:
"Whenever people are in distress,
I crawl to rescue them."
14.13 Chǔ Prime Minister Yúqiūzǐ reported to King Zhuāng:
"I have heard that upholding public duty and enforcing laws
can bring honor;
those with shallow abilities and meager conduct
should not hope for high positions;
those not renowned for benevolence and wisdom
should not seek prominence and glory;
where one's talents are not distinguished,
one should not occupy such positions.
I have served as Prime Minister for ten years,
yet the state has not become better governed,
legal disputes have not ceased,
reclusive scholars have not been promoted,
excessive disasters have not been punished,
long occupying this high position,
I block the path of many worthy men,
holding office without merit, feeding on empty rations,
my greed knows no satisfaction -
my crimes deserve investigation by reason.
I have privately selected a talented man from our state,
a scholar from the lower villages named Sūnshū Áo,
elegant and capable in many ways,
his nature free from desire.
If Your Majesty elevates him and entrusts him with governance,
then the state can be well-ordered,
and scholars and commoners will rally to him."
King Zhuāng said:
"You have assisted me,
enabling me to lead in the Central States,
with my commands reaching distant regions,
finally achieving hegemony over the feudal lords -
who but you made this possible?"
Yúqiūzǐ replied: [35"Those who long cling to emolument and position
are greedy;
those who do not advance the worthy and capable
are deceptive;
those who do not yield their positions
are corrupt.
Failing in these three aspects
constitutes disloyalty.
As a minister who is disloyal,
how could Your Majesty still regard me as your servant?
I wish to firmly resign."
King Zhuāng consented,
granted Yúqiūzǐ three hundred acres of land,
honoring him as "State Elder,"
and appointed Sūnshū Áo as Prime Minister.
Soon after,
someone from Yúqiūzǐ's household violated the law,
Sūnshū Áo arrested and executed him.
Yúqiūzǐ was pleased,
entered to see the king,
and said:
"What I said about Sūnshū Áo -
he indeed can be entrusted with state affairs,
upholding state laws without favoritism,
administering punishments without bending them -
he may be called just and fair."
King Zhuāng said: [62"This is your gift to me!"
14.14 Zhào Xuānzǐ recommended Hán Xiànzǐ to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"He is a man without partiality,
governs the multitude without disorder,
and faces death without fear."
The Marquis appointed him as Central Army Commander.
During the Battle of Héqū,
Zhào Xuānzǐ's chariot disrupted the formation,
Hán Xiànzǐ executed his charioteer.
People all said:
"Hán Xiànzǐ will surely die.
His patron promoted him in the morning, yet he executed his patron's servant by evening -
who could tolerate this?"
After the campaign ended,
Zhào Xuānzǐ hosted a feast for the high officials,
after three rounds of drinking,
he said:
"Gentlemen, you may congratulate me now."
The officials said:
"We don't know what to congratulate you for."
Xuānzǐ said:
"I recommended Hán Jué to our lord,
if my recommendation was inappropriate,
I would certainly receive punishment.
Now my chariot was out of formation and he executed my servant -
this shows he is without partiality,
proving my recommendation was correct."
The officials bowed twice and touched their heads to the ground, saying:
Not only is Jìn State fortunate to enjoy this,
but even Tángshū relies on this,
how dare we not bow twice and touch our heads to the ground?"
14.15 Duke Wén of Jìn asked Jiùfàn:
"Who can be appointed as Governor of Xīhé?"
Jiùfàn replied:
"Yú Zìgāo is suitable."
The Duke said:
"Isn't Zìgāo your enemy?"
He replied:
"Your Lordship asked who could serve as governor,
not who my enemies are."
Zìgāo visited Jiùfàn to thank him,
saying:
"Fortunately you pardoned my faults
and recommended me to the lord,
enabling me to become Governor of Xīhé."
Jiùfàn said:
"Recommending you
was public duty;
bearing resentment toward you
is personal matter.
I will not let private affairs harm public righteousness.
You should leave now,
but remember -
I could still shoot you!"
14.16 King Wén of Chǔ attacked Dèng,
sending Prince Gé and Prince Líng together to gather vegetables.
The two princes went out foraging,
saw an old man carrying a basket,
begged from him,
when he didn't give,
they assaulted him and seized his basket.
The king heard of this,
ordered both princes detained,
and planned to execute them.
A minister pleaded:
"Taking the basket
is indeed a crime,
but executing them
exceeds their crime -
why would Your Majesty execute them?"
As he finished speaking,
the old man came to the army camp and said:
"We attack Dèng because they are without morality,
yet now your princes assault me and seize my basket -
this is more immoral than Dèng."
He cried out to heaven and wailed.
When the ruler heard this,
all ministers were fearful.
The ruler appeared before him,
saying:
"Punishing crime yet violently seizing
is no way to prohibit brutality;
relying on strength to abuse the elderly
is no way to educate the young;
favoring my sons while abandoning law
is no way to protect the state.
Showing partiality to these two
destroys three principles of conduct,
this is no way to govern.
The old man may let this rest -
I apologize to him outside the army gate."
14.17 The clan of Chǔ's Lìngyǐn Zǐwén
had a member who violated the law.
The court magistrate arrested him,
but upon learning he was from the Lìngyǐn's clan, released him.
Zǐwén summoned the magistrate and reprimanded him,
saying:
"The reason for establishing the position of court magistrate
is to oversee violations of the king's decrees and investigate breaches of national law.
An upright officer upholding the law
should be gentle yet unbending,
firm yet unyielding.
Now you abandon the law, defy the decree, and release a lawbreaker—
this is administering justice unjustly,
harboring a biased heart.
How could this be my intention to seek private gain?
Why does the magistrate pervert the law?
I hold a high position to set an example for the officials and people.
If they bear grievances
and I cannot exempt myself from the law,
now that my clan member has clearly broken the law,
for the magistrate to release him out of consideration for my personal feelings
would make my unfairness glaringly evident to the whole state.
Holding the reins of the state
yet being known for partiality—
to live without righteousness
is worse than death for me."
Thereupon, he delivered his clansman to the magistrate, saying:
"If he is not punished,
I will die for it."
The magistrate, afraid,
then punished the clansman.
King Chéng heard of this,
and without even putting on his shoes, went to Zǐwén's residence, saying:
"I am young and inexperienced,
having appointed an unfit person as magistrate,
thus opposing your will, sir."
He then dismissed the magistrate and honored Zǐwén,
entrusting him with internal affairs.
The people of the state, upon hearing this, said:
"With a Lìngyǐn so just,
what have we to worry about!"
And together they composed a song:
"Zǐwén's clan
broke the state's laws.
The magistrate freed him,
but Zǐwén refused.
He heeded the sprouts of grievance,
upright and fair."
14.18 King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a law for the Máo Gate:
"Any minister, official, or prince entering court
whose horse's hoof treads beyond the eaves—
the court magistrate shall behead his chariot shaft and execute his driver."
The crown prince entered court,
and his horse's hoof trod beyond the eaves.
The magistrate beheaded the shaft and executed the driver.
The prince was furious,
went in and tearfully pleaded with the king:
"Execute the magistrate for me."
The king said:
"The law
serves to revere the ancestral temple and honor the state.
Thus, one who can establish laws, follow decrees,
and respect the state
is a loyal minister of the state.
How can he be executed?
To violate the law, discard decrees,
and disrespect the state
is for a minister to override the ruler,
for the lower to oppress the higher.
If ministers override the ruler, the sovereign loses authority;
if the lower oppress the higher, the throne is endangered.
If the state is not preserved,
what can I bequeath to my descendants?"
The prince then retreated to his quarters,
bowed twice, and begged for death.
14.19 During the time of King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
the crown prince's chariot stood inside the Máo Gate,
and Junior Tutor Qìng drove him away.
The prince, angered,
went in and reported to the king:
"Junior Tutor Qìng chased away my chariot."
The king said:
"Let it be.
He does not overstep in the presence of the elder ruler,
nor act presumptuously behind the young lord.
He is a treasure of the state."
14.20 King Hélú of Wú was about to raise an army for Wǔ Zǐxū to take revenge on Chǔ.
Zǐxū advised:
"A feudal lord does not raise armies for a commoner.
Moreover, serving a ruler is like serving a father.
To impair the ruler's righteousness
to avenge one's father—
I cannot do it."
Thus, he stopped.
Later, he avenged his father under different circumstances.
Zǐxū can be said not to have used public affairs for private ends.
14.21 When Confucius served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
he would always consult his teachers in judging cases.
Earnestly, they all stood,
and then the gentleman would advance and ask:
"What does so-and-so think?"
So-and-so would state his view.
Again he asked:
"What does so-and-so think?"
So-and-so would state his view.
After debate,
the gentleman would say:
"It seems we should follow so-and-so's opinion."
With the gentleman's wisdom,
was it necessary to wait for so-and-so's words
to know how to judge the case?
The gentleman's respect and deference
meant that in matters of discourse, whatever could be shared with others,
the gentleman did not keep to himself.
14.22 When Zǐgāo governed in Wèi,
he cut off a man's foot as punishment.
When turmoil arose among Wèi's ruler and ministers,
Zǐgāo fled to the outer gate,
but it was closed,
and the man whose foot he had cut off was guarding it.
He said:
"There's a breach over there."
Zǐgāo said:
"A gentleman does not climb over walls."
He said:
"There's a hole over there."
Zǐgāo said:
"A gentleman does not crawl through holes."
He said:
"There's a room here."
Zǐgāo entered.
When the pursuers gave up,
Zǐgāo prepared to leave
and said to the footless man:
"I could not undermine the sovereign's laws,
so I personally cut off your foot.
Now that I am in distress,
this is your chance for revenge.
Why do you help me escape?"
The man replied:
"Losing my foot was due to my own crime,
there was no help for it.
When you tried my case,
you weighed the laws carefully,
following legal procedures for me,
wishing I could be exempt from punishment—
I knew that.
After the verdict and sentencing,
when it came to carrying out the punishment,
you looked sorrowful and unhappy,
showing it in your expression—
I also knew that.
It was not that you favored me personally!
Heaven endows a benevolent heart,
and it is natural for you.
That is why I helped you escape."
Confucius, upon hearing this, said:
"A good official plants virtue,
a poor official sows enmity.
Acting with impartiality—
this refers to Zǐgāo, does it not!"
15.1 The "Sīmǎ Fǎ" states:
"A state, however large,
will perish if it loves war;
the world, however peaceful,
will face danger if it forgets war."
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"The gentleman maintains weapons to guard against unforeseen events."
Arms should not be treated lightly,
for lightness leads to loss of awe;
arms should not be abandoned,
for abandonment invites invasion.
In the past, King Fūchāi of Wú loved war and perished,
while King Yǎn of Xú lacked martial prowess and was also destroyed.
Thus, an enlightened king in governing the state
neither treats arms lightly above,
nor neglects the military below.
The "Yì Jīng" says:
"In security, do not forget danger."
Thus, one's person is safe, and the state can be preserved.
15.2 King Zhāo of Qín sighed during a morning court and said:
"The swords of Chǔ are sharp,
but their entertainers are unskilled.
Sharp swords mean the warriors are fierce and bold;
unskilled entertainers mean their thoughts are far-reaching.
I fear Chǔ is plotting against Qín."
This is called thinking of misfortune in times of luck,
and remembering peril while in safety,
which ultimately led to his achieving hegemony.
15.3 Wángsūn Lì said to King Wén of Chǔ:
"King Yǎn of Xú is fond of practicing the way of benevolence and righteousness,
and all thirty-two states east of the Hàn River have submitted to him.
If you, King, do not attack him,
Chǔ will surely end up serving Xú."
The King said:
"If he truly possesses the Way,
he cannot be attacked."
Wángsūn Lì replied:
"For the great to attack the small,
and the strong to attack the weak,
is like a big fish swallowing a small fish,
or a tiger devouring a piglet.
How could this be unjustified?"
King Wén then raised an army to attack Xú,
and devastated it.
As King Yǎn of Xú was about to die,
he said:
"I relied on civil virtue,
but neglected military preparedness;
I was fond of practicing the way of benevolence and righteousness,
but was unaware of the deceitful hearts of others,
thus I have come to this end!"
Truly, the ancient kings must have been prepared!
15.4 Wú Qǐ was the governor of Yuàn,
and while touring the counties,
he came to Xī,
and asked Qū Yíjiù:
"The King, unaware of my incompetence,
has made me governor of Yuàn.
What would you, sir, advise me?"
Lord Qū did not reply.
After one year,
the King appointed him Prime Minister,
and while touring the counties,
he came to Xī,
and asked Qū Yíjiù:
"I previously sought your advice,
but you, sir, did not instruct me.
Now the King, unaware of my incompetence,
has made me Prime Minister.
I ask you, sir, to observe how I will perform."
Lord Qū said:
"What do you intend to do?"
Wú Qǐ said:
"I will equalize the noble ranks of Chǔ and balance their emoluments;
reduce the surplus and supplement the deficiencies;
and sharpen armor and weapons to contend with the world at the appropriate time."
Lord Qū said:
"I have heard that
those who were good at governing states in the past did not alter their old ways,
nor change their constants.
Now you intend to equalize the noble ranks of Chǔ and balance their emoluments,
reducing the surplus and supplementing the deficiencies—
this is altering the old ways and changing the constants.
Moreover, I have heard that
weapons are instruments of ill omen,
and contention is contrary to virtue.
Now you secretly plan contrary to virtue,
and are fond of using instruments of ill omen—
these are what people reject,
the height of perversity.
They are wanton and excessive affairs,
and those who practice them will not benefit.
Moreover, when you used Lǔ's troops,
you should not have succeeded against Qí,
yet you succeeded;
when you used Wèi's troops,
you should not have succeeded against Qín,
yet you succeeded.
I have heard it said:
'Only those who bring misfortune can complete misfortune.'
I had been wondering why our King has repeatedly defied the Way of Heaven,
yet until now encountered no misfortune.
Ah!
It seems he was waiting for you, sir."
Wú Qǐ, alarmed, said:
"Can it still be changed?"
Lord Qū said:
"It cannot!"
Wú Qǐ said:
"What should I do, then?"
Lord Qū said:
"One who has formed his punishment
cannot change it anymore.
You'd better sincerely abide by your position and earnestly carry out your duties.
In Chǔ, nothing is more valued than recommending the worthy."
15.5 The Spring and Autumn Annals record the survival and fall of states to examine future generations.
Even with vast territory and numerous people,
strong armor and sharp weapons,
and fierce and brave generals,
if the soldiers are not attached to them,
they cannot achieve victory and merit in battle.
The Marquis of Jìn was captured at Hán,
Zǐyù (Déchén) of Chǔ was defeated at Chéngpú,
and Cài's multitude crumbled without waiting for the enemy.
Hence it is said:
"King Wén could not employ people who were not attached to him;
Xiān Zhěn could not fight with untrained troops;
Zàofǔ and Wáng Liáng could not drive broken carriages and feeble horses to speed and cover long distances;
Yì and Péng Méng could not shoot far and hit small targets with crooked arrows and weak bows."
Thus the essence of strength and weakness, success and failure
lies in attaching the soldiers and training them.
15.6 If internal order is not achieved,
one cannot rectify external affairs;
if the root benevolence is not cultivated,
one cannot control the branches.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals give priority to the capital and then to the central states,
and priority to the central states and then to the barbarians.
By the time of King Huì of Zhōu,
due to encountering a chaotic age,
and inheriting the system of the former kings,
while the powerful Chǔ claimed kingship,
and the feudal lords rebelled,
he wished to extend the mandate of the former kings,
and unify the world.
But without first broadly nurturing the capital and then the central states,
and the central states and then the barbarians,
internal order not being achieved,
he acted in anger without assessing his strength,
