or weighing gains and losses,
raised troops to campaign against the powerful Chǔ,
and his army was greatly defeated,
humiliated and unable to act,
greatly laughed at by the world.
Fortunately, he met Duke Huán of Qí,
and thus obtained safety and honor.
Therefore, if internal order is not achieved,
one cannot rectify external affairs;
if the root benevolence is not cultivated,
one cannot control the branches.
15.7 Regarding the general receiving command:
the commander enters,
the military officers all enter,
and all face north, bow twice, and kowtow to receive the command;
the Son of Heaven faces south and hands him the battle-axe,
then turns east,
and facing west, bows to him,
showing that he will not control him.
Thus, having received command and gone forth,
he forgets his state;
engaging in battle,
he forgets his family;
hearing the sound of the drum,
he only fears not achieving victory,
and forgets himself.
Thus he is resolved to die.
Being resolved to die is not as good as delighting in death;
delighting in death is not as good as being content in death;
being content in death is not as good as dying for righteousness;
dying for righteousness is not as good as looking upon death as going home.
This is what it means.
Thus if one man is resolved to die,
ten men cannot withstand him;
if ten men are resolved to die,
a hundred men cannot withstand them;
if a hundred men are resolved to die,
a thousand men cannot withstand them;
if a thousand men are resolved to die,
ten thousand men cannot withstand them;
if ten thousand men are resolved to die,
they can roam freely across the world.
With orders carried out and prohibitions heeded,
they are the army of a true king.
15.13 Confucius traveled north and
ascended Nóng Shān to the east;
Zǐlù, Zǐgòng, and Yán Yuān accompanied him.
Confucius sighed deeply and said:
"Climbing high and looking down
makes one's heart sorrowful!
You few disciples,
each speak your aspirations,
and I, Qiū, will listen to them."
Zǐlù said:
"I wish to have white plumes like the moon,
red plumes like the sun,
the sounds of bells and drums
rising to be heard by the heavens,
banners and flags fluttering,
sweeping down to cover the ground.
Yóu would then raise troops and attack,
surely seizing territory for a thousand lǐ,
something only Yóu can achieve.
Let those other two follow me."
Confucius said:
"How brave is this scholar!
How fervent he is!"
Zǐgòng said:
"Cì wishes for Qí and Chǔ to join battle in the vast wilderness,
with two fortresses facing each other,
banners and flags in sight,
dust and ashes connecting,
engaging in combat with weapons.
Cì wishes to don plain white garments and a white cap,
to discourse amidst the gleaming blades,
resolving the troubles of both states,
something only Cì can achieve.
Let those other two follow me."
Confucius said:
"How eloquent is this scholar!
How soaring he is!"
Yán Yuān alone did not speak.
Confucius said:
"Huí, come here,
why do you alone not wish to speak?"
Yán Yuān said:
"Matters of civil and military affairs,
those two have already spoken of them,
how dare Huí participate?"
Confucius said:
"If your humble heart does not wish to join in,
still, speak of it."
Yán Yuān said:
"Huí has heard that salted fish and fragrant orchids are not stored in the same box,
Yáo, Shùn, Jié, and Zhòu did not govern the same state,
the words of those two differ from Huí's.
Huí wishes to find an enlightened king or sage ruler and assist him,
so that city walls need not be built,
moats need not be crossed,
swords and halberds are forged into farming tools,
enabling the world to be free from the troubles of war for a thousand years.
If so, then why would Yóu fervently attack,
and why would Cì soaringly persuade?"
Confucius said:
"How beautiful is this virtue!
How sublime it is!"
Zǐlù raised his hand and asked:
"I wish to hear the Master's intention."
Confucius said:
"What I wish for
is Yán's plan.
I wish to carry my robes and cap and follow Master Yán."
15.14 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zhòngní:
"I wish to defend when small,
attack when large,
what is the way for this?"
Zhòngní said:
"If the court has propriety,
and superiors and inferiors are close,
the multitude of the people are all the ruler's charges,
whom would the ruler attack?
If the court lacks propriety,
and superiors and inferiors are not close,
the people are all the ruler's enemies,
with whom would the ruler defend?"
Thereupon, he abolished the prohibitions on marshes and weirs,
relaxed the taxes at passes and markets,
to provide benefits for the people.
15.15 King Wén said:
"I wish to use troops,
whom can I attack?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"The Mìxū clan is suspicious of us,
we can go attack them first."
Guǎn Shū said:
"No,
their ruler is an enlightened lord of the world,
attacking him would be unjust."
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"Your servant has heard that
the former kings attacked the crooked, not the compliant;
attacked the perilous, not the easy;
attacked the excessive, not the inadequate."
King Wén said:
"Good."
Then he attacked the Mìxū clan,
and destroyed them.
15.16 King Wǔ was about to attack Zhòu,
summoned Tàigōng Wàng and asked him:
"I wish to know victory without fighting,
know auspiciousness without divination,
and employ those not my people—
is there a way to do this?"
Tàigōng replied:
"There is a way.
If the king gains the hearts of the multitude to plot against the unprincipled,
then you can know victory without fighting;
if the worthy attack the unworthy,
then you can know auspiciousness without divination;
if they harm them,
and we benefit them,
even if not our people,
they can be obtained and employed."
King Wǔ said:
"Good."
Then he summoned Zhōu Gōng and asked him:
saying:
"Those in the world who plan affairs
all regard Yīn as the Son of Heaven,
and Zhōu as a feudal lord,
for a feudal lord to attack the Son of Heaven—
is there a way to victory?"
Zhōu Gōng replied:
"If Yīn is truly the Son of Heaven,
and Zhōu is truly a feudal lord,
then there is no way to victory,
how can they be attacked?"
King Wǔ angrily said:
"Is there an explanation for your words?"
Zhōu Gōng replied:
"Your servant has heard that
those who attack propriety are bandits,
those who attack righteousness are brutal.
If one loses the people,
one is reduced to a commoner.
The king attacks one who has lost the people,
why speak of attacking the Son of Heaven?"
King Wǔ said:
"Good."
Then he raised the masses and mobilized the army,
fought Yīn at Mùyě,
and greatly defeated the Yīn people.
Entering the hall, he saw jade,
and said:
"Whose jade is this?"
The reply was:
"The feudal lords' jade."
He immediately took it and returned it to the feudal lords.
The world heard of it and said:
"King Wǔ is incorruptible with wealth."
Entering the chambers, he saw women,
and said:
"Whose women are these?"
The reply was:
"The feudal lords' women."
He immediately took them and returned them to the feudal lords.
The world heard of it and said:
"King Wǔ is incorruptible with desire."
Then he distributed the grain from Jùqiáo,
scattered the gold and coins from Lùtái to give to the officers and people,
retired his war chariots and did not ride them,
laid aside his armor and weapons and did not use them,
released the horses at Huà Shān,
set loose the oxen at Táolín,
showing they would not be used again.
Those in the world who heard all said King Wǔ practiced righteousness under heaven,
is that not great indeed!
15.17 King Wén wished to attack Chóng,
first proclaiming:
"I have heard that Chóng Hóu Hǔ despises and insults fathers and brothers,
does not respect elders,
adjudicates cases unjustly,
distributes wealth unevenly,
the common people exhaust their strength yet cannot obtain clothing and food.
I will come to punish him,
solely for the people."
Then he attacked Chóng,
ordering no killing of people,
no destruction of houses,
no filling of wells,
no cutting of trees,
no disturbance of the six domestic animals,
and those who disobeyed the order would die without pardon.
The people of Chóng heard this,
and thus requested to surrender.
15.18 King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Chén,
and Wú came to its rescue.
It rained for ten days and ten nights,
then cleared.
The Grand Historian Yǐ Xiāng said:
"Wú will surely arrive by night.
With our armor arrayed and fortifications damaged,
they are bound to press upon us.
Why not form ranks, beat the drums, and go out to await them?"
When the Wú army arrived,
they saw the Chǔ forces in battle formation and turned back.
The Grand Historian Yǐ Xiāng said:
"Pursue them."
Wú marched sixty lǐ but achieved nothing,
and when their king halted his troops to rest,
Chǔ indeed attacked them,
routing the Wú army completely.
15.19 During the time of Duke Huán of Qí,
it rained continuously for a hundred days.
Duke Huán wished to attack Cáolíng,
as its walls, damaged by the rain, were not yet repaired.
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng arrived at the gate with soldiers and laborers.
Duke Huán said:
"What are the laborers for?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard that
rain brings opportunities.
Since Cáolíng cannot withstand the rain,
I request to attack it."
The Duke said:
"Good."
So he raised an army and attacked it.
Upon arrival,
the main force was outside the walls,
while the defenders were inside.
Duke Huán said:
"Could there be a sage among them?"
Then he turned his banners and left.
15.20 Sòng besieged Cáo but could not capture it.
Simǎ Zǐyú said to the ruler:
"When King Wén attacked Chóng,
the Chóng army defended their city,
and for thirty days they did not surrender.
He withdrew to cultivate his teachings,
then attacked again,
and they surrendered from their fortifications.
Might your virtue now be lacking in some way?
Why not withdraw to cultivate your teachings,
and act only when your virtue is without flaw?"
15.21 King Hélǘ of Wú battled the Jīng people at Bǎijǔ,
winning a great victory.
Advancing to the outskirts of Yǐng,
he defeated the Jīng people five times.
Five of Hélǘ's ministers remonstrated, saying:
"To penetrate deeply and seek vengeance from afar
is not to the king's advantage.
Should you not return?"
The five generals cut their hair,
but Hélǘ did not respond to them,
and the heads of the five men fell before his horse.
Hélǘ grew fearful,
summoned Wǔ Zǐxū, and asked him.
Zǐxū said:
"The five ministers were afraid,
but those who have been defeated five times
are even more terrified.
Your Majesty should advance a little further."
So they entered Yǐng,
reaching the river to the south,
and Fāngchéng to the north,
an area of three thousand lǐ square,
all submitting to Wú.
15.22 Tián Chéngzǐ often contended with Zǎi Wǒ.
Zǎi Wǒ hid soldiers by night,
intending to attack Tián Chéngzǐ,
and ordered among the troops:
"Do not rise until you see the banner signal."
Chīyí Zǐpí heard of this
and informed Tián Chéngzǐ.
Tián Chéngzǐ then used a banner signal to rouse Zǎi Wǒ's troops to attack him,
and thus destroyed him.
15.23 Duke Huán of Qí went north to attack the Shānróng tribe,
requesting troops from Lǔ,
but Lǔ did not provide them.
Duke Huán was angry
and prepared to attack Lǔ.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be done.
We have already punished the northern lords,
and now to attack Lǔ—
is that not inappropriate?
Lǔ will surely serve Chǔ,
and thus we would lose both in one move."
Duke Huán said:
"Good."
So he ceased the attack on Lǔ.
15.24 The sage governs all under heaven
by prioritizing civil virtue and only then employing military force.
All military actions arise from disobedience;
if civil transformation does not change them,
then punishment is imposed.
The incorrigibly foolish do not change;
where pure virtue cannot transform them,
military force is then applied.
the Duke of Zhōu killed Guǎn and Cài to quell rebellion,
Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī to curb extravagance,
and Confucius had Shǎozhèng Máo executed to transform the masses.
Not to punish the cunning and harmful is
the way to chaos.
The "Yì" says:
"If the small are not awed,
the great will not be punished;
this is the blessing of petty men."
15.25 The Five Emperors and Three Kings taught benevolence and righteousness,
and all under heaven transformed.
Confucius also taught benevolence and righteousness,
yet all under heaven did not follow—why is that?
In the past, enlightened kings had ceremonial caps to honor the worthy
and axes to execute the wicked,
so their rewards were extremely generous and their punishments extremely severe,
and thus all under heaven transformed.
Confucius honored Yán Yuān but had nothing to reward him with,
despised Rú Bēi but had nothing to punish him with,
hence all under heaven did not follow.
Therefore, the Way cannot be established without authority,
nor can it be practiced without power;
it is when the Way is revered that it is practiced.
15.26 When Confucius served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
on the seventh day he had Shǎozhèng Máo executed beneath the Eastern Tower.
His disciples heard of it and hurried to see him;
those who arrived said nothing,
their thoughts all the same.
Zǐgòng arrived last,
hurried forward, and said:
"This Shǎozhèng Máo
was a renowned man in the state of Lǔ.
You have just begun governing;
why did you first execute him?"
Confucius said:
"Cì,
this is beyond your understanding.
There are five types of offenders deserving execution by a king,
and theft is not among them:
first, those whose minds are discerning but dangerous;
second, those whose speech is false but eloquent;
third, those whose conduct is deviant but steadfast;
fourth, those whose knowledge is foolish but extensive;
fifth, those who comply with wrongs and glorify them.
These five all have reputations for intelligence and wisdom,
but not the reality.
If they act deceptively,
their wisdom is enough to sway the masses,
their strength enough to stand alone;
they are the champions of the wicked,
and must be executed.
Anyone with one of these five traits
cannot avoid execution;
now Shǎozhèng Máo had them all,
hence he was executed first.
In the past, Tāng executed Zhú Mù,
Tàigōng executed Pān Zhǐ,
Guǎn Zhòng executed Shǐ Fùlǐ,
and Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī;
none of these five escaped execution.
To say they were executed is not because they robbed by day
or burgled by night,
but because they were all subversive types.
This is what perplexes the noble man
and confuses the foolish.
The 'Shī' says:
'Anxious is my heart,
hated by a crowd of petty men.'
This refers to such cases."
15.27 A man from Qí named Wáng Mǎnshēng sought an audience with the Duke of Zhōu.
The Duke came out to receive him
and said,
"You have honored me from afar,
what instruction do you have for me?"
Wáng Mǎnshēng replied,
"Those who discuss internal affairs do so inside,
those who discuss external affairs do so outside.
Are we to discuss internal matters?
Or external matters?"
The Duke then led him inside.
Wáng Mǎnshēng said,
"I respectfully follow as you lay out the mat."
The Duke did not guide him to sit.
Wáng Mǎnshēng said,
"Those who discuss major matters sit,
those who discuss minor matters stand.
Are we to discuss major matters?
Or minor matters?"
The Duke then guided him to sit.
Wáng Mǎnshēng sat down,
and the Duke said,
"What instruction do you have for me?"
Wáng Mǎnshēng said,
"I have heard that a sage understands without words,
while a non-sage does not understand even with words.
Should I speak now?
Or remain silent?"
The Duke bowed his head in thought for a while but did not respond.
Wáng Mǎnshēng then took a brush and wrote on a tablet:
"The state is in peril."
He passed it close to his chest.
The Duke looked up, saw the writing, and said,
"Yes, yes,
I heed your command respectfully!"
The next day, he executed Guǎn and Cài.
16.1 If a ruler knows how to oversee his subordinates and govern the masses,
then his ministers will fear and obey him;
if he knows how to listen to advice and handle affairs,
then he will not be deceived or misled;
if he knows how to bring peace and benefit to the myriad people,
then the realm will surely be stable;
if he knows how to serve his superiors with loyalty and filial piety,
then the conduct of his subjects will be complete.
All those who are overthrown or assassinated
fail to understand the methods to control their ministers.
16.2 When officials are competent in their duties, affairs are well managed;
when affairs are well managed, benefits arise;
when they are incompetent, affairs become chaotic;
when affairs are chaotic, harm results.
16.3 The myriad affairs of the world
emerge with countless variations.
Some cling to emptiness,
others cling to substance.
Some prefer frivolity,
others value sincerity and determination.
Some act with calm ease,
others move with swift urgency.
From this perspective,
the world cannot be unified,
yet a sage king, ruling over the world, can unify it.
16.4 Attention cannot be sharply focused on two things at once,
and affairs cannot flourish in two areas simultaneously.
What flourishes there
must decline here;
what is long on the left
must be short on the right;
those who enjoy staying up late
cannot rise early.
16.5 Bells are attached to the bridle,
and chimes are set on the yoke.
When the horse moves, the bells ring;
when the bells ring, the chimes respond—
this is the rhythm of movement.
16.6 Without wealth, one cannot achieve greatness;
without generosity, one cannot unite kin.
When kin become distant, harm follows;
losing the support of the masses leads to failure.
Punishing without teaching is called cruelty;
demanding results without warning is called tyranny.
16.7 Water flows from the mountains into the sea;
grain grows in the fields and is stored in granaries.
The sage observes where things originate
and thus knows where they will end up.
16.8 The way of heaven spreads harmony,
human affairs involve taking and giving.
Hoarding without using
is called a storehouse of resentment;
thus, things should not be accumulated excessively.
16.9 A tree trunk one arm-span around
can support a roof weighing a thousand jun;
a key five inches long
can control opening and closing.
Is it because the material is fully adequate?
Rather, it is because it occupies a crucial position.
16.10 Small pleasures harm righteousness,
petty cleverness harms the way,
minor sophistries harm governance,
and a careless mind injures virtue.
Great governance is not perilous.
16.11 Though the dragon is divine,
it cannot leave its kind in broad daylight;
though the whirlwind is swift,
it cannot raise dust in rainy weather.
16.12 A village named Shèngmǔ (Victorious Mother),
Zēngzǐ would not enter;
a spring named Dàoquán (Bandit Spring),
Confucius would not drink from.
They detested the names.
16.13 A woman's gossip
can make one flee;
a woman's slander
can bring death and ruin.
16.14 Not cultivating one's own character
but demanding it of others
is called losing propriety;
not governing one's inner self
but adorning the exterior
is called great ruin.
16.15 Loading a cart until it is precarious
and then following it with a whip
is no way to preserve it intact.
16.16 If a scholar lies fallen across the road,
his limbs uncovered,
it is not the scholar's fault,
but the shame of those who possess the land.
16.17 When a ruler is about to prosper,
heaven sends him the way;
when a minister is about to prosper,
heaven sends him scholars;
when a commoner is about to prosper,
he must have worthy children.
16.18 With wise teachers and good friends at his side,
and the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music arrayed before him,
it is rare for one to abandon these and do evil.
16.19 A righteous man does not deceive his own heart;
a benevolent man does not harm living beings.
16.20 If plans are leaked, there will be no achievement;
if strategies are not devised, affairs will not succeed.
16.21 A worthy scholar does not serve what he disapproves of,
nor does he disapprove of what he serves.
16.22 The foolish become more stubborn in their errors;
the vulgar become more crude in their deceit.
16.23 No sound is too faint to be heard;
no action is too hidden not to be revealed.
16.24 The most divine can transform all things;
the most worthy can change all people.
16.25 If the superior is untrustworthy,
the subordinate will be disloyal;
if superiors and subordinates are not in harmony,
even if there is peace, danger will surely come.
16.26 Seeking by the right way, nothing is unattainable;
acting at the right time, nothing is unaccomplished.
16.27 If the time has not come,
one cannot force life;
if affairs are not ripe,
one cannot force success.
16.28 If the virtuous and good perish,
it is the lingering calamity of their ancestors;
if the reckless and stubborn survive,
it is the lingering merit of their ancestors.
16.29 In authority, choose the weighty;
in favor, choose the enduring.
16.30 If the talented and worthy are given light duties,
they will gain fame;
if the unworthy are given great responsibilities,
they will die and their names will be ruined.
16.31 A scholar does not shift for profit,
nor change for fear of trouble.
Once filial piety, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness are established,
he will not regret even death.
16.32 To be clever and use it for selfish ends
is不如不如 to be simple and use it for the public good.
Hence it is said:
"Cunning artifice is不如不如 clumsy sincerity."
16.33 Studying tirelessly
is the means to cultivate oneself;
teaching tirelessly
is the means to cultivate others.
The reason for valuing emptiness and non-being
is to be able to respond to change and accord with the times.
16.34 Though a cap be old,
it must be placed on the head;
though shoes be new,
they must be worn on the feet.
High and low have their distinctions,
which cannot be transgressed.
16.35 One heart can serve a hundred rulers,
but a hundred hearts cannot serve one ruler.
Hence it is said:
"Upright in heart and sparing in words."
16.36 All things that grasp their root will live;
all affairs that follow their principle will succeed.
Where the Way resides,
all under heaven turn to it;
where virtue resides,
all under heaven value it;
where benevolence resides,
all under heaven love it;
where righteousness resides,
all under heaven stand in awe of it.
A leaking house causes people to leave it;
shallow waters cause fish to flee them;
tall trees cause birds to roost in them;
profound virtue causes scholars to hasten to it;
one with propriety causes people to respect him;
one with loyalty and trustworthiness causes scholars to die for him.
16.37 Though clothes be worn,
conduct must be cultivated;
though hair be disheveled,
speech must be orderly.
16.38 Act in response to the time,
achieve through adaptation.
16.39 If a campaign is justified,
its blessings are fivefold;
if a campaign is unjustified,
its calamities are tenfold.
16.40 Nobility must have humility as its foundation;
height must have lowness as its base.
When heaven is about to bestow,
it first tests with hardship;
when heaven is about to destroy,
it first burdens with excess.
16.41 Be filial to parents,
trustworthy in friendships.
In a marsh of ten paces,
there must be fragrant grass;
in a town of ten households,
there must be loyal scholars.
16.42 Plants and trees die in autumn,
but pines and cypresses alone remain;
water floats all things,
but jade and stones sink and stay.
16.43 For the hungry and thirsty to obtain food,
who would not rejoice?
Relieve poverty and rescue the desperate,
why worry about having nothing?
16.44 Observe their motives,
watch their actions,
and then you may know them.
16.45 One who rides a carriage or horse reaches a thousand li without fatigue;
one who rides a boat crosses rivers and seas without swimming.
16.46 No wisdom is greater than refraining when in doubt;
no conduct is greater than having no regrets.
16.47 By judging one's residence and naming of children,
one can sufficiently observe the scholar.
16.48 Do not double profits,
do not double rewards.
16.49 Rash plans
should not be pursued;
anxious fears
should not be nurtured.
16.50 What heaven offers, if not accepted,
brings instead calamity;
when the time comes, if not welcomed,
brings instead disaster.
16.51 The way of heaven shows no favoritism,
but constantly sides with the good.
16.52 The way of heaven has constancy,
existing not for Yáo's sake,
nor perishing for Jié's sake.
16.53 Families that accumulate good deeds
will surely have abundant blessings;
families that accumulate evil deeds
will surely have abundant calamities.
16.54 Because of one choke,
to stop eating entirely;
because of one stumble,
to refuse walking further.
16.55 A heart as vast as heaven and earth is enlightened;
conduct as straight as a marking line is illustrious.
16.56 Those in high position with great virtue are followed,
those handling great affairs with small virtue meet misfortune.
16.57 Do not follow words that are doubtful,
do not emulate conduct that is suspect.
16.58 Moths can topple beams and pillars,
mosquitoes and gadflies can drive away cattle and sheep.
16.59 Do not respond to deceptive words and clever rhetoric,
do not praise strange tales and empty talk.
16.60 Plan before acting, and you will prosper;
act before planning, and you will perish.
16.61 Do not abandon your work due to indulgence,
do not demean yourself due to poverty and low status,
do not harm your body for the sake of preferences,
do not impair your life for the sake of desires,
do not seek fame through extravagance,
do not become arrogant due to honor and wealth.
16.62 Improper joy and anger
are called lack of clarity;
violence and cruelty that fail
instead bring harm upon oneself;
unavenged grievances arising
breed misfortune from fortune.
16.63 One wrong word spoken,
four horses cannot retrieve it;
one urgent word not spoken,
four horses cannot deliver it.
16.64 Flying with the wind
aids one's strength;
holding reeds while soaring
prepares against arrows and snares.
16.65 A mirror, being clear and bright,
reflects beauty and ugliness naturally;
a scale, being balanced and impartial,
weighs light and heavy accurately.
16.66 Weeds growing among hemps
straighten without support;
white sand entering mud
turns black along with it.
16.67 Time, oh time,
allows no space for planning;
when the moment reaches its peak,
there is not a breath's gap.
16.68 To labor without rest
will lead to natural cessation;
to possess without giving
will lead to natural loss.
16.69 For one who acts on all that should be done,
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished;
for one who desires all that should be desired,
there is nothing that cannot be obtained.
16.70 The accumulation of numerous righteous acts
brings blessings that reach all;
the accumulation of numerous wicked acts
brings calamities that befall all.
16.71 Strength overcomes poverty,
caution overcomes disaster,
prudence overcomes harm,
vigilance overcomes calamity.
16.72 Heaven rewards the good with virtue,
heaven rewards the evil with misfortune.
16.73 When a noble man gains opportunity, he is like water;
when a petty man gains opportunity, he is like fire.
16.74 Slandering those who surpass oneself
is a fault of the heart;
respecting those worthier than oneself
is a strength of the heart.
16.75 When the heart is attained,
all things are insufficient to sway it;
when the heart is lost,
even the heart alone cannot be maintained.
16.76 A son who is unfilial
is not my son;
a friend who is untrustworthy
is not my friend.
16.77 Feed the mouth, and all joints thrive;
water the root, and branches and leaves flourish.
If the root is injured, branches wither;
if the root is deep, the top grows thick.
16.78 Those who do good attain the Way,
those who do evil lose the Way.
16.79 Do not let vile words leave your mouth,
do not let careless words stay in your ears.
16.80 Forced pretense does not last long,
fondness for falsehood does not endure.
16.81 A righteous man does not deceive his own heart,
an honest man does not take what is not his.
16.82 Regard wealth as grass,
and your person as treasure.
Be kind and benevolent to the young,
and reverent and respectful to the elderly.
16.83 If dogs bark without causing alarm,
it is called a golden fortress;
constantly avoiding peril,
is called having no regrets.
16.84 In wealth, remember poverty;
in prime, remember old age;
though young in years,
plan for it early.
16.85 Those with propriety may die for each other,
those without propriety may also die for each other.
16.86 Nobility does not expect arrogance,
yet arrogance comes of itself;
arrogance does not expect ruin,
yet ruin arrives on its own.
16.87 A lame person day and night wishes to rise,
a blind person does not forget sight.
16.88 The wise begin with enlightenment,
and end in harmony;
fools begin with pleasure,
and end in sorrow.
16.89 Look up to the high mountain,
tread the bright path;
though strength may not suffice,
the heart must strive for it.
16.90 Be as cautious at the end as at the start,
always take it as a warning;
trembling with fear,
be prudent in affairs daily.
16.91 The sage's rectitude
is best in tranquility;
the worthy's governance,
thus differs from the masses.
16.92 Those fond of speaking ill of others,
will have their own faults spoken of;
those fond of hating others,
will also be hated by others.
16.93 With ample food and clothing,
one knows honor and shame;
with full granaries,
one knows rites and decorum.
16.94 When rivers overflow,
it lasts no more than three days;
a raging storm,
is over in a moment.
16.95 Fortune arises from subtlety,
calamity from neglect;
fearing day and night,
lest one not see it through.
16.96 Once carved and polished,
return to simplicity;
things in opposition,
revert to their origin.
16.97 Following the current downstream is easy to reach far,
riding the wind in haste is easy to go distant.
16.98 If troops are not prepared in advance,
there is no way to face the enemy;
if plans are not considered beforehand,
there is no way to respond to emergencies.
16.99 If the core is not square,
fame will not be illustrious;
if the exterior is not round,
it is the gate to disaster.
Straight but unable to bend,
cannot undertake great ventures;
square but unable to be round,
cannot long endure.
16.100 Be cautious in your person,
do not say it's mere talk.
16.101 The words of a madman,
the sage may select from.
16.102 Those who can endure shame find peace,
those who can endure humiliation survive.
16.103 When the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold.
When the river collapses,
its embrace is in the mountains.
16.104 Nothing harms wisdom more than wine;
nothing delays affairs more than pleasure;
nothing ruins integrity more than lust;
to break strength, turn oneself to weakness.
16.95 Wealth lies in knowing contentment,
nobility in seeking retreat.
16.106 Those who worry about affairs first find joy later,
those who are arrogant about affairs first find worry later.
16.107 Fortune lies in accepting advice,
the path to preservation.
16.108 Be reverent, humble, and yielding,
pure and incorruptible without slander;
be kind, benevolent, and love others,
and you will surely receive reward.
16.109 If advice is not heeded,
later none will contend.
If actions are improper,
the common people will slander.
Regret lies in recklessness,
calamity in taking the lead.
16.110 When Pú Qiū fine-tunes his arrow,
ducks and wild geese cry mournfully;
when Féng Méng grips his bow,
tigers and leopards roar at dawn.
16.111 The river winds and thus can flow far,
the mountain slopes gradually and thus can rise high.
The Way is leisurely and thus can transform,
virtue is pure and sincere and thus can be majestic.
16.112 Speaking of others' goodness,
is like a balm of moisture;
speaking of others' faults,
pains more than spear or dagger.
16.113 Doing good not uprightly,
will end in crookedness;
engaging in evil without release,
will end in wickedness.
16.114 Through one death and one life,
friendship is truly known.
Through one poverty and one wealth,
the nature of friendship is revealed.
Through one nobility and one baseness,
friendship is manifested.
Through one rise and one fall,
friendship emerges.
16.115 Virtue and righteousness come first,
the use of force comes after.
16.116 One who has just washed his hair must brush his hat,
one who has just bathed must shake his clothes.
16.117 A defeated general cannot speak of courage,
a minister of a fallen state cannot speak of wisdom.
16.118 A pit well has no giant softshell turtles,
because it is narrow;
a garden has no tall forests,
because it is small.
16.119 Minor loyalty
is a thief to great loyalty;
small profits
are destructive to great profits.
16.120 To cut ties oneself is easy,
to ask others to cut ties is difficult.
16.121 Water, when agitated, becomes fierce;
arrows, when propelled, fly far;
people, stirred by fame,
will not ruin their reputation.
16.122 An inferior man obtains office and dies for it,
a superior man obtains office and lives through it.
16.123 Fortune and calamity do not emerge from the earth,
nor descend from the sky;
they are born from oneself.
16.124 Remote villages often have crooked learning,
petty arguments harm great wisdom,
clever words ruin trust,
small favors hinder great righteousness.
16.125 To avoid distress lies in early consideration,
to avoid poverty lies in early preparation.
16.126 If you wish others not to know,
better not to do it;
if you wish others not to hear,
better not to say it.
16.127 Do not speak what should not be spoken,
to avoid its troubles;
do not do what should not be done,
to avoid its dangers;
do not take what should not be taken,
to avoid its deceit;
do not contend what should not be contended,
to avoid its noise.
16.128 The clear-sighted see in the dark,
the wise plan before forms take shape;
the sharp-eared hear in silence;
the prudent guard against what is not yet accomplished.
16.129 The world is turbid, but I alone am clear;
everyone is drunk, but I alone am sober.
16.130 The faults of discord,
none fail to arise;
the beginnings of ruin,
emerge from here.
Great breaches in rivers start from ant holes,
mountains collapse greatly from small landslides.
16.131 The gradual steps of debauchery,
transform into rise,
water, fire, metal, wood overcome each other in turn.
16.132 What is low and upright may be increased,
what is high and leaning is about to collapse.
Straight as an arrow leads to death,
straight as a plumb line earns praise.
16.133 Misfortune arises from desire for gain,
blessing comes from self-restraint.
16.134 The sage guides his ears and eyes with his heart,
the petty man guides his heart with his ears and eyes.
16.135 For those in high positions,
the worry lies in lack of clarity;
for those in subordinate positions,
the worry lies in lack of loyalty.
16.136 People know how to fertilize fields,
but do not know how to cultivate their hearts;
correct your posture and conduct,
and preserve yourself intact to this day.
16.137 Seeing disappearance, one knows existence;
seeing frost, one knows ice.
16.138 Magnanimity lies in loving benefit,
reverence lies in serving one's parents.
16.139 Following the times makes it easy to practice benevolence,
following the Way makes it easy to understand others.
16.140 Those who seek profit often face troubles,
those who make promises lightly seldom keep trust.
16.141 To desire worthiness, nothing is better than humbling oneself;
to crave wealth, nothing is better than preserving one's life;
wealth is not as lofty as righteousness,
power is not as revered as virtue.
16.142 A father cannot love a worthless son,
a ruler cannot love unruly people,
a ruler cannot reward ministers without merit,
ministers cannot die for a ruler without virtue.
16.143 To ask about skilled driving, none know better than the horses;
to ask about good governance, none know better than the people.
16.144 Taking the lowly as honorable,
taking contraction as extension.
What the sage follows,
is modeled on heaven.
16.145 The gentleman practices virtue to preserve himself whole,
the petty man practices greed to destroy himself.
16.146 Urging each other with ritual,
strengthening each other with benevolence,
one attains the Way in oneself,
and gains reputation among people.
16.147 Those who understand fate do not blame heaven,
those who know themselves do not blame others.
16.148 If a person lacks love,
then they cannot be benevolent;
if cunning but not skillful,
then they cannot be trusted.
16.149 When speaking of good, do not involve yourself;
when speaking of evil, do not involve others.
16.150 If the superior is pure and without desire,
then the subordinates will be upright and the people simple.
16.151 Future events can be pursued,
past events cannot be reached.
16.152 Without a thoughtful mind, one cannot comprehend;
without eloquent speech, one cannot delight.
16.153 Goodness cannot be achieved through pretense,
evil cannot be removed with words.
16.154 Near the market, there are no cheap deals;
in the fields, there is no wilderness;
goodness does not lodge as a traveler.
16.155 Without benevolence, righteousness, firmness, and martial prowess,
one cannot stabilize the world.
16.156 If water turns against its source, the river dries up;
if a person betrays trust, their name will not be known.
16.157 If righteousness overcomes trouble, it is auspicious;
if trouble overcomes righteousness, it brings ruin.
16.158 The strategies of five sages
are not as good as encountering the right time;
eloquence, wisdom, clarity, and intelligence
are not as good as meeting the right era.
16.159 One with a base heart
should not be given advantageous power;
one with a foolish nature
should not be entrusted with sharp tools.
16.160 More carelessness leads to more failures,
more words lead to more mistakes.
16.161 Caps and shoes are not stored together,
the worthy and unworthy do not share the same position.
16.162 High-ranking officials have deep worries,
those with large emoluments bear great responsibilities.
16.163 Accumulating virtue knows no small act,
accumulating resentment knows no large one,
whether much or little, it will surely be repaid,
such is the inevitable trend.
16.164 An owl met a dove,
the dove said:
"Where are you going?"
The owl said:
"I am moving east."
The dove said:
"Why?"
The owl said:
"The villagers all hate my cry,
so I'm moving east."
The dove said:
"If you can change your cry,
that would work;
if you cannot change your cry,
moving east will still make them hate your sound."
16.165 The clothing of the sage
fits the body to comfort the person;
his food
satisfies the stomach.
Suitable clothing and moderate eating,
not indulging the mouth and eyes.
16.166 Zēngzǐ said:
Eagles and hawks consider mountains low,
and build nests atop them;
turtles, alligators, fish, and softshell turtles consider deep pools shallow,
and burrow holes within them.
Ultimately, what captures them
is bait.
If a gentleman does not seek profit and emolument,
then he will not harm himself.
16.167 Zēngzǐ said:
"Too much familiarity leads to mutual neglect;
too much solemnity leads to lack of closeness.
Therefore, the gentleman's familiarity should suffice for joyful interaction,
and his solemnity should suffice to complete rituals."
16.168 Zēngzǐ said:
"When entering a state,
if your words are trusted by the ministers,
then you may stay;
if loyalty is practiced by the ministers,
then you may take office;
if kindness is extended to the common people,
then you may settle peacefully."
16.169 The mouth is a gate,
the tongue is a trigger;
once words are spoken improperly,
four horses cannot retrieve them.
The mouth is a gate,
the tongue is a weapon;
once words are spoken improperly,
they wound oneself in return.
Words come from oneself,
but cannot be stopped by others;
actions start nearby,
but cannot be halted at a distance.
Words and actions
are the pivotal mechanism of the gentleman.
The movement of this pivotal mechanism
is the root of honor and disgrace;
can one not be cautious?
Thus, Kuǎizǐyǔ said:
"Speaking is like archery;
once the arrow leaves the string,
even if one regrets it,
one cannot follow and retrieve it."
The *Book of Songs* says:
"A flaw in a white jade scepter
can still be ground away;
a flaw in these words
cannot be undone."
16.170 The silkworm moth resembles a silkworm,
the eel resembles a snake.
When people see snakes or moths,
none fail to shudder.
Women workers tend silkworms,
fishermen handle eels;
why do they not find them repulsive?
Because they desire to earn money.
Those chasing fish get wet,
those chasing beasts run;
not because they enjoy it,
but due to the exigency of their tasks.
16.171 Climbing high makes one want to gaze afar,
facing a deep pool makes one want to peer in;
why is that?
It is the nature of the place.
Driving a carriage makes one respectful,
archery makes one upright;
why is that?
Because the posture demands it.
16.172 People face five kinds of death,
of which the sage can eliminate three,
but cannot remove two.
Death from hunger and thirst
can be eliminated;
death from freezing and cold
can be eliminated;
death from encountering the five weapons
can be eliminated.
Death due to lifespan
cannot be eliminated;
death from abscesses and ulcers
cannot be eliminated.
Death from hunger and thirst
is due to internal insufficiency;
death from freezing and cold
is due to external forces overcoming the internal;
death from encountering the five weapons
is due to virtue not being sincere.
Death due to lifespan
is the end of one's allotted years;
death from abscesses and ulcers
is due to exhaustion of blood and qi.
Hence it is said:
If the internal is not upright,
external excesses arise.
When external excesses arise, many grievances and anomalies occur;
when there are many grievances and anomalies, illnesses are born.
Therefore, with clarity, stillness, and non-action,
blood and qi become balanced.
16.173 The foundation of all conduct
lies in a single word.
One word that is fitting
can repel enemies;
one word that is appropriate
can preserve the state.
An echo cannot produce sound alone,
a shadow cannot bend and become straight on its own;
things always follow their kind.
Therefore, the gentleman is cautious with the words that leave him.
16.174 Carrying a stone to throw oneself into an abyss
is a difficult act,
yet Shēntú Dí did it,
but the gentleman does not value it;
although Dào Zhì was violent and greedy,
his name is as renowned as the sun and moon,
passed down alongside Shùn and Yǔ without ceasing,
yet the gentleman does not value him.
16.175 The gentleman has five shames:
not sitting in court,
not discussing at banquets,
the gentleman is ashamed of this;
holding a position,
yet having no words to contribute,
the gentleman is ashamed of this;
having words to say,
but no actions to match,
the gentleman is ashamed of this;
having gained something,
then losing it again,
the gentleman is ashamed of this;
having abundant land but insufficient people,
the gentleman is ashamed of this.
16.176 The gentleman, though impoverished,
will not take a position in a doomed state;
though poor,
will not accept a salary from a chaotic ruler.
To be honored in a chaotic age,
to align with a tyrant,
is a shame to the gentleman.
The masses consider physical mutilation a disgrace,
the gentleman considers the destruction of righteousness a dishonor;
the masses value profit,
the upright value reputation.
16.177 The system of an enlightened ruler
gives rewards generously,
and punishments leniently.
Feeding people is measured by their strength,
employing people is graded by their age.
16.178 The gentleman's words are few but true;
the petty person's words are many but empty.
16.179 The gentleman's learning
enters the ear,
is stored in the heart,
and practiced with the body.
16.180 The gentleman's governance
begins where it is hardly noticeable,
and ends where it cannot be matched.
16.181 The gentleman considers blessings as if they may not come,
and calamities a hundredfold.
16.182 The gentleman chooses whom to take from,
but does not choose whom to give to.
16.183 The gentleman, though substantial, appears empty;
though possessing, seems to have nothing.
16.184 With proper preparation, the gentleman has no troubles.
16.185 The gentleman does not eat from shameful means,
nor gain through disgrace.
16.186 The gentleman delights in realizing his aspirations,
the petty person delights in accomplishing his tasks.
16.187 The gentleman does not extend what he dislikes to what he loves.
16.188 The gentleman has lifelong worries,
but not a moment's calamity;
he follows the Way in action,
speaks according to principle,
joy does not lead to carelessness,
anger does not lead to difficulty.
16.189 The gentleman's faults
are like eclipses of the sun and moon—
how do they harm the light?
The petty person's approvals
are like a dog barking at a thief,
or a wildcat seeing at night—
how do they contribute to goodness?
16.190 The wise do not act recklessly,
the brave do not strike recklessly.
16.191 The gentleman compares with righteousness,
the farmer compares with grain.
16.192 If one cannot advance his words in serving the ruler,
he should decline the rank;
if he cannot practice his righteousness,
he should decline the salary.
16.193 All know that taking is gaining,
but do not know that giving is also gaining.
16.194 Governance can invite bandits,
conduct can invite shame;
for these to come without being sought,
has never been heard of under heaven.
16.195 A fierce beast hesitating
is not as effective as a bee or scorpion delivering its poison;
lofty discussions that cannot be reached
are not as effective as humble talk that achieves results.
16.196 Qín trusted its own clan to rule,
but in its decline,
it was not because it changed its trust in the clan,
yet it perished and the state fell.
Therefore, the way a king governs the world
lies in implementing laws,
not in trusting the clan.
16.197 On high mountain peaks, there are no beautiful trees—
harmed by too much sun;
under large trees, there is no beautiful grass—
harmed by too much shade.
16.198 When Zhōng Zǐqī died, Bó Yá broke his zither strings and destroyed his instrument,
knowing the world had no one to play for;
when Huì Shī passed away, Zhuāngzǐ closed his eyes deeply and spoke no more,
seeing the world had no one to converse with.
16.199 Cultivating the self
is the storehouse of wisdom;
loving and giving
is the beginning of benevolence;
taking and giving
is the mark of righteousness;
feeling shame and disgrace
is the decision of courage;
establishing a reputation
is the ultimate of conduct.
16.200 Recommending the worthy receives high reward.
Obstructing the worthy incurs public execution,
an ancient universal principle;
enfeoffing men in court,
judging men in the market,
an ancient universal method.
16.201 The Way is subtle yet bright,
plain yet effective;
gaining not by the Way,
arising not in its time,
is called reckless success;
gaining then losing,
settled then overturned again.
16.202 Blessings
are the gate to calamity;
correctness
is the precursor to error;
order
is the forerunner of chaos.
For affairs without beginning or end to avoid calamity,
has never been heard of.
16.203 A branch should not forget its root,
virtue should not forget its reward,
seeing profit, one must think of harm to the self.
Therefore, the gentleman focuses his spirit and mind on these three,
and auspiciousness extends to his descendants.
16.204 Two heights cannot be superimposed,
two great things cannot be contained together,
two powers cannot coexist equally,
two nobles cannot stand as pairs.
Where superimposition, containment, coexistence, and pairing occur,
conflict over achievements is inevitable.
Thus, the gentleman moderates his desires,
each guarding his own sufficiency,
so that he may endure long.
By restraining desires and heeding advice,
respecting the worthy without neglect,
employing the capable without disdain,
if a ruler can practice these three,
his state will surely grow strong and great, and his people will not scatter.
16.205 Silence avoids excessive speech,
prudence avoids excessive action.
A wooden horse cannot walk,
nor does it consume fodder;
a Qílì horse gallops a thousand miles a day,
yet the whip never leaves its back.
16.206 Measuring inch by inch,
by the time it reaches a zhàng, error is certain;
weighing zhū by zhū,
by the time it reaches a dàn, excess is inevitable.
Weighing by the dàn and measuring by the zhàng,
direct and seldom erroneous;
counting silk threads and rice grains,
tedious and unclear.
Thus, broad comparisons are easy for wisdom,
while intricate arguments are difficult for insight.
16.207 A fish large enough to swallow a boat,
if tossed ashore and deprived of water,
can be subdued by ants,
for it has left its abode;
a monkey losing its trees,
captured by foxes,
is not in its proper place.
The flying serpent rides the mist to soar,
the Yìnglóng dragon mounts the clouds to rise,
the monkey secures trees to climb,
the fish gains water to dart,
each thrives where the environment suits.
16.208 The gentleman, broad in learning,
worries about not mastering it;
having mastered it,
worries about not being able to practice it;
being able to practice it,
worries about not being able to yield in it.
16.209 The gentleman is not ashamed to learn,
nor ashamed to ask.
Inquiring and seeking,
is the root of knowledge;
reflection and contemplation,
are the path to knowledge.
This means it is valuable to build upon others' knowledge to enhance one's own,
not valuable to rely solely on one's own intellect to know.
16.210 The way of heaven and earth:
at its extreme, it reverses;
full, it diminishes.
The five colors dazzle the eye,
yet they fade in time;
lush trees and abundant grass,
yet they wither in season.
All things have their flourish and decline,
how can they remain unchanged?
16.211 When people suffer, they become unkind;
when toiled, deceit arises;
in peace, they can be taught;
in peril, they strategize.
At the extreme, it reverses;
full, it diminishes.
Therefore, the gentleman avoids fullness and extremity.
17.1 The worthy and the gentleman
understand the timing of prosperity and decline,
discern the origins of success and failure,
observe the principles of order and chaos,
scrutinize human sentiments,
and know when to advance or withdraw.
Thus, though impoverished, they do not accept positions in a doomed state;
though poor, they do not take salaries from a corrupt ruler.
Hence, Tàigōng at seventy did not push for personal advancement,
Sūnshū Áo thrice left the chancellorship without regret.
Why?
They did not force alignment with the unfit.
Tàigōng aligned once with Zhōu and his lineage was enfeoffed for seven hundred years;
Sūnshū Áo aligned once with Chǔ and his fief lasted ten generations;
while Wén Zhǒng preserved the perishing Yuè and made Gōujiàn hegemon,
yet he was granted death before him;
Lǐ Sī amassed merits for Qín but ended up suffering the five punishments.
Though devoted and concerned for their rulers,
endangering themselves to secure the state,
their achievements were the same.
Some were enfeoffed and their lines continued;
some were ordered to die and punished.
Their aspirations and paths differed.
Thus, Jīzǐ abandoned his state and feigned madness,
Fàn Lǐ left Yuè and changed his name,
Zhìguā parted from his lord and brother and altered his surname,
all seeing far and recognizing subtleties,
and through benevolence, able to forsake wealth and power to avoid budding calamities.
As for tyrannical and chaotic rulers,
who can break free from their bonds to serve them,
and partake in their disasters?
Therefore, the worthy do not merely fear death and avoid harm,
but recognize that dying uselessly only exposes a tyrant's brutality.
Bǐgān died under Zhòu but could not correct his conduct;
Zǐxū died in Wú but could not save his state.
These two men,
by insisting on remonstrance unto death,
only served to highlight their rulers' tyranny,
without benefit as fine as a hair's tip.
Hence, the worthy conceal their wisdom,
suppress their abilities,
waiting for the right person to unite with.
Then, their words are all heeded,
their actions never doubted,
ruler and minister harmonize,
and they remain free from trouble for life.
If it is not the right time,
and the right person is absent,
yet one's personal convictions cannot be restrained,
grieving for the world's chaos,
worrying for the ruler's peril,
with a life of no worth,
treading a path of obstruction,
passing before slanderers,
approaching a ruler of no measure,
committing unforeseeable crimes,
harming one's innate nature—
is that not delusion?
Thus, Wénxìn Hóu and Lǐ Sī,
deemed worthy by the world,
in planning for the state,
gauging subtleties and targeting hidden issues,
were said to have no flawed strategies;
in victory and conquest,
were said to face no strong enemies.
Their accumulated merits were immense,
their power and profit exceedingly high,
yet the worthy were unused,
slanderers held sway.
Knowing they were not employed,
their benevolence could not compel them to leave.
In overcoming enemies and amassing achievements,
they erred not by a hair's breadth;
in avoiding calamities and harms,
they failed to see a mountain.
Accumulating what they desired,
they reached what they abhorred.
Were they not deluded by power and profit?
The Book of Songs says:
"People know one thing,
but know not the other."
This refers to such cases.
17.2 Zǐshí ascended Wú Mountain and gazed in all directions,
sighing deeply with lament,
saying:
"Alas,
how sorrowful!
Some in the world understand affairs clearly,
yet do not align with people's hearts;
some align with people's hearts,
yet do not understand affairs clearly."
His disciple asked:
"What does that mean?"
Zǐshí said:
"In the past, King Fūchāi of Wú did not heed Wǔ Zǐxū's loyal and utmost remonstrance,
and had his eyes gouged out and his body dismembered.
Grand Master Pǐ and Gōngsūn Luò, obsequious and accommodating,
followed Fūchāi's ambition to attack Qí,
and both sank in rivers and lakes,
their heads hung on Yuè's banners.
In earlier times,
Fèi Zhòng, È Lái, and Jiāo Gé,
with long noses and protruding ears,
and Chóng Hóu Hǔ,迎合 Zhòu's heart,
seeking to please his will,
but when King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
the four died in the wilderness of Mù,
their heads and feet separated.
Bǐgān, loyal to the end, had his heart cut out and died.
Now, to clarify affairs,
one fears the disaster of gouged eyes and cut-out hearts;
to align with people's hearts,
one dreads the peril of severed heads and feet.
From this perspective,
the gentleman's path is narrow indeed.
If one truly does not encounter an enlightened ruler,
within this narrow path,
it becomes perilous and blocked,
with no way out."
17.3 Qí Shèzǐ visited King Huì of Qín,
and the king was pleased with him.
Then Tánggū slandered him,
and when he had another audience,
King Huì received him with concealed anger.
It was not that his words were different,
but that the listener had changed.
Thus, mistaking a minor note for a major one
is not the fault of the strings;
taking sweet for bitter
is not the error of the taste.
17.4 Mí Zǐxiá was beloved by the Lord of Wèi.
According to the laws of Wèi,
stealing the lord's carriage warranted the punishment of foot amputation.
When Mí Zǐxiá's mother fell ill,
someone heard of it
and went to inform him at night.
Mí Zǐxiá presumptuously took the lord's carriage and went out.
The lord heard of it and praised him, saying:
"How filial!
For his mother's sake,
he risked the punishment of foot amputation!"
When accompanying the lord on a stroll in the fruit garden,
Mí Zǐxiá ate a peach and found it sweet,
so he offered the unfinished portion to the lord.
The lord said:
"He loves me so much he forgets his own taste."
But when Mí Zǐxiá's looks faded and the lord's affection waned,
and he incurred the lord's displeasure,
the lord said:
"This is the one who once arrogated my carriage,
and also once fed me his leftover peach."
Thus, Zǐxiá's conduct
had not necessarily changed from the beginning;
being praised earlier and condemned later
was due to the shift in love and hatred.
17.5 When Shùn was tilling the land,
he could not benefit his neighbors;
but when he became the Son of Heaven,
the whole world revered him.
Therefore, a noble person in poverty cultivates themselves well,
and in success benefits the world.
17.6 Confucius said:
"Since Jìsūn bestowed upon me a thousand zhōng, my friends have grown closer;
since Nángōng Jìngshū provided me with a carriage, my Way has been furthered.
Thus, the Way sometimes gains weight through timing,
and finds traction through influence.
Were it not for the gifts of these two men,
my Way would have nearly been abandoned."
17.7 Tàigōng's farming did not cover the cost of seeds,
his fishing did not cover the cost of nets,
yet he had wisdom to spare in governing the world.
Duke Wén planted rice,
Zēngzǐ herded sheep,
and Sūnshū Áo, after three years as chancellor of Chǔ,
did not know the yoke was behind the crossbar.
Those devoted to great matters naturally forget the small.
Zhì Bó's cook lost a roasting spit and he knew it,
but when Hán and Wèi rebelled, he was unaware.
Hándān Zǐyáng's gardener lost a peach and he knew it,
but when his state was lost, he did not know.
Those engrossed in small matters also forget the great.
17.8 Chúnyuán Kūn said to Mèngzǐ:
"Those who prioritize name and substance do so for others;
those who put them last do so for themselves.
You, sir, were among the three high ministers,
yet name and substance had not reached above or below when you left.
Would a benevolent person necessarily act thus?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"To dwell in a low position and not serve the unworthy with one's worth—that was Bóyí;
to five times approach Tāng and five times approach Jié—that was Yī Yǐn;
not to detest a corrupt lord nor decline a minor office—that was Liǔxià Huì.
These three men followed different paths,
but their aim was one.
What is that one?
It is benevolence.
A noble person simply seeks benevolence;
why must they be the same?"
Chúnyuán Kūn said:
"In the time of Duke Mù of Lǔ,
Gōngyí Zǐ was in power,
with Zǐsī and Zǐgēng as ministers,
yet Lǔ's decline worsened.
Does this not show that worthies are of no benefit to the state?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yú perished because it did not employ Bǎilǐ Xī,
while Duke Mù of Qín employed him and became hegemon.
Thus, not employing worthies leads to ruin;
how could mere decline be avoided?"
Chúnyuán Kūn said:
"In the past, Wáng Bào lived by the Qí River,
and west of the river people became good at singing;
Mián Jū lived in Gāotáng,
and the right side of Qí became good at songs.
The wives of Huá Zhōu and Qǐ Liáng
wept so skillfully for their husbands that they changed the state's customs.
What is within
must manifest without.
I have never seen one who acts without achieving results.
Therefore, there are no worthies;
if there were, I would surely recognize them."
Mèngzǐ said:
"When Confucius was Minister of Crime in Lǔ and was not employed,
he attended a sacrifice,
but the sacrificial meat did not arrive,
so he left without removing his ceremonial cap.
Those who did not know thought he left for the meat;
those who knew thought he left because of the disrespect.
But Confucius wished to depart over a minor fault,
not to leave without just cause.
Thus, what a noble person does
is naturally beyond the understanding of the masses."
17.9 When the chancellor of Liáng died,
Huìzǐ wished to go to Liáng.
While crossing the river, he suddenly fell into the water.
The boatman rescued him,
and said:
"Where are you going in such a hurry?"
Huìzǐ replied:
"Liáng has no chancellor;
I wish to go and become its chancellor."
The boatman said:
"You are helpless in a boat;
without me, you would have died.
How can you chancellor Liáng?"
Huìzǐ said:
"In managing boats and oars,
I am not your equal.
But in securing the state and preserving the altars of land and grain,
compared to me,
you are as unseeing as a blind puppy."
17.10 Xīlǘ Guò was crossing east over the river
when he drowned midstream.
The boatman pulled him out and asked:
"Where were you heading today?"
Xīlǘ Guò said:
"I wished to go east to persuade the feudal lords."
The boatman covered his mouth and laughed:
"You drowned midstream in the river,
unable to save yourself;
how can you persuade the feudal lords?"
Xīlǘ Guò said:
"Do not use your own abilities to belittle others.
Have you not heard of the Héshì Jade?
It is worth a thousand pieces of gold,
yet used to separate threads in weaving,
it is not even as good as a tile;
the Suíhóu Pearl,
a treasure of the state,
yet used to shoot at magpies,
is not as good as a mud pellet;
Qíjì and Lù'ěr,
harnessed to yoke and collar in a gallop,
can cover a thousand lǐ in a day—
this is extreme speed,
yet set to catch rats,
they are not as good as a cat worth a hundred coins;
Gānjiàng and Mòyé,
brushed against a bell without a clang,
tested on objects without notice,
raised to cut metal,
sever feathers, and split an iron axe—
this is extreme sharpness,
yet used to mend shoes,
they are not as good as an awl worth two coins.
Now you wield an oar in a small boat,
amidst vast waters,
facing the waves of Yáng Hóu and the deep currents—
that suits your abilities.
But if I were to take you east to persuade the feudal lords
and meet the lord of a state,
your blindness
would be no different from an unseeing puppy."
17.11 Gān Wù was sent on a mission to Qí.
While crossing the great river,
the boatman said:
"The river water
is merely a gap.
If you cannot cross it yourself,
how can you persuade kings?"
Gān Wù replied:
"Not so.
You do not understand.
Everything has its strengths and weaknesses.
A cautious and sincere person
may serve a ruler well
but is not suited for military command.
Fine horses like Qíjì and Lù'ěr
can cover a thousand lǐ,
but if confined to a palace
to catch mice,
they are less capable than a small cat.
The sword Gānjiàng is renowned for its sharpness,
famous throughout the world,
yet a craftsman using it to work wood
finds it inferior to an axe.
Now, wielding the oar to navigate the currents,
I am not your equal,
but in persuading rulers of states large and small,
you are not equal to Wù."
17.12 When the world changes, affairs transform;
when affairs transform, the times shift;
when the times shift, customs alter.
Therefore, a noble person first assesses the land and tailors the tools accordingly,
observes the customs and harmonizes with the practices,
consolidates diverse opinions to establish education.
A foolish person learning to shoot at distant targets
aims at the sky to shoot,
yet the arrow falls within five steps,
and he again aims at the sky to shoot.
The world has changed,
but if one does not adjust their methods,
it is like the fool learning to shoot afar.
One who focuses on the tip of an autumn hair
may fail to see Mount Tài;
one who listens to subtle musical tones
may not hear the roar of thunder.
Why is this?
Because their attention is diverted.
A hundred people trying to untie a knot
cannot make it secure;
a thousand people slandering a verdict
cannot produce a just statement;
ten thousand people conspiring in wrongdoing
cannot elevate a worthy person.
17.13 When deer gather in herds,
tigers and leopards avoid them;
when birds fly in formation,
eagles and vultures do not attack;
when the masses unite,
even sages do not oppose them.
The flying serpent moves through mist and dew,
riding the wind and rain to travel,
not stopping until a thousand lǐ,
yet at dusk it lodges in the burrows of loaches and eels.
Why does this happen?
Because its focus is not singular.
The earthworm has no strong sinews or bones within,
nor sharp claws or teeth without,
yet it drinks from the underworld springs below
and tills the dry soil above.
Why does this happen?
Because its focus is singular.
The hearing ear listens,
the seeing eye observes,
and with these faculties, benevolence becomes evident and integrity is distinguished.
Thus, pursuing a path not meant to be taken,
though toilsome, leads nowhere;
seeking what is not rightfully one's own,
though forced, yields nothing.
The wise do not engage in improper affairs,
the upright do not seek what is not theirs,
hence they avoid harm and their reputations shine.
The Book of Songs says:
"Without envy or greed,
what action would not be good?"
This refers to such virtue.
17.14 King Zhāo of Chǔ summoned Confucius,
intending to entrust him with governance and enfeoff him with seven hundred households.
Zǐxī said to the king of Chǔ:
"Does Your Majesty have ministers as skilled in warfare as Zǐlù?
Or as adept in diplomacy as Zǎi Yǔ?
Or as capable in administration as Zǐgòng?
In the past, King Wén resided in Fēng,
King Wǔ in Hào,
and between Fēng and Hào,
a territory of a hundred chariots,
they overthrew superiors and executed rulers,
establishing themselves as Sons of Heaven,
and the world hailed them as sage kings.
Now, with Confucius's virtue
and the land of seven hundred households,
aided by these three disciples,
it would not benefit Chǔ."
The king of Chǔ then desisted.
How difficult it is to distinguish good from evil,
that even a sage was doubted,
let alone other worthy individuals?
Thus, sages and worthies rarely find alignment,
while flattery and sycophancy often flourish.
Hence, there may be chaos for a thousand years,
but not stability for a century.
That Confucius was doubted
is indeed lamentable!
17.15 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"Do wise people live long?"
Confucius said:
"Yes.
There are three types of death that are not fate
but are brought upon by individuals themselves.
Those who sleep and rise irregularly,
eat and drink without moderation,
or exert themselves excessively in leisure or labor
are killed by disease;
those in low positions who offend their superiors,
or whose insatiable desires lead to endless pursuits
are killed by punishment;
those who few oppose many,
weak insult strong,
or act in anger without assessing their strength
are killed by warfare.
These three types of death are not fate
but are self-inflicted."
The Book of Songs says:
"If a person has no integrity,
why not die?"
This refers to such cases.
17.16 Confucius encountered hardship in the territory between Chén and Cài,
where supplies were cut off.
His disciples all showed signs of hunger,
yet Confucius sang between two pillars.
Zǐlù entered and asked:
"Is it in accordance with ritual,
Master, for you to sing?"
Confucius did not respond immediately,
but after finishing the song, said:
"Yóu,
when a gentleman delights in music,
it is to remain free from arrogance;
when a petty person delights in music,
it is to remain free from fear.
Who understands this?
Do you not understand me, yet follow me?"
Zǐlù was displeased,
took up a shield and danced,
and after three rounds of singing, left.
By the seventh day,
Confucius was still cultivating music without cease.
Zǐlù appeared resentful and said:
"Is it timely,
Master,
for you to cultivate music now?"
Confucius did not respond,
but after the music ended, said:
"Yóu,
in the past, Duke Huán of Qí's ambition for hegemony was born in Jǔ;
Gōujiàn's ambition for hegemony was born in Kuàijī;
Duke Wén of Jìn's ambition for hegemony was born in Líshì.
Thus, if one does not dwell in obscurity, one's thoughts will not be far-reaching;
if one's life is not restrained, one's wisdom will not be broad.
How can one know if one will not encounter such opportunities?"
With that, he rose.
The next day,
they were freed from the predicament.
Zǐgòng, holding the reins, said:
"We, your disciples, have followed you, Master, and encountered this difficulty;
it should not be forgotten."
Confucius said:
"Alas!
What is this?
Is it not said,
'After breaking his arm three times, one becomes a good physician'?
The hardship between Chén and Cài
was my fortune.
That you, my disciples, followed me
is also fortune.
I have heard that
a ruler does not become a true king without facing adversity,
and a worthy man does not achieve virtue without facing hardship.
In the past, Tāng was trapped in Lǚ,
King Wén was trapped in Yǒulǐ,
Duke Mù of Qín was trapped at Xiáo,
Duke Huán of Qí was trapped at Chángsháo,
Gōujiàn was trapped in Kuàijī,
Duke Wén of Jìn was trapped in Líshì.
The way of hardship
is like moving from cold to warmth,
and from warmth to cold;
only the wise truly understand it, yet find it hard to express.
The Yì Jīng says:
'Hardship
leads to success.
Perseverance.
For the great man, it is auspicious,
without blame.
But words are not believed.'
What the sage finds difficult to convey to others
is trustworthiness."
17.17 Confucius was trapped between Chén and Cài,
dwelling within a confined space,
sitting on a mat of three layers of reeds,
without food for seven days,
with only bland vegetable soup without grain,
his disciples all showing signs of hunger.
Yet he read the Shī Jīng and Shū Jīng,
and practiced rituals and music without cease.
Zǐlù came forward to admonish him:
"For ordinary people who do good,
heaven rewards them with fortune;
for those who do evil,
heaven rewards them with misfortune.
Now, Master, you have long accumulated virtuous deeds and done good;
could it be that you still have some fault,
that you live in such obscurity?"
Confucius said:
"Come here, Yóu,
you do not understand.
Sit,
and I will tell you.
Do you think the wise know everything?
Then why was Prince Bǐgān cut open and died?
Do you think remonstrators are always heeded?
Then why was Wǔ Zǐxū's eyes gouged out at the eastern gate of Wú?
Do you think the incorruptible are always employed?
Then why did Bóyí and Shūqí starve to death at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain?
Do you think the loyal are always employed?
Then why did Bào Zhuāng wither away,
why did Jīng's Prince Gāo never achieve prominence in his lifetime,
why did Bào Jiāo embrace a tree and stand until he withered,
and why did Jièzǐtuī climb a mountain and burn to death?
Thus, there are many gentlemen with broad learning and deep strategies who do not meet the right time;
how could I be the only one!
Being worthy or unworthy
is a matter of talent;
to act or not to act
is a matter of human effort;
to meet the right time or not
is a matter of timing;
life and death
are a matter of fate.
To have talent but not meet the right time,
even if talented, one is not employed;
but if one meets the right time,
what difficulty is there?
Thus, Shùn plowed at Lìshān and made pottery by the river,
and was made Son of Heaven
because he met Yáo;
Fù Yuè carried earth,
was released from his labor with planks and mortar, and was made a high minister assisting the Son of Heaven
because he met Wǔ Dīng;
Yī Yǐn,
originally a servant of the Yǒushēn clan,
carried cauldrons and stands,
blended the five flavors, and was made prime minister assisting the Son of Heaven
because he met Chéng Tāng;
Lǚ Wàng, at fifty,
sold food at Jíjīn,
at seventy,
slaughtered oxen at Zhāogē,
at ninety,
became the teacher of the Son of Heaven
because he met King Wén;
Guǎn Yíwú was bound and blinded,
confined in a prison cart,
yet rose from the cart to become 'Uncle'
because he met Duke Huán of Qí;
Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself for the price of five sheepskins,
herded sheep for the Bó clan,
yet was elevated to high minister
because he met Duke Mù of Qín;
Shěn Jūn was renowned throughout the land,
was made prime minister,
yet yielded to Sūnshū Áo,
because he met King Zhuāng of Chǔ;
Wǔ Zǐxū achieved many merits earlier,
but was executed later,
not because his wisdom declined,
but because he first met Hé Lú,
and later met Fū Chāi.
A fine horse, distressed and pulling a salt cart,
is not without the form of a fine horse,
but the world does not recognize it.
If the fine horse met Wáng Liáng or Zàofǔ,
would it not have the hooves to run a thousand lǐ?
When orchids grow in deep forests,
they do not fail to be fragrant because there is no one to smell them.
Thus, the purpose of learning
is not merely to achieve success,
but to be in hardship without being distressed,
to worry yet not let one's will decline,
to foresee the beginnings of fortune and misfortune and keep the heart unconfused.
The sage's deep thoughts, unique understanding, and unique vision—
Shùn was also a worthy sage,
facing south to govern the world,
only because he met Yáo.
Had Shùn lived in the time of Jié and Zhòu,
he might have barely avoided punishment and execution,
but what official position could he have held to govern?
Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān;
at that time,
was it because Guān Lóngpáng lacked wisdom or Bǐgān lacked ability?
It was because of the tyrannical era of Jié and Zhòu.
Therefore, the gentleman diligently studies,
cultivates his person and rectifies his conduct,
to await his time."
17.18 Confucius went to Sòng,
where Kuāng Jiǎnzǐ intended to kill Yánghǔ.
Confucius resembled him,
and armored soldiers surrounded Confucius's lodging.
Zǐlù was enraged,
brandished a halberd, and prepared to fight.
Confucius stopped him, saying:
"How can righteousness fail to transcend vulgar customs?
If I have not studied the Shī Jīng and Shū Jīng thoroughly,
or cultivated rituals and music properly,
that is my fault.
But if I resemble Yánghǔ,
that is not my fault;
it is fate!
Yóu, sing,
and I will join you."
Zǐlù sang,
Confucius joined him,
and after three rounds, the soldiers withdrew.
17.19 Confucius said:
"If one does not observe the high cliff,
how can one know the peril of falling;
if one does not approach the deep abyss,
how can one know the danger of drowning;
if one does not observe the sea,
how can one know the hazard of wind and waves.
Are not failures due to neglecting these?
A scholar who is cautious about these three things
will not bring trouble upon others."
17.20 Zēngzǐ said:
"The echo does not refuse the sound,
the mirror does not refuse the form,
the gentleman corrects himself and all things are accomplished.
Walking is not for the shadow, yet the shadow follows;
calling is not for the echo, yet the echo responds.
Thus the gentleman first achieves merit and fame follows."
17.21 Zǐxià asked Zhòngní:
"What kind of person is Yán Yuān?"
He replied:
"Huí's trustworthiness
surpasses mine."
Zǐxià asked:
"What kind of person is Zǐgòng?"
He replied:
"Cì's quick-wittedness
surpasses mine."
Zǐxià asked:
"What kind of person is Zǐlù?"
He replied:
"Yóu's courage
surpasses mine."
Zǐxià asked:
"What kind of person is Zǐzhāng?"
He replied:
"Shī's dignity
surpasses mine."
Thereupon Zǐxià rose from his mat and asked:
"Then why do these four men serve you, Master?"
He replied:
"Sit,
and I will tell you.
Huí can be trustworthy but cannot be flexible,
Cì can be quick-witted but cannot yield,
Yóu can be brave but cannot be cautious,
Shī can be dignified but cannot accommodate.
To combine all four qualities
is what I do not do."
The truly sage person
must understand the benefits of advancing and retreating, the uses of bending and stretching.
17.22 Dōngguō Zǐhuì asked Zǐgòng:
"Why is your Master's school so mixed?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"Beside the straightening tool there are many crooked woods,
at the good doctor's door there are many sick people,
near the whetstone there are many blunt tools.
Our Master cultivates the Way to await all under heaven,
those who come are not turned away,
hence the mixture."
The Book of Songs says:
"Luxuriant are those willows,
the cicadas chirp clearly,
deep is the pool,
reeds and rushes grow thickly."
This means that beside great things,
there is nothing that cannot be accommodated.
17.23 Once,
Nánxiá Zǐ visited Chéng Běnzǐ,
who cooked a salamander for him.
Nánxiá Zǐ said:
"I have heard that gentlemen do not eat salamanders."
Chéng Běnzǐ said:
"Is it that gentlemen don't eat it?
What has that to do with you?"
Nánxiá Zǐ said:
"I have heard that comparing upward with superiors broadens one's virtue,
comparing downward with inferiors narrows one's conduct.
Comparing with the good
is the stairway to self-advancement;
comparing with the bad
is the source of self-degradation.
The Book of Songs says:
'I look up to the high mountain,
I tread the great path.'
How dare I consider myself a gentleman?
I merely aspire to be one."
Confucius said:
"When you see a worthy, think of equaling him;
when you see an unworthy, examine yourself within."
17.24 Confucius was observing at Lǚliáng,
where a waterfall plunged forty fathoms,
swirling for ninety li,
fish and turtles could not pass,
giant sea turtles dared not dwell.
A man was about to cross it,
Confucius sent someone to stop him at the cliff's edge, saying:
"This waterfall plunges forty fathoms,
circles for ninety li,
fish and turtles dare not pass,
giant sea turtles dare not dwell,
I believe it would be difficult to cross."
The man paid no attention,
and crossed to emerge.
Confucius asked:
"Are you skillful?
Or do you have some special method?
How were you able to enter and emerge?"
The man replied:
"When I entered,
I began with loyalty and trustworthiness;
when I emerged,
I again followed loyalty and trustworthiness.
I entrusted my body to the waves,
but dared not use personal cunning,
that is how I could enter and reemerge."
Confucius said to his disciples:
"If even water can be approached long with loyalty, trustworthiness, and righteousness,
how much more so with people!"
17.25 Zǐlù appeared before Confucius in splendid attire,
Confucius said:
"Yóu,
what is this ostentatious display?
Formerly, the Jiāng River emerged from Mín Mountain,
at its source,
it was small enough to float a wine cup.
When it reached the river crossings,
without boats
and avoiding wind,
it could not be crossed.
Was this not because of the many streams joining downstream?
Now if your clothing is very splendid,
your countenance full of pride,
who in the world would wish to improve you?"
Zǐlù hurried out,
changed his clothes and returned,
composed as before.
Confucius said:
"Yóu, remember this,
I tell you.
Extravagance in speech
is flowery;
ostentation in action
is boastful.
Those who show off their wisdom and ability
are petty persons.
Therefore, the gentleman knows what he knows,
and does not know what he does not know -
this is the essence of speech;
can do what he can do,
and cannot do what he cannot do -
this is the perfection of action.
Essential speech leads to wisdom,
essential action leads to benevolence,
having both wisdom and benevolence,
what more could be added!
Yóu,
the Book of Songs says:
'Tāng descended without delay,
his sage reverence daily ascended.'
This refers to this."
17.26 Zǐlù asked Confucius:
"Does a gentleman also have worries?"
Confucius said:
"No.
When a gentleman cultivates his conduct,
before attaining it,
he delights in the intention;
after attaining it,
he delights in the understanding.
Thus he has lifelong joy,
and not a single day's worry.
The petty person is not like this,
before attaining something,
he worries about not getting it;
after attaining it,
he fears losing it.
Thus he has lifelong worries,
and not a single day's joy."
17.27 Confucius saw Róng Qǐqī wearing a deerskin robe,
playing the zither and singing.
Confucius asked:
"Master, what brings you such joy?"
He replied:
"I have many reasons for joy.
Heaven gives birth to all things,
yet only humans are most noble,
and I have already been born as human -
this is my first joy;
among humans, males are esteemed,
and I have already been born male -
this is my second joy;
some people die without seeing the sun and moon, without leaving their swaddling clothes,
yet I have already reached ninety-five years of age -
this is my third joy.
As for poverty,
it is the constant state of scholars;
as for death,
it is the ultimate end for all people.
Dwelling in constancy while awaiting the end,
what should I worry about?"
17.28 Zēngzǐ said:
"I have heard three sayings from the Master,
which I have not yet been able to practice.
The Master, upon seeing one good quality in a person, forgets their hundred faults -
this shows the Master's easiness to serve;
when the Master sees others possessing goodness,
he regards it as if he possessed it himself -
this shows the Master's non-competitiveness;
when hearing of goodness, he must personally practice it,
and only then does he teach it -
