this shows the Master's capacity for labor.
The Master's capacity for labor,
the Master's non-competitiveness,
the Master's easiness to serve -
I have learned these three sayings from the Master but have not yet been able to practice them."
17.29 Confucius said:
"Huí,
you possess four aspects of the gentleman's way:
strong in disciplining yourself,
yielding in accepting advice,
cautious in awaiting official salary,
and careful in maintaining personal conduct."
17.30 Zhòngní said:
"Shǐ Qiū possesses three aspects of the gentleman's way:
though not holding office, he respectfully serves superiors,
though not performing sacrifices, he respectfully serves spirits,
though upright, he can yield to others."
17.31 Confucius said:
"After my death,
Shāng will daily improve,
while Cì will daily decline.
Shāng enjoys associating with those more virtuous than himself,
while Cì enjoys pleasing those inferior to himself."
17.32 Confucius was about to travel,
and it was raining but he had no cover.
A disciple said:
"Zǐxià has a cover,
we could go."
Confucius said:
"Shāng's character
is very deficient in wealth matters.
I have heard that in dealing with others,
one should promote their strengths,
and avoid their weaknesses,
thus the relationship can endure long."
17.33 Zǐlù was about to travel,
and took leave from Zhòngní, saying:
"May I ask how to gain intimacy with new acquaintances?
How to have few words yet be effective?
How to long remain a good scholar without offense?"
Zhòngní said:
"To gain intimacy with new acquaintances,
rely on loyalty;
to have few words yet be effective,
rely on trustworthiness;
to long remain a good scholar without offense,
rely on ritual propriety."
17.34 Zǐlù was about to travel,
and took leave from Zhòngní,
who said:
"Should I give you a carriage as farewell gift?
Or should I give you words as farewell gift?"
Zǐlù said:
"Please give me words."
Zhòngní said:
"Without strength, you won't go far;
without labor, you'll achieve nothing;
without loyalty, you'll have no intimacy;
without trustworthiness, you'll have no response;
without respect, you'll have no ritual propriety.
Be careful with these five things,
and you can endure long."
17.35 Zēngzǐ followed Confucius in Qí,
and Duke Jǐng of Qí offered Zēngzǐ the ceremony for a lower minister's position,
but Zēngzǐ firmly declined.
When about to depart,
Yànzǐ saw him off, saying:
"I have heard that
when a gentleman gives farewell gifts, giving wealth
is not as good as giving words.
Now consider the orchid root -
it takes three years to mature,
then it's soaked in deer meat paste,
and when completed,
it can be exchanged for a team of horses.
It's not that the orchid root itself is beautiful,
but what soaks it is beautiful.
I hope you will carefully consider what soaks you.
Having found what soaks you,
also seek what can be soaked.
I have heard that
a gentleman in dwelling must choose his place,
in travel must choose his direction.
Dwelling must choose place
in order to seek scholars;
travel must choose direction
in order to cultivate the Way.
I have heard that what alters constant nature and changes character is desire,
therefore one cannot but be careful."
17.36 Confucius said:
"Regarding the nature of average people,
when they have surplus, they become extravagant;
when insufficient, they become frugal;
without prohibitions, they become dissolute;
without measure, they become lost;
indulging desires, they become ruined.
Food and drink should have limits,
clothing should have moderation,
housing should have measure,
livestock and stores should have number,
carriages and utensils should have bounds -
these are to prevent the source of chaos."
Therefore, measures and limits cannot be unclear,
and good advice cannot be unheeded.
17.37 Confucius said:
"The skillful who love measure will surely excel;
the brave who love cooperation will surely prevail;
the wise who love planning will surely succeed.
The foolish are the opposite."
Those who occupy important positions and monopolize favor,
who control affairs and envy the worthy -
this is the nature of the foolish.
Their will becomes arrogant and they take old grievances lightly.
Therefore, when position is exalted, danger surely follows;
when responsibility is heavy, collapse surely comes;
when favor is monopolized, disgrace surely results.
17.38 Confucius said:
"Children beaten with whips
do not follow their father's teachings;
people punished with executions
do not follow their ruler's governance.
This shows the difficulty of harsh methods.
Therefore, the gentleman does not rush to judgment,
nor issue arbitrary commands,
considering these sources of chaos."
17.39 Confucius said:
"To speak all day without leaving worries for oneself,
to act all day without leaving troubles for oneself -
only the wise have this.
Therefore, caution serves to eliminate troubles,
respect serves to overcome difficulties.
Working at something for a lifetime,
yet ruined by a single word -
can one not be careful!"
17.40 Confucius said:
"Those who, though wealthy and noble, humble themselves before others -
who would not associate with them?
Those who, with wealth and nobility, respect and love others -
who would not draw close to them?
When the multitude's words are not opposed,
one may be called knowing speech.
When one's words are followed by the multitude,
one may be called knowing timing."
17.41 Confucius said:
"Those who, being wealthy, can make others wealthy -
even if they desire poverty, cannot obtain it;
those who, being noble, can make others noble -
even if they desire lowliness, cannot obtain it;
those who, being successful, can make others successful -
even if they desire failure, cannot obtain it."
17.42 Zhòngní said:
"Plant in unsuitable ground,
and it will not grow;
speak to the wrong person,
and they will not listen.
With the right person,
it is like gathering sand and raining upon it;
with the wrong person, it is like gathering the deaf and drumming for them."
17.43 Confucius said:
"A boat cannot travel without water,
but if water enters the boat, it will sink.
A ruler cannot govern without the people,
but if the people defy their superiors, the state will topple."
Hence it is said:
The gentleman must be strict,
and the petty person must be restrained.
17.44 Confucius said:
"Rely on the virtuous and you will never be distressed;
rely on the wealthy and you will never be poor.
Why is it that a centipede can still walk after being cut?
Because it has many supporting legs."
17.45 Confucius said:
"If you do not know a man,
look at his friends;
if you do not know a ruler,
look at his envoys."
He also said:
"Living with good people,
is like entering a room of orchids and angelica;
after a long time, you no longer notice their fragrance,
for you have been transformed by them.
Living with bad people,
is like entering a fish market;
after a long time, you no longer notice the stench,
for you have been transformed by them too."
Hence it is said:
What is stored near cinnabar turns red;
what is stored near black pigment turns black.
Therefore, the gentleman is careful where he places himself.
17.46 Zǐgòng asked:
"When the gentleman sees great waters, he always contemplates them.
Why is this?"
Confucius said:
"Water is something with which the gentleman compares virtue.
It gives everywhere without selfishness,
resembling virtue;
wherever it flows, life follows,
resembling benevolence;
it flows low and follows contours,
always following principle,
resembling righteousness;
shallow places flow freely,
deep places are unfathomable,
resembling wisdom;
it plunges into hundred-ren valleys without hesitation,
resembling courage;
gentle yet penetrating everywhere,
resembling discernment;
it accepts impurities without protest,
resembling tolerance;
entering unclean,
emerging fresh and pure,
resembling transformation through goodness;
in measurement it is always level,
resembling justice;
full without needing leveling,
resembling moderation;
though winding thousands of times, it must flow east,
resembling purpose.
This is why the gentleman contemplates great waters."
17.47 Why does the wise take delight in water?
It is said:
Springs gush forth,
never ceasing day or night,
resembling strength;
flowing according to principle,
leaving no small gaps,
resembling impartiality;
moving downward,
resembling courtesy;
plunging into thousand-ren chasms without hesitation,
resembling courage;
contained by dams yet remaining clear,
resembling understanding of destiny;
entering unclean,
emerging fresh and pure,
resembling transformation through goodness;
all people draw from it equally,
all categories are properly supplied,
all things live by it,
and die without it,
resembling virtue;
profound and deep,
unfathomable,
resembling sageliness.
It moistens everywhere between heaven and earth,
helping states to form,
this is why the wise delights in water.
The Book of Songs says:
"How delightful is the Pàn water,
where we gather the water-shields;
the Marquis of Lǔ has arrived,
drinking at the Pàn palace."
This speaks of delight in water.
Why does the benevolent take delight in mountains?
It is said:
Mountains rise lofty and grand,
where all people gaze up in admiration.
Grasses and trees grow there,
numerous things stand there,
birds gather there,
beasts rest there,
treasures are produced there,
rare people dwell there,
nourishing all things tirelessly,
giving to all quarters without limit.
They produce clouds and wind,
connecting the energy between heaven and earth,
helping states to form,
this is why the benevolent delights in mountains.
The Book of Songs says:
"The Tài mountain stands majestic,
gazed upon by the Marquis of Lǔ."
This speaks of delight in mountains.
17.48 Jade has six beauties,
valued by the gentleman.
Viewed from afar, it is warm and smooth;
approached closely, it has fine texture;
its sound is gentle nearby yet heard far away;
it can be broken but not bent;
flawed but not weak;
sharp-edged but not cutting;
any flaw must be shown outwardly,
therefore it is valued.
Its warm and smooth appearance from afar
is compared by the gentleman to virtue;
its fine texture when approached closely
is compared to wisdom;
its gentle sound heard far away
is compared to righteousness;
being breakable but unbendable,
flawed but not weak
is compared to courage;
being sharp-edged but not cutting
is compared to benevolence;
showing any flaw outwardly
is compared to sincerity.
17.49 Dàowú asked the Master:
"Who is better - one who knows much or one who knows nothing?"
He replied:
"One who knows nothing
belongs to the category of the dead;
though not dead,
he must greatly burden others.
However, one who knows much
is fond of using his mind.
If his much knowledge
is used to benefit others, then it is good;
if used to harm others, then it is not good."
Dàowú said:
"Excellent!"
17.50 Yuè Shífù said:
"The unworthy consider themselves worthy;
the foolish think highly of themselves;
flatterers cannot examine their own hearts,
yet their mouths utter words,
and they tell others to keep silent.
This is like digging a well when thirsty,
or forging weapons when already in crisis -
though hastening, it will be too late."
17.51 Facing wealth, forget poverty;
facing life, forget death -
this can keep one from crime.
The gentleman treasures his speech,
the peacock treasures its feathers,
the tiger and leopard treasure their claws -
these are all ways to cultivate oneself.
Associating with superiors, one does not lose his emolument;
associating with inferiors, one does not fall into trouble.
Therefore, the gentleman chooses whom to associate with,
just as the farmer chooses which field to till.
The gentleman cultivates people,
the farmer cultivates fields.
The farmer selects seeds to plant,
and in good years must get grain;
the scholar selects people to cultivate,
and in good times must get emolument.
17.52 When the world loses the Way, then benevolence and righteousness arise;
when the state is not well-governed, then filial children emerge;
when the people contend without sharing, then kindness and generosity appear;
when the Way is violated and times are adverse, then stratagems and schemes come into being.
17.53 All that is good in life
stems from learning.
Within a single household,
there must be a guiding principle,
which refers to the parents.
Thus, if the ruler is upright, the common people are well-governed;
if parents are upright, children and grandchildren are filial and kind.
Therefore, the children in Confucius's household did not know how to curse,
and the children in Zēngzǐ's household did not know how to be lazy;
the reason for this
is that they were born into and taught goodness.
17.54 The benevolent prefer to unite people,
while the non-benevolent prefer to divide them.
Hence, when a noble person lives among others, there is order;
when a petty person lives among others, there is chaos.
The noble person seeks to harmonize people,
much like fire and water cannot naturally coexist,
but with a cauldron between them,
fire and water do not clash,
and they blend a hundred flavors.
Therefore, a noble person must be careful in choosing those among whom they dwell.
17.55 Qí Jǐnggōng asked Yànzǐ:
"I am sitting on the ground myself,
and all my ministers are sitting on the ground,
yet you alone pull up grass to sit on it;
why is that?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"I have heard
that only during mourning and in prison does one sit on the ground.
Now, I dare not treat sitting with my lord
as if it were a matter of mourning or imprisonment."
17.56 Qí Gāo Tíng asked Confucius:
"I have not neglected the mountains,
nor have I shirked the land,
wearing a straw raincoat,
carrying tools,
and with sincere spirit, I come to inquire about the way of serving a noble person;
I hope you will tell me."
Confucius said:
"Be steadfast in your duties,
respectful in your assistance,
and tireless in dealing with others.
When you see a noble person, promote them;
when you see a petty person, withdraw from them.
Rid yourself of malicious thoughts,
and be loyal to them.
Be diligent in your actions,
cultivate your manners,
and even a thousand miles away,
you will be as close as brothers.
If your actions are not diligent,
and your manners are not proper,
even those across the door will not communicate with you."
18.1 Yán Yuān asked Zhòngní:
"What is the conduct of a perfected person like?"
The Master said:
"The conduct of a perfected person
comprehends the principles of human nature,
penetrates the changes of all things,
understands the reasons behind the hidden and the manifest,
and sees the source of the floating energies.
One who is like this can be called a perfected person.
Having known the Way of Heaven,
they practice benevolence and righteousness personally,
and discipline themselves with ritual and music.
Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music
are the conduct of a perfected person.
To exhaust the spiritual and know transformation
is the height of virtue."
18.2 The "Yì" says:
"Looking up, we observe the celestial phenomena;
looking down, we examine the terrestrial patterns.
Therefore, we know the reasons behind the hidden and the manifest."
When the manifestations of celestial phenomena, terrestrial patterns, and human emotions are stored in the mind,
it becomes the repository of sage wisdom.
Thus, when the ancient sage kings ruled the world,
they necessarily adjusted to the four seasons,
established the calendar and pitch standards,
studied the celestial phenomena,
measured the changes of the times,
and ascended the spiritual terrace to observe the atmospheric signs.
Therefore, Yáo said:
"Oh, you, Shùn!
The celestial succession rests in your person;
hold faithfully to the mean,
and the four seas will be in distress."
The "Shū" says:
"Observe the jade transit-instrument and jade sight-tube,
to harmonize the seven governors."
The jade transit-instrument refers to the North Star, the Hooked Array, and the Pivot Star;
with the direction of its handle pointing to the twenty-eight lodgings,
it determines auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, fortune and misfortune.
The celestial phenomena and their lodgings,
the prognostication of expansions and contractions,
are each verified according to their categories.
The way of divining changes
is twofold.
These two
are the numbers of yīn and yáng.
Therefore, the "Yì" says:
"One yīn and one yáng is called the Way."
The Way
is that by which all things move without exception.
Thus, it originates from one,
forms from two,
completes from three,
circulates from four,
and acts from five.
Therefore, among the celestial images that are clearly manifested,
none are greater than the sun and moon;
in observing the movements of change,
none are more evident than the five planets.
The five planets of heaven circulate the energies of the five phases,
their origins still springing from yīn and yáng,
and their transformations culminate in eleven thousand five hundred and twenty.
The so-called twenty-eight stars are:
the eastern ones called Jiǎo, Kàng, Dī, Fáng, Xīn, Wěi, Jī;
the northern ones called Dǒu, Qiānniú, Xūnǚ, Xū, Wēi, Yíngshì, Dōngbì;
the western ones called Kuí, Lóu, Wèi, Mǎo, Bì, Zīxī, Shēn;
the southern ones called Dōngjǐng, Yúguǐ, Liǔ, Qīxīng, Zhāng, Yì, Zhěn.
The so-called lodgings
are where the sun, moon, and five planets reside.
Those outside and inside the lodgings' movements
are distinguished by official titles;
their roots all emanate from the earth,
and their blossoms take form in heaven.
The so-called five planets are:
first, the Year Star (Jupiter);
second, the Sparkling Deluder (Mars);
third, the Quelling Star (Saturn);
fourth, the Great White (Venus);
fifth, the Chronograph Star (Mercury).
Chānqiāng, comets, Xúnshǐ, Wǎngshǐ, and the banner of Chīyóu,
all are produced by the expansions and contractions of the five planets.
The transgressions of the five planets,
each are divined according to metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
In spring, autumn, winter, and summer, their appearances and disappearances have their times;
if they lose their regularity,
and deviate from their season,
then there are anomalies;
if they keep to their season,
and abide in their regularity,
this is called auspiciousness.
In ancient times, there were those in charge of the four seasons.
The one in charge of spring is Zhāng;
when it culminates at dusk,
grains can be sown,
reported upward to the Son of Heaven,
and proclaimed downward to the people;
the one in charge of summer is the Great Fire;
when it culminates at dusk,
millet and beans can be sown,
reported upward to the Son of Heaven,
and proclaimed downward to the people;
the one in charge of autumn is Xū;
when it culminates at dusk,
wheat can be sown,
reported upward to the Son of Heaven,
and proclaimed downward to the people;
the one in charge of winter is Mǎo;
when it culminates at dusk,
cutting, logging, hunting, and storing can be done,
reported upward to the Son of Heaven,
and proclaimed downward to the people.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven faces south and observes the culmination of the four stars,
knowing the urgency or leisure of the people;
in urgent times, he does not impose taxes or levies,
nor does he conscript labor.
The "Shū" says:
"Reverently grant the people the seasons." The "Shī" says:
"Things are abundant,
only if it is their time."
The reason things exist and do not cease
is that they move in their proper time.
18.3 The Book of Changes says:
"Heaven displays signs,
revealing good and bad fortune,
and the sages take them as models."
In ancient times, King Gāozōng of Shāng and King Chéng of Zhōu, moved by the omen of a pheasant crowing and the anomaly of a sudden storm,
cultivated themselves and reformed their conduct,
thus enjoying the blessings of prosperity and abundance.
When the First Emperor of Qín ascended the throne,
comets appeared four times,
locusts blotted out the sky,
there was thunder in winter and frost in summer,
meteorites fell in Dōngjùn,
giants appeared in Líntáo,
supernatural calamities manifested together,
Mars remained in the Heart constellation,
a comet swept across Tàijiǎo,
and Tàijiǎo was thereby lost,
yet in the end he did not reform.
When the Second Emperor took the throne,
he compounded these evils,
and upon his accession,
there were solar and lunar eclipses,
mountains and forests sank and vanished,
Mercury appeared during the four seasonal transitions,
Venus passed across the sky,
thunder sounded without clouds,
crooked arrows shone at night,
Mars assailed the moon,
calamitous fires burned the palaces,
wild birds frolicked in the court,
the capital's gates collapsed inward,
heavenly changes shook above,
ministers were confused at court,
the common people were in chaos below,
yet he failed to recognize this,
and thus perished.
18.4 Within the Eight Wildernesses are the Four Seas,
within the Four Seas are the Nine Provinces,
and the Son of Heaven resides in the Central Province to govern the eight directions.
The area between the two rivers is called Jìzhōu,
south of the river is Yùzhōu,
west of the river is Yōngzhōu,
south of the Hàn River is Jīngzhōu,
south of the river is Yángzhōu,
between the Jì and Hé rivers is Yǎnzhōu,
east of the Jì River is Xúzhōu,
Yān is Yōuzhōu,
Qí is Qīngzhōu.
Mountains, rivers, marshes, and wetlands,
hills, highlands, mounds, and ridges—
for these five types of land,
the sage kings followed their contours,
adapted to their advantages,
without losing their inherent nature:
on high land, millet;
on medium land, sorghum;
on low land, rice.
The uses of rushes, reeds, and sedges were never lacking,
hemp, wheat, millet, and grain were also abundant,
birds and beasts in the mountains and forests, fish and turtles in the rivers and marshes, all multiplied.
The king, from his capital extending in all directions, gathered and brought them in.
18.5 In the second year of King Yōu of Zhōu,
the three rivers of Western Zhōu all shook.
Bóyángfù said:
"Zhōu is about to perish!
Now the qì of heaven and earth
does not lose its order;
if it transgresses its order,
it is because the people have disturbed it.
When yang is suppressed and cannot emerge,
and yin is constrained and cannot rise,
then there are earthquakes.
Now that the three rivers shake,
it is because yang has lost its place and fills yin;
yang overflows and strengthens yin,
so the sources must be blocked.
If the sources are blocked,
the state must perish.
When water and soil are moist, the people's resources are sufficient;
if water and soil have nowhere to moisten,
the people will lack wealth and resources—
what can they await but destruction?
In the past, the Yī and Luò rivers dried up and Xià perished;
the Hé River dried up and Shāng perished.
Now the virtue of Zhōu is like that of the two dynasties in their final years;
its river sources are again blocked,
and blockage must lead to drying up.
A state must rely on mountains and rivers;
if the mountains collapse and the rivers dry up,
it is an omen of destruction.
When the rivers dry up,
the mountains must collapse.
If the state perishes, it will not exceed ten years,
for that is the cycle of numbers;
what heaven abandons does not exceed its cycle."
That very year,
the three rivers dried up,
and Qí Mountain collapsed;
in the eleventh year,
King Yōu was destroyed,
and Zhōu moved its capital eastward.
18.6 The Five Sacred Mountains—
what are they?
Tài Shān
is the Eastern Sacred Mountain;
Huò Shān
is the Southern Sacred Mountain;
Huà Shān
is the Western Sacred Mountain;
Cháng Shān
is the Northern Sacred Mountain;
Sōnggāo Shān
is the Central Sacred Mountain.
Why are the Five Sacred Mountains regarded as equivalent to the Three Dukes?
Because they can broadly spread clouds and rain,
and can greatly gather clouds and rain.
Clouds, touching the rocks, emerge;
gathering from a small area, they unite,
and before the morning is over, rain falls across the land.
Their bestowed virtue is vast and great,
so they are regarded as equivalent to the Three Dukes.
18.7 The Four Great Rivers—
what are they?
They are the Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Jì rivers.
Why are the Four Great Rivers regarded as equivalent to the feudal lords?
Because they can wash away filth and turbidity,
can channel all rivers to the sea,
and can produce clouds and rain across a thousand lǐ.
Their bestowed benefits are very great,
so they are regarded as equivalent to the feudal lords.
18.8 Mountains and rivers—
why are they regarded as equivalent to viscounts and barons?
Because they can produce things,
can moisten and nourish things,
and can generate clouds and rain.
Their kindness is abundant,
yet their categories number in the hundreds,
so they are regarded as equivalent to viscounts and barons.
The Book of Documents says:
"Offer sacrifices to the Six Honored Ones,
make orderly offerings to the mountains and rivers,
and extend them to all the spirits."
18.9 Duke Jǐng of Qí built a terrace for his open-air sleeping quarters.
Hearing an owl hoot and finding it repulsive,
he refused to ascend it even after its completion.
Bó Chángqiān said:
"The terrace was built with great urgency,
and now that it's finished,
why does Your Lordship not ascend it?"
The Duke replied:
"Indeed,
there was an owl that hooted before,
its sound foreboding all manner of ill omens,
I detest it deeply,
hence I do not ascend."
Bó Chángqiān said:
"I beg to perform an exorcism to drive it away."
The Duke asked:
"What preparations are needed?"
He answered:
"Build a new chamber and place white mao grass inside."
The Duke had the chamber built,
and when completed,
white mao grass was placed within.
Bó Chángqiān performed the ritual at night.
The next day, he asked the Duke:
"Did you hear the owl's call last night?"
The Duke said:
"It hooted once and was heard no more."
He sent someone to check,
and found the owl on the steps,
wings spread,
lying dead on the ground.
The Duke exclaimed:
"Your methods are so remarkably effective!
Can you also prolong my lifespan?"
He replied:
"I can."
The Duke asked:
"By how much can it be extended?"
He answered:
"For a Son of Heaven, nine years;
for a feudal lord, seven years;
for a high official, five years."
The Duke said:
"Will there be any omens to witness this?"
He replied:
"If longevity is granted,
the earth will tremble."
The Duke was delighted,
and ordered all officials to quickly prepare what Bó Chángqiān required.
As Bó Chángqiān departed,
he encountered Yànzǐ on the road,
bowed before his horse,
and explained:
"I performed an exorcism for the lord to kill an owl.
The lord said to me:
'Your methods are so remarkably effective,
can you also prolong my lifespan?'
I said:
'I can.'
Now I am about to conduct a grand sacrifice to pray for his longevity,
hence I inform you as I go."
Yànzǐ said:
"Ah,
how admirable!
That you can pray for the lord's longevity.
However,
I have heard that
only through governance and virtue that accord with the spirits
can longevity be increased.
Now, merely by sacrifice,
can longevity truly be enhanced?
Then, will there be auspicious signs?"
He replied:
"If longevity is granted,
the earth will tremble."
Yànzǐ said:
"Qiān,
previously I observed the linking stars severed,
the pivot stars scattered,
and the earth will tremble;
are you relying on this?"
Bó Chángqiān bowed his head for a moment,
then looked up and replied:
"Yes."
Yànzǐ said:
"Doing this brings no benefit,
nor harm if not done.
You should lighten taxes and levies,
not burden the people,
and let the lord know this."
18.10 Floods and droughts are both acts of the cosmic yīn and yáng in the world.
During great droughts, yú sacrifices are held to pray for rain;
during great floods, drums are beaten to coerce the earth god.
Why is this?
It is said:
Yáng is
the leader of yīn.
Among birds, the male is yáng and the female yīn;
among beasts, the male is yáng and the female yīn;
among people, the husband is yáng and the wife yīn;
in the family, the father is yáng and the child yīn;
in the state, the ruler is yáng and the minister yīn.
Thus yáng is noble and yīn base,
yáng honored and yīn humble,
as is the way of heaven.
In great drought,
yáng energy is overly abundant, suppressing yīn,
yīn is firmly oppressed by yáng,
and yáng becomes congested;
due to excessive congestion and suppression,
yīn cannot rise.
Hence, only yú sacrifices and prayers are made,
daring not to add more.
As for great floods and solar eclipses,
they occur when yīn energy is too strong, diminishing yáng essence from above,
allowing the base to ride over the noble,
the humble to override the honored,
which is greatly rebellious and unjust.
Therefore, drums are beaten to intimidate it,
and red strings are wound to coerce it.
From this perspective,
the Spring and Autumn Annals rectifies the positions under heaven,
exposes the failures of yīn and yáng,
directly rebukes the rebellious,
without shying away from difficulty,
demonstrating its fearlessness against the powerful.
Thus, coercing the solemn earth god does not alarm the spirits,
expelling the heavenly king does not disrespect the superior,
refusing Kuǎikuì's command does not disobey one's father,
severing ties with Wénjiāng does not mean lacking love for one's mother.
Has righteousness been fulfilled?
Has righteousness been fulfilled?
18.11 During a great drought in Qí,
Duke Jǐng summoned his ministers and asked:
"Heaven has not rained for a long time,
and the people are beginning to show signs of hunger.
I had it divined,
and the affliction lies in the high mountains and vast waters.
I wish to levy a small tax to sacrifice to the Spirit Mountain,
is that acceptable?"
None of the ministers responded.
Yànzǐ stepped forward and said:
"It is not acceptable;
sacrificing there will be of no benefit.
The Spirit Mountain has stones for its body,
and grass and trees for its hair.
If heaven does not rain for long,
its hair will scorch,
its body will grow hot;
does it not desire rain itself?
Sacrificing to it is futile."
Duke Jǐng said:
"If not,
I wish to sacrifice to the River Earl,
is that acceptable?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"It is not;
sacrificing there will be of no benefit.
The River Earl has water for his kingdom,
and fish and turtles for his people.
If heaven does not rain for long,
the springs will decline,
all rivers will dry up,
his kingdom will perish,
his people will vanish;
does he not need rain himself?
What good would sacrificing to him do?"
Duke Jǐng asked:
"What should be done now?"
Yànzǐ said:
"If you truly leave the palace and expose yourself to the elements,
sharing the worries of the Spirit Mountain and the River Earl,
perhaps heaven will fortunately send rain."
Thereupon, Duke Jǐng went into the wilderness and exposed himself,
for three days,
and heaven indeed sent heavy rain,
allowing the people to plant their crops fully.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Excellent!
Yànzǐ's words—
how can they be ignored?
It is because he possesses virtue."
18.12 When Heaven and Earth possess virtuous harmony,
then the vital energy has essence.
With the waxing and waning of yīn and yáng,
transformations occur in due time.
When the time is right, there is order;
when the time is right, there is transformation;
when the time is missed, there is chaos.
Therefore, humans are born lacking five capabilities:
eyes cannot see,
cannot eat,
cannot walk,
cannot speak,
cannot procreate.
Thus, after three months, the eyes develop and then they can see;
after seven months, teeth grow and then they can eat;
after one year, the knees form and then they can walk;
after three years, the fontanelle closes and then they can speak;
after sixteen years, the essence is fully developed and then they can procreate.
When yīn reaches its extreme, it reverts to yáng;
when yáng reaches its extreme, it reverts to yīn.
Thus, yīn changes through yáng,
and yáng changes through yīn.
Therefore, boys grow teeth at eight months,
lose their baby teeth at eight years,
and at two eights (sixteen), their essence transforms and begins to circulate;
girls grow teeth at seven months,
lose their baby teeth at seven years,
and at two sevens (fourteen), their essence transforms and begins to circulate.
For the unworthy, as soon as the essence transformation begins,
and the vital energy is stirred,
they indulge their emotions and desires,
thus reversing the process and disrupting transformation.
Therefore, the "Shī" says:
"Such a person,
longing for marriage,
greatly lacks fidelity,
and does not know destiny."
The virtuous are not like this;
when their essence transformation is complete and abundant,
they lament that the time may not be met,
and seeing no beginning of the Way,
they express their emotions and desires in song.
The "Shī" says:
"The quiet maiden is lovely,
waiting for me at the corner of the wall;
fond of me but not seen,
scratching my head, pacing back and forth."
"Gazing at the sun and moon,
my thoughts travel far;
the road is so distant,
how can you come!"
These are words of urgent times,
deeply felt,
hence they mention the sun and moon.
18.13 Measures and weights
are derived from the millet grain,
making one fēn,
ten fēn make one cùn,
ten cùn make one chǐ,
ten chǐ make one zhàng;
sixteen millet grains make one dòu,
six dòu make one zhū,
twenty-four zhū weigh one liǎng,
sixteen liǎng make one jīn,
thirty jīn make one jūn,
four jūn weigh one dàn;
one thousand two hundred millet grains make one yuè,
ten yuè make one gě,
ten gě make one shēng,
ten shēng make one dǒu,
ten dǒu make one dàn.
18.14 All the Six Classics recorded by the emperors and kings
invariably mention the four divine creatures.
When virtue flourishes, they are kept as domestic animals;
when governance is peaceful, they appear in due season.
Thus, the qílín has the body of a deer and the tail of an ox,
with a round head and a single horn.
It embodies benevolence and righteousness,
and its sounds match the musical pitches.
Its walking follows the compass,
and its turns follow the square.
It chooses the ground before stepping,
and settles only where the position is level.
It does not live in groups,
nor does it travel in flocks.
How elegant, possessing both substance and refinement!
In solitude, it is modest and orderly,
and in movement, it displays grace and dignity.
When Huángdì ascended the throne,
with his sage virtue receiving Heaven's mandate,
he cultivated the bright Way,
practicing only benevolence.
The world was peaceful and harmonious,
yet the fènghuáng had not appeared.
Thinking of its image,
he rose early each morning and night,
then inquired of Tiānlǎo,
saying:
"What is the fènghuáng like?"
Tiānlǎo replied:
"The fènghuáng
has the front of a swan and the rear of a qílín,
a snake's neck and a fish's tail,
the stance of a crane and the thought of mandarin ducks,
its aspirations transformed through beauty and resilience,
with dragon's patterns and a turtle's body,
a swallow's beak and a chicken's mouth,
and wings joined with centered grace.
Its head bears virtue,
its crest upholds righteousness,
its back carries benevolence,
and its heart holds wisdom.
In eating, it has substance;
in drinking, it has decorum;
when departing, it leaves elegance;
when arriving, it brings auspiciousness.
Its morning call is 'fāmíng',
its daytime call is 'bǎocháng',
its flying call is 'shàngxiáng',
and its perching call is 'guīchāng'.
Its wings clasp righteousness,
its bosom embraces loyalty,
its feet tread on rectitude,
and its tail ties to martial prowess.
Its soft sounds harmonize with metal,
its loud tones match the drum.
Stretching its neck and flapping its wings,
it displays all five lights,
its radiance arousing the eight winds,
its energy bringing timely rain.
This is the image of the fènghuáng.
Only the fènghuáng can comprehend all things,
penetrate heavenly blessings,
embody a hundred forms,
and reach the Way.
Its departure brings disasters,
its appearance brings fortune.
It surveys the nine provinces,
observes the eight extremities,
embodies both civil and martial virtues,
rectifies the royal domain,
shines sternly over the four directions,
and all sages and benevolent rulers submit.
Thus, if one obtains one aspect of its image,
the fènghuáng passes by.
If one obtains two,
it descends.
If one obtains three,
it descends in spring and autumn.
If one obtains four,
it descends in all four seasons.
If one obtains five,
it dwells for a lifetime."
Huángdì said:
"Alas!
How magnificent!"
Thereupon, he donned the yellow crown,
tied the yellow sash,
and fasted in the central palace.
The fènghuáng then blotted out the sun as it descended.
Huángdì descended the eastern steps,
facing west,
bowed his head and said:
"The August Heaven has bestowed this;
how dare I not accept the command!"
Then the fènghuáng settled in the eastern garden,
ate the emperor's bamboo seeds,
perched on the emperor's parasol tree,
and never left for life.
The Book of Songs says:
"The fènghuáng sings,
on that high ridge.
The parasol tree grows,
facing the morning sun.
Lush and luxuriant,
harmonious and chirping."
This refers to it.
The divine turtle has patterns of five colors,
resembling jade and gold,
with its back to the shade and facing the sun.
Its arched top symbolizes heaven,
its flat bottom imitates earth,
its spread resembles mountains,
its four feet moving in response to the four seasons,
and its markings represent the twenty-eight constellations.
With a snake's head and dragon's wings,
its left eye symbolizes the sun,
its right eye the moon,
transforming over a thousand years,
its energy ascending and descending,
able to know the changes of survival, demise, fortune, and misfortune.
In tranquility, it is faithful and steady;
in action, it becomes manifest.
The divine dragon can be high,
can be low,
can be large,
can be small,
can be hidden,
can be visible,
can be short,
can be long.
How illustrious in its height,
how profound in its depth,
reflecting the sky's light,
how elevated in its manifestation.
Now present, now absent,
subtle and fleeting,
beautifully patterned,
in emptiness, it is essence and harmony,
in motion, it is spirit and transformation.
Alas!
How true!
The nobleman is like a deity,
observing that majestic demeanor,
wandering in serene seclusion,
resembling the fènghuáng.
The Book of Documents says:
"The birds and beasts dance gracefully,
the fènghuáng comes to display its grace."
This refers to it.
18.15 During the time of King Chéng,
three seedlings of grain grew through a mulberry tree,
joining into one ear,
so large it nearly filled a cart,
so long it almost stuffed a box,
and the people presented it to King Chéng.
King Chéng asked the Duke of Zhōu:
"What does this mean?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Three seedlings joining into one ear suggests that the world may unite in harmony?"
Three years later,
the Yuèshāng clan came to court through multiple translations,
offering a white pheasant to the Duke of Zhōu,
saying:
"The road is long and distant,
mountains and rivers are treacherous and deep,
fearing one envoy might not get through,
so we came through triple translation to pay homage."
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"If virtue's grace does not reach,
the nobleman does not accept their tribute;
if governance and orders are not extended,
the nobleman does not subjugate their people."
The interpreter said:
"I received the command from the elders of our land:
'For long, Heaven has sent no violent winds or excessive rains;
could it be that the Central Kingdom has a sage?
If so, why not pay homage to him.'"
Only then did the Duke of Zhōu respectfully accept what they had brought.
18.16 In the fifteenth year of King Huì of Zhōu,
a spirit descended at Shēn.
The king asked Nèishǐ Guō, saying:
"What is the reason for this?
Does such a thing normally occur?"
He replied:
"It does.
When a state is about to flourish,
its ruler is reverent, enlightened, upright, pure, benevolent, and harmonious;
his virtue is sufficient to manifest its fragrant influence,
and his kindness is sufficient to unite his people.
The spirits enjoy his offerings and the people heed him,
with neither people nor spirits bearing grievances.
Thus, bright spirits descend there,
observe his governance and virtue, and equally distribute blessings.
When a state is about to perish,
its ruler is greedy, corrupt, wicked, dissolute, negligent, degenerate, and tyrannical;
his governance is foul,
and no fragrance ascends;
his punishments are false and unjust,
causing the common people to become disloyal.
The bright spirits do not cleanse it, and the people have thoughts of leaving;
both people and spirits are pained and resentful,
with nothing to rely on or cherish,
so spirits also go there,
observe its harshness and wickedness, and bring down calamities upon it.
Therefore, some see spirits and rise,
while others because of them perish.
In the past, when Xià was rising,
Zhùróng descended on Chóng Mountain;
when it perished,
Huílù stayed at Tíng Suì.
When Shāng was rising,
Táowù dwelled at Pī Shān;
when it perished,
Yíyáng appeared in the pastures.
When Zhōu was rising,
Yuèzhuó cried on Qí Shān;
when it declined,
Dù Bó shot King Xuān in Hào.
These are all instances recorded of the bright spirits."
The king said:
"Now, which spirit is this?"
He replied:
"Formerly, King Zhāo married a woman from Fáng,
called the Queen of Fáng,
who had a wanton virtue,
associating with Dān Zhū.
Dān Zhū embodied himself and matched with her,
giving birth to King Mù.
He oversees the descendants of Zhōu to bring them blessings or misfortunes.
A single spirit does not move far away;
if we look at it from this perspective,
could it be Dān Zhū?"
The king said:
"Upon whom will it bestow its influence?"
He replied:
"Upon Guó."
The king said:
"Then what will happen?"
He replied:
"I have heard that:
if one follows the Way and gains a spirit,
it is called abundant fortune;
if one is licentious and gains a spirit,
it is called covetous misfortune.
Now Guó is slightly decadent;
it will perish!"
The king said:
"What should I do then?"
He replied:
"Have the Grand Steward lead the invocators and scribes with the Lí clan,
presenting sacrificial animals, grain offerings, jades, and silks to make an offering there,
without making any requests."
The king said:
"How long will Guó last?"
He replied:
"In the past, Yáo oversaw the people with a cycle of five;
now his descendant appears;
when ghosts and spirits manifest,
they do not miss their timing.
If we look at it from this perspective,
it will not exceed five years."
The king sent Grand Steward Jǐfù to lead the Fù clan along with invocators and scribes,
presenting sacrificial animals and jade cups to make an offering.
Nèishǐ Guō accompanied them;
when they reached Guó,
the Duke of Guó also sent invocators and scribes to request land.
Nèishǐ Guō heard about Guó's plea for fate,
returned,
and reported to the king, saying:
"Guó is sure to perish.
Not offering sincere sacrifices to the spirits yet seeking blessings from them,
the spirits will surely bring misfortune upon it;
not being close to the people yet seeking to use them,
the people will surely turn away.
To offer with sincere intent is true sacrifice;
to kindly protect the common people is closeness.
Now the Duke of Guó exhausts the people's resources to fulfill his own transgressions,
alienating the people and angering the spirits while seeking profit—
is that not difficult indeed!"
In the nineteenth year,
Jìn took Guó.
18.17 Duke Huán of Qí campaigned north against Gūzhú.
Before reaching Bēi'ěr Valley, about ten lǐ away,
he suddenly halted,
staring wide-eyed.
After a while,
he held an arrow but dared not shoot.
He sighed deeply and said:
"Will our endeavor not succeed?
There was a person a foot tall,
wearing a large crown,
fully formed in features,
with his left sleeve draped,
running in front of the horses."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The endeavor will surely succeed.
This person
is the spirit who knows the way.
Running in front of the horses
means he is guiding;
his left sleeve draped
indicates there is water ahead,
and we should cross from the left side."
After traveling ten lǐ,
indeed there was water called Liáo River.
They marked it,
and crossing from the left reached ankle-depth,
while crossing from the right reached knee-depth.
After crossing,
the endeavor indeed succeeded.
Duke Huán bowed twice before Guǎn Zhòng's horse and said:
"Zhòngfù's sageliness reaches such heights;
I have long offended you."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Yíwú has heard that
sages foresee things before they take form.
Now that it has taken form and I knew it,
this shows Yíwú is good at receiving teachings,
not that he is a sage."
18.18 Wú attacked Yuè,
destroyed Kuàijī,
and obtained a bone segment that filled a cart.
They sent an envoy to ask Confucius, saying:
"Which bone is the largest?"
Confucius said:
"Yǔ assembled his ministers at Kuàijī Mountain;
Fángfēng shì arrived late,
and Yǔ killed and exposed his body,
his bone segment filling a cart.
This is the largest."
The envoy said:
"Who guards as spirits?"
Confucius said:
"The numinous powers of mountains and rivers
that are sufficient to order the world—
their guardians are spirits;
those of the state altars are dukes and marquises;
the sacrifices to mountains and rivers are for the lords,
all belonging to the king."
He said:
"What did Fángfēng shì guard?"
Confucius said:
"He was the lord of Wāngmáng shì,
guarding Fēng and Yú Mountains.
His spirit bore the surname Lí;
in Yú and Xià, he was called Fángfēng shì,
in Shāng, Wāngmáng shì,
in Zhōu, Chángdí shì,
and now he is called the Great Man."
The envoy said:
"How tall are people?"
Confucius said:
"Jiāoyáo shì are three chǐ tall,
the shortest of all;
the tallest do not exceed ten,
the extreme of numbers."
The envoy said:
"Excellent!
You are a sage."
18.19 Confucius was in Chén when
a falcon landed in the court of the Marquis of Chén and died,
pierced by an arrow of thornwood,
with a stone arrowhead,
measuring one chi and eight cun in length.
The Marquis of Chén sent someone to inquire of Confucius,
who said:
"This falcon has come from afar;
this is an arrow of the Sùshèn people.
Long ago, when King Wǔ conquered the Shāng,
he opened routes to the Nine Yí and Hundred Mán tribes,
ordering each to bring their local products as tribute,
so they would not neglect their duties.
Thus, the Sùshèn people offered arrows of thornwood with stone arrowheads,
measuring one chi and eight cun in length.
The former king, wishing to display how his virtuous influence reached distant lands,
showed it to later generations,
that they might forever remember it.
Therefore, he inscribed on the arrow's shaft:
'Tribute arrow of thornwood from the Sùshèn people.'
He bestowed it upon his eldest daughter Dà Jī,
who was married to Yú Húgōng and enfeoffed in Chén.
Dividing precious jades among those of the same surname
was to display kinship;
assigning distant tributes to those of different surnames
was to ensure they did not forget their service.
Hence, Chén was given the arrow of the Sùshèn people.
Try seeking it in the old treasury."
And indeed, it was found there.
18.20 Jì Huánzǐ, while digging a well, unearthed an earthen jar,
inside which was a sheep.
He asked Confucius about it,
claiming he had found a dog.
Confucius said:
"From what I have heard,
it is not a dog,
but a sheep.
The monsters of wood and stone
are Kuí and Wǎngliǎng;
the monsters of water
are dragons and Wǎngxiàng;
the monster of earth
is the fényáng,
not a dog."
Huánzǐ exclaimed:
"How profound!"
18.21 King Zhāo of Chǔ was crossing the river when
an object as large as a dou measure
struck his boat directly
and came to rest in it.
Greatly astonished, King Zhāo
sent an envoy to consult Confucius.
Confucius said:
"This is called a píngshí (duckweed fruit),
which can be cut open and eaten.
Only a hegemon can obtain it;
it is an auspicious sign."
Later, in Qí, a flying bird
with one leg
descended
and stopped before the palace hall,
spreading its wings and hopping.
The Marquis of Qí was greatly puzzled
and also sent an envoy to ask Confucius,
who said:
"This is called a shāngyáng;
urgently advise the people to hasten the repair of ditches and canals,
for heavy rain is imminent."
They acted accordingly,
and heavy rain indeed fell,
flooding many states,
while Qí alone remained safe.
When Confucius returned,
his disciples asked him about it.
Confucius said:
"In the past,
children chanted a rhyme:
'The King of Chǔ, crossing the river, obtained a píngshí,
as big as a fist,
red as the sun,
cut it open and ate it, sweet as honey.'
This was the fulfillment for Chǔ.
There was also another where children held hands in pairs,
bent one leg, and hopped, singing:
'Heaven is about to send heavy rain,
the shāngyáng dances.'
Now that Qí has encountered it,
it is also its fulfillment.
After such rhymes,
there is always a corresponding event."
Thus, a sage does not merely hold to the Way;
he observes things and records them,
thereby understanding their correspondences.
18.22 Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng sent Gōngsūn Chéngzǐ (Zǐchǎn) on a mission to Jìn.
Duke Píng was ill,
and Hán Xuānzǐ assisted
in hosting the guest.
The guest inquired about the ruler's illness,
to which he replied:
"Our ruler has been ill for a long time;
we have prayed to all deities above and below,
yet it remains unrelieved.
Now he dreams of a yellow bear entering his chamber door.
Is it a human ghost?
Or perhaps a malevolent spirit."
Zǐchǎn said:
"With your ruler's wisdom
and you in charge of governance,
how could there be a malevolent spirit?
I have heard that
long ago, Gǔn defied the emperor's command,
was executed at Yǔshān,
and transformed into a yellow bear,
entering the Yǔyuān abyss.
He became the object of sacrifice in the Xià dynasty's suburban altar,
continued by the Three Dynasties.
Where ghosts and spirits are concerned,
if not of their own clan,
then they are attended by those of equal rank.
Thus, the Son of Heaven sacrifices to the Supreme Deity,
lords and marquises to the various gods,
and officials below ministers only sacrifice to their own clan.
Now that the Zhōu court has declined somewhat,
Jìn has succeeded it.
Could it be that you have not performed the Xià suburban sacrifice?"
Xuānzǐ reported this,
and they performed the Xià suburban sacrifice,
with Dǒng Bó acting as the representative of the deceased.
In five days, the duke recovered.
The duke met Zǐchǎn
and rewarded him with a ceremonial tripod from Jǔ.
18.23 The Duke of Guó dreamed he was in the temple
where a spirit,
with a human face, white hair, and tiger claws,
stood holding a battle-axe in the western corner.
The duke fled in fear.
The spirit said:
"Do not flee!
The Emperor's command states:
'Let Jìn attack at your gate.'"
The duke bowed and kowtowed,
then awoke.
He summoned the historian Yín to interpret the dream,
and Yín said:
"From your description,
it is Rùshōu,
the god of punishment from Heaven,
whose affairs are determined by celestial officials."
The duke imprisoned him
and even had the people celebrate the dream.
Zhōu Zhīqiáo told his fellow nobles:
"Guó will not last long;
I now realize this.
Our ruler, instead of reflecting, rejoices at a great state's attack—
what good is that to us?
I have heard it said:
'When a great state follows the Way and a small state is attacked, it is called submission;
when a small state is arrogant and a great state attacks, it is called punishment.'
The people resent the ruler's extravagance,
hence they act against his commands.
Now he celebrates this dream;
his extravagance will surely grow.
This is Heaven depriving him of insight and worsening his flaws.
The people detest his behavior,
and Heaven deceives him further.
When a great state comes to punish,
his orders will be defied;
the ancestral state is already weakened,
and other states will distance themselves.
With no allies inside or out,
who will save him!
I cannot bear to wait."
He prepared to leave
and moved his clan to Jìn.
Three years later,
Guó perished.
18.24 When Duke Píng of Jìn was constructing the Shīqí Palace,
a stone was heard speaking.
Duke Píng asked Shī Kuàng:
"Why did the stone speak?"
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Stones cannot speak.
There must be a spirit inhabiting it,
or else
the people are hearing things erroneously.
I have heard it said:
'When actions are taken untimely,
causing resentment and slander among the people,
then even speechless things will speak.'
Now, with the palace being excessively extravagant,
the people's strength exhausted,
the commoners suffering and resentful,
and none able to live peacefully,
is it not fitting
that the stone speaks?"
18.25 Duke Píng of Jìn went out hunting
and saw a nursing tigress crouching motionless.
He turned to Shī Kuàng and said:
"I have heard that
when a hegemon king appears,
fierce beasts crouch and dare not rise.
Today, as I went out,
I saw a nursing tigress crouching motionless.
Is this not such a fierce beast?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"Magpies eat hedgehogs,
hedgehogs eat jùnyì birds,
jùnyì birds eat leopards,
leopards eat bó beasts,
and bó beasts eat tigers.
The bó beast looks similar to a dappled horse.
Today, when my lord went out,
were you perhaps driving dappled horses to hunt?"
The duke said:
"Yes."
Shī Kuàng said:
"I have heard that
one who deceives himself once will face hardship,
twice will face disgrace,
thrice will face death.
Now, the reason the tiger did not move
was because of the dappled horses,
not due to my lord's virtue and righteousness.
How can you, my lord, deceive yourself this once?"
Another day, when Duke Píng was leaving court,
a bird circled around him and would not leave.
Duke Píng turned to Shī Kuàng and said:
"I have heard that
when a hegemon king appears,
phoenixes descend to him.
Today, as I left court,
a bird circled around me,
not leaving all morning.
Could this be the phoenix?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"In the east, there is a bird called jiànkē.
This bird
has patterned feathers and red feet,
hates other birds but loves foxes.
Today, did my lord wear a fox fur robe when leaving court?"
Duke Píng said:
"Yes."
Shī Kuàng said:
"I have already said it before:
one who deceives himself once will face hardship,
twice will face disgrace,
thrice will face death.
Now, the bird stayed because of the fox fur robe,
not due to my lord's virtue and righteousness.
How can you, my lord, deceive yourself a second time?"
Duke Píng was displeased.
Another day, he hosted a banquet at the Shīqí Tower
and had his officer Mǎ Zhāng spread caltrops on the steps,
then summoned Shī Kuàng.
When Shī Kuàng arrived,
he walked up in his shoes.
Duke Píng said:
"How can a subject walk in shoes into his lord's hall?"
Shī Kuàng removed his shoes, piercing his feet,
crawled on his knees, piercing them,
and looked up to heaven with a sigh.
The duke rose and led him by the hand, saying:
"Today, I was just joking with you, old man.
Why are you so quickly troubled?"
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Troubled,
for meat that breeds worms ends up eaten by them;
wood that breeds borers ends up carved by them;
man who creates anomalies ends up harmed by them.
The vessels of the five tripods
should not grow weeds;
the hall and temple of a lord
should not sprout caltrops."
Duke Píng said:
"What should be done now?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"The anomaly is already present,
nothing can be done!
On the eighth day of next month,
when you review the officials
and establish the crown prince,
you, my lord, will die!"
When the eighth day of the next month arrived,
at dawn,
Duke Píng said to Shī Kuàng:
"Old man, you set today as the deadline.
How am I doing?"
Shī Kuàng was not pleased,
requested to leave,
and shortly after he left, Duke Píng died.
Thus it was known that Shī Kuàng had divine insight.
18.26 Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào asked Zhái Fēngtú:
"I have heard that in Dí it rained wheat for three days.
Is it true?"
He replied:
"True."
"And I heard it rained blood for three days,
is it true?"
He said:
"True."
"And I heard horses gave birth to oxen,
and oxen to horses,
is it true?"
He said:
"True."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"How great!
These anomalies
are enough to destroy a state!"
Zhái Fēngtú replied:
"The wheat rained for three days
was blown by the wind;
the blood rained for three days
was from birds of prey striking above;
horses giving birth to oxen,
oxen to horses,
is due to mixed herding;
these are not Dí's true anomalies."
Jiǎnzǐ asked:
"Then what are Dí's true anomalies?"
He replied:
"The state is frequently dispersed,
its ruler young and weak,
its high ministers corrupt,
its officials forming cliques to seek rank and salary,
its officers acting arbitrarily with no one to appeal to,
its government orders unstable and frequently changing,
its scholars crafty, greedy, and resentful;
these are its true anomalies."
18.27 Duke Āi shot and hit the altar of Jì,
then developed a mouth ailment,
unable to eat meat.
He sacrificed to Jì and improved,
then consulted a shaman official.
The shaman official altered the story, saying:
"Jì, carrying the five grains,
descended from heaven holding onto a stalk,
but the stalk broke before reaching the ground.
An old man from Liègǔ spread his lapel to catch it.
Why not offer sacrifices to him?"
The duke followed this advice, and his ailment vanished.
18.28 Biǎn Què passed through Zhào,
where the crown prince of the King of Zhào had died suddenly from a violent illness.
Biǎn Què went to the palace gate and said:
"I have heard that something involving earth has abruptly occurred in the state,
could it be an emergency?"
A court official fond of medicine came out to respond to him:
"Indeed.
The crown prince has died suddenly from a violent illness."
Biǎn Què said:
"Go in and report that the physician from Zhèng, Qín Yuèrén, can revive the crown prince."
The official challenged him:
"I have heard that in high antiquity, there was a physician called Miáo Fù.
When Miáo Fù practiced medicine,
he used reeds for a mat,
straw for dogs,
faced north and prayed,
uttering only ten words,
and all those who came supported by others,
or carried on litters,
recovered fully as before.
Can your methods achieve this?"
Biǎn Què said:
"They cannot."
The official continued:
"I have heard that in middle antiquity, there was a physician called Yú Fū.
When Yú Fū practiced medicine,
he manipulated brains and marrow,
tied the diaphragm and membranes,
applied heat to the nine orifices to stabilize the channels and collaterals,
causing the dead to become living again,
hence he was called Yú Fū.
Can your methods match this?"
Biǎn Què said:
"They cannot."
The official said:
"If your methods are like this,
it is like looking at the sky through a tube,
or piercing the ground with an awl,
what you aim to see is vast,
but what you actually see is very little.
If your methods are all like this,
how could they suffice to startle even a child?"
Biǎn Què said:
"Not so.
There are things like hitting a mosquito's head by groping in the dark,
or distinguishing black from white while blindfolded.
The crown prince's illness
is what is called corpse syncope.
If you doubt this,
let me try to go in and diagnose him;
the inside of the crown prince's thigh should be warm,
and in his ears, there is a shrill sound,
as if someone is whistling.
In such a case,
it can be treated."
The official went in to report to the King of Zhào,
who rushed out barefoot,
and upon reaching the gate said:
"You have honored us from afar, sir,
gracing this humble person.
If you are fortunate enough to have a cure,
then this child of the dust
may tread heaven and earth and live long as a man.
If you do not have it,
he will fill the ditches before even the dogs and horses."
Before he finished speaking,
his tears soaked his lapels.
Biǎn Què then proceeded to diagnose him,
first building a Xuānguāng stove,
preparing an eighty-percent decoction,
sharpening needles and stones,
selecting the three yang and five transport points,
with Zǐ Róng pounding medicine,
Zǐ Míng blowing into the ears,
Yáng Yí restoring the spirit,
Zǐ Yuè supporting the body,
and Zǐ Yóu applying manipulation,
the crown prince was thus revived.
When the world heard of it, all said:
"Biǎn Què can bring the dead to life."
Biǎn Què declined, saying:
"I cannot bring the dead to life;
I only enable those who are meant to live to survive.
The dead cannot be revived with medicine."
Alas!
The misrule of a chaotic ruler cannot be cured with medicine.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"When it blazes fiercely,
it cannot be saved by medicine."
These are words of extreme description.
18.29 Confucius stood in his hall one morning,
and heard the sound of someone weeping very sorrowfully.
Confucius took up his lute and played it,
and the music matched the weeping.
Confucius went out,
and among his disciples, there was one sighing.
He asked:
"Who is it?"
The reply was:
"It is Huí."
Confucius said:
"Why are you sighing, Huí?"
Huí said:
"Just now, there is someone weeping,
and the sound is very sorrowful,
not only mourning the dead,
but also weeping for the living separated."
Confucius said:
"How do you know?"
Huí said:
"It resembles the birds of Wán Mountain."
Confucius said:
"What do you mean?"
Huí said:
"The birds of Wán Mountain
give birth to four chicks,
and when their wings are fully grown,
they leave for the four seas.
The parents cry mournfully to see them off,
for they are going away and will not return."
Confucius sent someone to ask the weeping person,
who said:
"My father died and the family is poor,
so I am selling my child to bury him,
and now I am about to part with him."
Confucius said:
"Excellent,
he is a sage!"
18.30 Duke Jǐng was hunting at Wú Qiū,
and the night was still early,
so the duke sat down to nap.
He dreamed of five men facing north, leaning on a hut,
claiming they were innocent.
The duke woke up,
summoned Yàn Zǐ and told him his dream,
saying:
"Could it be that I have once killed the innocent and executed the guiltless?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Formerly, our previous lord, Duke Líng, was hunting,
and five men set a net and frightened the game,
so he had them killed.
Their heads were cut off and buried.
The place was named 'Mound of the Five Men.'
Could it be this?"
The duke ordered men to dig and search,
and indeed five heads were found together in one hole.
The duke said:
"Alas!"
And ordered officials to bury them.
The people of the state did not know about his dream,
and said:
"Our lord pities even white bones,
how much more the living!
He spares no effort,
and does not withhold any wisdom."
Hence it is said:
It is easy for a ruler to do good.
18.31 Zǐ Gòng asked Confucius:
"Do the dead have consciousness, or are they without it?"
Confucius said:
"If I say the dead have consciousness,
I fear filial sons and devoted grandsons might harm the living to bury the dead;
if I say they have no consciousness,
I fear unfilial descendants might abandon their relatives without burial.
Cì, if you wish to know whether the dead have consciousness or not,
you will know it soon enough after death,
and it will not be too late then."
18.32 Prince Jiàn was sent to guard Chéngfù,
and he met Chéng Gōng Gān in a field,
asking:
"What is this?"
Chéng Gōng Gān said:
"It is a hemp field."
"What is a hemp field for?"
"It is for growing hemp."
"What is hemp for?"
He said:
"It is for making clothes."
Chéng Gōng Gān said:
"Formerly, King Zhuāng attacked Chén,
and stayed at the house of Yǒu Xiāo,
saying to the people in the road-house:
'Is the alley not in bad condition?
Why is the ditch not dredged?'
King Zhuāng still knew if an alley was in bad condition,
or a ditch not dredged.
Now you, sir, do not know that the field is for hemp,
or that hemp is for clothes;
I fear you, sir, will not rule the state!"
The prince indeed did not ascend the throne.
19.1 When the Way prevails under heaven,
rites, music, and military campaigns emanate from the Son of Heaven.
When achievements are accomplished, rites are established;
when governance is stabilized, music is composed.
Rites and music
are the great means for implementing transformation.
Confucius said:
"For transforming customs and practices,
nothing is better than music;
for securing superiors and governing the people,
nothing is better than rites."
Therefore, the sage kings cultivated ritual refinement,
established schools,
displayed bells and drums,
with the Son of Heaven having the Pìyōng,
and the feudal lords the Pàngōng,
all to carry out virtuous transformation.
The Book of Songs says:
"At the Pìyōng in Hàojīng,
from west to east,
from south to north,
none do not submit."
This expresses it.
19.2 Accumulated kindness becomes love,
accumulated love becomes benevolence,
accumulated benevolence becomes numinousness.
The reason the Língtái is called numinous
is because it accumulates benevolence.
The divine numinous
is the foundation of heaven and earth,
and the beginning of all things.
Thus, King Wén began by connecting with the people through benevolence,
and all under heaven became benevolent;
this is the ultimate in civil virtue.
If virtue does not reach its peak, it cannot be refined.
19.3 Shāng means constancy,
constancy means substance,
substance governs heaven;
Xià means greatness,
greatness means refinement,
refinement governs earth.
Therefore, the king alternates between Shāng and Xià,
a twofold repetition;
primary colors, a threefold repetition;
flavor favors sweetness,
sound favors the gōng note,
a single repetition;
thus, the methods of the Three Dynasties cycle like a circle.
Hence, the Xiàhòu clan taught loyalty,
and the noble person became loyal;
the commoners' flaw was crudeness,
and nothing remedies crudeness like reverence;
thus, the Yīn people taught reverence,
and the noble person became reverent.
The commoners' flaw was superstition,
and nothing remedies superstition like refinement;
thus, the Zhōu people taught refinement,
and the noble person became refined.
The commoners' flaw was superficiality,
and nothing remedies superficiality like loyalty.
Therefore, the sage's approach to sageliness
is like the square's triple integration,
the compass's triple integration,
completing a cycle and starting anew,
reaching the end and returning to the origin.
The Book of Songs says:
"Carved and polished, their patterns;
like gold and jade, their substance."
This speaks of the beauty of refinement and substance.
19.4 The Tradition says:
Following emotions and indulging desires
is called being a beast;
acting arbitrarily if possible
is called being a rustic;
clinging to the old and resisting change
is called being one of the masses;
distinguishing right from wrong,
comprehending the ways of past and present,
is called being a scholar;
promoting the worthy and enabling the capable
is called being a senior official;
revering superiors and caring for inferiors
is called being a feudal lord;
covering like heaven and supporting like earth
is called being the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, scholars wear the fǔ pattern,
senior officials the fú pattern,
feudal lords the fire pattern,
the Son of Heaven the mountain and dragon pattern.
The more abundant the virtue, the more elaborate the refinement;
the more ordered the inner self, the more manifest the refinement.
19.5 The Book of Songs says:
"To the left, to the left,
the noble person is suited for it;
to the right, to the right,
the noble person possesses it."
The Tradition says:
The noble person
is suited for everything.
Thus, wearing ceremonial robes and headdress, standing solemnly
in the temple court above,
all officials and attendants are reverent;
wearing mourning garments of cut hemp,
with hempen girdles and staff,
standing in the mourning order,
guests offering condolences all grieve;
clad in armor and helmet,
standing amid the drumbeats of war,
no soldier fails to be brave.
Thus, their benevolence is sufficient to cherish the hundred surnames,
their courage to secure endangered states,
their trustworthiness to bind feudal lords,
their strength to withstand calamities,
their authority to lead the three armies.
Hence it is said:
Suited for the left,
suited for the right,
for the noble person, nothing is unsuitable—
this expresses it.
19.6 Duke Jǐng of Qí ascended for archery,
while Yànzǐ prepared the rites and waited.
The duke said:
"The rites of selective archery—
I am weary of them!
I wish to gather the brave warriors of the world
and plan the state with them."
Yànzǐ replied:
"A noble person without rites
is a commoner;
a commoner without rites
is a beast.
If ministers have excessive courage, they assassinate their lord;
if sons have excessive strength, they assassinate their elders.
Yet they dare not do so
solely because of what rites dictate.
Rites are the means to govern the people;
reins are the means to control horses.
That one can govern the state without rites—
I have never heard of it."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Well said."
Thereupon, he ordered the archery ground refurbished and seats changed,
honored Yànzǐ as his foremost guest,
and inquired about rites all day long.
19.7 The Book of Documents says:
"Of the five matters,
the first is demeanor."
Demeanor
is how men show respect and reverence,
and how women appear graceful and lovely.
Walking steps hit the square,
turning movements hit the circle;
standing, they curve like a chime stone;
bowing, they embrace like a drum.
Entering the ruler's court with it,
they are dignified and solemn;
they are reverent and loyal;
entering the village with it,
they are harmonious and compliant;
entering the communities, clans, and associations with it,
they are harmonious and affectionate.
The Book of Songs says:
"The mild and respectful person
makes virtue the foundation."
Confucius said:
"Respectfulness approximates rites
and keeps disgrace and insult at a distance."
19.8 Clothing and appearance
are what please the eye;
speech and responses
are what please the ear;
desires and preferences
are what please the heart.
When the gentleman's clothing is appropriate
and his appearance is proper,
then the people's eyes are pleased;
when his words are smooth
and his responses are adequate,
then the people's ears are pleased;
when he approaches benevolence and distances himself from what is not benevolent,
then the people's hearts are pleased.
These three reside in the heart,
flow through the body,
and manifest in movement and stillness;
even if not in office,
this is called genuine conduct.
Thus, a loyal heart that loves goodness and renews itself daily,
finds joy in virtue when alone,
pleased internally and manifested externally.
The Book of Songs says:
"Why does he stay?
He must have companions.
Why does he last so long?
He must have a reason."
Only those who have a reason can live long and see much without being burdened by material things.
19.9 Those who understand the way of heaven wear the jué crown;
those who understand the way of earth wear qú shoes.
Those capable of managing troubles and resolving chaos carry the xī;
those skilled in archery and charioteering wear the shè;
those who can command the three armies hold the jìn hù.
Clothing must bear the compass and square,
carrying the plumb line and setting the standard below.
Thus, the gentleman's clothing is appropriate and his appearance proper,
matching his attire to reflect his virtue,
so that by observing his jade-like appearance, his conduct and abilities can be ascertained.
The Book of Songs says:
"The branches of the wánlán plant,
a youth wears the xī."
This speaks of conduct and ability.
19.10 The cap is used to distinguish adults.
Cultivating virtue and restraining oneself,
to self-discipline,
thereby checking wicked thoughts
and preserving correct intentions.
A gentleman, upon first capping, must be blessed,
completing the ritual by adding the cap,
to sharpen his mind.
Thus, a gentleman, upon adulthood, must wear cap and girdle to conduct affairs,
abandoning the playful and lazy heart of youth,
and steadfastly pursuing the ambition to advance virtue and cultivate work.
Therefore, even if attire does not form a complete image,
the inner heart does not change;
the inner heart cultivates virtue,
externally adorned with ritual refinement,
thus achieving a manifest and good reputation.
Hence, the leather cap and plain attire
remain unchanged through a hundred kings,
both to cultivate virtue
and to correct appearance.
Confucius said:
"Straighten his clothes and cap,
dignify his gaze,
solemnly, people look upon him with awe—
is this not authority without fierceness?"
19.11 When King Chéng was about to be capped,
the Duke of Zhōu had祝雍 (Zhù Yōng) bless the king,
saying:
"Let the words be expressive but not verbose."
祝雍 (Zhù Yōng) said:
"May the king draw near to the people,
keep away from flatterers,
be sparing with time,
generous with wealth,
and employ the worthy and able."
At this moment of initiation,
the blessing was recited four times with additions before retiring.
For a duke's capping,
he himself acts as host,
with ministers as guests,
feasted with the triple-offering ritual;
the duke first adds the dark formal robe and leather cap,
each time necessarily in court attire and dark crown, capped four times.
For the capping of feudal lords' heirs or other sons,
the duke acts as host,
the ritual being the same as for scholars.
Capped in the ancestral temple, it is said:
"On this auspicious month and day,
we add to you the primary headdress,
remove your childish aims,
and follow your accomplished virtue."
The capping ritual at nineteen signifies correctness and capping,
an ancient universal rite.
19.12 "In summer, the duke went to Qí to fetch a bride."
"Why is it recorded?
To personally welcome her
is the rite."
How is the ritual conducted?
It is said:
Feudal lords present two pairs of shoes with a cóng jade,
while ministers, scholars, and commoners present two pairs of shoes with two bundles of dried meat.
Saying:
"The humble consort of a certain state
has sent me with this unworthy cóng
and unworthy shoes,
to ritually honor the lady, a chaste maiden."
The lady replies:
"I, born in a secluded chamber of lowly estate,
untaught by governesses,
yet granted the duty of holding your garments,
dare not but reverently bow and pray."
The officiant returns the bow,
the lady accepts the cóng,
takes one pair of shoes to fit the maiden,
adjusts her hairpin and robes, and commands her:
"Go forth,
serve your parents-in-law well,
with obedience as your household rule,
do not waver in heart,
do not dare to turn back."
The maiden bows,
then she is led by the hand
and given to her husband at the door.
The husband leads her out the door,
he walks ahead,
she follows,
bows in farewell to her father in the hall,
and to her aunts at the main gate.
The husband first ascends the carriage and takes the reins,
then the maiden ascends the carriage;
the wheels turn three times,
after which the husband descends and proceeds ahead.
Ministers, scholars, and commoners refer to their father, saying:
"So-and-so's father,
so-and-so's teacher and friend,
has sent me with these unworthy shoes
and unworthy dried meat,
daring not but to reverently ritually honor such-and-such clan's chaste maiden."
The mother says:
"I, a product of the thatched hut,
unpracticed in weaving and spinning tasks,
yet granted the duty of holding broom and dustpan,
dare not but reverently bow."
19.13 The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
"On rénshēn,
the duke passed away in the Gāo Qǐn."
The Commentary says:
"What is the Gāo Qǐn?
It is the main寝 (qǐn, chamber).
Why sometimes say Gāo Qǐn,
and sometimes Lù Qǐn?"
It is said:
"Feudal lords have three main寝 (qǐn):
one is called Gāo Qǐn,
two is called Zuǒ Lù Qǐn,
three is called Yòu Lù Qǐn.
The Gāo Qǐn
is the寝 (qǐn) of the founding lord;
the two Lù Qǐn
are the寝 (qǐn) of the succeeding lords."
"Why two?"
It is said:
"A son does not occupy his father's寝 (qǐn),
hence two寝 (qǐn).
A succeeding lord generation after generation cannot reside in the寝 (qǐn) of the high ancestor,
thus there is the Gāo Qǐn,
named 'high'."
"How are the Lù Qǐn arranged?"
"The Gāo Qǐn stands in the center,
the Lù Qǐn to the left and right."
The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
"The Heavenly King entered Chéngzhōu."
The Commentary says:
"What is Chéngzhōu?
It is Eastern Zhōu."
"Then how about the Son of Heaven's寝 (qǐn)?"
It is said:
"Also three.
The寝 (qǐn) of the successor who carries on the bright and upholds culture
are called the left and right Lù Qǐn."
"Why called Chéngmíng (carrying brightness)?"
It is said:
"They carry on after the Mingtáng (Bright Hall).
Thus, with the three寝 (qǐn) of Son of Heaven and feudal lords established, name and reality are correct,
the principle of father and son is clear,
matters of honor and humility are distinguished,
and the virtues of great and small are differentiated."
19.14 The Son of Heaven uses chàng as a ceremonial gift.
Chàng is
the essence of all herbs.
It ascends and flows through the heavens,
descends and flows through the earth,
there is nowhere it does not flow,
thus the Son of Heaven uses chàng as a ceremonial gift.
Feudal lords use guī as a ceremonial gift.
Guī is
jade.
Thin yet unyielding,
sharp-edged yet not cutting,
if there is a flaw within,
it will inevitably show on the outside,
thus feudal lords use jade as a ceremonial gift.
High ministers use gāo as a ceremonial gift.
Gāo is
a lamb.
Sheep gather in groups but do not form cliques,
thus high ministers use sheep as a ceremonial gift.
Grand officers use yàn as a ceremonial gift.
Yàn are
geese that form ranks with rituals of seniority and juniority,
thus grand officers use them as a ceremonial gift.
Scholars use zhì as a ceremonial gift.
Zhì are
pheasants, chosen because they cannot be lured by pointing at food, caged, or tamed through familiarity,
thus scholars use pheasants as a ceremonial gift.
Commoners use wù as a ceremonial gift.
Wù are
ducks.
Ducks are used because they have no other intentions,
thus commoners use ducks as a ceremonial gift.
A ceremonial gift is
that which serves as a pledge.
19.15 Feudal lords present scholars to the court once every three years.
One proper selection is called favoring virtue,
a second proper selection is called honoring the worthy,
a third proper selection is called having merit.
For having merit,
the Son of Heaven first bestows carriages, robes, bows, and arrows,
secondly bestows chàng,
thirdly bestows a hundred tiger warriors,
and confers the title of "Mandated Feudal Lord."
A Mandated Feudal Lord gains the authority to conduct punitive expeditions independently,
if a neighboring state has a minister who assassinates his ruler,
or a concubine's son who kills the legitimate heir,
even without requesting permission from the Son of Heaven, he may launch an expedition against them.
After the expedition, he returns the land to the Son of Heaven.
When feudal lords present scholars,
one improper selection is called a fault,
a second improper selection is called arrogance,
a third improper selection is called deception.
For deception,
the Son of Heaven demotes them,
first demotion involves reduction in rank,
second demotion involves reduction in territory,
third demotion results in complete loss of territory.
If feudal lords fail to present scholars, it is called not following the proper way,
for not following the proper way,
the Son of Heaven demotes them,
first demotion involves reduction in rank,
second demotion involves reduction in territory,
third demotion results in complete loss of territory,
then the Son of Heaven annually reviews officials without documented achievements and dismisses them,
replacing them with scholars presented by the feudal lords.
The Book of Songs says:
"With many officials in earnest,
King Wén found peace."
This expresses that meaning.
19.16 In ancient times, there were certainly people who were commended,
those among the people who could respect elders, pity orphans, choose to yield, and devote effort to their duties,
were commended by their ruler.
Only after receiving commendation could they ride in decorated carriages with paired horses,
those who had not received commendation were not permitted to ride,
and those who rode without permission were all punished.
Thus, although the people might have surplus wealth and luxurious goods,
if they lacked benevolence, righteousness, merit, or virtue,
