then there was no use for their surplus wealth and luxurious goods.
Therefore, the people all promoted benevolence and righteousness while disdaining wealth and profit,
disdaining wealth and profit led to no contention,
no contention meant the strong did not bully the weak,
and the many did not oppress the few.
This is why Táng and Yú established symbolic punishments,
and the people dared not break the laws,
thus disorder was stopped.
The Book of Songs says:
"Admonish your people,
be careful in your feudal duties,
to guard against the unexpected."
This expresses that meaning.
19.17 For the Son of Heaven, it is called inspection tours;
for feudal lords, it is called reporting on duties.
Inspection tours mean
inspecting what they guard;
reporting on duties means
reporting on their official responsibilities.
In spring, he inspects plowing,
to assist those in need;
in autumn, he inspects harvesting,
to aid those with shortages.
The Son of Heaven conducts inspection tours once every five years.
In the second month of the year,
he tours east,
reaching the Eastern Peak,
where he offers burnt offerings and performs sacrifices to the mountains and rivers from a distance,
receives feudal lords,
and inquires after centenarians.
He orders the Grand Music Master to present folk songs,
to observe the customs of the people.
He orders markets to report prices,
to observe what the people like and dislike,
and those with decadent tastes and peculiar preferences.
He orders the Minister of Rites to examine the seasons and months,
fix the days,
unify pitch standards, rituals, music, systems, and clothing,
and correct them.
If sacrifices to the mountain and river deities are neglected, it is considered disrespect,
for disrespect,
the ruler is demoted in rank.
If ancestral temple ceremonies are not in order, it is considered unfilial,
for unfilial conduct, the ruler has his territory reduced.
Those who have achieved merit and benefited the people
then have their territory increased.
Upon entering a territory,
if the land is well-cultivated and cleared,
the elderly are respected and the worthy are honored, then there is reward,
and their territory is increased;
upon entering a territory,
if the land is barren and neglected,
the elderly are abandoned and the worthy are lost,
and extortionate officials hold positions, then there is reprimand,
and their territory is reduced.
One failure to attend court results in demotion of rank;
a second failure to attend court results in reduction of territory;
a third failure to attend court leads to mobilization of the six armies against them.
In the fifth month of the year,
he tours south,
reaching the Southern Peak,
following the same rituals as the eastern inspection tour.
In the eighth month of the year,
he tours west to the Western Peak,
following the same rituals as the southern inspection tour.
In the eleventh month of the year,
he tours north,
reaching the Northern Peak,
following the same rituals as the western inspection tour.
Upon return, he reports at the temples of ancestors and father,
using a single sacrificial animal.
19.18 The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"In the first month,
the duke hunted at Láng."
The Commentary explains:
"Spring hunting is called sōu,
summer hunting is called miáo,
autumn hunting is called xiǎn,
winter hunting is called shòu."
"What does miáo mean?"
It says:
"Miáo means taking the furred ones,
capturing them without surrounding the marshes,
not ambushing the whole herd,
taking game without harming fawns or eggs,
not killing pregnant animals;
spring sōu hunting
does not kill young fawns or pregnant animals;
winter shòu hunting takes all.
All the common people go out,
maintaining proper chariot speed,
not colliding with game,
not hunting deceitfully,
pursuing without crossing boundaries -
this is the meaning of miáo, sōu, and shòu.
Thus the rituals of miáo, sōu, and shòu
simplify military affairs.
Therefore miáo means taking the furred ones,
sōu means searching thoroughly,
shòu means guarding and remaining."
"Why is there no hunting in summer?"
It says:
"It is the time when heaven and earth, yīn and yáng, are at their peak of growth.
Fierce beasts do not seize prey,
birds of prey do not strike,
venomous creatures do not sting.
If even birds, beasts, insects, and snakes know to respond to heaven,
how much more should humans?
Therefore the ancients necessarily had enclosures for rearing animals.
Why is it called tián (field/hunting)?
The sage, when undertaking affairs, must return to the root.
The five grains
are used to serve the ancestral temple
and nourish the myriad people.
To remove the birds and beasts that harm the crops,
it is therefore called tián.
When the sage creates names and terms,
the meaning of affairs can be known."
19.19 The Son of Heaven and the feudal lords
when there are no state affairs, hunt three times per year -
first for the dried meat offerings,
second for guests,
third to supply the ruler's kitchen.
Not hunting when there are no state affairs
is called disrespect;
hunting not according to ritual
is called wasting heaven's creatures.
The Son of Heaven does not completely surround [an area],
feudal lords do not ambush whole herds.
When the Son of Heaven kills game, the large tassels are lowered;
when feudal lords kill game, the small tassels are lowered;
when high officials kill game, the assisting chariots stop;
when the assisting chariots stop, the common people may hunt.
When otters sacrifice fish,
then fishermen may enter the marshes and weirs;
when jackals sacrifice game,
then hunting may begin;
when turtledoves transform into hawks,
then nets may be set;
when plants and trees wither and fall,
then one may enter the mountain forests.
Before insects hibernate,
one should not use fire in hunting;
do not take fawns or eggs,
do not kill the pregnant,
do not kill the young,
do not overturn nests.
These are all examples of
when sages are above,
gentlemen in position,
and capable people in office -
the manifestation of great virtue.
Thus when Gāo Yáo was Minister of Justice,
justice prevailed,
and the people each obtained what was truly due them;
when Bó Yí presided over rites,
high and low all practiced deference;
when Chuí was Chief Artisan,
the hundred craftsmen achieved merit;
when Yì was in charge of conservation,
mountains and marshes were opened and regulated;
when Qì was in charge of agriculture,
the hundred grains grew timely and lush;
when Xiè was Minister of Education,
the hundred families were intimate and harmonious;
when Lóng was in charge of guests,
people from distant lands came;
when the twelve shepherds traveled, none in the nine provinces dared to be perverse;
when Yǔ dammed the nine mountains,
dredged the nine marshes,
opened the nine roads,
settled the nine provinces,
each came with tribute according to their office,
not missing what was appropriate.
The territory extended five thousand lǐ square,
reaching the wild domains.
To the south, he pacified Jiāozhǐ, Dàfā, Xīróng, Xīzhī, Qúsōu, Dī, Qiāng;
to the north, he reached Shānróng, Fā, Sùshèn;
to the east, he reached Chángyí, Dǎoyí.
Within the four seas,
all praised Emperor Shùn's achievements.
Thereupon Yǔ raised up the music of Jiǔsháo,
attracted rare creatures,
and phoenixes came soaring.
The bright virtue of all under heaven began with Emperor Yú.
19.20 The archer must have a calm mind and correct posture,
hold bow and arrows,
steadily and firmly,
then the archer can hit the target.
The Book of Songs says:
"The great target is raised,
bows and arrows are drawn,
the archers are assembled,
display your shooting skill."
This refers to this.
The bow (hú) means preparation.
Preparation means
preparing our intention.
Therefore in ancient times, when a boy was three days old,
they used six mulberry bows and arrowweed arrows
to shoot toward heaven, earth, and the four directions.
Heaven, earth, and the four directions
are where a man's affairs lie.
He must be mindful of his affairs
before daring to eat grain.
Therefore it is said:
"Not eating plain meals" - this refers to this.
19.21 When people interact with each other in life,
it is called retaining guests.
From the Son of Heaven to the common officers, each has their own order.
Presenting gifts for the dead without reaching the coffin and corpse,
or offering condolences to the living without expressing grief,
is contrary to the rites.
Therefore, in ancient times, one traveled fifty lǐ for auspicious occasions,
and one hundred lǐ for mourning.
Presenting funeral gifts and handling affairs in a timely manner is called timeliness.
Timeliness
is a major aspect of the rites.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
"The Heavenly King sent Zǎi Xuǎn to come and present funeral gifts for Huì Gōng and Zhòngzǐ."
What are funeral gifts?
In funeral matters, there are those who present gifts;
typically, they use a team of horses and bolts of silk.
Carriages and horses are called fèng,
money and goods are called fù,
clothing and coverings are called suì,
objects for the mouth are called hán,
and items for enjoyment are called zèng.
Those who know the deceased give fù and fèng,
while those who know the dead give zèng and suì.
Zèng and suì are for sending off the dead,
while fù and fèng are for assisting the living.
Carriages and horses, bolts of silk, money and goods, clothing and coverings, and items for enjoyment—
what are their quantities?
It is said:
The Son of Heaven has six horses,
feudal lords have four horses,
senior officials have three horses,
principal officers have two horses,
and junior officers have one horse.
The Son of Heaven has five bolts of silk,
three black and two crimson,
each fifty feet long;
feudal lords have three black and two crimson,
each thirty feet long;
senior officials have one black and two crimson,
each thirty feet long;
principal officers have one black and one crimson,
each two zhàng long;
junior officers have one bolt each of plain and patterned silk;
commoners have one bolt each of cloth and silk.
The Son of Heaven's fèng
includes six horses
and a carriage;
feudal lords have four horses,
and a carriage;
senior officials are said to have a triple carriage;
principal and junior officers do not use carriages.
The Son of Heaven has one set each of embroidered garments,
reaching the ground;
feudal lords cover the instep,
senior officials reach the ankle,
and officers reach the thigh.
The Son of Heaven fills the mouth with pearls,
feudal lords with jade,
senior officials with pearls,
officers with shells,
and commoners with grains.
For those of high rank, great virtue, and close kin,
the fù, fèng, hán, and suì are generous,
and there are also differences based on wealth and poverty,
with quantities of two, three, four, or five,
derived from heaven and earth to establish odd and even numbers,
measuring human emotions to set rituals and patterns,
which is called having a basis,
the great foundation of the rites.
19.22 The *Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
"On the gēngxū day,
the Heavenly King passed away."
The *Commentary* says:
"Why is the burial of the Heavenly King not recorded?
For the Son of Heaven, the passing is recorded but not the burial,
because it must occur at its proper time;
for feudal lords, both the death and burial are recorded,
as with the Son of Heaven present,
it cannot be fixed at a specific time."
"What does 'must occur at its proper time' mean?"
"The Son of Heaven is encoffined after seven days,
and buried after seven months;
feudal lords are encoffined after five days,
and buried after five months;
senior officials are encoffined after three days,
and buried after three months;
officers and commoners are encoffined after two days,
and buried after two months."
"Why is it so in all cases?"
It is said:
"Rites do not prepare for inauspicious events in advance;
only after death are mourning garments prepared,
mourning clothes worn,
inner and outer coffins decorated,
the grave dug and the burial site prepared,
after which the mourning rituals are complete,
all external relatives have arrived,
the burial mound is gathered,
and the kindness of filial sons and loyal ministers is fully expressed.
Thus, the Son of Heaven is buried after seven months,
when all within the same realm have arrived;
feudal lords are buried after five months,
when all within the same alliance have arrived;
senior officials are buried after three months,
when all within the same court have arrived;
officers and commoners are buried after two months,
when all external relatives have arrived."
19.23 Yánlíng Jìzǐ went to Qí.
On his return,
his eldest son died between Yíng and Bó,
and he was buried there.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ
is one well-versed in the rites of Wú."
He sent Zǐgòng to observe.
The grave was dug not deep enough to reach water,
and the burial was in everyday clothes.
After the burial, the grave was sealed,
the mound covering the pit,
its height just enough to lean on.
After sealing the grave,
he bared his left arm,
circled the grave to the right,
and wailed three times,
saying:
"Flesh and bones return to the earth,
such is fate;
but the soul and spirit go everywhere,
they go everywhere!"
And then he departed.
Confucius said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ's actions are in accordance with the rites."
19.24 A child is born and for three years,
only then is it free from the care of its parents,
hence the three-year mourning period is established,
to repay the kindness of parents.
The one-year mourning period
applies to feudal lords,
while the three-year mourning period
applies to the Son of Heaven,
this is the constant rule of the rites.
19.25 Zǐxià, after completing the three-year mourning period,
went to see Confucius.
Confucius gave him a zither,
and had him play it.
He took the zither and played,
joyfully and happily,
then rose and said:
"The ancient kings established the rites,
I dare not fall short."
The Master said:
"He is a nobleman!"
Mǐnzǐ Qiān, after completing the three-year mourning period,
went to see Confucius.
Confucius gave him a zither,
and had him play it.
He took the zither and played,
sorrowfully and sadly,
then rose and said:
"The ancient kings established the rites,
I dare not exceed."
Confucius said:
"He is a nobleman!"
Zǐgòng asked:
"Mǐnzǐ's grief was not exhausted,
yet you said 'nobleman';
Zǐxià's grief was exhausted,
yet you also said 'nobleman'.
I am confused,
may I ask what this means?"
Confucius said:
"Mǐnzǐ's grief was not exhausted,
but he could restrain it according to the rites,
hence he is a nobleman;
Zǐxià's grief was exhausted,
but he could extend and express it,
hence he is a nobleman.
The three-year mourning period
is indeed what the superior can endure,
and the inferior can strive for."
19.26 King Xuān of Qí said to Tián Guò:
"I have heard that Confucian scholars mourn their parents for three years
and their ruler for three years.
Which is more important, the ruler or the father?"
Tián Guò replied:
"Perhaps the ruler is not as important as the father."
The king angrily said:
"Then why do you leave your parents to serve the ruler?"
Tián Guò replied:
"Without the ruler's land,
I would have no place to house my parents;
without the ruler's stipend,
I would have no means to support my parents;
without the ruler's ranks and positions,
I would have no way to honor and glorify my parents.
What I receive from the ruler,
I dedicate to my parents.
All service to the ruler
is for the sake of my parents."
King Xuān was disgruntled but had no reply.
19.27 In ancient times, when there was a disaster it was called a plague,
the ruler would wear plain garments for a period,
dispatch officials to condole the dead and inquire after the sick,
show concern through shamans and doctors,
crawl on hands and knees to rescue them,
and provide hot soup and porridge as remedies.
The well-off must first assist the widowed, orphaned, and solitary.
For those too ill to care for each other,
or who die with no means for burial,
then bury them.
Do not call at the door of those mourning a parent;
those wearing the coarse hemp of mourning for close relatives
are exempt from labor conscription for five months;
those in lighter mourning garments
before burial
are exempt from labor conscription.
When there are many deaths from severe contagion,
gather groups of youths,
beat drums and light torches,
to enter and use them in the official residences and wards.
Each beats drums and lights torches,
driving out from the official residences and wards.
The head of the household,
wearing his cap,
stands at the eastern steps.
When the task is done,
they exit the ward gate,
exit the city gate,
proceeding to the wilds.
This is the way to crawl and rescue from plague.
The same applies when an army is badly defeated.
19.28 Fasting means
thinking of where the deceased lived,
thinking of their laughter and speech,
thinking of their actions.
After three days of fasting,
one then sees the purpose of the fasting.
On the day of sacrifice,
as one is about to enter the door,
dimly as if seeing their countenance,
circling and exiting the door,
sighing as if hearing the sound of their sighs.
The visage of the ancestors does not fade from sight;
their voices, coughs, and spittle
do not fade from hearing;
their likes, dislikes, desires, and aversions
are not forgotten in the heart.
This is the fasting of a filial son.
19.29 Spring sacrifice is called cí,
summer sacrifice is called yuè,
autumn sacrifice is called cháng,
winter sacrifice is called zhēng.
In spring, offer leeks and eggs;
in summer, offer wheat and fish;
in autumn, offer millet and pork;
in winter, offer rice and wild geese.
Every three years, hold a xiá;
every five years, hold a dì.
Xiá means
to combine;
dì means
to scrutinize.
Xiá is
the great combined sacrifice in the ancestral temple;
dì is
scrutinizing their virtue to rank excellence.
When a sage ruler is about to sacrifice,
he must purify himself through fasting and concentrate his thoughts,
as if his parents were present,
just arising, not yet ascended,
earnestly and intently,
focusing his mind to envision his parents' likeness,
this is the sincerity of a filial son.
Those from all quarters assisting in the sacrifice,
who come empty return full,
who arrive void return substantial,
all taking this as their model.
19.30 Hán Hèzǐ was crossing the river,
the ferryman said:
"People crossing here
none fail to make an offering,
will you not do so?"
Hán Hèzǐ said:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to the spirits within the seas,
feudal lords sacrifice within their domains,
great officers sacrifice to their parents,
scholars sacrifice to their ancestors.
I, Hè, am not entitled to serve the River Earl."
The ferryman plied his oar,
water entered the boat and it drifted.
The ferryman said:
"Earlier I insisted on telling you,
but you, sir, did not heed my words.
Now water is in the boat and it drifts,
very perilous,
shall we prepare baggage and clothes to swim ashore?"
Hánzǐ said:
"I do not change my aim because others dislike me,
nor change my righteousness because I may die."
Before he finished speaking,
the boat moved smoothly on.
Hán Hèzǐ said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'Dense are the kudzu vines,
spreading over branches and stems,
genial and virtuous nobleman,
seek blessings without deviation.'
If even ghosts and spirits do not deviate,
how much more should men?"
19.31 Confucius said:
Rites without form
are reverence;
mourning without garments
is grief;
music without sound
is joy.
Without speaking, there is trust;
without moving, there is dignity;
without giving, there is benevolence—
this is due to intention.
The sound of bells and drums,
struck in anger is martial,
struck in sorrow is mournful,
struck in joy is happy.
When the intention changes,
the sound also changes.
If the intention is sincere,
it penetrates metal and stone,
how much more so people?
19.32 Gōng Mèngzǐgāo visited Zhuānsūn Zǐmò and said:
"May I ask about the rites of a nobleman?"
Zhuānsūn Zǐmò said:
"Discard your external show,
harmonize your inner self,
if expression overcomes and the heart follows it,
remove these three and it will suffice."
Gōng Mèng did not understand,
and told Zēngzǐ,
Zēngzǐ looked solemn, hesitated and said:
"Great are these words!
Those with external show must break internally,
those whose expression overcomes and heart follows
are sure to be enslaved by others.
Therefore, a nobleman completes his virtuous conduct yet appears unaware,
broad in knowledge and learning yet does not contend in speech,
subtle and penetrating in wisdom and thought yet capable of not being foolish."
19.33 Zēngzǐ was ill,
Mèng Yí went to inquire after him.
Zēngzǐ said:
"When a bird is about to die,
its song is mournful;
when a nobleman faces great departure,
his words are temperate.
In rites, there are three principles—
do you know them?"
He replied:
"I do not."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Sit,
and I will tell you.
A nobleman cultivates rites to establish his aim,
then greedy desires do not arise;
a nobleman reflects on rites to cultivate his person,
then negligence, laziness, disrespect, and carelessness do not come;
a nobleman cultivates rites with benevolence and righteousness,
then contentious, violent, and disorderly words are kept afar.
As for setting up vessels and stands,
arranging baskets and dishes,
these are the tasks of officials.
Even if a nobleman cannot do them,
it is acceptable."
19.34 Confucius said:
"Acceptable,
but simplistic."
Simplistic here means
rustic and uncultured.
Being rustic and uncultured means
lacking ritual refinement.
When Confucius visited Zǐsāng Bózi,
Zǐsāng Bózi received him without wearing formal hat and clothes.
His disciples asked:
"Why does our master visit this man?"
Confucius replied:
"His natural substance is excellent but lacks refinement,
I wish to persuade him to cultivate refinement."
After Confucius left,
Zǐsāng Bózi's disciples were displeased,
asking:
"Why did you receive Confucius?"
He answered:
"His natural substance is excellent but overly refined,
I wished to persuade him to discard some refinement."
Hence it is said:
One who cultivates both substance and refinement is called a gentleman;
one who has substance but no refinement is called rustic.
Zǐsāng Bózi being rustic
would reduce human relations to the level of oxen and horses,
therefore Zhònggōng said:
"Too simplistic."
Above, there was no enlightened Son of Heaven;
below, no worthy feudal lords;
the world was without the Way.
Ministers assassinated their rulers,
sons murdered their fathers.
If one had power to punish them,
it was acceptable to do so.
In Confucius' time,
there was no enlightened Son of Heaven above,
hence he said "Yōng could be made to face south."
Facing south
signifies the position of the Son of Heaven.
The reason Yōng earned this description
was his asking Confucius about Zǐsāng Bózi.
Confucius said:
"Acceptable,
but simplistic."
Zhònggōng replied:
"If one maintains reverence and governs with simplicity to guide the people,
would that not be acceptable?
But if one lives simply and governs simplistically,
would that not be too simplistic?"
The Master said:
"Yōng's words are correct."
Zhònggōng understood transformative arts,
Confucius was versed in the kingly way,
yet could find no improvement to Zhònggōng's words.
19.35 When Confucius reached outside the outer gate of Qí's capital,
he met a child carrying a pot,
walking together with him.
The child's gaze was pure,
his heart upright,
his behavior proper.
Confucius said to his driver:
"Quick, drive faster,
drive faster!
The Sháo music is beginning."
When Confucius arrived there and heard the Sháo music,
he did not notice the taste of meat for three months.
Thus music serves not only to please oneself,
but also to please others;
not only to rectify oneself,
but also to rectify others.
How great it is!
Those who experience this music
never imagined music could reach such heights.
19.36 The Yellow Emperor ordered Líng Lún to create musical pitches.
Líng Lún went west from Dàxià,
then to the northern slopes of Kūnlún,
gathered bamboo from Xiègǔ valley,
selecting pieces with evenly spaced nodes of uniform thickness,
cut between two joints,
making tubes nine inches long to blow through,
establishing the Huángzhōng pitch as the fundamental note,
called Hánshǎo,
then making twelve pipes.
At the foot of Kūnlún,
he listened to the phoenix's cries,
distinguishing the twelve pitches:
six from the male's song,
six from the female's song,
comparing them with the Huángzhōng pitch,
finding they matched the Huángzhōng pitch perfectly.
All could be generated from it,
forming the basis of the pitch system.
Therefore it is said:
Huángzhōng is subtle yet balanced, pure yet unharmful,
as the fundamental note it stands alone in honor,
symbolizing the great sage's virtue,
illuminating the utmost worthy's achievements.
Hence it is presented in ancestral temples,
singing to welcome virtuous accomplishments,
never forgotten through generations.
Thus Huángzhōng generates Línzhōng,
Línzhōng generates Dàlǚ,
Dàlǚ generates Yízé,
Yízé generates Tàicù,
Tàicù generates Nánlǚ,
Nánlǚ generates Jiázhōng,
Jiázhōng generates Wúyì,
Wúyì generates Gūxǐ,
Gūxǐ generates Yìngzhōng,
Yìngzhōng generates Ruíbīn.
Divide the generating pitch into three parts,
add one part for ascending generation;
divide the generating pitch into three parts,
subtract one part for descending generation.
Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Tàicù, Jiázhōng, Gūxǐ, Zhònglǚ, Ruíbīn are ascending;
Línzhōng, Yízé, Nánlǚ, Wúyì, Yìngzhōng are descending.
In the age of great sages and perfect governance,
heaven and earth's energies combine to produce winds.
As the sun reaches each position, it moves these winds,
generating the twelve pitches.
Thus at the winter solstice in midwinter,
Huángzhōng is generated;
late winter generates Dàlǚ;
early spring generates Tàicù;
midspring generates Jiázhōng;
late spring generates Gūxǐ;
early summer generates Zhònglǚ;
at the summer solstice in midsummer,
Ruíbīn is generated;
late summer generates Línzhōng;
early autumn generates Yízé;
midautumn generates Nánlǚ;
late autumn generates Wúyì;
early winter generates Yìngzhōng.
When heaven and earth's winds are proper,
the twelve pitches are perfectly established.
19.37 The sages created the táo drum, gǔ drum, qiāng, jié, xūn, and chí -
these six instruments
produce virtuous sounds.
Then with bells, chime stones, yú reed organs, and sè zithers they harmonize them,
then with shields, axes, ox-tail banners, and pheasant feathers they dance to them.
This is how they sacrifice in the temples of former kings,
this is how they offer and reciprocate toasts.
This establishes official ranks and social hierarchy appropriately,
this demonstrates to later generations the order of respect, seniority, and age.
19.38 Bell sounds are resounding,
resonance establishes commands,
commands establish authority,
authority establishes military spirit.
Gentlemen hearing bell sounds think of military officers.
Stone chimes are clear,
clarity establishes distinction,
distinction leads to readiness for death.
Gentlemen hearing chime sounds think of border-defending ministers.
Silk strings sound sorrowful,
sorrow establishes integrity,
integrity establishes resolve.
Gentlemen hearing qín and sè sounds think of principled ministers.
Bamboo instruments sound expansive,
expansiveness establishes gathering,
gathering assembles crowds.
Gentlemen hearing yú, shēng, xiāo, and guǎn sounds think of ministers who gather and store resources.
Drum sounds are exciting,
excitement establishes movement,
movement advances crowds.
Gentlemen hearing drum sounds think of commanding officers.
When gentlemen listen to music,
they don't just hear the melodious sounds -
they also find something that resonates with them.
19.39 Music is what the sages delighted in,
and it can improve the hearts of the people.
It deeply moves people,
transforms customs and practices,
hence the former kings emphasized its role in education.
People possess the nature of vitality and consciousness,
but lack constancy in sorrow, joy, anger, or pleasure;
they respond to external stimuli and are moved,
after which their mental dispositions take form.
Thus, when melancholic and distressed music is played,
the people become sorrowful;
when harmonious, flowing, and rhythmically rich music is played,
the people become content and joyful;
when harsh, forceful, and激昂 music is played,
the people become resolute and firm;
when upright, strong, dignified, and sincere music is played,
the people become respectful and reverent;
when generous, smooth, and harmoniously moving music is played,
the people become kind and loving;
when decadent, dissolute, and chaotic music is played,
the people become licentious and disorderly.
Therefore, the former kings based it on human emotions and nature,
examined it through measures and numbers,
regulated it with ritual and righteousness,
embraced the harmony of vital energy,
guided the conduct of the five constant virtues,
making it yang without dissipation,
yin without闭塞,
strong气 without anger,
soft气 without fear,
with the four通畅交互 within and manifesting outwardly,
all maintaining their positions without encroaching on each other.
Then they established levels of learning,
broadened its rhythms,
refined its patterns,
to measure moral depth.
They balanced the proportions of large and small,
arranged the sequence of beginnings and ends,
to symbolize affairs and conduct,
making the principles of closeness and distance, nobility and baseness, elder and younger, male and female
all visible in music.
Hence it is said:
"Music,
observe its depth!"
If the soil is impoverished, grass and trees will not grow;
if the waters are troubled, fish and turtles will not grow large;
if the vital energy declines, living things will not thrive;
if the age is chaotic, rituals become corrupt and music becomes excessive.
Therefore, its sound is sorrowful but not dignified,
joyful but not tranquil,
careless and violating rhythm,
drifting and forgetting the root.
Broad, it容纳奸邪;
narrow, it stirs desires;
evoking restless energy and extinguishing the virtue of peace,
thus the gentleman despises it.
Whenever corrupt sounds move people, perverse energy responds;
when perverse energy takes form, decadent music arises.
When upright sounds move people, harmonious energy responds;
when harmonious energy takes form, harmonious music arises.
Singing and responding correspond,
deviations and rectitude each return to their place,
and the principles of all things
each move according to their kind.
Therefore, the gentleman returns to his nature to harmonize his will,
compares with categories to perfect his conduct.
He does not accustom his ears to corrupt sounds and disorderly sights,
does not allow decadent music and corrupt rituals into his heart,
does not let lazy, arrogant, and perverse energies inhabit his body,
making ears, eyes, nose, mouth, mind, and all parts follow harmony and correctness to practice righteousness,
then expresses it through sounds,
adorns it with qín and sè,
moves with shields and axes,
decorates with feathers and ox-tails,
accompanies with pipes,
arousing the light of ultimate virtue,
moving the harmony of the four energies,
to manifest the principles of all things.
Thus, its clarity resembles heaven,
its vastness resembles earth,
its beginning and end resemble the four seasons,
its revolutions resemble wind and rain;
five colors form patterns without chaos,
eight winds follow pitch pipes without deviation,
all measures attain numbers with constancy;
small and large complete each other,
beginning and end generate each other,
high and low, clear and turbid,
alternate to form the warp.
Thus, when music is practiced, human relations are clear,
ears and eyes are sharp and clear,
vital energy is peaceful,
customs are transformed,
all under heaven is tranquil.
Hence it is said:
"Music is joy."
The gentleman delights in obtaining the Way,
the petty person delights in satisfying desires.
Using the Way to control desires,
then there is joy without disorder;
forgetting the Way for desires,
then there is confusion without joy.
Therefore, the gentleman returns to his nature to harmonize his intent,
broadens music to complete its teaching,
so when music is practiced, the people turn toward direction,
and virtue can be observed.
Virtue is the pinnacle of nature;
music is the flower of virtue;
metal, stone, silk, and bamboo are the instruments of music.
Poetry expresses its intent;
song prolongs its sound;
dance moves its form.
These three originate from the heart,
and then the energy of music follows.
Thus, when emotion is deep, patterns are brilliant;
when energy is abundant, transformation is spiritual;
harmony and smoothness accumulate within and splendor blossoms outward—
only music cannot be falsified.
Music is the movement of the heart;
sound is the image of music;
patterns and rhythms are the adornment of sound.
The gentleman moves its root,
delights in its image,
then orders its adornment.
Therefore, first drumming to warn and alert,
three steps to show direction,
repeating the beginning to emphasize progression,
returning to disorder to adorn the conclusion,
vigorous yet not excessive,
profoundly subtle yet not obscure.
He delights solely in his will,
never weary of the Way;
fully practicing the Way,
not indulging his desires.
Thus, emotion is revealed and righteousness established,
music ends and virtue is honored.
The gentleman thereby loves goodness,
the petty person thereby掩盖 his faults.
Hence it is said:
"In the way of nurturing the people,
music is of great importance."
19.40 Among instruments suitable for refined cultivation, the qín is most appropriate.
Gentlemen approach it because it can cultivate virtue.
All music arises from the human heart.
The movement of the human heart is caused by external things.
Moved by things, it then manifests in sound;
sounds correspond and produce variation;
variation formed into patterns is called melody;
setting melody to music, along with shields, axes, feathers, and ox-tails, is called yuè (music).
Music is what is produced from melody,
its root lies in the human heart being moved by things.
Thus, when a sorrowful heart is moved, the sound is焦急 and fading;
when a joyful heart is moved, the sound is舒缓 and gentle;
when a delighted heart is moved, the sound is expansive and scattered;
when an angry heart is moved, the sound is forceful and harsh;
when a respectful heart is moved, the sound is straight and upright;
when a loving heart is moved, the sound is harmonious and tuned.
Good and evil in people are not innate,
but arise from being moved by things;
hence the former kings were cautious about what influenced them.
Thus, ritual stabilizes their intentions,
music harmonizes their nature,
governance unifies their conduct,
punishment prevents their transgressions.
Ritual, music, punishment, and governance
share the same ultimate goal:
to unite the people's hearts and establish the way of order.
19.41 All music originates from the human heart.
When emotions stir within, they take form in sound;
when sounds are patterned, they are called music.
Therefore, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
reflecting harmonious governance;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
reflecting perverse governance;
the music of a perishing state is sorrowful and pensive,
reflecting the hardship of its people.
The way of sound and music
is interconnected with governance.
Gōng represents the ruler,
shāng represents the officials,
jué represents the people,
zhǐ represents affairs,
yǔ represents things.
If these five notes are disordered, there is no standard.
The music without standards:
if gōng is disordered, it becomes wild,
indicating the ruler's arrogance;
if shāng is disordered, it becomes uneven,
indicating the corruption of officials;
if jué is disordered, it becomes mournful,
indicating the people's resentment;
if zhǐ is disordered, it becomes sorrowful,
indicating excessive toil in affairs;
if yǔ is disordered, it becomes perilous,
indicating scarcity of resources.
If all five are disordered,
and they encroach upon each other, it is called dissolution.
In such a case,
the state's destruction is imminent.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi
is the music of a chaotic age,
comparable to dissolution.
The music of Sāngjiān and Púshàng
is the music of a perishing state;
its governance is fragmented,
its people are adrift,
and deceit toward superiors and pursuit of selfish desires become unstoppable.
19.42 Whenever people suffer calamities and misfortunes,
they arise from licentiousness, excess, violence, and arrogance.
The root of licentiousness, excess, violence, and arrogance
lies in drinking alcohol.
Therefore, the ancients were cautious about the rituals of drinking,
making the ears listen to elegant music,
the eyes behold proper demeanor,
the feet walk with correct posture,
and the mind discuss the right path.
Thus, they could drink all day without fault.
In the short term over days,
in the long term over months,
all would cultivate virtue through this to enhance goodness.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Drunk with wine,
satiated with virtue."
This refers to this.
19.43 Of all things that enter from without,
none penetrate deeper than sound,
transforming people most profoundly.
Therefore, the sages shaped it with virtue, calling it music.
Music
is the wind of virtue.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Dignified and solemn in demeanor,
virtuous and orderly in sound."
This refers to ritual and music.
Thus, the nobleman uses ritual to rectify the external,
and music to rectify the internal.
If internally one departs from music even briefly,
then evil influences arise;
if externally one departs from ritual even briefly,
then arrogant behavior emerges.
Therefore, the ancient emperors and lords listened to bell sounds,
never leaving the court;
ministers and officials listened to qín and sè,
never leaving their presence,
so as to nurture a righteous heart and eliminate corrupting influences.
When music moves within,
it makes people easily follow the Way and love goodness;
when music manifests outwardly,
it makes people warm, respectful, and refined.
The sounds of Yǎ and Sòng move people, and upright energy responds;
harmonious and accomplished, graceful sounds move people, and harmonious energy responds;
harsh, fierce, and violent sounds move people, and angry energy responds;
the sounds of Zhèng and Wèi move people, and licentious energy responds.
Therefore, the nobleman is cautious about what he uses to move others.
19.44 Zǐlù played the sè with the tones of the northern borders.
Confucius heard it and said:
"Indeed,
Yóu is untalented."
Rǎn Yǒu was in attendance,
and Confucius said:
"Qiú, come here.
Why don't you tell Yóu?
The ancient kings' creation of music
involved playing central tones
and maintaining central rhythm,
flowing toward the south,
not returning to the north.
The south is the region of life and growth,
the north is the domain of killing and conquest.
Thus, the nobleman holds to the center as the foundation,
and focuses on life as the basis.
Therefore, his music is gentle and harmonious, centered,
symbolizing the energy of life and growth.
Feelings of sorrow, grief, and pain
do not touch his heart;
actions of violence, harshness, licentiousness, and wildness
do not reside in his body.
Such is the atmosphere of order and preservation,
the work of peace and joy.
Petty men are not like this;
they grasp the trivial to discuss the fundamental,
and focus on harshness as the basis.
Therefore, their music is shrill, harsh, and petty,
symbolizing the energy of killing and conquest.
Feelings of harmony, moderation, centrality, and uprightness
do not touch their hearts;
actions of warmth, dignity, respect, and solemnity
do not reside in their bodies.
Such killing
is the atmosphere of chaos and destruction,
the work of defeat and flight.
In the past, Shùn created the sounds of the southern wind;
his rise was sudden and great,
and to this day, kings and lords speak of it without ceasing;
Zhòu made the sounds of the northern borders;
his fall was swift,
and to this day, kings and lords laugh about it.
That Shùn, as a common man,
accumulated uprightness and embodied benevolence,
trod the central path and practiced goodness, and ultimately rose;
Zhòu, as the Son of Heaven,
loved arrogance, licentiousness, and wildness,
was harsh, violent, and cruel, and ultimately perished.
Now Yóu is but a common man,
a lowly cloth-robed fellow,
who not only disregards the system of the ancient kings
but also plays the music of a perishing state.
How can he preserve his seven-foot body?"
Rǎn Yǒu told Zǐlù this.
Zǐlù said:
"It is Yóu's fault.
A petty man is incapable,
and having fallen into this state,
the Master's words are fitting!"
Thereupon he repented,
refrained from eating,
and after seven days, was nothing but skin and bones.
Confucius said:
"Yóu's reform
goes too far."
20.1 Confucius divined
and obtained the hexagram "Bì".
He sighed, looking up,
feeling unsettled.
Zǐ Zhāng approached,
raised his hand, and asked:
"I have heard that 'Bì' is an auspicious hexagram; why do you sigh over it?"
Confucius said:
"Bì
is not a true color,
hence I sigh.
I think of substance:
plain,
white should be pure white,
black should be pure black.
What, then, is substance?
I have also heard
that vermilion lacquer needs no pattern,
white jade needs no carving,
precious pearls need no adornment.
Why?
When substance is abundant,
it does not receive adornment."
20.2 Those who believe in ghosts and spirits lose their strategies,
and those who believe in auspicious days miss their opportunities.
How do we know this is so?
The sages and worthies possess comprehensive knowledge,
and can achieve success without relying on specific days or times;
they respect laws and decrees,
value merits and achievements,
and remain fortunate without divination;
they are careful with benevolence and righteousness,
follow principles and reason,
and receive blessings without praying at temples.
Therefore, performing numerous divinations, selecting dates,
purifying through fasting,
fattening sacrificial animals,
adorning with jade tablets,
and meticulously conducting sacrifices
ultimately cannot eliminate the calamity of rebellion.
If one serves deities believing they are aware,
yet intends to act recklessly against the Way,
and seeks blessings through sacrifices,
the deities will surely oppose it.
The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the Five Sacred Mountains, and the Four Great Rivers;
feudal lords sacrifice to the gods of soil and grain;
high officials sacrifice to the five household gods;
scholars sacrifice at their gates and doors;
commoners sacrifice to their ancestors.
The sage kings, in accordance with the will of Heaven,
established rituals to define distinctions.
In ancient times, those who selected days for divination
aimed to assist in resolving doubts through the Way,
showing precedence and not daring to act arbitrarily,
not seeking to secure safety through perverse evils.
Confucius said:
"To sacrifice to spirits not one's own is flattery."
Thus, Mount Tài never accepted the sacrifices of the Jì family.
The Yì jīng states, "The eastern neighbor's sacrifice of an ox
is not as good as the western neighbor's simple offering,"
emphasizing that what matters is the reverence in the ritual, not the value of the offerings,
valuing sincerity over extravagance.
With genuine virtue and its extension,
one can succeed anywhere.
Therefore, when sages observe people's outward refinement,
they must examine their inner substance.
20.3 The farmers at Lìshān were prone to encroaching on each other's fields,
so Shùn went to plow there;
the fishermen at Léizé often fought over fishing grounds,
so Shùn went to fish there;
the pottery in the eastern regions was of poor quality,
so Shùn went to make pottery there.
Thus, plowing, fishing, and pottery were not Shùn's original duties,
but he undertook them
to remedy these failings.
Human nature often cannot overcome desires,
leading them to abandon substance for superficiality,
hence the production of inferior utensils
and the outbreak of conflicts,
and once conflicts arise,
deceit follows.
Why is this so?
It is because they turn from sincerity to deceit,
forsaking simplicity for falsity,
chasing after trivialities without rest.
If sages restrain the ornamental and uphold the substantial,
the world will return to its roots.
20.4 The Shī jīng says:
"The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree,
with its seven young ones;
the good and noble person,
their demeanor is uniform."
The commentary states:
The reason the cuckoo can nurture its seven young
is its single-mindedness;
the reason the noble person can govern all things
is their consistent principle.
Governing things with one principle
is the mind of Heaven.
When the five elements do not separate,
but unite as one,
it is called the mind of Heaven.
If we can deeply anchor our intentions in oneness,
then one heart can serve a hundred rulers,
but a hundred hearts cannot serve one ruler;
thus, sincerity is not far away.
Sincerity is oneness,
and oneness is substance;
though the noble person may have outward refinement,
it never departs from inner substance.
20.5 In Wèi, there were five old men
who carried jars to the well
to water leeks,
managing only one plot all day.
Dèng Xī passed by,
got off his carriage, and advised them:
"Make a machine,
heavy at the back,
light at the front,
called a lever;
you could water leeks all day,
covering a hundred plots without tiring."
The five old men said:
"Our teacher said:
'Where there is the cleverness of machinery,
there will be the failure of machinery.'
It's not that we don't know,
but we do not wish to do it.
You may go on your way;
we will water with single-mindedness,
and will not change."
Dèng Xī left,
and after traveling several dozen lǐ,
his expression was displeased,
feeling troubled.
His disciple said:
"Who are these people to resent you, my lord?
Allow me to kill them for you."
Dèng Xī said:
"Let them be.
They are what are called true men;
they can be entrusted to guard the state."
20.6 Qín Gǔlí asked Mòzǐ, saying:
"What use are embroidered silks and fine linens?"
Mòzǐ replied:
"Alas!
These are not our proper concerns.
In ancient times, there were those who achieved success without ornamentation—
Xià Yǔ was such a man.
He built humble, small palaces,
reduced and simplified his diet,
had earthen steps of only three levels,
and wore clothing of plain cloth.
In that era,
elaborate embroidery had no use, and the focus was on durability and strength.
Yīn's Pángēng
enlarged his ancestral king's residence
yet moved the capital to Yīn,
leaving the thatched roofs untrimmed
and the wooden rafters uncarved,
to change how the world viewed things.
At that time,
where would brocaded silks
have been applied?
The common people have no fixed mind of their own
but take the ruler's as their guide.
If those above do not act,
how would those below use such things?
These two kings led by personal example for all under heaven,
hence their influence flourished in their time,
and their fame endures to this day.
Moreover, embroidered silks and fine linens
are creations of chaotic rulers,
their origin all arising from Qí.
Duke Jǐng delighted in extravagance and forgot frugality;
fortunately, Yànzǐ was there to admonish him with frugality,
yet it was almost not enough to prevail.
How can extravagance ever be exhausted?
Zhòu built the Lùtái terrace and a hill of dregs,
pools of wine and forests of meat,
palace walls painted with patterns,
carved and engraved,
brocades covering the halls,
gold and jade treasures,
women and performers,
bells, drums, pipes, and strings—
indulgence unchecked,
while the world grew increasingly depleted.
Thus, he ultimately met personal death and the state's ruin,
condemned by all under heaven.
Was it not precisely because of the use of embroidered silks and fine linens?
Now, in a year of famine,
suppose someone wanted to give you the Pearl of the Marquis of Suí,
saying:
'You cannot sell it;
it is a treasure to be used as an ornament.'
Another wanted to give you a zhōng of grain.
If you take the pearl, you cannot have the grain;
if you take the grain, you cannot have the pearl.
Which would you choose?"
Qín Gǔlí said:
"I would take the grain,
for it can relieve poverty."
Mòzǐ said:
"Indeed, so.
Then why engage in extravagance,
promoting the useless,
indulging in frivolous excess?
These are not the urgent matters of the sage.
Thus, one must first have constant fullness in eating,
then seek refinement;
one must first have constant warmth in clothing,
then seek beauty;
one must first have constant security in dwelling,
then seek pleasure.
To act in ways that can be sustained,
to conduct oneself in ways that can endure,
substance first and ornament later—
this is the task of the sage."
Qín Gǔlí said:
"Well said."
20.7 After Qín Shǐ Huáng had unified the empire,
he became extremely extravagant and wasteful.
Even in the thirty-fifth year of his reign, he did not cease,
constructing the Grand Imperial Highway,
which stretched from Jiǔyuán to Yúnyáng,
cutting through mountains and filling valleys,
making a direct route.
Dissatisfied with the smallness of the former kings' palaces,
he then between Fēng and Hào,
the locations of King Wén and King Wǔ,
built a court palace in the Shanglin Park south of the Wèi River.
First, he constructed the front hall, Ēpáng,
five hundred paces from east to west,
fifty zhang from north to south,
capable of seating ten thousand people above,
and below, able to hoist a flag of five zhang.
Surrounding it were elevated passageways,
stretching straight from the hall's base to the Southern Mountains.
The peaks of the Southern Mountains were marked as gate towers.
He built elevated roads,
crossing the Wèi River from Ēpáng,
connecting to Xiányáng,
to mirror the celestial pole's passage across the Milky Way to the Encampment constellation.
He also initiated the project at Líshān,
sealing it deep to the bottom of three springs.
Within the Guānzhōng region, he built three hundred detached palaces,
and outside Guānzhōng, four hundred,
all furnished with bells, chimes, curtains, and canopies,
as well as women, singers, and actors.
He erected a stone gate tower on the Qú Mountain boundary by the Eastern Sea,
to serve as the eastern gate of Qín.
At this time, the fangshi Hán visitor Hóu Shēng and Qí visitor Lú Shēng conspired together, saying:
"These times are unfit to live in;
the emperor delights in using punishments and executions to assert his might,
while those below fear punishment and cling to their salaries,
none daring to be fully loyal.
The emperor hears no faults and grows more arrogant daily,
and those below, cowed, resort to flattery and deceit to gain favor,
advisers are not heeded,
and the deviation from the right path worsens,
if we stay long,
we will be harmed."
So they fled together.
Upon hearing this, Qín Shǐ Huáng
was greatly enraged and said:
"I once treated Lú Shēng generously,
honoring him with rank and employing him,
yet now he slanders me.
I hear many scholars spread evil words,
to mislead the common people."
He then ordered the censors to round up all the scholars,
and through mutual accusations, over 460 scholars implicated in breaking the law
were all buried alive.
Lú Shēng was not caught, but Hóu Shēng was later captured.
Qín Shǐ Huáng heard of it,
summoned and saw him,
ascending the Ādōng Tower,
overlooking the four-way street,
intending to condemn and have him torn apart by chariots.
Seeing Hóu Shēng, Qín Shǐ Huáng
angrily said:
"You old villain, wicked,
slandering your lord,
how dare you face me again!"
When Hóu Shēng arrived,
he looked up at the tower and said:
"I have heard that one who knows death is bound to be brave;
will Your Majesty listen to one word from me?"
Qín Shǐ Huáng said:
"What do you wish to say?
Speak."
Hóu Shēng said:
"I heard that Yǔ set up a slander pole,
wishing to know his errors.
Now, Your Majesty is extravagant and has lost the root,
indulgent and drawn to trivialities.
Palaces, towers, and pavilions,
connected and piled high;
pearls, jade, and precious treasures,
accumulated into hills;
brocades, embroideries, and patterned silks,
fill the storehouses to excess;
women, singers, and actors,
number in the tens of thousands;
music of bells and drums,
flows endlessly;
fine wines and delicacies,
spread in abundance before you;
clothing light and warm,
carriages and horses adorned.
All that serves your comfort,
is splendid and dazzling,
beyond measure.
The common people are exhausted,
their strength depleted,
yet you remain unaware.
Moreover, you are quick to punish slander,
sternly intimidating those below,
resulting in mute subjects and a deaf ruler,
which is why we left.
We do not regret our own lives,
but lament the impending fall of Your Majesty's state!
I have heard that the wise kings of old,
ate only until full,
wore only until warm,
dwelled in palaces just sufficient,
and used carriages and horses only for travel.
Thus, they were not abandoned by Heaven above,
nor by the common people below.
Yáo had thatched roofs untrimmed,
rough-hewn rafters uncarved,
earthen steps of three levels,
yet he was content his whole life,
because he valued simplicity over ornamentation.
Dān Zhū was arrogant and cruel,
fond of indulgence and excess,
neglecting governance and transformation,
and thus did not rise.
Now, Your Majesty's excesses,
surpass Dān Zhū ten thousandfold and overshadow Kūnwú, Jié, and Zhòu a thousandfold;
I fear that for Your Majesty, ten parts are lost and not one remains."
Qín Shǐ Huáng remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"Why did you not speak earlier?"
Hóu Shēng replied:
"Your Majesty's mind,
was soaring on blue clouds,
floating amidst displays of literary elegance,
considering yourself wise and strong,
insulting the Five Emperors above,
oppressing the Three Kings below,
abandoning simplicity,
embracing superficial skills,
the signs of Your Majesty's downfall have been evident for long.
We feared speaking would be futile,
and only lead to our own deaths,
so we fled and dared not speak.
Now that I face certain death,
I thus state this to Your Majesty,
though I cannot prevent your fall,
I wish to make you aware of it."
Qín Shǐ Huáng asked:
"Can I change?"
Hóu Shēng said:
"The form is already set;
Your Majesty can only sit and await ruin!
If you wish to change,
can you be like Yáo or Yǔ?
If not,
there is no hope.
Your assistants are also unfit,
I fear even change cannot save it."
Qín Shǐ Huáng sighed deeply,
and then released him without execution.
Three years later,
Qín Shǐ Huáng died,
the Second Emperor ascended the throne,
and in three years, Qín fell.
20.8 Wèi Wén Hóu asked Lǐ Kè:
"From where do punishments and penalties originate?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"They arise from wicked, immoral, and licentious behavior.
All wicked intentions
stem from hunger and cold;
licentiousness
is the deceit born of prolonged hunger.
Carving and engraving patterns
harm agricultural work;
weaving brocades and ornate ribbons
injure women's labor.
If farming is harmed,
it is the root of hunger;
if women's work is injured,
it is the source of cold.
When hunger and cold come together,
and one can avoid turning to wickedness,
it has never happened.
When men and women adorn themselves to show off,
and can remain without licentiousness,
it has never been so.
Therefore, if the ruler does not restrict craftsmanship,
the state will be poor and the people extravagant;
with a poor state and extravagant people,
the poor will commit wicked acts,
and the wealthy will indulge in licentiousness,
thus driving the people to evil.
When the people turn to evil,
and laws are enforced to punish them,
without pardoning their crimes,
it is setting a trap for the people.
The origin of punishments has a source;
if the ruler does not block the root but instead attacks the branches,
it is a way to harm the state!"
Wèi Wén Hóu said:
"Well said."
And adopted it as a guiding principle.
20.9 Duke Mù of Qín casually asked Yóu Yú:
"The wise kings and sage emperors of ancient times,
how did they gain or lose their states,
and what was the reason?"
Yóu Yú replied:
"I have heard that
they gained them through frugality,
and lost them through extravagance."
Duke Mù said:
"I wish to hear about the principles of extravagance and frugality."
Yóu Yú said:
"I heard that when Yáo possessed the empire,
he ate from earthenware bowls,
drank from earthenware vessels,
yet his territory extended south to Jiāozhǐ,
north to Yōudū,
and east-west to where the sun and moon rise and set,
with none failing to submit.
When Yáo relinquished the empire,
and Shùn received it,
he made eating vessels
by cutting and shaping wood,
smelting copper and iron to sharpen their edges,
and lacquering them black for use as food containers,
but the feudal lords considered this more extravagant,
and thirteen states became insubordinate.
When Shùn relinquished the empire and Yǔ received it,
he made sacrificial vessels,
lacquering the outside and painting the inside vermilion,
using silk for cushions,
with wine cups and ladles colorfully decorated,
this was even more extravagant,
and thirty-two states became insubordinate.
After the Xià dynasty perished,
and Yīn and Zhōu received it,
they made grand vessels,
erected nine banners,
carved and polished eating vessels,
engraved wine cups and ladles,
adorned four walls with four curtains,
and embroidered mats with patterns,
this was even more extravagant,
and fifty-two states became insubordinate.
If the ruler favors ornate decorations,
those who submit will become more extravagant.
Therefore it is said:
Frugality is the Way."
After Yóu Yú left,
Duke Mù summoned his Neishǐ Liào and told him:
"I have heard that when a neighboring state has a sage,
it is a worry for rival states.
Now Yóu Yú is a sage,
I am troubled by this,
what should I do?"
Neishǐ Liào said:
"The Róng people are remote and distant,
and have not heard the music of the Central States.
You should send them female musicians,
to disrupt their governance,
and generously request an extension for Yóu Yú,
to create distance between them.
When there is a rift between ruler and minister,
then you can make your move."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
So he sent three groups of nine female musicians to the Róng king,
and requested an extension for Yóu Yú.
The Róng king agreed,
and indeed upon seeing the female musicians grew fond of them,
setting up banquets and listening to music,
not moving for a whole year,
with half his horses, cattle, and sheep dying.
Yóu Yú returned to remonstrate,
but his advice was not heeded,
so he left and went to Qín,
where Duke Mù welcomed him and appointed him as chief minister,
asking about the military situation and geographical advantages.
Having obtained this information,
he raised an army and attacked them,
annexing twelve states,
and expanding territory by a thousand li.
Duke Mù, though an extravagant ruler,
could listen to worthies and accept advice,
thus he dominated the Western Róng.
The Western Róng, indulging in pleasure,
seduced by profit,
lost their state,
because they departed from simplicity."
20.10 Jīng Hóu went to visit the crown prince of Wèi,
wearing a feathered jade sword on his left,
and jade pendants on his right,
the left shining on the right,
the right shining on the left.
After sitting for a while,
the crown prince neither looked at them,
nor asked about them.
Jīng Hóu said:
"Does the state of Wèi also have treasures?"
The crown prince said:
"Yes."
Jīng Hóu said:
"What are these treasures like?"
The crown prince said:
"The ruler's trustworthiness and ministers' loyalty,
the people's support for their superiors,
these are the treasures of Wèi."
Jīng Hóu said:
"What I asked about
was not this kind,
but rather about objects."
The crown prince said:
"Yes,
there is Túshī Zhǎo who governs Wèi,
and the markets have no inflated prices;
Qìe Xīn who governs Yáng,
and lost items are not picked up on the roads;
Máng Mǎo who serves at court,
and worthy men from neighboring states all come to visit.
These three great officers
are the great treasures of Wèi."
At this, Jīng Hóu fell silent and did not respond,
removed the jade sword from his left,
took off the pendants from his right,
left them on his seat,
stood up ashamed,
silently without bidding farewell,
hurried out,
got in his carriage and drove away.
The crown prince of Wèi sent horsemen carrying the sword and pendants to catch up with Jīng Hóu,
having them tell Jīng Hóu:
"I lack the virtue to treasure what cannot be preserved by pearls and jades,
these cannot be worn when cold,
nor eaten when hungry,
do not leave me with harmful things."
Thereupon Jīng Hóu secluded himself and did not go out,
and was reported to have died.
20.11 Duke Píng of Jìn made a racing chariot,
with dragon banners of various colors,
adorned with rhinoceros and elephant [designs],
inlaid with feathers and auspicious herbs.
When the chariot was completed,
he set a price of a thousand yi of gold,
placed it below the palace steps,
and ordered his ministers to come view it.
Tián Chà passed by three times without a single glance.
Duke Píng, enraged, changed countenance and asked Tián Chà:
"You passed by three times without a single glance,
why is that?"
Tián Chà replied:
"I have heard that one pleases the Son of Heaven with the empire,
pleases feudal lords with their states,
pleases senior officials with their offices,
pleases scholars with affairs,
pleases farmers with food,
pleases women with weaving.
Jié was destroyed by extravagance,
Zhòu fell by dissipation,
therefore I dare not look."
Duke Píng said:
"Well said."
Then he ordered his attendants:
"Remove the chariot."
20.12 The royal granary of Marquis Wén of Wèi caught fire.
Marquis Wén donned plain mourning garments,
avoided the main hall,
and for five days,
all his ministers also wore plain clothes to offer condolences.
Only Gōngzǐ Chéngfù did not come to condole.
When Marquis Wén returned to the main hall,
Gōngzǐ Chéngfù hurried in to congratulate him, saying:
"This is truly excellent,
the fire in the royal granary."
Marquis Wén changed countenance and said displeasedly:
"The royal granary
is where I store my treasures.
Now it has suffered a fire disaster,
I have donned plain garments,
avoided the main hall,
and all ministers have worn plain clothes to condole,
yet you, sir, did not come to condole.
Now that I have already returned to the hall,
why do you still come to congratulate me?"
Gōngzǐ Chéngfù said:
"I have heard it said:
The Son of Heaven stores his treasures throughout the four seas,
feudal lords store theirs within their domains,
high officials store theirs in their homes,
scholars and commoners store theirs in boxes and chests.
If treasures are not stored in their proper places,
if there is no natural disaster,
there will surely be human calamity.
Now fortunately there is no human calamity,
but only a natural disaster,
is that not excellent?"
Marquis Wén sighed deeply and said:
"Well said."
20.13 Duke Huán of Qí said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"My state is very small,
and our financial resources are very limited,
yet my ministers' clothing, carriages, and horses are extremely extravagant.
I wish to prohibit this,
is it permissible?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I have heard it said:
What the ruler tastes,
the ministers will eat;
what the ruler favors,
the ministers will wear.
Now, when you eat,
it must be cinnamon-flavored broth,
you wear robes of refined purple silk,
and furs of white fox,
this is why your ministers are so excessively luxurious.
The Book of Songs says:
'If he does not personally act,
the common people will not believe.'
If you wish to prohibit extravagance,
why not start with yourself?"
Duke Huán said:
"Well said."
Thereupon he changed to wearing robes of plain silk,
and a plain white cap.
After one year at court, the state of Qí became frugal.
20.14 Jì Wénzǐ served as prime minister of Lǔ.
His concubines did not wear silk,
his horses did not eat grain.
Zhòngsūn Tuó remonstrated, saying:
"You are the chief minister of Lǔ,
yet your concubines do not wear silk,
your horses do not eat grain.
People will think you are stingy,
and that you do not bring splendor to the state."
Wénzǐ said:
"Is that so?
I observe that the parents of our state's people
wear coarse clothes and eat simple vegetables,
therefore I dare not do otherwise.
Moreover, I have heard that a gentleman brings splendor to the state through virtue,
not through his concubines and horses.
Virtue
benefits both myself and others,
therefore it can be practiced.
If one indulges in luxury and extravagance,
sinks into ornate appearances,
and cannot restrain oneself,
how can one protect the state?"
Zhòngsūn Tuó withdrew in shame.
20.15 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ rode in worn-out carriages with lean horses,
and wore sheepskin furs.
His steward remonstrated, saying:
"New carriages are safer,
fat horses travel faster,
white fox furs are warm and light,
you should change these."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"It's not that I don't know this.
I have heard it said:
When a gentleman wears fine clothes, he becomes more humble,
but when a petty person wears fine clothes, he becomes more arrogant.
Now I maintain this humble preparation
for fear of developing the heart of a petty person."
The Tradition says:
"The more honorable Duke Zhōu's position became, the more humble he was;
the more enemies he defeated, the more fearful he became;
the wealthier his family became, the more frugal he was.
Therefore, the Zhōu dynasty lasted over eight hundred years."
This refers to this principle.
20.16 When Lǔ was building the Láng park,
Jì Píngzǐ wanted it completed quickly.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"What's the use of rushing its completion
by oppressing the people?
Is that permissible?
It would be better to have no park
than to have no people.
How can we bear to hear of pleasure excursions
that exhaust the people from their proper governance?"
20.17 Shūsūn Wénzǐ of Wèi asked Wángsūn Xià:
"The temple of my late lord is too small,
I wish to rebuild it,
is this permissible?"
He replied:
"The gentlemen of old
regarded frugality as propriety,
but gentlemen today
replace it with extravagance.
Though Wèi is poor,
could we not exchange one pair of patterned shoes
for ten embroidered ceremonial robes?
But this would be considered improper."
Wénzǐ then abandoned the plan.
20.18 Duke Wén of Jìn assembled the feudal lords and made a covenant, saying:
"I have heard that when a state becomes disordered,
it is not due to music and women,
but inevitably due to corrupt profits.
Those who delight in music and women
are licentious,
those greedy for corrupt gains
are deluded.
A state that is licentious and deluded
will either perish or be crippled.
From now on,
let no one allow beautiful concubines to alienate his wife,
let no one allow music to interfere with governance,
let no one allow private affairs to harm public duty,
let no one use goods and profits to tempt inferiors.
Those who have such practices
are called those who cut at the root and foundation,
letting it flow to the flowers and leaves.
If this happens, they will have troubles without relief,
and enemies without quelling.
Those who do not comply with these words will be shown the covenant."
Thereupon, gentlemen who heard this said:
"Does Duke Wén not understand the Way?
That he did not become king
was only because he lacked proper support."
20.19 Yànzǐ was hosting Duke Jǐng at a drinking party.
As dusk fell,
the duke called for torches to be prepared.
Yànzǐ declined, saying:
"The Book of Songs says:
'How the tilted cap slopes,'
speaking of loss of virtue.
'Repeatedly dancing, unrestrained,'
speaking of loss of decorum.
'Drunk with wine,
satiated with virtue.'
'When drunk, one should leave,
then both receive blessing,'
this is the ritual between host and guest.
'If drunk but does not leave,
this is called harming virtue,'
this is the fault of both host and guest.
I, Yìng, have divined for the day,
but not for the night."
The duke said:
"Well said."
He raised his cup in offering,
bowed twice, and departed.
He said:
"How could I find fault with him?
I have entrusted the state to Yànzǐ.
Though his household is poor,
he serves me well,
not wishing me to indulge in extravagance,
how much more so when he counsels with me on state affairs!"
20.20 Yáng Wángsūn fell ill and was near death,
when he instructed his son, saying:
"Upon my death, I wish to be buried naked,
to return to my true essence.
You must not alter my intention."
Marquis Qí heard of this
and went to admonish him, saying:
"I have privately heard that you, Wángsūn, have ordered your burial
to be conducted naked into the earth.
If it must be as I have heard,
I foolishly believe it should not be done.
If the dead have no consciousness, then it ends there;
but if the dead do have consciousness,
this would be to desecrate the corpse underground.
How then would one face one's ancestors?
I foolishly believe it should not be done."
Wángsūn replied:
"I intend to use this to rectify the world.
Extravagant burials truly offer no benefit to the deceased,
yet the world competes to outdo one another in this,
squandering wealth and exhausting resources,
only to let them rot underground.
Some are buried today and unearthed tomorrow—
how does this truly differ from exposing bones in the wilderness?!
Moreover, the deceased
represent the transformation at life's end,
the return of beings to their origin.
Those who return attain their destination,
and those who transform achieve change,
this is each thing returning to its true essence.
That true essence is dark and obscure,
looking at it, it has no form,
listening to it, it has no sound,
thus it aligns with the nature of the Dào.
To adorn the exterior to boast to the crowd,
and use lavish burials to distort the truth,
causing those who should return not to reach their destination,
and those who should transform not to achieve change,
this is to make each thing lose its natural state.
Furthermore, I have heard:
the spiritual essence
belongs to Heaven.
The physical form
belongs to Earth.
When the spiritual essence departs from the form,
each returns to its true origin,
hence it is called a ghost (guǐ),
for 'ghost' means 'to return' (guī).
The corpse lies alone, a mere lump,
how could it have consciousness?
To wrap it thickly with silks and fabrics,
to send it off with abundant wealth and goods,
is to rob the living of their resources.
The ancient sages, considering human feelings,
could not bear to see their kin suffer,
thus established rituals for them.
Now these are exceeded,
and so I wish to be buried naked to rectify this.
In the past, when Yáo was buried,
a hollow log served as his coffin,
and vine tenders as the bindings.
The digging of the grave did not reach the springs below,
nor release odors above.
Thus, the sages in life were easy to honor,
and in death easy to bury,
adding nothing useless,
and wasting nothing unbeneficial.
To say that now we spend wealth on lavish burials,
where the dead do not know,
and the living cannot use,
is absurd indeed!
This can be called a grave delusion!"
Marquis Qí said:
"Well said."
And so, he was buried naked.
20.21 In Lǔ, there was a frugal man
who cooked food in an earthenware pot,
and finding it delicious,
served it in a clay vessel
to offer to Confucius.
Confucius accepted it
with joy and pleasure,
as if receiving a grand sacrificial offering.
His disciples said:
"An earthenware bowl
is a crude vessel,
and the cooked food
a humble meal.
Why then is our master so pleased with it?"
Confucius said:
"I have heard that one who enjoys remonstrance thinks of his ruler,
and one who eats well remembers his parents.
It is not that I consider the fare sumptuous,
but that I think of my parents because he shared his delicious food with me."
20.22 Yànzǐ fell ill
and was near death.
He cut a pillar to place a writing inside,
and said to his wife:
"When the pillar speaks,
wait until our son is grown to look at it."
When the son grew up and opened the writing,
the words said:
"Cloth and silk are not to be exhausted, for once exhausted, they cannot adorn;
oxen and horses are not to be exhausted, for once exhausted, they cannot be harnessed;
a scholar should not be exhausted, for once exhausted, he cannot be entrusted.
Exhaustion, oh exhaustion,
it is exhaustion indeed."
20.23 Zhòngní asked Lǎodān:
"How extreme it is that the Dào is difficult to practice in these times!
I have been upholding the Dào and presenting myself
to seek out the rulers of the age,
yet none accept me.
The Dào is indeed difficult to practice now!"
Lǎozǐ said:
"Those who persuade may drift in their listening,
and those who speak may confuse with their words.
With these two conditions,
the Dào cannot be entrusted lightly."
20.24 Zǐgòng asked Zǐshí:
"Have you not studied the 'Book of Songs'?"
Zǐshí replied:
"Do I have the leisure?
My parents require me to be filial,
my brothers require me to be fraternal,
my friends require me to be trustworthy.
Do I have the leisure?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Then let me set aside my 'Book of Songs'
to learn from you."
20.25 Gōngmíng Xuān studied under Zēngzǐ
for three years
without reading any books.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Xuān, you have been at my door for three years without studying.
Why is that?"
Gōngmíng Xuān replied:
"How dare I reside at the master's door without learning?
I have observed the master at home,
with parents present,
where not even a harsh word was directed at dogs or horses.
I admired this
and tried to learn it, but could not achieve it.
I have observed the master receiving guests,
respectful and frugal without slackness,
I admired this
and tried to learn it, but could not achieve it.
I have observed the master at court,
stern yet not harming his subordinates,
I admired this
and tried to learn it, but could not achieve it.
I admire these three things
and have tried to learn them but could not.
How dare I reside at the master's door without learning?"
Zēngzǐ rose from his mat and apologized, saying:
"I am not as good as Xuān.
He has truly learned."
20.26 A man from Lǔ was skilled at weaving sandals himself,
and his wife at weaving plain silk,
and they wished to move to Yuè.
Someone told them:
"You will surely become impoverished."
The man from Lǔ asked:
"Why?"
The person said:
"Sandals are for wearing on the feet,
and plain silk is for making caps,
but the Yuè people go barefoot and cut their hair short.
To go to a country where these are not used,
how can you expect not to be impoverished?"
21.1 Mǐn Zǐqiān and his brother,
after their mother passed away,
their father remarried,
and they gained two more brothers.
Once, while Zǐqiān was driving the chariot for his father,
he dropped the reins,
and his father held his hand,
noticing his clothes were very thin.
Upon returning home,
the father called his stepmother's sons,
held their hands,
and felt their thick, warm clothing.
He then said to his wife:
"The reason I married you
was for the sake of my sons,
but now you deceive me.
Leave,
do not stay!"
Zǐqiān stepped forward and said:
"With Mother here, one son suffers the cold;
if Mother leaves, all four sons will be cold."
His father fell silent.
Hence it is said:
"How filial is Mǐn Zǐqiān,
with one word, his mother stayed,
with another, three sons were kept warm."
Quoted from "Yìwén Lèijù," volume 20, page 369.
21.2 Jìn Línggōng built a nine-story tower,
spending billions in resources,
and declared to his attendants:
"Anyone who dares to remonstrate will be executed!"
Sūn Xī then advised him:
"I can stack thirteen chess pieces
and place nine eggs on top."
The duke said:
"I have studied little,
and never seen such a thing;
please demonstrate for me."
Sūn Xī then placed the chess pieces underneath
and stacked nine eggs on top.
The attendants were terrified.
Línggōng crouched down,
breathless with fear.
He exclaimed:
"How perilous,
how perilous!"
Sūn Xī said:
"I consider this not perilous,
for there is something even more dangerous."
The duke said:
"I wish to see it."
Sūn Xī replied:
"This nine-story tower,
taking three years to build,
prevents men from farming,
women from weaving,
depletes the state's treasury,
reduces the population,
causes officials and people to rebel and flee,
and invites neighboring states to plot,
preparing to raise armies.
If the state falls and perishes,
what hope remains for you, my lord?"
Línggōng said:
"My fault
has reached such extremes."
He immediately ordered the nine-story tower demolished.
Quoted from "Lèijù," volume 24, page 436.
21.3 Sūn Xī studied mournful songs on the ancient qin,
and once played melodies of Zhèng and Wèi on the instrument.
Línggōng was deeply moved,
so he composed the tune "Duke of Wèi,"
singing in harmony with it.
Quoted from "Běitáng Shūchāo," volume 106, page 409.
21.4 The King of Qí erected a nine-tiered tower,
offering rewards to skilled painters in the state.
Jìng Jūn, who often suffered from hunger and cold,
had a wife of exquisite beauty.
Being a skilled painter,
he coveted the reward to paint the tower,
but after being away from home for many days,
he missed his wife dearly,
so he painted her portrait
and smiled at it.
Someone nearby saw this and reported it to the king.
The king summoned and questioned him,
to which he replied:
"Having such a wife,
and being away from home for so long,
I constantly think of her,
so I secretly painted her image
to comfort my longing heart,
unaware that it would come to your attention."
The king then set out wine,
enjoying the company of Jìng Jūn.
He said to Jìng Jūn:
"Among the women presented in the state, none are beautiful;
I offer a million coins for your wife,
is that acceptable?
If not,
I will kill you."
Jìng Jūn, terrified, reluctantly agreed.
Quoted from "Lèijù," volume 32, page 561, and "Tàipíng Yùlǎn," volume 381, page 1758.
21.5 Lǚ Wàng, at seventy years old,
was fishing at the Wèi River's shore,
for three days and nights,
without a single fish biting.
He spoke with a farmer,
who was an ancient wise man,
and the farmer
said to Wàng:
"When you fish again,
use a fine line,
fragrant bait,
cast it gently,
and do not startle the fish."
Wàng followed his advice.
First, he caught a crucian carp,
then a carp,
and upon cutting it open, found a document inside,
which read:
"Lǚ Wàng will be enfeoffed in Qí."
Wàng knew then that he was destined for nobility.
Quoted from "Lèijù," volume 66, page 1178.
21.6 Qí sent Chúnyú Kūn to Chǔ,
who was short in stature,
and the King of Chǔ looked down on him,
saying:
"Has Qí no one else?
That they send you?
What are you skilled at?"
He replied:
"I have no particular skills,
but with the seven-foot sword at my waist,
I intend to behead an unworthy king."
The king said:
"Stop,
I was only joking with you."
He then drank with Kūn,
and the King of Chǔ said to Chúnyú Kūn:
"I have an enemy in Wú,
can you avenge me?"
He replied:
"I once saw a rustic by the roadside,
holding a single fish,
praying in the field:
'May the high yield be ten thousand sheaves,
the low yield a thousand hectoliters.'
I secretly laughed at him,
thinking his offering meager yet his hopes great.
Now, you give me half a day's pleasure and entrust me with Wú;
this is not a wise plan, my king."
The King of Chǔ fell silent.
Quoted from "Yùlǎn," volume 378, page 1745; "Lèijù," volume 96, page 1671; and "Yùlǎn," volume 736, page 3264.
21.7 Jìn Wéngōng attacked Chǔ,
and upon returning, distributed rewards,
with Hú Yǎn receiving the highest honor.
Someone said:
"In the matter of Chéngpú,
it was Xiān Zhěn's strategy."
Wéngōng replied:
"At Chéngpú,
Yǎn advised me not to break my promise,
upholding the covenant of three retreats.
Xiān Zhěn's plans for military affairs
I used to achieve victory,
but that was a temporary strategy,
while Yǎn's words secured a merit for ten thousand generations.
How can temporary gain outweigh eternal merit?
Thus, he comes first."
Everyone was convinced and satisfied.
Quoted from "Yùlǎn," volume 279, page 1302.
