21.8 Lord Liáng went out hunting,
and saw a flock of white wild geese.
Lord Liáng descended from his carriage,
drew his bow and intended to shoot them.
A traveler on the road was watching,
and urged Lord Liáng to stop,
causing the flock of geese to take fright.
Lord Liáng became angry,
and wanted to kill the traveler.
His charioteer Gōngsūn Lóng descended from the carriage and replied:
"In the past, during the time of Duke Jǐng of Qí,
there was a drought for three years.
A divination was performed and it said:
'You must sacrifice a human,
then it will rain.'
Duke Jǐng said:
'The reason I sought rain in the past was for my people.
Now, if sacrificing a human will make it rain,
I myself will serve as the sacrifice.'
Before his words were finished,
heavy rain fell across a thousand lǐ.
Now, my lord, because of the white wild geese, you wish to kill him,
this is no different from being a wolf or tiger."
Lord Liáng took him by the hand,
and together they mounted the carriage,
returning to enter the city gate,
where he exclaimed 'Long live!',
and said:
"How joyful!
Today's hunt,
uniquely yielded excellent words."
Cited from Tàipíng Yùlǎn, vol. 390, p. 1804.
21.9 Qí dispatched troops to attack Lǔ,
and they saw a woman,
fleeing with two young children,
carrying the small one and leading the large one by the hand.
Seeing the large army about to arrive,
she then carried the large one and led the small one by the hand.
The envoy found it very strange,
and questioned her.
The woman said:
"The larger one is the son of my husband's elder brother,
the smaller one is my own son.
The son of my husband's brother represents public duty,
my own son represents personal duty.
Should I not rather save the public and abandon the personal?"
The envoy was deeply moved,
admired her words,
and immediately called off the army and returned.
He reported to the King of Qí, saying:
"Lǔ cannot be attacked.
If even a common woman's sense of duty is like this,
how much more so the ministers of the court?"
Cited from Tàipíng Yùlǎn, vol. 422, p. 1948.
21.10 In Lǔ there was a virtuous woman,
a daughter of the Cìshì family,
just twenty years of age,
who was well-versed in the classics,
often standing in attendance while chanting,
weeping tears like rain.
Someone who recognized her said:
"Do you wish to marry?
Why is your sorrow so profound?"
She replied:
"The ruler of Lǔ is old,
and the crown prince is still young.
I worry that treacherous ministers will arise."
Cited from Tàipíng Yùlǎn, vol. 469, p. 2156.
21.11 Zhào Xiāngzǐ asked Wáng Lí:
"Why is it that states perish?"
He replied:
"Because the ruler is stingy and yet capable of tolerance,
that is why they perish."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Why do you say so?"
He said:
"Stinginess means he cannot reward the worthy,
tolerance means he cannot punish the guilty.
If the worthy are not rewarded,
and the guilty are not punished,
if the state does not perish, then what?"
Cited from Tàipíng Yùlǎn, vol. 633, p. 2840.
21.12 Sū Qín arrived in Qí,
and the King of Qí treated him generously.
The various great officials were jealous of him,
and sent someone to assassinate Qín, but he did not die.
The King of Qí brought out treasures to offer a reward and seek the assassin, but could not find him.
As Sū Qín was near death,
he said to the King of Qí:
"If Your Majesty truly wishes to find the assassin for your servant,
after your servant dies,
I beg you to have my corpse torn apart by chariots in the marketplace,
and proclaim:
'Sū Qín was working for Yān intending to bring chaos to Qí.
Now that he is dead,
I am very pleased,
hence I have torn him apart.
If the one who killed him is found,
I will heavily reward and enfeoff him.'
If you do this,
the one who assassinated me will surely come forth."
The King of Qí followed his advice,
tore the corpse apart and proclaimed it,
and the assassin of Qín indeed came forth to seek the reward.
Cited from Tàipíng Yùlǎn, vol. 633, p. 2840.
21.13 A man on the northern frontier
had his horse wander into Hú territory.
Everyone condoled with him.
His father said:
"How do we know this may not turn out to be a blessing?"
After several months,
his horse returned leading a fine Hú steed.
Everyone congratulated him.
His father said:
"How do we know this may not turn out to be a misfortune?"
The family became wealthy with fine horses,
and his son enjoyed riding,
but fell and broke his thigh bone.
Everyone condoled with him.
His father said:
"How do we know this may not turn out to be a blessing?"
After one year,
the Hú tribes massively invaded,
and all able-bodied men took up bows and fought.
Among the frontier people,
nine out of ten died,
but this son alone, because he was lame,
ensured that father and son preserved each other.
Cited from Tàipíng Yùlǎn, vol. 896, p. 3980.
21.14 Duke Píng of Jìn asked Zhào Wǔ:
"Zhōngmóu
is the thigh and arm of the three states,
the shoulder and thigh of Hándān.
I wish to have a good magistrate for it.
The magistrate post is vacant,
whom should we send?"
Zhào Wǔ said:
"Xíng Bózi is suitable."
The Duke said:
"Is not Xíngzi your enemy?"
He replied:
"Personal enmity does not enter the public gate."
He asked again:
"The post of the central treasury magistrate is vacant,
whom should we send?"
Zhào Wǔ said:
"My son is suitable."
Thus, in external recommendation he did not avoid enemies,
in internal recommendation he did not avoid his son.
Cited from Lèishū Jíjù, vol. 50, p. 907.
21.15 A turtle of a thousand years
can speak with humans.
Cited from Lèishū Jíjù, vol. 96, p. 1668.
21.16 Drums emulate Heaven,
bells emulate Earth.
Cited from Shūchāo, vol. 108, p. 412.
21.17 The brave warrior Mèi Bēn, in water does not avoid jiāo dragons,
on land does not avoid tigers and wolves.
Cited from Wénxuǎn, annotation to "Rhapsody on the Imperial Hunt," p. 168.
21.18 Music that is harmonious and fine accords with the feeling of the song,
and fully expresses the meaning of the dance.
Cited from Wénxuǎn, annotation to "Rhapsody on Dance," p. 320.
21.19 Zǐ Qí, at eighteen years of age,
was sent by the ruler of Qí to govern Dōng'ē,
and Dōng'ē was greatly transformed.
Cited from Hòu Hàn Shū, annotation to "Biography of Hú Guǎng," p. 1508.
21.20 During the time of Duke Píng of Jìn,
the land was barren for a thousand lǐ.
Cited from Hòu Hàn Shū, annotation to "Biography of Zāng Gōng," p. 696.
21.21 In the state of Wáng, the former wife's son was Bó Qí,
the later wife's son was Bó Fēng.
The stepmother wanted her own son to be established as crown prince,
and persuaded the king, saying:
"Bó Qí makes advances to me."
The king did not believe it.
His mother said:
"Have Bó Qí go to the rear garden,
and I will pass by his side.
If Your Majesty watches from the terrace,
you will know immediately."
The king did as she said.
When Bó Qí entered the garden,
the stepmother secretly took more than ten bees and placed them inside her single-layer garment.
Passing by Bó Qí's side, she said:
"The bees are stinging me."
Bó Qí then reached into her garment, took the bees, and killed them.
The king saw this from afar,
and then banished Bó Qí.
Cited from Hòu Hàn Shū, annotation to "Biography of Huáng Qióng," p. 2039.
21.22 Duke Wén of Jìn was served roasted meat with a hair wrapped around it.
The chef said:
"I sharpened my dagger,
its edge rivaling Gānjiàng's blades,
yet when cutting the meat the hair remained unsevered—
this is my first crime;
I inspected each slice carefully but failed to see the hair—
this is my second crime;
the stove fire burned red-hot yet the hair endured—
this is my third crime."
Duke Wén replied:
"Ah,
the truth lies elsewhere."
He then summoned the assistant chef for questioning,
and the confession followed.
Cited in Shu Chao, vol. 5, p. 175.
21.23 When Liǔxià Huì died,
people intended to compose a eulogy for him.
His wife said:
"To recount my husband's virtues,
none of you know him as well as I do."
She then wrote the eulogy:
"My husband never boasted,
never sought advancement,
his posthumous title should be Huì (Benevolent)."
The disciples heard this and complied.
Cited in Shu Chao, vol. 102, p. 391.
21.24 The Master said:
"Judging by appearance,
one errs with Zǐyǔ;
judging by speech,
one errs with Zǎiyǔ."
Dàntái Zǐyǔ
had the demeanor of a noble man,
but upon long acquaintance,
his words fell short of his appearance;
Zǎiyǔ's eloquence
was refined and cultured,
yet with prolonged interaction,
his wisdom did not match his rhetoric.
Cited from Sòng Xuējù's Collected Sayings of Confucius, Chapter of King Zhāo of Chǔ.
21.25 Duke Líng of Wèi dug a pond in cold weather.
Wǎn Chūn admonished:
"Starting labor in winter
may exhaust the people."
The Duke asked:
"Is it cold?"
Chūn replied:
"You wear fox fur,
sit on bear mats—
thus feel no cold,
but the people suffer greatly from it."
The Duke then halted the project.
Cited in Imperial Readings, vol. 27, p. 127.
21.26 Chúnyú Kūn posed three challenges,
and Zōu Jì answered all three correctly.
Kūn and his companions, defeated in debate, departed.
Thus, the value of swords like Gānjiàng and Mòyé lies in their instant cutting.
Cited in annotations to Wénxuǎn, Reply to Prince of Dōng'ā's Letter, p. 750.
21.27 Under Yīn law,
dumping ashes in the street was punishable.
Cited in Shu Chao, vol. 43, p. 121.
21.28 The Pìyōng
was where the Son of Heaven held rural banquets.
Cited in Imperial Readings, vol. 534, p. 2422.
21.29 When Qín Èrshì ascended the throne,
shooting stars lit the night sky.
Soon after, the empire fell into chaos,
and Èrshì was killed.
Cited in Imperial Readings, vol. 875, p. 3884.
21.30 Yǔ governed the world
by listening through five tones,
hanging bells, drums, chimes, and stone chimes at his gate, with a hand-drum,
to welcome scholars from all lands.
Cited in Chuxue Ji, vol. 9, p. 206.
21.31 Duke Wén enjoyed eating pickled calamus root,
which is sweetflag.
Cited in Imperial Readings, vol. 999, p. 4421.
21.32 When Gōngsūn Qiáo served as minister of Zhèng,
lost items lay unclaimed on roads,
peaches and plums hung over streets,
yet none dared take them.
Cited in Imperial Readings, vol. 967, p. 4288.
21.33 Rats in the beams grew fat listening to elders' discussions.
Cited in Imperial Readings, vol. 911, p. 4037.
21.34 Marquis Wén of Chǔ said:
"The local elites often suppress the good and promote the evil;
one should question them personally."
Cited in annotations to Wénxuǎn, Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital.
21.35 Chūlǐzǐ, nearing death,
said:
"Bury me east of Zhāngtái Terrace, south of the Wèi River;
in a hundred years, an imperial palace will flank my tomb."
When Hàn rose,
the Chánglè Palace stood to its east,
the Wèiyāng Palace to its west,
with the Armory directly above.
Cited in Essential Collection of Texts and Affairs 56, and Complete Classified Compendium Past and Present 66.
21.36 Once the Marquis of Suí traveled
and encountered a large snake cut in half.
Suspecting its divinity,
he had it treated with medicine.
The snake then could leave.
Hence, the place was named Duànshé Qiū (Broken Snake Hill).
Over a year later,
the snake brought a luminous pearl,
an inch in diameter,
pure white and glowing,
thus called the Suí Pearl.
Cited in Correct Meanings of Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Lǐ Sī.
21.37 Zǐ Qí, aged eighteen,
was sent by the ruler of Qí to govern Ā.
After his departure,
the ruler regretted it,
dispatching a messenger to recall him.
The messenger returned saying:
"Zǐ Qí will surely succeed;
his companions are all white-haired elders."
Upon reaching Ā,
Zǐ Qí melted weapons into farm tools.
Wèi, hearing a youth ruled
with empty armories
and granaries,
launched an attack.
The people of Ā, fathers leading sons,
elder brothers leading younger,
fought with private weapons,
and defeated Wèi's army.
Cited in annotations to Wénxuǎn, Pān Zhèngshū's Poem for Héyáng.
21.38 The King of Gāopíng sent an envoy to borrow grain from Marquis Wén of Wèi.
The Marquis said:
"Wait until my rent grain from the estates arrives."
The envoy replied:
"On my way here,
I saw a fish in a ditch gasping,
who said to me:
'I'm trapped in shallow water,
my life hangs by a breath;
can you water me?'
I told it:
'Wait until I go south to see the Lord of the River Dikes,
to release water from the Jiāng and Huái to fill your mouth.'
The fish said:
'My life is but a moment;
if I must wait for the Jiāng and Huái's flow,
by the time you return,
you'll find me in the dried fish market.'
Now Gāopíng is impoverished,
so I come to borrow grain,
yet you say to wait for rent grain—
by then, Great King, you'll seek me in the graveyard."
Cited in Yìwén Lèijù 85, Imperial Readings 840, Complete Classified Compendium Past and Present 57, Tiānzhōng Jì 45, and Yuānjiàn Lèihán 395.
21.39 When Zǐchǎn died,
maidens wept in their chambers,
farmers mourned in the fields.
Cited in Běitáng Shūchāo 35.
21.40 After Zǐchǎn's ministership in Zhèng and his death,
women discarded hairpins and earrings,
men set aside lutes and zithers.
Cited in Běitáng Shūchāo 35.
21.41 The imagery of music:
whether zithers are plain or fine, they harmonize in music.
Cited in Běitáng Shūchāo 109.
21.42 Duke Líng of Jìn loved mournful songs and zither playing.
Cited in Běitáng Shūchāo 109 and Yuānjiàn Lèihán 188.
21.43 The imagery of music:
its modulations reflect all things.
Cited in Běitáng Shūchāo 111.
21.44 Lightning's dark brilliance strikes and flashes.
Cited in Běitáng Shūchāo 152.
21.45 Yùzǐ said:
"Yǔ governed the world
by listening through five tones,
hanging chimes, bells, and hand-drums at his gate to welcome scholars from all lands."
Cited in Chuxue Ji 9.
21.46 Within ten steps, there is fragrant grass.
Cited in Book of Later Hàn, Biography of Wáng Fú, and Yuānjiàn Lèihán 408.
21.47 Long ago, when Zōu Jì served as Prime Minister of Qí,
seventy-two scholars including Master Chúnyú Kūn from Jìxià
all looked down upon Zōu Jì
and devised clever arguments to test him.
Chúnyú Kūn made three allusions,
and Zōu Jì understood all three,
responding like an echo,
leaving Kūn and his peers speechless, and they departed.
Thus, the reason Gānjiàng and Móyé swords are esteemed
is for their ability to cut instantly;
the reason Qíjì horses are valued
is for their immediate arrival;
if one must take many days and a long time,
even a silk thread can wear through a stone,
and a nag can travel far;
therefore, intelligence and quick-wittedness
are admirable qualities in a person.
Annotation from Hòu Hàn Shū · Cuī Yīn Biography; annotation from Wén Xuǎn · Chén Kǒngzhāng's Reply to the King of Dōng'ē; Tài Píng Yù Lǎn 432.
21.48 Bào Jiāo wore bark as clothing,
and ate wild fruits.
Annotation from Hòu Hàn Shū · Cuī Yīn Biography.
21.49 Nìng Qì fed his ox on the broad road,
striking a cart spoke and singing "Shuò Shǔ";
Fù Yuè, replacing a convict, built walls in the wilderness of Fù Yán,
and Emperor Gāozōng dreamed of finding him.
Annotation from Hòu Hàn Shū · Mǎ Róng Biography.
21.50 Unprincipled theories,
unguarded actions,
and unrefined words—
the noble person is cautious of them.
Yáng Liàng's annotation from Xúnzǐ · "Correct Naming" chapter.
21.51 When starving horses fill the stable,
and hungry dogs are in the courtyard,
upon seeing hay and bones,
they cannot be restrained from moving.
Shì Lèi Fù 23.
21.52 To serve Zhòngní as a minister
is like scooping with a cup to drink from the river and sea—
one cannot know its depth.
Tài Píng Yù Lǎn 2; Jì Zuǎn Yuān Hǎi 43.
21.53 Marquis Wén of Wèi's teacher Lǐ Kuī authored six books on law.
Gǔ Jīn Hé Bì Shì Lèi Bèi Yào Wài Jí 17.
21.54 Tián Yīng said:
"Those who die for righteousness do not fear the threat of the axe;
those impoverished for righteousness do not accept the gift of high office.
To live without righteousness
is worse than to die with righteousness."
Jì Zuǎn Yuān Hǎi 54.
21.55 Seeking profit through lowly associations,
without any shame;
contending for the slightest gain,
knowing yet insisting on fighting for it.
Jì Zuǎn Yuān Hǎi 54.
21.56 To mistake Zhǐ for Yǔ—
it is not the fault of the string;
to take sweet for bitter—
it is not the fault of the taste.
Jì Zuǎn Yuān Hǎi 55.
21.57 Shè Gōng Zhū Liáng asked Lè Wáng Fù:
"What kind of person is Minister Zhào Wénzǐ of Jìn?"
He replied:
"He loves learning and accepts admonition."
Shè Gōng said:
"I suspect that's not all."
He replied:
"To love learning is wisdom;
to accept admonition is benevolence.
The Jiāng River emerges from Wénshān,
its source as narrow as a jar's mouth;
by the time it reaches Chǔ,
it is ten lǐ wide.
There is no other reason—
it has many tributaries below.
For a person to love learning and accept admonition,
how fitting that they establish themselves!"
Tiān Zhōng Jì 9.
21.58 King Wǔ asked Tài Gōng:
"Do wealth and poverty come from fate?"
Tài Gōng said:
"If one's efforts are not thorough,
or thorough yet not wealthy,
thieves are in their house."
King Wǔ said:
"What are these thieves?"
Tài Gōng said:
"Poor planning—
the first thief.
Untimely sowing and harvesting—
the second thief.
Marrying an incapable woman—
the third thief.
Raising too many daughters—
the fourth thief.
Neglecting duties for drink—
the fifth thief.
Extravagant clothing—
the sixth thief.
Careless storage—
the seventh thief.
Inefficient wells and stoves—
the eighth thief.
Borrowing for ceremonies—
the ninth thief.
Lighting lamps unnecessarily—
the tenth thief.
How can one become wealthy with these?"
King Wǔ said:
"Well said."
Tiān Zhōng Jì 39.
21.59 Two nobles cannot coexist equally,
two powers cannot stand as pairs.
Yáng Shèn's Yì Lín Fá Shān 17.
21.60 When Lǔ Xiànzǐ was a guest in Jìn,
Xuānzǐ hosted a banquet for him,
moving three times,
yet the bells and stones were already in place without moving.
Xiànzǐ said:
"How rich your household is!"
Xuānzǐ said:
"How does your household compare to mine in wealth?"
Xiànzǐ replied:
"My household is very poor,
but I have two scholars named Yán Huí and Zī Wúlíng,
who bring peace to my state and household,
and harmony to the people.
That is all I have,
and I am content with it!"
After the guest left,
Xuānzǐ said:
"He is a noble man,
who considers nurturing worthies as wealth;
I am a vulgar man,
who sees bells and stones as wealth."
Confucius said:
"Mèng Xiànzǐ's wealth deserves to be recorded in the Chūn Qiū."
Jiāo Shì Lèi Lín 1B.
21.61 Mǐnzǐ Qiān lost his mother early
and suffered under his stepmother,
who clothed him in reed catkins in winter,
while her own two sons wore silk floss.
His father ordered Mǐnzǐ to drive the cart,
but he was too cold and dropped the reins,
earning his father's scolding,
yet Mǐnzǐ did not defend himself.
Upon discovering the truth,
the father returned and said to his wife:
"I married you
for the sake of my son;
now you deceive me,
leave and do not stay."
Zǐ Qiān stepped forward and said:
"With mother here, one son is cold;
if mother leaves, three sons will be destitute."
His father fell silent.
Thus it is said:
How filial was Mǐnzǐ Qiān!
One word brought his mother back,
another kept three sons warm.
Yuān Jiàn Lèi Hán 271.
21.62 The Marquis of Lí lost his state,
long dwelling in Wèi,
but Wèi did not aid him,
so his ministers urged his return,
and he composed "Zhōng Lù."
Yuān Jiàn Lèi Hán 10.
21.63 Sāng Jūn took medicine from his bosom and gave it to Biǎn Què,
instructing him to drink it with Shàng Chí water,
which, before reaching the ground,
was collected as dew from bamboo and trees.
Yuān Jiàn Lèi Hán 10.
21.64 King Chéng of Zhōu was playing with his young brother
and picked up a leaf from the ground,
giving it to his brother, saying:
"I grant you Táng with this."
Duke Zhōu said:
"Choose an auspicious day."
The King said:
"It was just a joke,
I won't actually enfeoff him."
Duke Zhōu said:
"A king values his words;
to enfeoff someone and then regret it is untrustworthy."
So he proceeded to enfeoff him.
Yuān Jiàn Lèi Hán 118.
21.65 Wáng Zhāng, as a scholar,
studied in Cháng'ān,
living alone with his wife.
When Zhāng fell ill and had no quilt,
he lay in a cowhide cover,
bidding farewell to his wife,
weeping and sobbing.
His wife scolded him angrily, saying:
"Zhòngqīng,
in the capital, the esteemed and noble are at the imperial court—
who surpasses Zhòngqīng?
Now, in illness and distress,
instead of rousing yourself with determination,
you instead weep and sob—
how shameful!"
From "Yuānjiàn Lèihán" 267.
21.66 Zhū Yún, over seventy years old, passed away at home,
refusing to call a doctor or take medicine when ill.
His final wish was to be buried in the clothes he wore,
with a coffin fitting his body,
and earth surrounding the outer coffin.
From "Yuānjiàn Lèihán" 267.
21.67 Xí Sīmí went to see Tián Chéngzǐ.
Tián Chéngzǐ ascended a tower with him to look in all directions;
three sides were unobstructed,
but looking south,
the trees from Xí's home blocked the view.
Tián Chéngzǐ said nothing.
Xí returned home,
had someone cut down the trees,
but after a few axe cuts,
Xí stopped them.
His steward asked:
"Why change your mind so quickly?"
Xí replied:
"There is an ancient saying:
'Knowing the fish in the deep pool brings misfortune.'
Tián Chéngzǐ is about to take action;
if I show him that I perceive subtle signs in such a major matter,
I will surely be in danger.
Not cutting the trees
incurs no crime;
but knowing what others do not speak of—
that crime is great."
So, he did not cut them down.
From "Yuānjiàn Lèihán" 276.
21.68 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ hunted on the southern slope of Jìn Mountain,
and sighing while holding the reins, said:
"I have thousands of grain-fed horses,
and hundreds of strong warriors,
intending to hunt beasts—
yet I fear neighboring states may nurture talents to hunt me."
How wise!
Jiǎnzǐ excelled at self-reflection.
From "Yuānjiàn Lèihán" 277.
